[^15]: The controversy concerning the arrangement and number of the particles of bread extracted from the prosphora and placed upon the diskos during the Proskomedia was one of the sharpest liturgical debates in the late 16th- and early 17th-century Ruthenian Church, with significant divergences between South Slavic/Athonite manuscripts, Muscovite practices, and Venetian Greek printed euchologia.

[^16]: Patriarch Jeremiah II Tranos of Constantinople visited the Ruthenian lands in 1588–1589, issuing canonical regulations and clarifying liturgical customs for the Kyivan Metropolia.

[^17]: In the outer margin of the leaf, the printer placed the callout *зри* ("Note well" / *nota bene*), drawing the reader's attention to the patriarchal authority underpinning these rubrical decisions.

[^18]: The rites for receiving converts from Protestantism (Calvinism, Lutheranism, and Antitrinitarian Socinianism) and Roman Catholicism, which formed an essential part of the 16th-century Ruthenian Trebnyk tradition amidst the intense religious polemics of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.

[^19]: The Order of the Consecration of the Great Myron (Chrism), customarily performed by the primate or bishop on Great and Holy Thursday, preserved here from ancient Kyivan and South Slavic codices to maintain complete episcopal and parish liturgical self-sufficiency.

[^20]: Slavonic *маслосщ҃е́нїе* (*maslosviashcheniie*), the Holy Mystery of Unction (Greek: Εὐχέλαιον, *Euchelaion*), traditionally celebrated by seven priests with seven epistles, gospels, and prayers.

[^21]: Dionysius the Areopagite (Corpus Dionysiacum), *De Ecclesiastica Hierarchia* (*On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*), which provided the foundational patristic justification for liturgical symbolism and sacramental structures.

[^22]: St. Basil the Great, *On the Holy Spirit* (*De Spiritu Sancto*), ch. 27, §66, defending apostolic liturgical customs transmitted through unwritten oral tradition.

[^23]: St. John Chrysostom, *Homily 4 on Second Thessalonians*, §2 (PG 62:488), on 2 Thess 2:15: "Therefore, brethren, stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle."

[^24]: The episcopal printing shop of Krylos (near Halych), where Bishop Hedeon Balaban had set up printing operations in 1606 to print biblical and patristic editions, including the Psalter and the *Didactic Gospel* (*Yevanheliie Uchytel’ne*).

[^25]: Many young Ruthenian Orthodox nobles traveled to Italy (particularly to the University of Padua) for higher education in the late 16th and early 17th centuries, where they encountered Roman Catholic theology and post-Tridentine polemics, which frequently led to conversions or abandonment of ancestral Eastern Orthodox practices.

[^26]: Teodor Yurievych Balaban died on May 24, 1606, while the Striatyn Trebnyk was still on the press. The publication was completed under the direct supervision of Bishop Hedeon Balaban and his master printer, Pamvo Berynda.

[^27]: Slavonic *пове́рста чл҃чскаго въ́зраста*: structured systematically according to the human lifecycle, beginning with childbearing and baptism, progressing through marriage, monastic life, illness, and burial, and concluding with general blessings and canonical regulations.

[^28]: Refers to the canonical Nomocanon collection appended to the end of the 1606 Trebnyk, providing practical canonical and penitential guidance for parish priests who did not have access to a full *Kormchaia Kniga* (Syntagma/Nomocanon).

[^29]: "Dread, bloodless sacrifice" (*страшна́я же́ртва безкро́вная*) is the classical patristic and liturgical designation for the Holy Eucharist (Divine Liturgy).

[^30]: The preface concludes with an episcopal valediction and call for mutual prayer. At the bottom right of the leaf is a typographical catchword (*Боу́недающу*), marking the transition to the main text of the codex, which opens on physical leaf p19 (fol. 1r).

[^31]: Fol. 1r. Slavonic *Чи́нъ ѡ҆бновле́нїе ѻ҆троча́те* translates the Greek Τάξις εἰς τὸ ἀνακαινίσαι παιδίον ("Order to dedicate/renew a child"), the ancient Byzantine rite for the naming and signing of an infant on the eighth day after birth in imitation of Christ's Circumcision and naming (Luke 2:21).

[^32]: Slavonic *ѡ҆ба́бы* (*от бабы*), that is, by the midwife (повивальная бабка), who according to ancient liturgical custom presented the newborn child at the entrance of the church prior to the mother's forty-day purification.

[^33]: Cf. Psalm 4:7 (LXX 4:6): "The light of Thy countenance, O Lord, is signed upon us." Masoretic numbering: Ps 4:6.

[^34]: The prayer looks forward from the eighth-day naming rite to the child's future Holy Baptism, Chrismation ("the seal"), and first reception of Holy Communion ("the most pure and dread Mysteries").

[^35]: The eighth-day naming and dedication rite (begun on fol. 1r, p19) concludes with this solemn Trinitarian doxology and dismissal at the entrance of the church.

[^36]: Slavonic *Мл҃тва ба́бѣ по прїѧ́тїи мл҃нца* translates the Byzantine euchological prayer for the midwife (*ба́ба* / *повитуха*) who received the newborn child, purifying her and blessing her return to the liturgical assembly.

[^37]: Fol. 2v. Slavonic *Чи́нъ въ тре́тїй де́нь женѣ̀ пороже́нїи ѻ҆троча́те* ("Order on the third day for a woman after giving birth to a child"). Whereas many classical Greek and South Slavic euchologia designate these prayers for the first day after childbirth, the Striatyn Trebnyk assigns them specifically to the third day in the child's home.

[^38]: Fol. 3r. The Troparion (*Рожество̀ твоѐ Бц҃е Дв҃о*) and Kontakion (*І҆ѡакі́мъ и҆ А҆́нна поноше́нїа безча́дства*) of the Nativity of the Most Holy Theotokos (September 8), Tone 4, are appointed as the opening hymnody, theologically framing all Christian childbearing within the salvation-historical mystery of the Virgin's birth.

[^39]: Fol. 3v. The prayer quotes the ancestral curses upon Adam and Eve following the Fall: Genesis 3:19 ("In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread") and Genesis 3:16 ("In sorrow shalt thou bring forth children"), contrasting mortal labor and sorrow with Christ's sinless Nativity from the Virgin.

[^40]: Fol. 4r. Slavonic *соумнѣ́нїе* reflects Greek δισταγμός or ῥύпас, denoting the natural spiritual distress, emotional turmoil, and vulnerability experienced by the mother in childbed.

[^41]: Fol. 4r. Slavonic *ѿ съжи́тельства дїа́воля, и҆ ро́да вся́каго пога́нствїа* ("from the cohabitation of the devil, and from every manner of defilement/paganism"). The petition reflects the pastoral exorcistic protection invoked by the Church against demonic harassments and pagan folk superstitions historically associated with post-partum recovery.

[^42]: Fol. 4v. The third prayer is explicitly addressed not only to the mother, but also to the kinswomen and neighbors who assisted at the birth (*жена́мъ прилꙋчи́вшимїся на рожде́нїи то́мъ*), extending the Church's blessing and sanctification to the entire household.

[^43]: Fol. 5r. The prayer emphasizes the patristic dogma of the Virgin Mary's painless parturition (*неболѣ́знноу съблю́лъ є҆сѝ*), by which the curse of Eve was healed in the uncorrupt birth of Christ.

[^44]: Fol. 5v. "Bath of regeneration" translates the Pauline phrase *ба́ня па́кибытїѧ́йская* (Titus 3:5, Greek: λουτρὸν παλιγγενεσίας), referring to the forthcoming Holy Mystery of Baptism.

[^45]: Fol. 6r. In the outer margin, the red callout *зрѝ* ("Note well") highlights this pastoral rubric, which mandates immediate emergency baptism for sickly infants and forbids delaying until the customary fifth, sixth, eighth, or fortieth day.

[^46]: Fol. 6r. The citation of legal and canonical penalties for miscarriages occurring after five months of gestation reflects Byzantine and Slavic canonical jurisprudence (e.g. Canons of St. Basil the Great, Canons 2 and 8; Council in Trullo, Canon 91; Syntagma / *Kormchaia Kniga*), which classified the destruction of a formed fetus as homicide.

[^47]: Fol. 6v. Slavonic *въ цр҃ковьсти́тися* (to be churched, воцерковлятися; Greek: Σαранτισμός / εἰσκκλησιασμός) opens the solemn Order of Churching on the Fortieth Day, patterned upon the Presentation of Christ in the Temple (Luke 2:22–39) and the Mosaic purification (Leviticus 12:1–8).

[^48]: Fol. 6v. The rubric prescribes that the mother present the child before the church doors, accompanied by the intended sponsor (godparent) who will receive the child after baptism.

[^49]: Fol. 6v. Troparion of the Meeting of the Lord (Presentation of Christ in the Temple, February 2), Tone 1 (*Ра́дꙋйся ѡ҆брадо́ванная Бц҃е Дв҃о*), sung as the child is brought to the sanctuary doors.

[^50]: Fol. 7r. Continuation and conclusion from fol. 6v (p30) of the Troparion of the Meeting of the Lord (Presentation of Christ in the Temple, February 2), Tone 1 (*Ра́дꙋйся ѡ҆брадо́ванная Бц҃е дв҃о...*), quoting Luke 2:29–32.

[^51]: Fol. 7r. Kontakion of the Meeting of the Lord (*І҆́же оу҆тро́бꙋ дв҃ичю ѡ҆ст҃ивъ рожество́мъ си...*). Although in later standard liturgical editions this kontakion is appointed under Tone 1, some Ruthenian sources designate it Tone 1 while preserving the archaic pre-Nikonian petitions.

[^52]: Fol. 7r. Slavonic *оу҆мирѝ въ бра́нехъ житїѐ и҆ оу҆крѣпѝ цр҃ѧ [царѝ] и҆́хъже възлюби́лъ є҆си* ("grant peace in wars to life, and strengthen the kings/rulers whom Thou hast loved"). The Striatyn Trebnyk preserves the traditional Byzantine/Ruthenian civil petition for Christian rulers facing wartime adversity.

[^53]: Fol. 7v. This conditional rubric accounts for pastoral situations of neonatal infant mortality occurring before the completion of the forty days. If the child has died, the prayer of churching serves purely as the post-partum purification of the mother, omitting the child-oriented petitions.

[^54]: Fol. 7v. The Greek euchological theology contrasts "sensory light" (*свѣ́тъ чю́вственый*, Greek: αἰσθηтὸν φῶς) of physical birth into the material world with "spiritual/intelligible light" (*вразꙋ́мный свѣ́тъ*, νοηтὸν φῶς) imparted in Holy Illumination (Baptism).

[^55]: Fol. 8r. The second prayer of churching is designated to be recited secretly (*втаѝ*, Greek: μυστικῶς) while the mother and infant bow their heads before the entrance of the nave. It prays specifically for the mother's readmission to the Holy Mysteries of the Eucharist after her forty days of seclusion.

[^56]: Fol. 8v. Slavonic *жръто́вникъ* (literally "altar of sacrifice" or "prothesis") is used interchangeably here with *ѡ҆лта́рь* (sanctuary/chancel). The rubric directs the priest to receive the male infant into his arms and carry him into the sanctuary through the Holy Doors.

[^57]: Fol. 8v. The traditional canonical distinction in the rite of churching between male and female infants: male infants are carried through the Holy Doors around the Holy Table (*ст҃а́ѧ трапе́за*), whereas female infants are brought up to the Holy Doors (*сты̑ѧ две́ри*) and venerate the principal icons of the iconostasis.

[^58]: Fol. 9r. The Canticle of Symeon (Luke 2:29–32, *Nunc Dimittis* / *Нн҃ѣ ѿпоуща́еши*) is recited by the priest at the conclusion of bringing the child into the sanctuary, directly identifying the infant's reception in the church with Christ's Presentation in the Temple.

[^59]: Fol. 9v. The prescription of forty prostrations or metanias (*покло́новъ четыредесѧ́ть*) performed by the mother before the principal icon of the Theotokos symbolizes the completion of the forty days of post-partum purification, echoing the scriptural number of purification and testing.

[^60]: Fol. 9v. Slavonic *прїе́мникъ же гле́тсѧ, коу́мъ* ("and the receiver is called the koum [godparent/sponsor]"). *Koum* (Ukrainian/East Slavic *кум*, from Latin *compater*) is the vernacular East Slavic term for the baptismal sponsor who officially receives the child at the church doors.

[^61]: Fol. 10r. The opening canonical florilegium of the Striatyn Trebnyk introduces the Holy Mystery of Baptism through ancient conciliar and patristic canons, establishing valid Trinitarian baptismal form and canonical criteria for the reconciliation of converts.

[^62]: Fol. 10r. Apostolic Canon 47 imposes deposition upon any bishop or presbyter who either repeats a valid baptism or recognizes invalid heretical baptism, affirming the unrepeatable character of Christian illumination (cf. Ephesians 4:5).

[^63]: Fol. 10r. Canon 50 of the Council of Carthage (Canon 57 in the Greek Syntagma / African Code) addresses the reception of Donatist infants and schismatics, forbidding the rebaptism of those baptized in the Catholic Church who fell into heresy.

[^64]: Fol. 10r. The printed text reads Canon 44 (*м҃д*), an erratum for Apostolic Canon 49 (*м҃ѳ*), which prescribes baptism in the threefold Name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit (cf. Matthew 28:19) and deposes any cleric who baptizes into "three unoriginate" or "three sons."

[^65]: Fol. 10v. The theological gloss on Apostolic Canon 49 expounds classic Greek patristic Trinitarian monarchia: the Father alone is Unoriginate (*безначя́льный*) and without cause (*за є҆́же не и҆мѣ́ти вины̀*, Greek: ἀναίτιος); the Son is generated ineffably (*неизрече́ннаго ра́ди рожде́нїа*); and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Unbegotten (*и҆схоже́нїа ра́ди ѿ нероже́нна*).

[^66]: Fol. 10v. Apostolic Canon 50 mandates three distinct immersions (*трѝ погрꙋже́нїа*) in the single Mystery of Baptism, invoking each Person of the Holy Trinity separately, and deposes anyone performing a single immersion into Christ's death.

[^67]: Fol. 11r. Eunomius of Cyzicus (d. c. 393), leader of the radical Anomoean Arians, rejected traditional threefold immersion and introduced single immersion into Christ's death, which was condemned at the Second Ecumenical Council (Constantinople I, 381).

[^68]: Fol. 11r. Canon 7 of the Second Ecumenical Council (Constantinople I, 381) establishes the classical Byzantine threefold classification for receiving converts: by Chrismation (Arians, Macedonians, Novatians, Quartodecimans, Apollinarians); by libellus/profession of faith (Nestorians, Monophysites); and by Baptism (Eunomians, Montanists, Sabellians, and pagans).

[^69]: Fol. 11v. Novatians (*наватїа́ны* / Cathari) referred to themselves as "the pure" (*каѳаро́й* / *чи́сты*). The enigmatic Slavonic phrase *и҆ лѣ́вы* translates Greek ἀριστερούς ("those on the left" or "the strict/left-handed"), an ancient colloquial or sect epithet referenced in Byzantine canonical commentaries (e.g. Balsamon, Zonaras).

[^70]: Fol. 11v. Second Ecumenical Council Canon 7 prescribes the sealing with Holy Myron of the forehead, eyes, nostrils, mouth, and ears with the sacramental formula: "The seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit" (*Σφραγὶς δωρεᾶς Πνεύματος Ἁγίου* / *Печа́ть да́ра Свѧта́го Дꙋ́ха*), quoting 2 Corinthians 1:22.

[^71]: Fol. 12r. Continuation of the canonical florilegium on baptism from Canon 7 of the Second Ecumenical Council (Constantinople I, 381; cf. Trullo Canon 95). Radical Anomoean Arians (Eunomians) who rejected threefold immersion, Montanists (Phrygians), and Sabellians who taught "Son-Fatherhood" (*сн҃оѡтче́ство*, Greek: υἱοπατορία, modalistic monarchianism conflating the Persons of the Trinity) are classified with unbaptized pagans and must be received exclusively by baptism *de novo*.

[^72]: Fol. 12r. Canon 48 of the Synod of Laodicea (c. 363–364) mandates post-baptismal chrismation with heavenly myron (*Ὅτι δεῖ τοὺς φωτιζομένους μετὰ τὸ βάπτισμα χρίεσθαι...*). The printed Slavonic witness reads *и҆нѣ́нымъ ... пома́зоватисѧ мѵ́ромъ просвѣща́емымъ оу҆законя́етъ*, an archaic scribal or compositor variant for the newly enlightened (*новопросвѣщаемымъ*) or "others" (*инѣмъ*), syntactically paired with *просвѣща́емымъ*.

[^73]: Fol. 12v. Canon 6 of the Council of Neocaesarea (c. 314–325) permits pregnant women to receive baptism at any time during gestation. The canonical argument establishes that the unborn child does not automatically share in the mother's illumination, since moral disposition (*προαίρεσις* / *произволе́нїе*) is an individual act of free volition.

[^74]: Fol. 13r. Fol. 12v–13r. The Ruthenian text directly incorporates the Greek technical canonical term *anadochoi* (*младе́нци же а҆надо́хоумъ*, Greek: ἀναδόχοις) followed by its Slavonic gloss (*сирѣ́чь въспрїе́мникомъ*, "that is, the sponsors/receivers"), establishing that infants are illumined through the proxy confession and liturgical guarantees of their baptismal godparents.

[^75]: Fol. 13r. Canon 6 of the Canonical Answers of St. Timothy, Patriarch of Alexandria (c. 381), directing that a female catechumen experiencing her menstrual period on the day appointed for baptism should have her illumination deferred until she is purified.

[^76]: Fol. 13r. Canon 1 of St. Timothy of Alexandria, cited in the Slavonic text as *прѣ́все* (Greek: πρὸ πάντων / Question 1), deciding that a catechumen child or adult who unwittingly partakes of the Holy Eucharist during the Divine Liturgy must be baptized immediately, having been called by the Lord.

[^77]: Fol. 13v. Canon 4 of the Canonical Epistle of St. Cyril of Alexandria (to Domnus of Antioch). Catechumens who incurred disciplinary excommunication or heavy penance and face mortal danger must not be allowed to die unbaptized, but are to receive illumination so as not to depart destitute of divine loving-kindness and human mercy (*бл҃гти чл҃чкыѧ*, translating Greek φιλανθρωπία).

[^78]: Fol. 13v. Canon 2 of St. Timothy of Alexandria. Catechumens afflicted with demonic possession are barred from receiving the illumination of the Holy Spirit while dominated by an unclean spirit, but in case of mortal peril (*in extremis*) they must be baptized before death.

[^79]: Fol. 14r. Canon 4 of St. Timothy of Alexandria. A catechumen incapacitated by delirium, fever, or mental illness who cannot make a personal profession of faith may be baptized without hesitation if witnesses confirm that he had previously expressed a conscious desire for baptism.

[^80]: Fol. 14r. Canon 121 of the Council of Carthage (418/419; Canon 111 in the Greek Syntagma / African Code Canon 125). Promulgated against the Pelagian heresy, this canon defines that baptismal grace confers not merely the negative pardon of past sins (*remissio peccatorum*), but positive supernatural power and divine assistance (*adiutorium*) enabling the Christian to resist future sin.

[^81]: Fol. 14v. The grotesque mascaron tailpiece (Renaissance woodcut cul-de-lampe featuring a bearded mask with strapwork volutes, floral crest, and looped ribbon handles) marks the typographical conclusion of the Canonical Florilegium on Baptism (Part II).

[^82]: Fol. 15r. Part III marks the start of the liturgical celebration of Holy Baptism itself, beginning with the Rite of Making a Catechumen (*Чинъ быва́емый на оглаше́нїе*). The opening leaf is adorned with a monumental Renaissance strapwork headpiece featuring a central medallion of Christ the Great High Priest / Emmanuel blessing with both hands, flanked by adoring angels, cornucopias, and pomegranates.

[^83]: Fol. 15r. The introductory rubrics prescribe the ancient Byzantine posture of the candidate at the church doors: facing eastward toward the sanctuary, stripped of outer garments down to the tunic, ungirded, bareheaded, and barefoot, with hands lowered at the sides, symbolizing the renunciation of worldly adornments and submission to Christ.

[^84]: Fol. 15r. The triple ritual action opening the catechumenate: threefold insufflation (*доу́нетъ три́щи*) driving out the enemy, threefold signing of the brow and breast with the Cross, and imposition of the priest's right hand (*cheirothesia*) claiming the candidate for Christ.

[^85]: Fol. 15v. The First Prayer of the Catechumenate (*Ѡ҆ и҆́мени твое́мъ Гд҃и Бж҃е и҆́стины...*) is an ancient euchological formula attested in the 8th-century Barberini Euchologion (Barberini Gr. 336, fol. 195r). It quotes Ezekiel 20:11 and Leviticus 18:5 (*"which if a man do, he shall live in them"*; cf. Romans 10:5).

[^86]: Fol. 16r. Scriptural allusions to the "book of life" (*кни́гы живо́тныѧ*, Revelation 3:5; 20:12) and Christ's spiritual flock (Psalm 27:9 / LXX 28:9; 1 Peter 5:3).

[^87]: Fol. 16v. The First Exorcism (*Запрѣще́нїе пръ́вое*), traditionally attributed to St. Basil the Great, commands the devil to depart by virtue of Christ's incarnation, His Passion on the Cross, the harrowing of Hades, and His destruction of the power of death (Hebrews 2:14; Matthew 27:51–53; Jude 1:9).

[^88]: Fol. 17r. Continuation of the First Exorcism of St. Basil the Great from Fol. 16v. The euchological text asserts the absolute cosmic sovereignty of God over Satan, citing the primordial placement of the cherubim and the turning flaming sword to guard the Tree of Life (Genesis 3:24), Christ walking upon the sea as upon dry land (Matthew 14:25), rebuking the winds and sea (Mark 4:39), the drying up of the deeps at His glance (Nahum 1:4), and the melting of mountains at His rebuke (Psalm 96:5 / LXX 96:5). The exorcism explicitly bans demonic intrusion across all temporal divisions (night, day, hour, and noonday).

[^89]: Fol. 17v. The demonic host is commanded to depart into tartarus (*тартаръ*, the abyssal prison of fallen spirits; cf. 2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6) until the Great Day of Judgment. The prayer invokes the celestial hierarchy—angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, principalities, authorities, powers, many-eyed cherubim (Ezekiel 1:18; 10:12), and six-winged seraphim (Isaiah 6:2)—and quotes Psalm 103:3–4 (LXX 103:3–4: *"Who walks upon the wings of the wind; Who makes His angels spirits, and His ministers a flame of fire"*). The candidate is solemnly designated as the "newly chosen soldier of Christ our God" (*ново и҆ꙁбра́ннаго во́ина Хрⷭ҇та̀ Бг҃а на́шего*), evoking the patristic typology of baptism as the enlistment oath (*sacramentum militare*) of the Christian soldier.

[^90]: Fol. 18r. The Second Exorcism (*Запрѣще́нїе вто́рое*), likewise attributed in classical Byzantine and Ruthenian euchologia to St. Basil the Great. The priest acts not by his own power, but in persona Christi through whom God Himself commands Satan and his allied force (*споспѣ́шная си́ла*, Greek: συνεργὸς δύнаμις) to depart from the candidate newly signed with the sign of the Cross (*новознамена́нный*).

[^91]: Fol. 18v. Dominical and scriptural catena demonstrating the complete impotence of demonic power before Christ: the exorcism of the deaf and dumb spirit (*ре́кшаго глоухо́моу и҆ беꙁгла́номоу бѣ́соу: и҆ꙁы́ди ѿ чл҃ка...*, Mark 9:25) and Christ's permission to the Legion demons to enter the herd of swine (Matthew 8:31–32; Mark 5:12–13; Luke 8:32–33), proving that demons cannot harm even animals without divine permission. These dominical miracles are framed within Old Testament cosmological proofs of God's almighty creative power: establishing the earth upon the waters (Psalm 135:6 / LXX 135:6), weighing the mountains and valleys (Isaiah 40:12), setting the sand as the eternal bound of the sea (Jeremiah 5:22), and touching the mountains so that they smoke (Psalm 103:32 / LXX 103:32).

[^92]: Fol. 19r. Continuation of the cosmological praise from Psalm 103 (LXX 103:2, 3, 5): wrapping Himself in light as in a garment, laying the beams of His chambers in the waters, and establishing the earth upon its foundations never to be moved. The exorcism culminates in an eschatological adjuration by Christ's saving Passion, precious Body and Blood, and His fearful Second Coming, in which He shall not delay (Habakkuk 2:3; Hebrews 10:37) to judge the world and cast the demonic powers into the unquenchable fire and the undying worm of Gehenna (Isaiah 66:24; Mark 9:44, 48).

[^93]: Fol. 19v. The Third Exorcism Prayer (*Мл҃тва запрѣще́нїю тре́тїа*), attributed in Byzantine euchologia to St. John Chrysostom. The petition invokes the "Lord Sabaoth, God of Israel" (*Гдⷭ҇и саваѡ́ѳъ Бг҃е і҆и҃левъ*) to heal the candidate and crush Satan under his feet shortly, directly citing Romans 16:20 (*"And the God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly"*).

[^94]: Fol. 20r. The Fourth Exorcism Prayer (*Мл҃тва д҃, запрѣще́нїю*), also attributed to St. John Chrysostom. The prayer recalls the creation of humanity in the image and likeness of God (Genesis 1:26), the tragedy of the Fall, and the divine economy of salvation through the Incarnation of Christ (John 3:17; 1 Timothy 1:15). It petitions God to open the noetic/spiritual eyes (*мы́сленѣи ѻ҆́чи*, Greek: νοεροὺς ὀφθалμούς; Ephesians 1:18) of the candidate.

[^95]: Fol. 20v. The prayer petitions God to assign to the candidate an "angel of light" (*а҆́гг҃лъ свѣ́телъ*) to preserve him from all hostile assaults, the encounter of the adversary, the noonday demon (*бѣ́съ полоу́денный*, Greek: δаймо́нїон месемврїно́н; Psalm 90:6 / LXX 90:6), and evil apparitions. The rubrics instruct the priest to breathe thrice upon the candidate and sign his brow, mouth, and breast, followed by the threefold expulsion formula commanding the departure of the spirits of error, deceit, idolatry, covetousness, lying, and uncleanness.

[^96]: Fol. 21r. The positive transformation of the candidate into a reason-endowed sheep (*ѻ҆́вча слове́сно*, Greek: πρόβατον λογικόν) of Christ's flock (John 10:14–16), an honorable member of the Church (1 Corinthians 12:27), a consecrated vessel (2 Timothy 2:21), a child of light (Ephesians 5:8), and an heir of the Kingdom (Romans 8:17). The candidate is exhorted to keep the baptismal seal (*печа́ть*, Greek: σфραγίς) unbroken and the white baptismal robe (*ри́за*, Greek: χιτών) undefiled (Galatians 3:27; Revelation 3:4). The prayer closes with the classical Trinitarian ekphonesis.

[^97]: Fol. 21v. The Rite of Renunciation of Satan (*Apotaxis* / *Ѽрица́нїе*). The candidate is divested of outer garments and untied, symbolizing the shedding of fallen mortality and earthly entanglements, and turned toward the West (the symbol of darkness, sunset, and demonic power) with hands raised in repudiation. The 1606 Striatyn edition incorporates distinct Ruthenian pastoral rubrics, using both *по́пъ* and *сщ҃енникъ* for priest, and introducing the vernacular term *коу́мъ* (godparent / sponsor) alongside the classical term *въспрїе́мникъ* (*anadochos*). Specific pastoral provisions allow the godparent to answer on behalf of infants unable to speak (*а҆́ще ли бꙋ́детъ мла́до...*) and non-Slavonic foreigners (*и҆ноплеме́нни*). The term *стоу́да є҆го̀* translates Greek *πομπῆς αὐτοῦ* ("his pomps/parade").

[^98]: Fol. 22r. The transition from the Renunciation of Satan (*Apotaxis*) to the Adherence to Christ (*Syntaxis*). Note the distinctive Ruthenian euchological terminology: while modern Synodal Church Slavonic editions employ the verb *сочетава́тися* (*сочетава́еши ли сѧ Хрїстꙋ̀*, rendering Greek συντάσσομαι), the 1606 Striatyn imprint uses *ѡ҆бѣщава́тися* (*Ѡ҆бѣща́еши ли сѧ Хрⷭ҇тꙋ̀* / *Ѡ҆бѣща́юсѧ*), emphasizing the covenantal pledge/vow made to Christ. Also noteworthy is the pastoral provision continuing from Fol. 21v permitting the godparent (*коу́мъ*) or the deacon to respond on behalf of foreigners (*и҆ноплеме́нни*) unable to speak Church Slavonic. The candidate is directed to turn eastward with hands lowered (symbolizing submissive devotion, in contrast to hands raised westward during the renunciation of Satan), followed by the profession of the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed thrice.

[^99]: Fol. 22v. The post-credal confirmation: the priest interrogates the candidate in the perfect tense (*Ѡ҆бѣща́лъ ли сѧ є҆сѝ Хрⷭ҇тꙋ̀* / *Ѡ҆бѣща́хсѧ*), followed by the act of adoration (*proskynesis*) before the Holy Trinity. The priest recites the dominical doxology quoting 1 Timothy 2:4 (*"Who wills all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth"*). Then follows the final pre-baptismal prayer of the catechumenate (*Влⷣко Гдⷭ҇и Бг҃е на́шъ, призовѝ раба̀ твое́го...*), petitioning God to summon the candidate to the "holy illumination" (*ст҃ое просвѣще́нїе*, the ancient patristic term for baptism, Greek: φωτισμός).

[^100]: Fol. 23r. Conclusion of the prayer of the catechumenate. The euchological text draws upon Johannine and Pauline theology: the washing away of the "oldness" (*ѻ҆ветша́нїе*, Romans 6:6; Ephesians 4:22), rebirth unto eternal life (John 3:3–5; Titus 3:5), and transformation from a mere "child of the flesh" (*ча́до тѣле́сное*, Romans 9:8) into a "child of the kingdom" (*ча́до црⷭ҇твїа*). The prayer concludes with the full Trinitarian ekphonesis and a Renaissance floral woodcut tailpiece marking the structural close of the Office of the Catechumenate.

[^101]: Fol. 23v. Woodcut headpiece and title for the Order of Holy Baptism (*ПОСЛѢ́ДОВАНЇЕ СВѦТА́ГѠ КРЕЩЕ́НЇА*). The woodcut cartouche features an iconographic representation of infant immersion in a chalice-shaped font (*коу́пѣль*), captioned *КР҃ЩЕНЇЕ Ѻ҆ТРОЧАТА* ("The Baptism of an Infant"). In early printed Ruthenian euchologia, the Catechumenate and Baptism proper are demarcated as distinct liturgical orders, each preceded by its own decorative headpiece.

[^102]: Fol. 23v. The opening vestiary and rubrical prescriptions: the priest vests in white vestments (*бѣ́лаѧ ѡ҆де́жда*) and cuffs (*нарꙋ́квицѣ*, epimanikia), symbolizing the paschal joy and purity of baptismal illumination. All tapers are kindled, and the priest performs a solemn censing around the baptismal font, after which the deacon initiates the service with the classical dialogue formula: "Bless, Master" (*Бл҃гословѝ, влады́ко*).

[^103]: Fol. 24r. The Great Litany (*Вели́каѧ є҆кте́нїа*) of Holy Baptism. In accordance with early printed liturgical shorthand, the initial petitions of the general Great Litany are recorded in abbreviated incipits (concluding before the standard response *Гдⷭ҇и поми́лꙋй*), while the baptism-specific petitions are given in full. Note the petition for the local hierarch (*Ѡ҆ а҆рхїепи́скопѣ на́шемъ*), reflecting the diocesan episcopal structure of the Kyivan Metropolia under the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.

[^104]: Fol. 24v. The special baptismal petitions of the Great Litany invoking the "supersubstantial Trinity" (*пресꙋще́ственнаѧ тро́ица*, Greek: ὑπερούσιος Τριάς). These petitions articulate the theological fruits of baptismal water: purification, illumination of the intellect (*просвѣще́нїе ра́зꙋма*), defense against invisible demonic assaults, incorruption, and adoption as a "child of light" (*сы́нъ свѣ́та*, Ephesians 5:8).

[^105]: Fol. 25r. Pauline baptismal theology in the litany: conforming unto the likeness of Christ's death and resurrection (*съѡ́бразенъ и҆ приѡбщи́тель сме́рти и҆ воскресе́нїю*, Romans 6:4–5). The preservation of the white baptismal robe (*ѡ҆де́жда кр҃ще́нїѧ*) is linked with the "betrothal of Christ" (*ѡ҆брꙋче́нїе Хрⷭ҇то́во*), expressing the mystical nuptial union between the baptized soul and Christ the Bridegroom.

[^106]: Fol. 25r. The litany designates the baptismal water as the "laver of regeneration" (*ба́нѧ па́кибытїѧ̀*, Greek: λουτρὸν палиγγενεσίας; Titus 3:5), granting remission of sins and the garment of incorruptibility. The leaf concludes with the standard concluding litany petitions: deliverance from affliction and the petition *Застꙋпѝ, сп҃сѝ...* (*Help us, save us...*).

[^107]: Fol. 25v. The conclusion of the Great Litany: the commemoration of the Theotokos (*Прⷭ҇тꙋ́ю, чⷭ҇тꙋю и҆ пребл҃гослове́ннꙋю Влⷣчцꙋ...*) and the final commendation (*Са́ми себѐ и҆ дрꙋ́гъ дрꙋ́га...*).

[^108]: Fol. 25v. The Priest's Secret Prayer during the Baptismal Litany (*Бл҃гоꙋтро́бный и҆ ми́лостивый Бг҃е...*). In the Byzantine and Ruthenian tradition, while the deacon intones the Great Litany at the font, the officiating presbyter recites this apologia pro seipso in a low voice (*чте́тъ въ себѣ̀ мл҃твꙋ сїю̀ та́и*). The prayer alludes directly to Psalm 7:9 (LXX 7:10: *"God tries the hearts and reins"*), Hebrews 4:13 (*"all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of Him with Whom we have to do"*), and Wisdom 11:23 (*"overlookest the sins of men unto repentance"*), pleading that the unworthiness of the minister may not impede the efficacy of the sacrament.

[^109]: Fol. 26r. Continuation of the priest's secret prayer. The text draws on 1 Corinthians 9:27 (*"lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway"*, Slavonic: *неискоу́шенъ*) and Galatians 4:19 (*"until Christ be formed in you"*). The petition frames the newly baptized candidate within the ecclesiological architecture of Ephesians 2:20 (*"built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets"*) and the prophetic metaphor of the planting of truth (*са́дъ и҆́стинный*, Isaiah 60:21; 61:3) in the Catholic Church.

[^110]: Fol. 26v. Rubric regarding the conclusion of the priest's secret prayer: the priest does not chant an audible exclamation (*ни въꙁглаша́етъ*), but recites even the concluding "Amen" secretly within himself (*но и҆ а҆ми́нь въ себѣ̀ гле́тъ*), preserving liturgical silence while the deacon finishes the litany petitions.

[^111]: Fol. 26v. The Great Prayer of Sanctification of the Baptismal Waters (*Ве́лїй є҆сѝ, Гдⷭ҇и, и҆ чю́дна дѣла̀ твоѧ̀...*), traditionally attributed in Byzantine and Ruthenian euchologia to St. Sophronius of Jerusalem (and identical in its opening stanzas to the Great Blessing of the Waters at Theophany). The threefold opening acclamation of God's unutterable cosmic wonders is followed by the cosmological anamnesis of creation ex nihilo (*ѿ небытїа̀ въ бытїѐ*) and divine providence (*про́мыслъ*). The text here introduces the ancient physical theory of the four elements (*ѿ четы́рехъ съста́въ*, the four elements: earth, water, air, fire).

[^112]: Fol. 27r. The cosmological anamnesis of the Great Sanctification of the Waters (*Ве́лїй є҆сѝ, Гдⷭ҇и...*). The text invokes the cosmic obedience of creation to the Creator: the crowning of the yearly cycle (Psalm 64:12 LXX), the trembling of the intelligible/spiritual powers (Greek: νοεραὶ δυνάμεις), the supplication of the stars, the stretching out of the heavens like a curtain (Psalm 103:2 LXX), the founding of the earth upon the waters (Psalm 135:6 LXX), and the bounding of the sea with sand (Jeremiah 5:22). Note the archaic Ruthenian dual/plural forms *мнѡгоѡчи́таѧ хероуві́мъ* and *шестокрила́таѧ серафи́мъ*.

[^113]: Fol. 27v. The Christological anamnesis and the purpose of the Incarnation. God, being uncircumscribed (*неописа́ненъ*, Greek: ἀπερίγραπτος), without beginning (*безнача́ленъ*, ἄναρχος), and ineffable (*неизглаго́ланъ*, ἀνεκλάλητος), took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7), dwelling among men (Baruch 3:38 LXX), and sanctifying the virginal womb by His Nativity. The euchology proclaims the three theological duties: "We confess Thy grace, we proclaim Thy mercy, we conceal not Thy benefactions."

[^114]: Fol. 28r. The epiclesis upon the baptismal waters: *Са́мъ оу҆́бо чл҃колю́бче цр҃ю, прїидѝ и҆ннѣ̀ прише́ствїемъ ст҃а́го твое́го дх҃а. и҆ ѡ҆свѧтѝ во́доу сїю̀* ("Do Thou Thyself, therefore, O King, Lover of mankind, come even now through the descent of Thy Holy Spirit, and sanctify this water"). The text explicitly references the crushing of the dragons' heads in the Jordan (Psalm 73:13 LXX: "Thou didst crush the heads of the dragons upon the water"). The priest repeats the epiklesis thrice, accompanied by the threefold blessing with the hand.

[^115]: Fol. 28v. The breathing and signing of the waters. The priest breathes upon the surface of the water thrice (*доу́нетъ на́ водꙋ г҃.*) and signs it with the sign of the Cross (*прекрⷭ҇титъ рꙋкою*), reciting the apotropaic prayer: *Да съкроуша́тсѧ позна́менїемъ въѡбраже́нїа крⷭ҇та твоего̀ всѧ̑ проти́вныѧ си́лы* ("Let all adversary powers be crushed beneath the sign of the representation of Thy Cross") thrice. This is followed by the deprecation of airy and invisible phantoms (Greek: ἀέρια καὶ ἀφανῆ εἰδώλια) and demons of darkness, invoking Psalm 22:2 LXX (*во́дꙋ поко́ѧ*, "water of refreshment/repose").

[^116]: Fol. 29r. Baptism as ontological regeneration. The euchological catalogue enumerates the sevenfold gifts of baptismal grace: remission of sins, illumination of souls, the laver of regeneration (Titus 3:5), renewal of the Spirit, the gift of adoption (Romans 8:15), the garment of incorruptibility, and the fountain of life. Quoting Isaiah 1:16 LXX (*"Wash you, make you clean, put away evil from your souls"*), the prayer petitions that the candidate may put off the "old man" and put on the "new man" created after the image of God (Ephesians 4:22–24; Colossians 3:10).

[^117]: Fol. 29v. The famous typographical erratum and insertion (*вы́но* / *здѣ́*). In the printed text of Fol. 29v, the typesetter originally omitted the clause *и҆ въскр҃нїа бꙋ́детъ. и҆ сохрани́въ* (rendering Greek καὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως γένηται, καὶ φυλάξας) between *прича́стникъ* on line 1 and *да́ръ* on line 2. Discovering the error during presswork, the Striatyn printers placed an asterisk above line 1 with the marginal notation *вы́но,* (Early Modern East Slavic: *вынос*, denoting an omission/insertion) and printed the missing line at the foot of the page (line 16) preceded by *здѣ́* ("here") and a corresponding red asterisk. The prayer concludes with the Pauline allusions to the prize of the high calling (Philippians 3:14) and enrollment among the firstborn in heaven (Hebrews 12:23).

[^118]: Fol. 29v–30r. The Rite of the Oil of Catechumens / Oil of Gladness (*є҆ле́й ра́дости*, Greek: ἔλαιον ἀγαλλιάσεως). The priest salutes the people with "Peace be unto all", instructs them to bow their heads, and bowing over the oil vessel, breathes upon it thrice and blesses it with his hand. The deacon holds the holy oil and intones "Let us pray to the Lord", introducing the ancient pre-baptismal prayer of blessing the oil (*Влⷣко Гдⷭ҇и Бг҃е ѻ҆ц҃ъ на́шихъ...*).

[^119]: Fol. 30r. Typological exegesis of Noah's dove and the olive branch (Genesis 8:11). The prayer explains the olive branch carried by the dove as an archetypal sign of reconciliation (*премѣне́нїа знаме́нїе*) and salvation from the flood, prefiguring the sacrament of baptismal grace and the confection of holy unction. The text affirms that the olive fruit served the mysteries of both the Old Covenant (consecration under the Law) and the New Covenant (perfection under Grace).

[^120]: Fol. 30v. The blessing and infusing of the oil into the font. The prayer requests that the oil become an "anointing of incorruption, an armor of righteousness [2 Corinthians 6:7], a renewal of soul and body, a fountain of life". Following the audible ekphonesis and choir's "Amen", the deacon calls "Let us attend" (*Вънме́мъ*), and the priest takes the oil and pours it dropwise upon the water in the form of three crosses, while singing *Alleluia* thrice with the congregation.

[^121]: Fol. 31r. The Pre-Baptismal Anointing (*Chrismation of the Catechumen* with the Oil of Gladness). Following the priestly blessing based on John 1:9 (*"Blessed is God, Who illuminates and sanctifies every man that comes into the world"*), the infant is brought to the priest. The priest dips his thumb/finger into the consecrated oil and signs the child in the form of a cross upon the forehead (*чело̀*), breast (*пръ́си*), face (*лицѐ*), and shoulders (*пле́щи*), reciting the formula of anointing: *Пома́зꙋетсѧ ра́бъ бж҃їй [и҆мⷬ҇къ], є҆ле́ѡмъ ра́дости...* (Psalm 44:8 LXX / Hebrews 1:9).

[^122]: Fol. 31r–31v. The bodily member formulas of anointing: breast ("Unto the healing of soul and body"), ears ("Unto the hearing of faith", Romans 10:17), feet ("That he may walk in Thy steps", 1 Peter 2:21; Psalm 118:105 LXX), and hands ("Thy hands have made me and fashioned me", Psalm 118:73 LXX / Job 10:8). In the 1606 Striatyn imprint, the formulas for the ears, feet, and hands are preserved in full liturgical order.

[^123]: Fol. 31v. The Canonical Baptismal Formula and Threefold Immersion. The priest holds the candidate upright, facing eastward, and pronounces the passive Byzantine baptismal formula (*Кр҃ща́етсѧ ра́бъ Бж҃їй [и҆́мѧ ре́къ]...*), immersing the candidate completely beneath the water at each of the three Persons of the Holy Trinity (*въ и҆́мѧ ѻ҆ц҃а... и҆ сн҃а... и҆ дх҃а ст҃а́го*). The Striatyn rubrics explicitly specify that the candidate is immersed and lifted up once at each Person (*низводѧ̀ є҆го̀ въ во́доу, и҆ възводѧ̀*), sealing the sacramental regeneration in accordance with Apostolic Canon 50.

[^124]: Fol. 32r. Psalm 31:1–6a LXX (*Блаже́ни и҆́мже ѿпоусти́шасѧ безако́нїа...* / *Beati quorum remissae sunt iniquitates*). In early Byzantine and Ruthenian euchologia, Psalm 31 is the joyful post-baptismal thanksgiving psalm chanted immediately following the candidate's emergence from the font. It proclaims the core mystery of baptismal regeneration: the absolute remission and covering of sins (Romans 4:7–8), the lifting of guilt, and deliverance from ungodliness. Note the archaic Ruthenian graphic variants in Fol. 32r: *възврати́хсѧ на стра́сть, є҆гда̀ оу҆нзѐ ми те́рнъ* (rendering LXX ἐν τῷ ἐνпаγῆναί μοι ἄκανθαν) and the abbreviation *позна̑* for *позна́хъ*.

[^125]: Fol. 32v. Psalm 31:6b–11 LXX and the threefold repetition (*Сї́й же ѱло́мъ гл҃етсѧ г҃.*). The euchology contrasts the spiritual understanding granted to the newly illuminated with the uncomprehending brute nature of the horse and mule (v. 9), whose jaws must be held with bit and bridle. The rubric requiring the psalm to be sung thrice reflects the ancient baptismal station before the chrismation and vesting, mirroring the Trinitarian nature of the mystery.

[^126]: Fol. 33r. The Ruthenian Pastoral Rubric on Infant Baptism vs. Candidates of Understanding (*смы́сленъ*). In this celebrated historical rubric, the 1606 Striatyn Euchologion records the early modern Ruthenian pastoral practice: if the candidate is an infant, the priest seats him in the font with the water reaching unto his neck, holding him securely with the left hand, and pours warm water over his head with the right hand (*водѣ̀ соу́щи по́шїю, придръжа̀ лѣ́вою роуко́ю. де́сноюже прїе́мъ те́плою во́доу възлива́етъ на главоу̀ є҆го̀*), explicitly citing pastoral prudence and safety lest the infant drown (*зане́же блюстѝ зали́тисѧ младе́нца*). If, however, the candidate has reached understanding (*а́ще ли є҆́стъ смы́сленъ кр҃ща́емый*), the priest immerses him completely in three immersions (*погружа́етъ є҆го̀ въ трѝ погроуже́нїа*).

[^127]: Fol. 33r. The Vesting of the Newly Baptized in the Robe of Righteousness (*ѡ҆де́жда пра́вды*, Greek: χιτὼν δικαιοσύνης). The priest clothes the newly illuminated in a clean white tunic or garment, pronouncing the Trinitarian vesting formula. The white garment represents the recovery of the robe of light and glory originally given to Adam in Paradise before the Fall, now restored through baptismal incorruption, prefiguring the eschatological wedding garment (Matthew 22:11–12; Galatians 3:27; Revelation 7:9).

[^128]: Fol. 33v. The Baptismal Troparion in Tone 8: *Ри́зоу ми пода́ждь свѣ́тлꙋ, ѡ҆дѣѧ́йсѧ свѣ́томъ ꙗ҆́ко ри́зою...* ("Grant unto me a robe of light, O Thou that deckest Thyself with light as with a garment..."). Based upon Psalm 103:2 LXX, this troparion is sung while the sponsor and priest arrange the white baptismal robe upon the child. It expresses the mystical illumination (*photismos*) of the soul through Christ, Who wraps Himself in uncreated light.

[^129]: Fol. 33v–34r. The Pre-Chrismation Euchological Prayer (*Блгⷭ҇ве́нъ є҆си Гдⷭ҇и Бг҃е въседръжи́телю...* / Greek: Εὐχὴ τοῦ ἁγίου Μύρου). Addressed to God the Father as the "Sun of Righteousness" (Malachi 4:2), this prayer explicitly articulates the indivisible organic unity of the three traditional mysteries of Christian initiation: cleansing in holy water (Baptism), the seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit through the life-creating anointing (Chrismation), and the immediate worthy reception of the Body and Blood of Christ (Eucharist: *и причаще́нїе ст҃а́го тѣ́ла, и҆ чт҃ныѧ кро́ве Хрⷭ҇та твое́го*).

[^130]: Fol. 34v. The Priestly Ekphonesis of Chrismation (*Ꙗ҆́ко ты̀ є҆си Бг҃ъ на́шъ Бг҃ъ ми́ловати и҆ сп҃сати насъ...*). The doxology seals the invocation of the Holy Trinity with the Father Paul standard ("now and ever, and unto ages of ages"), concluding the solemn prayer of consecration before the sacramental unction.

[^131]: Fol. 34v. The Holy Mystery of Chrismation (*Myropomazanie* / Greek: Χρῖσμα). The priest takes the consecrated Holy Chrism (*ст҃ымъ мѵ́ромъ*) and anoints the five bodily sensory centers in the form of the Cross: forehead (*чело̀*), eyes (*ѡ҆чеса̀*), breast (*пръ́си*), hands (*роу́цѣ*), and feet (*но́зѣ*), sealing each with the statutory biblical formula: "The seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit. Amen" (*Печа́ть да́ра ст҃го дх҃а, а҆ми́нь*; cf. 2 Corinthians 1:21–22; Ephesians 1:13; 4:30; Council of Laodicea, Canon 48).

[^132]: Fol. 34v. The Baptismal Circular Procession (*ѡ҆бхо́дѧтъ ѡ҆́крꙋгъ а҆нало́ѧ*). The priest, sponsor (*въспрїе́мникъ* / *кумъ*), and newly illuminated process three times around the analogion (or font) while chanting the ancient baptismal entrance hymn: *Є҆ли́ци въ Хрⷭ҇та̀ крⷭ҇ти́стесѧ, въ Хрⷭ҇та̀ ѡ҆блеко́стесѧ, а҆ллилоу́їа* (Galatians 3:27, sung thrice). The circular motion symbolizes the eternal, unending nature of the new covenant with Christ and participation in the joy of the heavenly choir.

[^133]: Fol. 34v. The Baptismal Prokeimenon in Tone 3 from Psalm 26:1 LXX (*Гдⷭ҇ь просвѣще́нїе моє̀ и҆ сп҃си́тель мо́й, кого́ сѧ оу҆бою̀...* / "The Lord is my illumination and my Savior; whom shall I fear?"). Illumination (*просвѣще́нїе*, Greek: φωτισμός) serves as the primary patristic term for Holy Baptism (cf. Justin Martyr, *First Apology* 61; Gregory of Nazianzus, *Oration 40*).

[^134]: Fol. 35r–35v. The Baptismal Epistle: Romans 6:3–11 (Pericope 91). The locus classicus of Pauline baptismal theology. St. Paul teaches that baptism is not a mere symbolic washing, but a mystical co-burial (*съпогребо́хомсѧ*) into the death of Christ and a resurrection unto newness of life, crucifying the "old man" and destroying the "body of sin" so that the believer is liberated from servitude to sin.

[^135]: Fol. 35v. Conclusion of the Epistle and the Liturgical Gospel Dialogue. The Pauline pericope culminates in the exhortation to reckon oneself dead unto sin, but alive unto God in Christ Jesus (Romans 6:11). The deacon then commands liturgical vigilance: *Премоу́дрость прѡ́сти оу҆слы́шимъ ст҃го є҆ѵⷢгліа* (Greek: Σοφία. Ὀρθοί. Ἀκούσωмен τοῦ ἁγίου εὐαγγελίου), answered by the announcement of the Holy Gospel according to Matthew.

[^136]: Fol. 35v–36r. The Great Commission Gospel: Matthew 28:16–20 (Pericope 116). The final verses of the Gospel of Matthew, proclaimed at every Byzantine baptism. The resurrected Lord, having received all power in heaven and earth, commissions the eleven apostles to go forth, make disciples of all nations, baptize them into the threefold Name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and keep His commandments, concluding with the perpetual promise: "And lo, I am with you always, even unto the end of the age."

[^137]: Fol. 36r. The Baptismal Augmented Litany (*є҆ктенїа̀*). In addition to the civil petitions for the sovereign and the hierarchy (the local bishop), the euchology introduces a unique personal petition for the sponsor/godparent (*ра́боу Бж҃їю [и҆́мѧ ре́къ въспрїе́мникоу]*), praying for mercy, life, peace, health, and remission of sins in recognition of the sponsor's grave spiritual sponsorship and covenantal pledge made at the font.

[^138]: Fol. 36v. The Petition for the Newly Illumined and the Baptismal Dismissal (*ѿпоу́стъ*). The litany concludes with a fervent supplication that the newly baptized child may be preserved in the "faith of a pure confession" (*въ вѣ́рѣ чи́стаго и҆сповѣда́нїа*) all the days of his life. The euchology then prescribes the proper baptismal dismissal formula commemorating Christ's baptism in the Jordan by John (*И҆́же въ І҆ѿрда́ни ѿ І҆ѡа́нна на́шего ра́ди сп҃се́нїа кр҃ти́тисѧ прїе́мый...*), which concludes on the succeeding folio (Fol. 37r / p91).

[^139]: Fol. 37r. Conclusion of the Baptismal Dismissal (*ѿпоу́стъ*). The text completes the liturgical formula begun on Fol. 36v: *ꙗ҆́ко бл҃гъ и҆ чл҃колꙕ́бецъ* ("...for He is good and the Lover of mankind"). In early modern Ruthenian euchologia, the dismissal seals the triple mystery of initiation (Baptism, Chrismation, and the subsequent Communion), acknowledging Christ's condescension to be baptized in the Jordan and invoking the intercession of the Theotokos, the precious Cross, and all the saints.

[^140]: Fol. 37r. The Great Transfer / Entrance (*вели́кїй перено́съ* / Greek: μεγάλη εἴσοδος) and Post-Baptismal Communion. The 1606 Striatyn Euchologion provides crucial historical evidence for the liturgical integration of Baptism within the Divine Liturgy. If the Liturgy is celebrated, the newly baptized infant is solemnly carried with tapers at the Great Transfer (*на вели́комъ перено́сѣ*), whereas an adult candidate walks in personal procession immediately preceding the Holy Gifts, holding a lighted taper in both hands (*дръжа̀ по свѣщѝ въ ѻ҆бо́ю рꙋкоу*). Both infant and adult immediately partake of the Holy Mysteries of Christ, preserving the undivided primitive order of Christian initiation. Furthermore, upon dismissal, the neophyte is escorted in joyful triumph back to his home bearing burning tapers.

[^141]: Fol. 37v. The Baptismal Octave of Illumination (*да́же до ѿсма́го днѐ*). In strict accordance with ancient Byzantine and Jerusalem practice (witnessed in the mystagogical catecheses of St. Cyril of Jerusalem and St. John Chrysostom), the newly illumined Christian wore the white baptismal robe (*chiton* / *kryzhmo*) and carried the lighted baptismal candle to church daily for seven consecutive days, attending Vespers, Matins, and the Divine Liturgy. Only on the eighth day (*ѿсмы́й дн҃ь*) was this octave brought to a liturgical close by the solemn ritual of Ablution and Hair-Tonsure.

[^142]: Fol. 38r. Part V: The Order for the Ablution of the Baptized on the Eighth Day (*ПОСЛѢДОВÁНЇЄ ВЪ Є҆́ЖЕ ѼМЫ́ТИ КР҃ТИ́ВШАГО СѦ ВЪ Ѽ́СМЫЙ ДН҃Ь* / Greek: Εὐχαὶ τῆς Ἀπολούσεως μεθ' ἡμέρας ὀγδόην). Folio 38r opens with a monumental full-width woodcut headpiece characteristic of the Striatyn printing house (depicting two classical floral urns flanked by rolling acanthus scrolls), introducing the distinct liturgical office for releasing the candidate from the baptismal garments and washing away the physical chrism so as to guard the holy mystery from profane contamination.

[^143]: Fol. 38r. The Loosing of the Baptismal Garments and the Ruthenian Term *па́пишъ* (*раздрѣша́етъ ꙗ҆́же па́пишъ ѿ кр҃ще́нїа ѻ҆дѣва́ла , и҆ по́ѧсъ*). The rubric specifies that the priest unlooses the belt and the baptismal garments designated as *па́пишъ* (repeated on Fol. 40r: *ѻ҆дѣва́ло и҆́же па́пишъ*). In western Ukrainian and Galician-Ruthenian historical dialect, *папуш* / *папиш* designates a swaddled bundle, wrap, or linen infant binder (cognate with Romanian *păpușă* / Latin *pupa*, and related to Galician *папуша* for a wrapped sheaf or swaddling bundle). Here it serves as a vernacular technical term for the white swaddling cloth or baptismal wrapper (*savanon* / *kryzhmo*) wrapped securely around the infant over the white tunic.

[^144]: Fol. 38v. The First Euchological Prayer of Ablution (*И҆́же и҆збавле́нїе съгрѣше́нїемъ ра́ди ст҃го кр҃ще́нїа...* / Greek: Ὁ τὴν ἄφεσιν τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν διὰ τοῦ ἁγίου βαπτίσματος...). The prayer addresses God as the Author of spiritual regeneration, petitioning that the divine illumination of His countenance may shine perpetually in the candidate's heart, that the "shield of faith" may be guarded from demonic ambush, and that the "garment of incorruptibility" (*нетлѣ́нїе ѻ҆дѣѧ́нїа*) and "spiritual seal" (*дх҃овнаѧ печа́ть*) received in Chrismation may remain spotless, inviolate, and unassailable.

[^145]: Fol. 39r. The Second Prayer of Ablution: Heavenly Illumination and the Unstolen Pledge (*Влⷭ҇ко Гн҃и Бг҃е на́шь , и҆́же ра́ди коу́пели нб҃наго ѻ҆сїѧ́нїа...* / Greek: Δέσποτα Κύριε ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν, ὁ διὰ τῆς κολυμβήθρας...). The euchology commemorates the font as the conduit of heavenly illumination (*нб҃ное ѻ҆сїѧ́нїе* / οὐράνιος ἔλλαμψις) and invokes the divine hand of protection over the child to keep the "pledge of the Spirit" (*ѻ҆броуче́нїе дх҃а*, Greek: ἀρραβὼν τοῦ Πνεύματος; cf. 2 Corinthians 1:22, 5:5; Ephesians 1:14) "unstolen" (*некра́домо* / ἄσυλον) by adversary powers.

[^146]: Fol. 39v. The Prayer of Bowing of Heads: The Neophyte as an Unconquered Champion (*Ѻ҆дѣ́выисѧ въ тѧ̀ Хрⷭ҇та̀ и҆ Бг҃а на́шего...* / Greek: Ὁ ἐνδυσάμενος σὲ τὸν Χριστὸν...). Reflecting the Pauline imagery of Galatians 3:27 ("as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ"), the prayer portrays the baptized person as an athlete or champion (*подви́жникъ* / Greek: ἀθλητής) entering the spiritual arena against invisible foes, beseeching the Lord to grant him final victory and the crown of incorruption.

[^147]: Fol. 40r. The Ritual Ablution and Sacramental Formula (*Кр҃ти́лсѧ є҆сѝ . просвѣти́лсѧ є҆си . мѵ́ромъ пома́залсѧ є҆сѝ...*). The rubric directs the priest to unbind the belt and the baptismal swaddling cloth (*па́пишъ*), dip their extremities into the water, sprinkle the child with the declaration "Thou hast been justified, thou hast been enlightened" (1 Corinthians 6:11), and then wipe the anointed sensory centers (head, face, breast) with a fresh sponge saturated with water. The formula explicitly enumerates the stages of initiation: baptism (*кр҃ти́лсѧ є҆си*), illumination (*просвѣти́лсѧ є҆си*), chrismation (*мѵ́ромъ пома́залсѧ є҆си*), sanctification (*ѡ҆ст҃и́лсѧ є҆си*), and washing (*ѡ҆мы́лсѧ є҆си*).

[^148]: Fol. 40v. The Mystery of the Tonsure of Hair: The Theological Anthropology of the Craftsman (*МЛ҃ТВА на постриже́нїе вла́сѡвъ* / Greek: Εὐχὴ ἐπὶ κουρᾷ τριχῶν). This profound euchological prayer develops a classical Patristic theology of the human organism (drawing upon Gregory of Nyssa and Nemesius of Emesa): God is hailed as the "excellent Craftsman" (*до́брый хꙋдо́жникъ* / ἄριστος τεχνίτης) Who endowed man with a rational soul (*дꙋша́ слове́снаѧ*) and an harmonious physical body, setting the head as a citadel upon the heights, adorning it with unconfused sensory organs, and covering it with hair as a shield against meteorological tempests.

[^149]: Fol. 41r. The Apostolic Mandate and the Dedication of the First-Fruits (*сътвори́ти нача́токъ стри́щи вла́сы*). The prayer cites the apostolic rule of St. Paul—the "chosen vessel" (Acts 9:15)—to do all things unto the glory of God (1 Corinthians 10:31). The clipping of the hair is offered not as an aesthetic trimming, but as a sacrificial first-fruits (*aparchē* / *нача́токъ*) of the candidate's body offered unto Christ in thanksgiving for his illumination.

[^150]: Fol. 41v. The Royal Anointing of David and the Blessing of Old Age (Psalm 127:5 LXX). The concluding prayer of tonsure typologically links the blessing of the candidate's head with the biblical anointing of King David by the Prophet Samuel at Bethlehem (1 Samuel / 1 Kings 16:13). The priest prays that the newly enlightened Christian may advance in age from infancy unto venerable grey hairs (*сѣди́ны ста́рости* / πολιὰ γήρως), beholding the prosperity of the mystical Jerusalem all the days of his life (Psalm 127:5 LXX; Masoretic Psalm 128:5).

[^151]: Fol. 42r. The Post-Baptismal Hair Tonsure Formula (*Пострига́етсѧ ра́бъ бж҃їи...* / Greek: Κείρεται ὁ δοῦλος τοῦ Θεοῦ...). The priest clips the hair of the neophyte crosswise (*пострига́етъ є҆го̀ крⷭ҇тоѻбра́зно*), beginning on the crown of the head, then the back, and the right and left sides, dedicating the first-fruits of bodily growth unto God. The active indicative passive formula ("The servant of God is shorn...") seals the completion of the mystery of illumination, expressing the yoke of Christ and royal servitude under the divine King.

[^152]: Fol. 42r. The Capping with the *Koukoulion* or *Klobuchets* (*посе́мъ возлага́етъ нань коу́коль, ре́кше клобоу́чецъ гл҃ѧ: Ѻ҆дѣва́етсѧ ра́бъ Бж҃їи... въ коу́коль незло́бїа* / Greek: κουκούλλιον τῆς ἀκακίας). The 1606 Striatyn Euchologion witnesses the ancient post-baptismal investiture with the baptismal cowl or white cap (*klobuchets*), designated the "koukoulion of innocence" (or guilelessness / harmlessness; cf. 1 Corinthians 14:20: "in malice be ye children"). In early Byzantine and Old Slavonic ritual tradition (preserved in early manuscripts such as Euchologion Sinait. gr. 959 and Barberini gr. 336), this white headpiece remained upon the child's head throughout the seven days of the baptismal octave to protect the consecrated chrism upon the crown and brow until the eighth-day ablution.

[^153]: Fol. 42r. The Post-Baptismal Litany and Royal Commemoration (*є҆кте́нїа, вне́йже помина́етъ цр҃ѧ, и҆ въспрїе́мника съ новопросвѣще́нны[мъ]*). The litany following the tonsure and capping includes an explicit petition for the reigning sovereign: *Є҆ще мо́лимсѧ ѡ҆ бл҃гочтивомъ цр҃и нашемъ* ("Again we pray for our pious king..."). In the historical context of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth under King Sigismund III Vasa (reigned 1587–1632), the Ruthenian Orthodox Church preserved the traditional euchological title *цр҃ь* / *коро́ль* alongside supplications for the sponsor (*въспрїе́мникъ*) and the newly illumined child.

[^154]: Fol. 42v. Conclusion of the Eighth-Day Ablution Office and the Customary Dismissal (*И҆ быва́етъ по ѻ҆бы́чаю ѿпоу́стъ*). Following the ekphonesis of the fervent litany, the priest imparts the canonical liturgical dismissal (*apolysis*), formally concluding the eighth-day octave rites of ablution and tonsure.

[^155]: Fol. 43r. Part VI: The Reception of Converts and Ancient Conciliar Canons (*ЧИ́НЪ КА́КО ПОДОБА́ЄТ ПРЇИМА́ТИ и҆́же ѿ є҆ре́ти́къ...* / Greek: Τάξις πῶς δεῖ δέχεσθαι τοὺς ἐξ αἱρέσεων προσερχομένους...). The opening rubric of Part VI cites almost verbatim the canonical legislation established by the Second Ecumenical Council (Constantinople I, 381, Canon 7) and confirmed by the Quinisext Council in Trullo (692, Canon 95). These canons classify heterodox converts into three distinct canonical categories according to their baptismal status: (1) those requiring full threefold baptism (e.g. Eunomians, Montanists, Sabellians); (2) those received by chrismation and formal written abjuration (*libellus* / *и҆зрече́нїе*), comprising Arians, Macedonians (Pneumatomachians, *дх҃оу съпоста́ты*), Novatians/Catharoi (conflated here under *Савва́тники*), Quartodecimans (*четырина́десѧтники, рекѡ́мїи тетради́те*), and Apollinarians; and (3) those received solely through abjuration and the profession of the Orthodox faith (e.g. Nestorians, Monophysites).

[^156]: Fol. 43v. The Preparatory Fast, Catechetical Discipline, and the Term *па́надиѧ* (*пости́ти дни̑и д҃і , и҆ли па́надиѧ*). Before reconciliation, the candidate is placed under a strict fourteen-day ascetical regimen: fasting for fourteen days (*дни̑и д҃і*), attending morning and evening church services daily, and learning the Psalter (*оу҆чѧ́щоусѧ ѱалмы̀*) in the manner of a formal catechumen (*ꙗ҆́ко ѻ҆глаше́нъ*). The alternate phrase *и҆ли па́надиѧ* (or *панаги́а*) refers in Ruthenian and Greek monastic parlance to the two-week Dormition Fast preceding the Feast of the All-Holy Mother of God (*Panagia*, August 1–14), which constitutes an exact fourteen-day fast.

[^157]: Fol. 44r. The Recitation of the Creed and the Rubric *кр҃ща́ѧисѧ* (*приклона́етъ гла́вꙋ кр҃ща́ѧисѧ*). The candidate recites the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed verse by verse; if illiterate or unfamiliar with Church Slavonic, the sponsor dictates it for him line by line. The rubric denotes the candidate as *кр҃ща́ѧисѧ* ("the one being baptized"), reflecting the ancient euchological terminology where persons undergoing any stage of the catechumenate or sacramental reconciliation are designated broadly by the verbal noun of illumination.

[^158]: Fol. 44r. The Euchological Prayer of Reception: 1 Timothy 2:4 and Deliverance from Deception (*Бг҃е ст҃ы́й и҆ сп҃сителю на́шъ, хотѧ́й въсѣ́мъ чл҃кѡмъ сп҃тисѧ...* / Greek: Ὁ Θεὸς ὁ ἅγιος καὶ σωτὴρ ἡμῶν, ὁ πάντας ἀνθρώπους θέλων σωθῆναι...). The prayer opens with the apostolic proclamation of 1 Timothy 2:4 that God wills all men to be saved and to come unto the knowledge of the truth. It describes the convert as one who has "scarcely recovered himself from deception" (*є҆два̀ въскло́ньшагосѧ ѿ ле́сти*, Greek: μόλις ἀνανεύσαντα ἀπὸ τῆς πλάνης), petitioning the Divine Shepherd to receive him back into the rational sheepfold.

[^159]: Fol. 44v. The Johannine Theology of the One Flock (John 10:16). The euchology explicitly quotes Christ's discourse on the Good Shepherd in John 10:16: "Other sheep I have which are not of this fold; them also I must bring, and they shall hear My voice; and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd" (*ꙗ҆́ко и҆ и҆ны́ѧ ѻ҆́вца и҆́мамъ...*). This Scripture grounds the theological reconciliation of schismatics and heretics not as an innovation, but as the fulfillment of Christ's cosmic gathering of scattered souls into the unity of the Church through the seal of holy Chrismation and partaking of the Holy Mysteries.

[^160]: Fol. 45r. Post-Reconciliation Chrismation (*пома́зоуетъ є҆го̀ мѵ́ромъ ꙗ҆́ко новопросвѣще́ннаго, то́жде нарица́нїе творѧ̀ надъ ни́мъ*). Following the anathemas and profession of faith, the priest anoints the candidate with holy myron using the canonical sacramental formula identical to that of baptismal illumination: "The seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit. Amen." This reflects the second-class reception established by Canon 7 of Constantinople I and Canon 95 of Trullo, validating the outward Trinitarian form of their previous water immersion while imparting the sacramental grace of the Holy Spirit through Orthodox Chrismation.

[^161]: Fol. 45v. The Seven-Day Fasting and Octave Injunction (*повелѣва́етъ є҆мꙋ̀ з҃ дн҃ии ма́са не ꙗ҆́сти, и҆ лица̀ не оу҆мыва́ти*). Following Holy Communion, the newly reconciled Christian is instructed to observe seven days of meatless fasting and to refrain from washing his face, remaining in the spiritual state of a newly baptized person (*ꙗ҆́коже новокрща́емый та́ко пребыва́ти*), returning on the eighth day for the ritual ablution of the holy chrism.

[^162]: Fol. 45v. The Enrolment and Naming of a Convert from Paganism (*Мл҃тва знамена́ти чл҃ка прише́дша ѿ пога́ныхъ кр҃титисѧ, и҆ и҆́мѧ є҆моу̀ нарещѝ* / Greek: Εὐχὴ εἰς τὸ σημειῶσαι ἄνθρωπον ἐξ ἐθνῶν ἐρχόμενον βαπτισθῆναι, καὶ ὄνομα αὐτῷ ἐπιθεῖναι). This euchological prayer serves as the adult liturgical equivalent to the naming of an infant on the eighth day (*Chindanye* / *Пострижины*). It marks the formal signing with the cross on the brow and the bestowing of a Christian baptismal name upon an unbaptized catechumen converting from paganism (*ѿ пога́ныхъ*).

[^163]: Fol. 46r. Renunciation of Pagan Nomenclature and the Dignity of an "Equal Christian" (*да бꙋ́детъ и҆ се́и раве́нъ хрⷭ҇тїа́нинъ, зна́емъ ѿ дне́шнего днѐ*). The prayer explicitly beseeches God to purge the convert of every former pagan and heretical name (*всѧ́кого и҆́мене є҆рети́ческаго*), making him a "chosen vessel" (Acts 9:15) and an "equal Christian" (*раве́нъ хрⷭ҇тїа́нинъ* / Greek: ἰσοχριστιανός), invested with full spiritual citizenship in the Body of Christ without distinction of prior ethnicity or background (Galatians 3:28).

[^164]: Fol. 46v. Canonical Reception of Armenians and Jacobites (*А҆РМЕ́НИ Ѡ҆БРАЩА́ЮЩЕИСѦ... не кр҃щаютсѧ, но пома́зоуютсѧ му́ромъ*). In strict fidelity to the Byzantine canonical tradition (summarized in the Nomokanons and the *Syntagma* of Matthew Blastares), Non-Chalcedonians—specifically Armenians and Syrian Jacobites—are received into the Orthodox Church through Chrismation and the abjuration of their characteristic recensional and theological peculiarities, rather than by re-baptism, recognizing their valid historical Trinitarian baptism.

[^165]: Fol. 46v. The Renunciation of Armenian, Chazinzarian, and Jacobite Errors (*въсѧ́коую є҆́ресь а҆рме́нскоую, и҆ ханзиза́рскоую, и҆ і҆аковити́коую*). The abjuration formula explicitly targets three interrelated Oriental non-Chalcedonian groups: (1) the Armenians (*а҆рме́нскоую*); (2) the Chazinzarians (*ханзиза́рскоую* / Greek: Χαζινζάριοι, Chatzitzarioi, or Staurolatrae, from Armenian *khach* / *khachazart*, "worshippers of the Cross", a 7th-century Armenian sect or polemical epithet applied in Byzantine anti-Armenian treatises by Nicetas Choniates and Demetrius of Cyzicus); and (3) the Jacobites (*і҆аковити́коую*, Syrian Miaphysites following Jacob Baradaeus). The convert also explicitly renounces their liturgical customs: the use of unmixed wine in the eucharistic chalice, azymes (unleavened bread), and their distinctive fasting ordinances (such as the Fast of the Artzivourion / St. Sarkis).

[^166]: Fol. 46v. The Holy Symbol of Faith as *ст҃ыи ѻ҆́бразъ* (*И҆ гл҃етъ ве́сь ст҃ыи ѻ҆́бразъ, є҆́же є҆́стъ Вѣ́рꙋю въ є҆ди́наго Бг҃а*). In Church Slavonic euchological rubrics, the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed is frequently termed *ст҃ыи ѻ҆́бразъ* (translating the Greek τύπος τῆς πίστεως or σύμβολον τῆς πίστεως, "the sacred pattern / type / symbol of the faith"), which the convert recites in its entirety before being anointed with holy chrism.

[^167]: Fol. 47r. The Christological Confession and Conciliar Anathemas of the Non-Chalcedonian Convert (*и҆ є҆ди́но оу҆́бѡ є҆стество̀ ст҃ѣ́и трⷪ҇ци и҆сповѣ́дꙋю...*). The penitent's profession of faith articulates the classic Chalcedonian Christological dogma against Monophysitism/Miaphysitism: confessing two distinct natures (*двѣ̀ є҆стествѣ̀*) in the incarnate Lord Jesus Christ—unconfused, unchangeable, indivisible, and inseparable (Council of Chalcedon, 451)—and affirming the impassibility of the divine nature (*Бж҃тво безстра́стно є҆́стъ*) against Theopaschism. The convert formally assents to the Seven Ecumenical Councils (*се́дмь събѡ́ровъ*) and pronounces anathema against ancient heresiarchs: Simon Magus (*Си́монъ пръ́выи є҆ретикъ*); Manes (founder of Manichaeism); Marcion; Arius and Eunomius (Arianism and Anomoeanism); Macedonius (Pneumatomachianism); Apollinarius; Paul of Samosata (Monarchianism); Sabellius (Modalism); Theodore of Mopsuestia (condemned at Constantinople II, 553); Nestorius (Nestorianism, Ephesus 431); and the Monophysite leaders Eutyches, Dioscorus of Alexandria (Chalcedon 451), Theodosius of Alexandria, and Timothy Aelurus.

[^168]: Fol. 47v. Anathemas against the Aphthartodocetic, Monophysite, and Monothelite Leaders (*І҆ꙋлїа́на. Петра̀ мо́гка...*). The catalogue continues with Julian of Halicarnassus (advocate of Aphthartodocetism); Peter Mongus (*Пе́тръ мо́гкъ*, Patriarch of Alexandria) and Peter the Fuller (*Пе́тръ крафе́й* / Gnapheus, Patriarch of Antioch), who interpolated the Theopaschite clause (*"Who was crucified for us"*) into the Trisagion; Severus of Antioch (*Севи́ръ безгла́вныи*), termed "headless" as leader of the Acephali; his organizer Jacob Baradaeus (*І҆а́ковъ цанца́лъ* / Zanzalus), from whom the Jacobite Syrian Church derives its historical appellation; Cyrus of Phasis/Alexandria and Marcian; Sergius I and Pyrrhus, Patriarchs of Constantinople and proponents of Monothelitism; and Polychronius (*Полихро́нїй младооу́мныи ста́рецъ*), the elderly Monothelite monk condemned at the Sixth Ecumenical Council (Constantinople III, 680–681) for attempting to prove his doctrine through an unsuccessful resurrection of the dead.

[^169]: Fol. 47v. The Imprecatory Oath and Civil Penalties of Perjury (*А҆́ще ли съ лже́ю и҆ ле́стїю сѐ творю̀...*). The candidate binds his conscience under an inviolable self-imprecation (*anathema*) invoking canonical and Scriptural archetypes of divine retribution: the perpetual vagabondage and trembling of fratricidal Cain (Genesis 4:12–14, LXX) and the incurable clinging leprosy of Gehazi, servant of Elisha, struck down for simony and deceit (4 Kingdoms 5:27 / 2 Kings 5:27). The formula combines spiritual damnation (*ѿринове́нъ, и҆ про́клѧтъ*) with explicit submission to the capital and corporeal penalties of imperial Byzantine civil jurisprudence (*гра́дскїи зако́нъ* / the *Basilika* and *Ecloga*), which prescribed severe civic infamy, banishment, and confiscation for relapsed heretics and perjured converts.

[^170]: Fol. 48r. The Threefold General Anathema and the Term *ѻ҆бновлѧ́емый* (*Въсѣ̑мъ є҆рети́кѡ́мъ а҆наѳе́ма, По три́щи. И҆ приклони́тъ гла́вꙋ ѻ҆бновлѧ́емый*). Following the recitation of specific heresiarchs and errors, the candidate seals his renunciation by proclaiming anathema against all heretical teachings three times (*по три́щи*). The rubrics designate the candidate as *ѻ҆бновлѧ́емый* ("the one being renewed" / regenerated; Greek: ὁ ἀνανεούμενος), denoting his sacramental rehabilitation from schism into the living communion of the Church.

[^171]: Fol. 48r. Scriptural Topoi of Reconciliation: 1 Timothy 2:4 and John 10:16 (*Бг҃е сп҃сителю на́шь, хотѧ́й всѣ̑мъ чл҃кѡмъ сп҃тисѧ...*). The euchological prayer grounds the reconciliation of Oriental non-Chalcedonians upon two central Scriptural passages: St. Paul's pastoral declaration of universal salvific intent in 1 Timothy 2:4 (*"Who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth"*), and Christ's parable of the Good Shepherd in John 10:16 (*"And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring, and they shall hear My voice; and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd"*). The phrase *є҆два̀ възъноу́вша ѿ ле́сти* (variant for *въскло́ньшагосѧ*, Greek: μόλις ἀνανεύσαντα ἀπὸ τῆς πλάνης) captures the image of one who has barely raised his head or awakened from the slumber of deception.

[^172]: Fol. 48v. Post-Abjuration Chrismation and Sacramental Integration (*пома́зоуетъ є҆го̀ му́ромъ ꙗ҆́ко новопросвѣще́ннаго. То́жде нарица́нїе творѧ̀ на́дъ нимъ*). The rubric specifies that the priest anoints the reconciled convert with holy myron (*мѵ́ро*) in the exact manner of a newly baptized person (*ꙗ҆́ко новопросвѣще́ннаго*), employing the canonical sacramental seal (*то́жде нарица́нїе* / "The seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit. Amen"). This conforms to Canon 95 of the Council in Trullo (692), which prescribes that Monophysites and Armenians, having retained valid historical Trinitarian baptism, are received into Orthodox communion through holy Chrismation and the immediate partaking of the Holy Mysteries (*прича́стїю чⷭ҇тнаго тѣ́ла, и҆ кро́ве*).

[^173]: Fol. 49r. The Post-Chrismation Clothing, Seven-Day Octave Fast, and Eighth-Day Ablution (*И҆ та́ко ѻ҆дѣва́етъ и҆̀. И҆ пороучи́тъ є҆моу̀ се́дмь дн҃ии ма́са не ꙗ҆́сти...*). The newly chrismated convert is invested in clean Christian garments (*ѻ҆дѣва́етъ и҆̀*), symbolizing the white baptismal robe of justification (*хитѡ́нъ пра́вды*). He is placed under an ascetical discipline for the duration of the seven-day octave: abstaining from meat (*ма́са не ꙗ҆́сти*) and refraining from washing his face, thereby preventing any profanation of the holy chrism upon his brow, eyes, nostrils, lips, ears, breast, and hands. On the eighth day (*въ ѻ҆смы́и же де́нь*), he returns to the church for the solemn liturgical washing (*ѻ҆мыва́нїе*), completing his sacramental integration into the Orthodox Church.

[^174]: Fol. 49v. Part VII: The Rite for the Reception of Latins in the 1606 Striatyn Trebnyk (*ЧИ́НЪ КА́КО ПОДОБА́ЄТ ПРЇИМА́ТИ приходѧ́щихъ ѿ лати́нъ...*). Part VII witnesses the official liturgical rite of the Ruthenian Orthodox Church under the jurisdiction of the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople for receiving Roman Catholics into Orthodoxy following the Council of Brest (1596). The Balaban print strictly adheres to the decisions of the Council of Constantinople (1484), which repealed the Union of Florence and decreed that Latins are received through renunciation of errors, anointing with holy chrism (*myron*), and holy communion, rather than through re-baptism. This practice stood in contrast both to the late-Byzantine rigorism of the 13th–14th centuries and to the later 1620 Moscow Council of Patriarch Filaret Romanov, which mandated re-baptism of Latins until the Pan-Orthodox Synod of Moscow in 1667 formally restored reception by Chrismation.

[^175]: Fol. 49v. The Renunciation of Latin Sabbath-Fasting and "Peter the Stammerer" (*Ѡ҆рица́ешилисѧ вѣ́ры лати́ньскыѧ, и҆ сꙋбо́тства и҆́хъ, є҆́же Пе́тръ гоугни́выи въ ри́мѣ оу҆ста́вилъ є҆́стъ*). The abjuration singled out by the opening interrogation focuses on two traditional Byzantine grievances: (1) Latin fasting on Saturdays (*сꙋбо́тство* / Sabbath-fasting), prohibited by Apostolic Canon 64 and Trullan Canon 55; and (2) the polemical figure of "Peter the Stammerer" (*Пе́тръ гоугни́выи* / *Petr Gugnivyi*). In medieval East Slavic and Ruthenian polemical literature—most notably the popular 14th–16th century *Tale of Peter the Stammerer* (*Сказание о Петре Гугнивом*), frequently interpolated into the Slavonic *Kormchaia Kniga* (Nomokanon)—the historical divergence of the Latin Church was mythologized as having been instituted by an alleged Roman bishop or cleric named Peter the Stammerer, who was said to have corrupted Roman liturgical traditions after the severance of communion. Modern historical scholarship identifies this epithet as a polemical transposition and conflation of Peter the Fuller (*Petros Gnapheus*) or Peter Mongus (*Petros Moggos*, literally "the stammerer" or "hoarse-voiced") into Roman church history.

[^176]: Fol. 50r. Internal Folio Cross-Reference to the Reception Prayer (*Смотрѝ наза́дъ ѡ҆братѝ два̀ листы ѡ҆брѧ́щеши...*). The rubric instructs the priest to turn back two physical leaves to Fol. 48r (leaf p113), where the euchological prayer of reconciliation (*"O God our Savior, Who willest all men to be saved..."*) is printed in full. This cross-referencing practice illustrates the typographer's economy of space in the 1606 Balaban print, avoiding the duplicate typesetting of lengthy prayers common to both the reconciliation of Non-Chalcedonians and that of Western Christians.

[^177]: Fol. 50r. Pre-Chrismation Ablution with Holy Water (*И҆ по мл҃твѣ да́сть є҆мꙋ̀ во́дꙋ ст҃ще́ннꙋ. И҆ ѻ҆мы́етъ и҆̀ по лицоу̀ и҆ по роука́ма...*). Prior to anointing with holy chrism, the candidate's face and hands are washed with sanctified water (*во́да свѧще́ннаѧ* / *hagiasma*). This symbolic purification signifies the washing away of Latin ritual customs and heterodox communion, serving as an outward lustrative preparation before receiving the unction of holy myron (*му́ромъ сты́мъ ꙗ҆́ко новокрще́ннаго*) as an illuminated member of the Orthodox Church.

[^178]: Fol. 50v. The Sanctity of the Ablution Water and Prohibition against Desecration (*да̀ ѻ҆мы́етсѧ на чи́стѣ мѣ́стѣ, ꙗ҆́ко ненастоупи́тисѧ водѣ̀ то́й*). The rubric mandates that on the eighth day the post-chrismation ablution must take place in an untrodden, clean place (*на чи́стѣ мѣ́стѣ*) to ensure that the water containing dissolved holy chrism is not stepped on (*ненастоупи́тисѧ водѣ̀ то́й*). In canonical Orthodox pastoral practice, this ablution water was poured directly into the *thalassidion* (piscina / sacrarium) of the church altar or into a dry well or under the roots of a fruit-bearing tree, guarding the sanctified chrism from profanation.

[^179]: Fol. 50v. Psalm 22 (LXX 22 / MT 23) as the Mystagogical Octave Psalm (*ѱало́мъ, к҃в. Гдⷭ҇ь пасе́тъ мѧ̀...*). The recitation of Psalm 22 according to Septuagint versification (*"The Lord shepherds me, and nothing shall fail me"*, LXX Psalm 22 [MT Psalm 23]) forms an integral part of the early Byzantine post-baptismal octave mystagogy. Commented upon by St. Cyril of Jerusalem in his *Mystagogical Catecheses* (Catechesis IV), the psalm prophetically details the sacramental journey of the neophyte: the green pasture and water of rest (baptism), the oil anointing the head (chrismation), and the prepared table and cup of unmixed wine (the Holy Eucharist).

[^180]: Fol. 51r. The Eighth-Day Ablution Prayer (*[И҆́]же и҆збавле́нїе съгрѣше́нїемъ ра́ди ст҃го кр҃ще́нїа рабꙋ̀ твое́моу дарова́въ...*). This prayer adapts the ancient eighth-day euchology of post-baptismal ablution found in the Barberini Euchologion (gr. 336) and early Slavonic Trebnyks for use over a reconciled Latin convert. It celebrates the convert's remission of sins (*и҆збавле́нїе съгрѣше́нїемъ*), petitions for the illumination of his heart with the light of the divine countenance (Psalm 4:7 / 66:2), and prays for the preservation of the incorrupt baptismal robe (*нетлѣ́нїе ѻ҆дѣѧ́нїа*) and the intact seal of the Holy Spirit (*нероуши́ма дх҃овнаѧ печа́ть*).

[^181]: Fol. 51v. The Ritual Ablution Formula and Head-Bowing Prayer (*Кр҃ти́лсѧ є҆сѝ. Просвѣти́лсѧ є҆сѝ. Ѻ҆мы́лсѧ є҆сѝ. Ѻ҆с͠ти́лсѧ є҆сѝ...*). The priest performs the ritual ablution of the holy chrism using warm water and a sponge (*гоу́ба* / Greek: σπόγγος), wiping the loci of anointing while reciting the ancient quadruplicate baptismal declaration: "Thou art baptized. Thou art illumined. Thou art washed. Thou art sanctified..." (cf. 1 Corinthians 6:11: "but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God"). This is immediately followed by the liturgical greeting of peace and the silent inclination prayer (*мл҃тва та́йнѡ* / *εὐχὴ κеклиμένη*), which echoes Galatians 3:27 (*"For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ"*) and petitions for the convert's victory as an "unconquered champion" against the spiritual adversary.

[^182]: Fol. 52r. The Communion of the Reconciled Latin Penitent and Concluding Rites of Part VII (*и҆ причаща́етъ є҆го̀ ст҃ы́хъ та́инъ...*). The reception of Roman Catholics culminates in their immediate admission to the Holy Mysteries (*прича́стїе ст҃ы́хъ та́инъ*), following the ancient canonical principle articulated by Canon 95 of the Council in Trullo (692) and confirmed by the Council of Constantinople (1484). Having abjured Latin liturgical divergence, confessed the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed without the *Filioque*, and received the unction of holy chrism (*myron*), the penitent is admitted to full Eucharistic fellowship, followed by the concluding litany and dismissal (*ѿпоу́стъ*).

[^183]: Fol. 53r. Part VIII: The Office of Betrothal, the Royal Doors, and the Gold and Silver Rings on the Altar (*ПОСЛѢ́ДОВА́НЇЕ БЫВА́ЄМОЕ Ѡ҆ БРꙊЧЕ́НЇЮ*). In the 1606 Striatyn Trebnyk, Betrothal (*Обруче́нїе* / ἀρραβών) is preserved as a distinct liturgical office conducted immediately following the Divine Liturgy (*По Бж҃тве́нои литꙋргі́и*). The bridal pair stands outside the iconostasis before the Royal Doors (*предъ ст҃ы́ми двьрьмѝ*), the bridegroom on the right and the bride on the left. The two rings—one gold and one silver—are placed upon the right side of the holy altar table (*ст҃а́ѧ трапе́ꙁа*). The Ruthenian text specifies: *зла́тыи перше́ный, сре́брный ѹ҆кланѧ́ѧсѧ къ де́снымъ, зла́тыи же къ шꙋ́и̑мъ* ("the golden one first, [and the] silver [one]; the silver leaning toward the right, and the golden toward the left, near one another").
