In Byzantine and Ruthenian mystagogy (commented upon by St. Symeon of Thessalonica, *De Sacramentis* 273), the gold ring signifies the solar brilliance of Christ and the authority of the husband, while the silver ring signifies the lunar radiance of the Church and the spouse; their proximity on the altar sanctifies their impending exchange and marital bond.

[^184]: Fol. 53v. The Signing of the Bridal Pair, Lighted Tapers, Entrance, and Initial Blessing (*зна́менаетъ гла́вы новобра́чныхъ г҃. и҆ да́стъ и҆̀мъ свѣ́ща въжже́ны...*). The priest blesses the bridal pair by making the sign of the cross thrice over their heads and gives them lighted tapers, symbolizing the lamps of the wise virgins awaiting the Heavenly Bridegroom (Matthew 25:1–13) and the spiritual joy and purity of Christian union. The rubric directs him to lead them within the nave of the church (*вну́тръ въ цр҃ковь*) and cense cruciformly. The deacon petitions: "Bless, Master" (*Бл҃ви влⷣко*), and the priest initiates the rite with the euchological doxology: "Blessed is our God always, now and ever, and unto ages of ages" (*Бл҃ве́нъ Бг҃ъ на́шъ...*), followed immediately by the Great Litany (*Ми́ромъ Гдⷭ҇у помоли́мсѧ*).

[^185]: Fol. 54r. Special Petitions of the Betrothal Litany (*Ѡ҆ рабѣ́хъ Бж҃їихъ, и҆́мѧ ре́къ, и҆́же нн҃ѣ ѡ҆брꙋча́ющихсѧ дроу́гъ дроу́гꙋ...*). The Great Litany is enriched with specific euchological petitions for the betrothed couple, faithfully translating the Byzantine Greek Euchologion (*ὑπὲρ τῶν δούλων τοῦ Θεοῦ τῶν νῦν ἀρραβωνιζομένων ἀλλήλοις*): praying for their mutual salvation; for the granting of children for the succession of the human race (*ча́да къ воспрїѧ́тїе ро́да* / Greek: εἰς διαδοχὴν γένους); for the sending down upon them of perfect and peaceful love and divine assistance (*любвѝ съвръше́ннѣй ми́рнѣй, и҆ по́мощи*); and for their blessing in conjugal unity.

[^186]: Fol. 54v. The Petition for an Honorable Marriage and Undefiled Bed (*Ꙗ҆́ко да̀ Гдⷭ҇ь Бг҃ъ на́шъ да́рꙋетъ и҆̀мъ бра́къ че́стенъ, и҆ ло́же несквръ́но...*). The litany weaves the apostolic injunction of Hebrews 13:4 ("Marriage is honorable in all, and the bed undefiled") directly into the liturgical petition, praying that the Lord God grant them an honorable marriage and an undefiled bed, and that they may be preserved in blameless conduct (*непоро́чное пребыва́нїе*) and unwavering faith (*твръ́даѧ вѣ́ра*).

[^187]: Fol. 55r. The First Euchological Prayer of Betrothal: Isaac and Rebecca (*Бж҃е вѣ́чный, и҆́же раздѣле́ннаѧ събра́въ въ є҆ди́нство...*). This ancient euchological prayer (Greek: Ὁ Θεὸς ὁ αἰώνιος, ὁ τὰ διῃρημένα συναγαγὼν εἰς ἑνότητα) invokes the biblical archetype of Isaac and Rebecca (Genesis 24) as the historical pattern of divinely guided marital union and inheritance of the covenant promise (*наслѣ́дники тѣ́хъ свое́му ѡ҆бѣтова́нїю*). God is addressed as the One Who establishes an indissoluble bond of love (*сою́ꙁъ любвѐ положи́въ нераздрꙋши́мъ*), gathering together disparate persons into ontological conjugal unity.

[^188]: Fol. 55v. The Bridal Ecclesiology of the Church and the Bestowal of the Rings (*и҆́же ѿ ꙗ҆ꙁы́къ пре́ѡ҆броучи́въ цр҃ковь дв҃оу чи́стоую...*). The second prayer roots Christian betrothal in Pauline bridal ecclesiology (2 Corinthians 11:2: "For I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ"), confessing Christ as having pre-espoused the Church from among the Gentiles. The priest takes the rings from the altar table and bestows the gold ring first upon the bridegroom and then the silver ring upon the bride, pronouncing the sacramental declaration: *Ѡ҆броуча́етъ ра́бъ Бж҃їи...* ("The servant of God is betrothed unto the handmaid of God...").

[^189]: Fol. 56r. The Threefold Cross with the Rings, the Sponsor (*Kum*), and the Friend of the Bridegroom (*по́семъ и҆ꙁмѣнѧ́етъ пе́рстени новобра́чныхъ, кꙋ́мъ, и҆лѝ дрꙋ́гъ женихо́въ...*). The rubric specifies that the priest makes the sign of the cross thrice with the ring over the head of each candidate before placing it upon their right hands (*на де́сныхъ и҆́хъ пе́рстѣхъ*). The subsequent threefold exchange of rings is performed not by the priest, but by the sponsor (*коу́мъ* / *kum*) or the best man / friend of the bridegroom (*дрꙋ́гъ женихо́въ*, rendering the Greek παράνυμφος), reflecting the ancient customary participation of the wedding sponsor in sealing the covenant.

[^190]: Fol. 56v. Eliezer's Mission in Mesopotamia and the Water Pitcher Sign (*ходата́йствомъ водоно́са ѡ҆броучи́ти реве́коу ѿкры́въ...*). The lengthy final prayer of betrothal (Greek: Κύριε ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν, ὁ τῷ παιδὶ τοῦ πατριάρχου Ἀβραὰμ συμπορευθεὶς ἐν τῇ Μεσοποταμίᾳ) recalls the mission of Abraham's servant Eliezer to Haran in Mesopotamia (Genesis 24). Eliezer prayed for a divine sign at the well of water: that the maiden who offered to draw water from her pitcher (*водоно́съ* / ὑδρία) for him and his camels would be the bride appointed by God for Isaac. The prayer proclaims God as the Creator of male and female (Genesis 1:27, Matthew 19:4), establishing woman as a helper unto man (Genesis 2:18) and for the continuation of mankind (*прїѧ́тїе ро́да чл҃ча* / διαδοχὴν τοῦ γένους τῶν ἀνθρώπων).

[^191]: Fol. 57r. Biblical Typology of the Ring: Joseph, Daniel, Tamar, and the Prodigal Son (*пе́рстенѧ ра́ди да́стьсѧ вла́сть і҆ѡ́сифоу въ є҆гѵ́птѣ...*). This euchological prayer marshals a sequence of Old and New Testament precedents illustrating the signet ring (*пе́рстень* / δακτύλιος) as the divine token of authority, vindication, covenant fidelity, and paternal adoption: Pharaoh investing Joseph with his signet ring as viceroy of Egypt (Genesis 41:42); the sealing of the lions' den and Daniel's deliverance in Babylon (Daniel 6:17, Bel and the Dragon 14:11–14); Tamar's vindication before Judah by means of his signet ring, cord, and staff (Genesis 38:18, 25); and the father bestowing the signet ring upon the repentant prodigal son as the restoration of sonship (Luke 15:22). The prayer links these historical tokens to the cosmic covenant established by the right hand of God, which divided the Red Sea under Moses (Exodus 15:6) and founded the heavens by the Word of Truth (Psalm 32:6 LXX [MT 33:6]).

[^192]: Fol. 57v. The Cosmic Foundation and the Angelic Guide of the Espoused (*землѧ̀ ѡ҆сно́вана... и҆ а҆́гг҃лъ Гдⷭ҇нь да пре́йдетъ пре́д ними...*). Continuing the betrothal prayer (Greek: Ὁ Θεὸς ὁ αἰώνιος...), the euchology extends God's cosmic ordering—the establishment of the heavens and foundation of the earth (Psalm 103:5 LXX [MT 104:5])—unto the micro-cosmos of the Christian home. The priest petitions for the angel of the Lord to precede the couple as their guardian and companion throughout all the days of their earthly life, evoking the angel who guided Eliezer (Genesis 24:7) and Raphael who accompanied Tobias (Tobit 5:16–22).

[^193]: Fol. 57v. The Betrothal Exclamation and Insistent Litany (*Та́же є҆кте́нїа: Поми́лꙋй на́съ Бж҃е...*). Following the euchological doxology ("For Thou art He Who blesses and sanctifies all things... unto ages of ages"), the deacon intones the Insistent Litany (*Сугубая ектения* / ἐκτενὴς ἱκεσία). In the 1606 Striatyn imprint, the litany contains specific petitions for the ruling bishop and for the newly betrothed couple (*ѡ҆ рабѣ́хъ Бж҃їихъ... ѡ҆броуча́ющихсѧ дроу́гъ дроу́гоу*), culminating in the communal petition *реце́мъ всѝ* ("let us all say").

[^194]: Fol. 58r. Autonomous Betrothal Dismissal and Structural Independence of the Rite (*Та́же ѿпоу́стъ*). In early Byzantine and 16th–17th century Ruthenian liturgical practice, Betrothal (*Обруче́нїе*) frequently remained an autonomous liturgical office celebrated weeks or months prior to the solemn Crowning (*Вѣнча́нїе*), rather than immediately conflated with it as in standard modern practice. The rubric *Та́же ѿпоу́стъ* ("Then the dismissal") followed by an ornamental tailpiece confirms the completion of Betrothal as a self-contained liturgical unit.

[^195]: Fol. 58v. Part IX: The Order of Crowning, the Entrance into the Nave, and Psalm 127 (*ПѠСЛѢДОВА́НЇЕ ВѢНЧА́НЇЮ* / *А҆́щели же въсхо́щꙋтъ а҆́бїе вѣнча́тисѧ...*). Part IX opens with an elaborate Renaissance woodcut headpiece depicting the Mystery of Crowning celebrated under an architectural baldachin before the tetrapod. The transitional rubric specifies: *А҆́щели же въсхо́щꙋтъ а҆́бїе вѣнча́тисѧ...* ("And if they wish to be crowned immediately, they enter into the church with lighted tapers..."). The celebrant precedes them into the nave with the censer, chanting Psalm 127 LXX [MT 128], the ancient bridal processional psalm (*Блаже́ни всѝ боѧ́щїисѧ Гдⷭ҇а...* / "Blessed are all they that fear the Lord").

[^196]: Fol. 59r. The Concluding Verses of Psalm 127 and the Hierarchical Petition (*Ѡ҆ а҆рхїепⷭ҇пѣ наше[мъ]...*). Psalm 127 concludes with the eschatological and familial blessing of Zion: children as olive shoots, seeing children's children, and peace upon Israel (Psalm 127:3–6 LXX). Immediately upon the psalm's completion, the deacon initiates the Great Litany of Crowning (*Ми́ромъ Гдⷭ҇у помоли́мсѧ*). The petition for the hierarchy uses the title *Ѡ҆ а҆рхїепⷭ҇пѣ наше[мъ]* ("For our archbishop"), reflecting the Ruthenian provincial terminology for the Metropolitan of Kyiv and Galicia or the diocesan eparch.

[^197]: Fol. 59v. Special Euchological Petitions of the Crowning Litany (*Ѡ҆ рабѣ́хъ Бж҃їихъ... и҆́же нн҃ѣ съчетава́ющихсѧ дроу́гъ дроу́гоу къ бра́ка приѡбще́нїе...*). The Crowning litany incorporates distinctive euchological petitions: praying that the marriage be blessed after the model of Cana of Galilee (*ꙗ҆́коже въ ка́нѣ Галиле́йстѣ*); for chastity (*цѣломꙋ́дрїе* / σωφροσύνη); for the fruit of the womb (*пло́дъ чре́вный*); for joy in the sight of sons and daughters; and for the granting of fair offspring (*бл҃гоча́дїе* / εὐτεκνία) and blameless conduct of life (*незазо́рное пребыва́нїе*).

[^198]: Fol. 60r. The First Euchological Prayer of Crowning: Creation of Eve and the Primordial Blessing (*Бг҃е пречи́стыи, и҆ вьсѧ́коѧ тва́ри създа́телю...*). The solemn prayer of Crowning (Greek: Ὁ Θεὸς ὁ ἄχранτος, καὶ πάσης κτίσεως δημιουργός...) roots the sacrament in the primordial creation narrative of Genesis 1–2: God fashioning Eve from Adam's rib out of His love for mankind, imparting the primordial mandate to increase, multiply, and have dominion over the earth (Genesis 1:28), and establishing husband and wife as one flesh (*є҆ди́нъ оу҆́дъ* / ἓν μέλος).

[^199]: Fol. 60v. The Old and New Testament Patriarchal Chain of Marriage (*и҆ и҆́хже Бг҃ъ съпрѧжѐ чл҃къ да не раꙁлоуча́етъ...*). The prayer recites the foundational covenantal marriages of salvation history: Adam and Eve (Genesis 2:24, Matthew 19:6); Abraham and Sarah's miraculous conception in old age (Genesis 17:4–5, 18:10–14); Isaac and Rebecca (Genesis 24); Jacob and Rachel with the twelve patriarchs (Genesis 29–35); Joseph and Aseneth with their sons Ephraim and Manasseh (Genesis 41:45–52); Zechariah and Elizabeth giving birth to St. John the Baptist (Luke 1); culminating in the rod of Jesse blossoming into the Theotokos (Isaiah 11:1).

[^200]: Fol. 61r. The Christological Transfiguration of Marriage at Cana (*прише́дъ въ ка́ноу Галиле́йскоую, и҆ сꙋ́щїи та́мо бра́къ бл҃вивъ...*). Christian matrimony finds its supreme sanction and sanctification in Christ's presence and first miracle at the wedding of Cana of Galilee (John 2:1–11). The prayer confesses that by His presence Christ revealed lawful wedlock (*зако́нное сꙋпрꙋ́жество*) and childbearing (*чадотворе́нїе*) to be His holy will, petitioning for His invisible episcopal oversight (*неви́димымъ твои́мъ прѣдстоѧ́тельствомъ*) to bless the bridal pair.

[^201]: Fol. 61v. Patriarchal Blessings of Dew, Fatness, and Generous Almsgiving (*ѿ росы̀ нб҃ныѧ свы́ше, и҆ ѿ тꙋ́ка земна́го...*). The conclusion of the first Crowning prayer adopts the patriarchal blessing of Isaac upon Jacob: "God give thee of the dew of heaven, and the fatness of the earth, and plenty of corn and wine" (Genesis 27:28). This abundance of wheat, wine, and oil (*пшени́ца, вина̀ и҆ є҆ле́а*) is sought not for self-indulgence, but so the newlyweds may exercise generous Christian charity and almsgiving (*да преподаю́тъ и҆ тре́боующимъ*), securing both earthly longevity and an unfading crown of celestial glory.

[^202]: Fol. 62r. Christ as the Priest and Lawgiver of Mystical Marriage (*та́йнаго и҆ прⷭ҇чтаго бра́ка сщ҃еннодѣ́йственникъ...*). Explaining the euchological title `ἱερουργός` / `сщ҃еннодѣ́йственникъ` applied to God/Christ in this second prayer of Crowning (Greek: Εὐλογητὸς εἶ, Κύριε ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν, ὁ τοῦ μυστικοῦ καὶ ἀχράντου γάμου ἱερουργὸς...), which defines God not merely as the creator of physical humanity, but as the active liturgical celebrant and consecrator of holy matrimony, establishing its sacramental character and guarding its incorruptibility against worldly decay.

[^203]: Fol. 62r. Primordial Creation and the Institution of Marriage (Genesis 2:18, 23). The euchology quotes the divine counsel prior to the creation of Eve: "It is not good for man to be alone; let us make him a helper fit for him" (Genesis 2:18), followed by Adam's ecstatic prophetic recognition of woman as bone of his bones and flesh of his flesh upon awakening from his deep sleep (Genesis 2:23).

[^204]: Fol. 62v. Scriptural Genesis and Synoptic Conflation (*сего̀ ра́ди ѡ҆ста́витъ чл҃къ ѿца̀ своего̀...*). The prayer combines the primordial covenantal formula of Genesis 2:24 ("Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife, and they shall be one flesh") with Christ's solemn dominical ratifying gloss in Matthew 19:6 and Mark 10:9: "What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder."

[^205]: Fol. 63r. The Typology of Divine Preservation (*съхранѝ и҆̀хъ... ꙗ҆́коже съхрани́лъ є҆сѝ...*). A liturgical litany of Old Testament salvific deliverances petitioned on behalf of the spouses: Noah preserved from the universal cataclysm within the ark (Genesis 7–8); Jonah preserved alive within the belly of the sea-monster (Jonah 2); and the Three Holy Youths (Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael) preserved unburnt in the fiery furnace of Babylon by the angel who made the midst of the furnace as it were a moist whistling wind (Daniel 3:49–50 LXX).

[^206]: Fol. 63v. The Joy of St. Helen and the Crowning of the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste (*бл҃же́наѧ є҆ле́на... ст҃ы́ѧ ти четыридесѧ́тъ мч҃никы...*). The euchology links matrimonial joy to the exalted spiritual joy of St. Helen upon discovering the True and Life-Giving Cross in Jerusalem (c. 326 AD), while the petition remembering the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste (d. 320 AD)—who received forty celestial crowns descending from heaven as they froze in the icy lake—explicitly establishes the bridal crowns as crowns of martyrdom, bearing witness to selfless ascetic sacrifice and victory over worldly passions.

[^207]: Fol. 63v. The Parental Blessing Establishing the Home (*занѐ мл҃твы роди́телей оу҆твръжа́ютъ ѡ҆снова́нїа дѡмо́въ...*). Quoting the canonical wisdom of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 3:9: "The blessing of the father establishes the houses of children; but the curse of the mother roots out foundations." The prayer explicitly extends the circle of euchological remembrance to the parents and sponsors assembled for the wedding feast.

[^208]: Fol. 64r. Vegetative Imagery of Blessing and Procreation (*ке́дры лива́нскыѧ, ꙗ҆́коже ло́зоу бл҃говѣ́твеноу...*). Integrating Old Testament poetic imagery of vital flourishing from Psalm 91:13 LXX [MT 92:12] ("the righteous shall flourish like a palm tree; he shall grow like a cedar of Lebanon") and Psalm 127:3 LXX [MT 128:3] ("thy wife shall be as a fruitful vine... thy children like olive plants round about thy table"), coupled with the apostolic benediction of 2 Corinthians 9:8 and the celestial luminescence of Philippians 2:15 ("among whom ye shine as lights in the world").

[^209]: Fol. 64v. The Third Crowning Prayer: Divine Imposition and Climax of Matrimonial Consecration (*Сщ҃е́нникъ па́ки мл҃твꙋ сїю̀ гл҃етъ велегла́сно: Бж҃е ст҃ы́и...*). This third euchological prayer (Greek: Ὁ Θεὸς ὁ ἅγιος, ὁ πλάσας ἐκ τοῦ χοὸς τὸν ἄνθρωπον...) constitutes the direct consecratory climax of the Crowning office. The rubric prescribes that the celebrant recite it *велегла́сно* ("with a loud voice" / ἐκφώνως), entreating God to reach down His invisible right hand from His holy habitation to yoke the bridegroom and bride together in mutual chastity and love prior to the imposition of crowns.

[^210]: Fol. 65r. The Rite of Imposition of Crowns (*прїе́мъ сщ҃е́нникъ вѣнца̀, вѣнча́етъ ѡ҆жени́вшагосѧ...*). The ritual imposition of wreaths or metallic crowns upon the heads of the couple constitutes the central sacramental act of Byzantine matrimony, signifying royal dignity as heads of a domestic church, mutual dominion over passions, and the crown of martyrdom.

[^211]: Fol. 65r. The Striatyn Crowning Formula: Recensional Witness (*Вѣнча́етсѧ ра́бъ Бж҃їи [и҆́мѧ], въ и҆́мѧ ѿц҃а...*). The 1606 Striatyn imprint preserves the concise archaic formula *Вѣнча́етсѧ ра́бъ Бж҃їи [и҆́мѧ], въ и҆́мѧ ѿц҃а и҆ сн҃а и҆ ст҃го дх҃а* without the explicit dative complement *рабѣ̀ Бж҃їей [и҆́мѧ]* found in standard later editions, reflecting an archaic early Byzantine euchological witness documented in Sinait. Gr. 959 and early South Slavic and Ruthenian imprints.

[^212]: Fol. 65r. The Triple Nuptial Blessing: Inked Recensional Witness (*Гдⷭ҇и Бж҃е на́шъ сла́вою и҆ чⷭ҇тїю вѣнча́лъ є҆сѝ и҆́хъ*). The 1606 text physically prints the past/perfect indicative form: *вѣнча́лъ є҆сѝ и҆́хъ* ("hast Thou crowned them"), directly citing the indicative wording of Psalm 8:6 LXX [MT 8:5] (*δόξῃ καὶ τιμῇ ἐστεφάνωσας αὐτόν* / *сла́вою и҆ че́стїю вѣнча́лъ є҆сѝ є҆го̀*), in contrast to the later harmonized precative imperative *вѣнча́й ѧ҆̀* ("crown them").

[^213]: Fol. 65r. The Nuptial Prokeimenon (Psalm 20:4 LXX [MT 21:3]). Tone 8: "Thou hast set upon their heads crowns of precious stones."

[^214]: Fol. 65v. The Prokeimenon Half-Verse (Psalm 20:5 LXX [MT 21:4]). "They asked life of Thee, and Thou gavest it them: length of days unto ages of ages." Note the grammatical dual verbal form in Church Slavonic: *проси́ста* ("they two asked"), precisely denoting the bridal pair.

[^215]: Fol. 65v. The Prokeimenon Verse (Psalm 20:2 LXX [MT 21:1]). "O Lord, in Thy strength the king shall be glad, and in Thy salvation how greatly shall he rejoice."

[^216]: Fol. 65v. The Nuptial Epistle Lection (Ephesians 5:20–33). Pericope 230: The foundational Pauline text setting forth the sacramental mystery of Christian marriage as the earthly mirror and icon of Christ's sacrificial love for His Bride, the Church.

[^217]: Fol. 66r. The Washing of Water by the Word (Ephesians 5:26). Alluding to baptismal rebirth (*τῷ λουτρῷ τοῦ ὕδατος ἐν ῥήмаτι* / *ба́нею водно́ю гл҃омъ*), through which the Church is purified and sanctified to become the unblemished Bride of Christ.

[^218]: Fol. 66v. The Conjugal Epilogue (Ephesians 5:33). Concluding the apostolic instruction with the call to mutual sacrificial love and reverence (*да бои́тсѧ* / *ἵνα φοβῆται*), understood not as servile terror, but as holy and affectionate awe within the hierarchy of love.

[^219]: Fol. 66v. The Nuptial Alleluia Tone 5. In Ruthenian chant tradition, the nuptial Alleluia is sung in Tone 5 with verses selected from Psalm 11 LXX.

[^220]: Fol. 66v. Nuptial Alleluia Verse (Psalm 11:8 LXX [MT 12:7]). "Thou, O Lord, shalt keep us, and shalt preserve us, from this generation, and forever."

[^221]: Fol. 66v. The Nuptial Gospel Lection (John 2:1–11). Pericope 6: The account of the Marriage at Cana of Galilee, where Jesus performed His first miracle at the request of His mother, changing water into wine and manifesting His glory.

[^222]: Fol. 67r. The Six Stone Waterpots and Nuptial Transformation (John 2:6–10). Explaining the euchological and typological significance of the six stone waterpots (*водоно́съ ка́менныхъ ше́сть*) in the Johannine wedding pericope (John 2:1–11, Pericope 6). In patristic and liturgical theology (e.g., St. John Chrysostom, *Homily 21 on John*, and St. Cyril of Alexandria), the waterpots of Jewish purification signify the old covenant of the Law and the Prophets, which Christ elevates and transforms by the New Covenant of grace into the rich nuptial wine of the Kingdom, prefiguring the Eucharistic communion of the Church and the spiritual sanctification of matrimonial union.

[^223]: Fol. 67v. The Johannine Conclusion and Manifestation of Glory (John 2:11). The conclusion of the nuptial Gospel pericope, noting the manifestation of Christ's divine glory (*и҆ ꙗ҆вѝ сла́воу свою̀*) and the awakening of apostolic faith at the wedding feast of Cana, which Byzantine euchologies identify as the sanctifying archetype for all Christian marriages.

[^224]: Fol. 67v. The Nuptial Augmented Litany (*Є҆ктенїа̀ согꙋ́баѧ*). The 1606 Striatyn text prints the petitions of the Augmented Litany in compressed epigraphic form, supplying the incipits of the opening petitions (*Ѿ всеѧ̀ дꙋша̀...*, *Гдⷭ҇и вседръжи́телю...*, *Поми́лоуй на́съ Бж҃е...*) followed by the proper nuptial petition remembering the newly-crowned spouses by name. In accordance with Rule 16, these incipits are preserved as printed without silent unwritten expansion.

[^225]: Fol. 67v. Sacerdotal Memento of the Spouses (*Е҆ще мо́лимсѧ ѡ҆ рабѣ́хъ Бж҃їй [и҆мк]...*). The rubric specifies that the deacon or priest explicitly commemorates the bridegroom and bride by name (*ре́къ: И҆ помина́етъ и҆́хже хо́щетъ*), praying for their health, preservation, and salvation in their newly consecrated estate.

[^226]: Fol. 68r. Sacerdotal Prayer After the Nuptial Gospel (*Гдⷭ҇и Бж҃е на́шъ, и҆́же сп҃си́телнымъ свои́мъ смотре́нїемъ...*). Greek: *Κύριε ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν, ὁ ἐν τῇ σωτηριώδει σου οἰκονομίᾳ καταξιώσας ἐν Κανᾷ τῆς Γαλιλαίας τίμιον ἀναδεῖξαι τὸν γάμον...* This classic post-Gospel prayer of the Byzantine Crowning rite beseeches Christ to manifest His presence once again as at Cana, preserving the marital bed undefiled (*небла́знено и҆́хъ ло́же съблюдѝ*), granting mutual concordance (*въ ми́рѣ и҆ съединенїи*), and bringing the couple unto ripe old age (*къ ста́рости масти́тѣ сконча́тисѧ*) in fulfillment of the divine commandments.

[^227]: Fol. 68v. The Litany of Supplication (*Проси́тельнаѧ є҆ктенїа̀* / *Aitēseis*). Printed in the Striatyn Trebnyk with incipits for each petition (*Застоупѝ сп҃сѝ...*, *Днѐ въсего̀ съвръше́нна...*, *А҆́гг҃ла ми́рна...*, *Млⷭ҇ть и҆ ѡ҆ставле́нїе...*, *Дѡ́бры и҆ поле́зны...*, *Про́чее лѣ́тъ...*, *Хрⷭ҇тїа́нскыѧ кончи́ны...*, *Съєдине́нїе вѣ́ры...*). In historical liturgical practice, this litany precedes the Lord's Prayer, mirroring the structure of the Divine Liturgy and highlighting matrimony as a sanctified ecclesial entrance into divine communion.

[^228]: Fol. 68v. The Introductory Embolism to the Lord's Prayer (*И҆ сподо́би ны, влⷣко, съ дръзнове́нїемъ...*). Sacerdotal exclamation introducing the recitation of the Dominical Prayer (Greek: *Καὶ καταξίωσον ἡμᾶς, Δέσποτα, μετὰ παῤῥησίας, ἀκατακρίτως τολμᾶν ἐπικαλεῖσθαι σὲ τὸν ἐπουράνιον Θεὸν Πατέρα, καὶ λέγειν*), emphasizing the filial boldness (*παῤῥησία* / *дръзнове́нїе*) granted to believers through adoption in Christ.

[^229]: Fol. 68v. The Dominical Prayer (*Ѿче на́шъ*). In the ancient Byzantine nuptial ordo, the chanting of the Lord's Prayer by the assembled congregation originally preceded the reception of Holy Communion by the newly married couple from the Pre-Sanctified Gifts, a rite later transformed into the drinking of the Common Cup.

[^230]: Fol. 69r. The Rite of the Common Cup (*Ѻ҆́бщаѧ ча́ша* / *Κοινὸν ποτήριον*). The presentation and blessing of the common cup of wine constitutes a surviving historical vestige and surrogate of the ancient reception of Holy Communion at the nuptial Divine Liturgy. In late Byzantine and Ruthenian practice, unconsecrated wine blessed with this sacerdotal prayer is shared mutually by the bridegroom and bride as a symbol of shared life, common sorrow, and unified joy.

[^231]: Fol. 69r. Prayer of Blessing Over the Common Cup (*Бж҃е, и҆́же всѧ̀ сътвори́выи крѣ́постїю свое́ю...*). Greek: *Ὁ Θεός, ὁ πάντα ποιήσας τῇ ἰσχύϊ σου, καὶ στερεώσας τὴν οἰκουμένην, καὶ κοσμήσας τὸν στέφανον πάντων τῶν ὑπὸ σοῦ γεноμένων...* The euchological text recalls God's creative cosmic fashioning and petitions a spiritual blessing (*бл҃гослове́нїемъ дх҃овнымъ*) upon the cup of wine presented to the spouses.

[^232]: Fol. 69v. The Nuptial Dance of Isaiah (*Хѡжде́нїе ѡ҆́кръстъ а҆нало́ѧ*). The circular procession around the analogion or tetrapod three times represents eternity, unbroken marital fidelity, and liturgical rejoicing. The rubric specifies that the best man or sponsor (*дроу́гоу женихо́воу*) holds the crowns over the heads of the bridegroom and bride as they are led by the celebrant.

[^233]: Fol. 69v. The First Nuptial Troparion: "O Isaiah, Dance" (*І҆са́їа ликоу́и* / *Ἡσαΐα χόρευε*). Tone 5: Citing the messianic prophecy of Isaiah 7:14 and Zechariah 6:12 (*въсто́къ и҆́мѧ є҆моу́* / *Ἀνατολὴ ὄνομα αὐτῷ*), this hymn is chanted identically at holy ordinations, monastic tonsures, and weddings, linking marital union to the incarnation of Christ and celebrating the virgin birth as the fountain of all Christian sanctity.

[^234]: Fol. 69v. The Second Nuptial Troparion: "O Holy Martyrs" (*Ст҃їи мч҃нци* / *Ἅγιοι μάρτυρες*). Tone 7: Commemorating the martyrs who received heavenly crowns (*и҆ вѣнча́вшеисѧ*), this hymn directly interprets the wedding crowns as emblems of martyric self-denial and patient suffering in the domestic church.

[^235]: Fol. 70r. The Third Nuptial Troparion: "Glory to Thee, O Christ God" (*Сла́ва тебѣ̀ Хрⷭ҇ѐ Бж҃е* / *Δόξα σοι, Χριστὲ ὁ Θεός*). Concluding the analogion procession with apostolic praise and confession of the Holy Trinity, identical to the dismissal troparion at priestly ordination.

[^236]: Fol. 70r. The Rite of Deposition of Crowns (*С̾ѧ́тїе вѣнце́въ*). The ceremonial removal of the crowns from the bridegroom and bride, accompanied by personalized patriarchal blessings evoking the righteous couples of the Old Covenant.

[^237]: Fol. 70r. Benediction Over the Bridegroom (*Възвели́ченъ бꙋ́ди, женишѐ, ꙗ҆́ко же А҆враа́мъ...*). Invoking the three great Patriarchs of Israel: Abraham, known for magnified faith and hospitality (Genesis 12:2, 17:5); Isaac, known for divine blessing and peaceful submission (Genesis 26:12); and Jacob, known for abundant fruitfulness and endurance (Genesis 28:14, 30:43).

[^238]: Fol. 70r. Benediction Over the Bride (*И҆ ты̀, невѣ́сто, възвели́чена бꙋ́ди, ꙗ҆́ко же Са́рра...*). Invoking the righteous Matriarchs: Sarah, magnified as mother of nations (Genesis 17:15–16; 1 Peter 3:6); Rebecca, renowned for bridal joy and beauty (Genesis 24); and Rachel, celebrated for abundant motherhood and love (Genesis 29–30; Jeremiah 31:15; Ruth 4:11). The Slavonic witness prints *Ра́хи[ль]* abbreviated with titlo as *Рах̑и,*.

[^239]: Fol. 70v. Prayer at the Deposition of Crowns (*Гдⷭ҇и Бж҃е на́шъ, прише́дыи въ Ка́ноу Галиле́йскоую...*). Greek: *Κύριε ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν, ὁ παραγενόμενος ἐν Κανᾷ τῆς Γαλιλαίας, καὶ τὸν ἐκεῖσε γάμον εὐλογήσας...* Beseeching God to receive the bridal crowns into His celestial kingdom (*въспрїимѝ вѣнца̀ и҆́хъ въ црⷭ҇твїе твоѐ*), signifying that the earthly dignity and ascetic struggle of Christian marriage find their ultimate fulfillment in the everlasting Kingdom of God. The blessing of "comings-in and goings-out" (*въхѡ́ды и҆ и҆схѡ́ды*) cites Psalm 120:8 LXX [MT 121:8].

[^240]: Fol. 71r. Sacerdotal Prayer of Head-Bowing and Solemn Trinitarian Blessing (*Ѿц҃ъ и҆ сн҃ъ и҆ дх҃ъ ст҃ыи...*). Greek: *Ὁ Πατὴρ, καὶ ὁ Υἱὸς, καὶ τὸ Ἅγιον Пνεῦμα, ἡ παναγία καὶ ὁμοούσιος καὶ ζωаρχικὴ Тριάς...* This exalted prayer of benediction invokes the Holy Trinity to bestow upon the spouses longevity (*длъгожи́тїе*), fair children (*бл҃гоча́дъство* / *εὐτεκνία*), spiritual advancement (*преспѣва́нїе животоу̀ и҆ вѣ́рѣ*), abundance of earthly goods, and eternal salvation.

[^241]: Fol. 71r. Concluding Congratulatory Rubric and Complete Dismissal (*Съвръше́нный ѿпоу́стъ*). The rubric prescribes mutual fraternal congratulations (*здравствоу́ютъ и҆́хъ*) and the ritual bridal kiss (*цѣлоу́етъ дроу́гъ дроу́га*) prior to the solemn dismissal (*ἀπόлυσις*) pronounced by the celebrant.

[^242]: Fol. 71v. Nuptial Dismissal Patrons (*Ст҃ы́хъ Бг҃овѣнча́нныхъ цр҃еи... ст҃го великомч҃ника Проко́пїа...*). The proper nuptial dismissal commemorates: (1) St. Constantine and St. Helen, the first Christian sovereigns crowned by God (*Θеоστεφεῖς* / *Бг҃овѣнча́ннїи*); and (2) the Great-Martyr Procopius (d. 303 AD), who according to ancient tradition encouraged twelve Christian women to endure martyrdom by comparing their suffering to glorious bridal adornment, establishing him as a patron of Christian marriage.

[^243]: Fol. 71v. The Office of the Dissolution of Crowns on the Eighth Day (*Мл҃тва на раздрѣше́нїе вѣнце́въ, въ ѡ́смыи дн҃ь*). Greek: *Εὐχὴ ἐπὶ ἀπολύσει στεφάνων εἰς τὴν ὀγδόην ἡμέραν*. In ancient Byzantine usage, the bridegroom and bride wore their wedding crowns for seven days following the nuptial mystery, returning to the church on the eighth day for a solemn rite of uncrowning and prayer before returning to daily secular life. While in later practice the crowns were removed at the end of the Crowning service, the prayer on the eighth day was retained in the euchologies. The opening words of the prayer evoke Psalm 64:12 LXX [MT 65:11] ("Thou shalt bless the crown of the year of Thy goodness").

[^244]: Fol. 72r. The Conclusion of the Prayer of the Dissolution of Crowns and the Prayer of Head-Bowing (*Съгла́снѣ прише́дше рабѝ твоѝ Гдⷭ҇и...* / *Εἰς συμφωνίαν ἐλθόντες...*). Explaining the Greek phrase *τὰ ἐν αὐτῷ σύμβολα συστείλαντες* rendered into Church Slavonic as *съпрѧта́вше ꙗ҆́же въ не́мъ знаме́нїа* ("having folded away / stowed the tokens that were therein"). In Byzantine and Ruthenian euchological practice, this refers to the formal ceremonial deposition and stowing of the bridal crowns, the common cup, and the nuptial ribbons, marking the liturgical termination of the marriage celebrations and the return of the couple to ordinary domestic life under divine protection.

[^245]: Fol. 72v. Patriarch St. Nicephorus the Confessor and Byzantine Canonical Discipline Concerning Digamy (*Гла́вы Ники́фора Патрїа́рха... ѡ двобра́чныхъ*). St. Nicephorus I, Patriarch of Constantinople (806–815, d. 828), championed icon veneration and authored authoritative canonical rulings (*κανόνες* / *главы*). In Byzantine sacramental theology, a first marriage uniquely icons the eternal, indissoluble mystery of Christ and the Church (Ephesians 5:32). Subsequent marriages (digamy and trigamy), while tolerated by pastoral condescension (*oikonomia*) to avert greater moral lapse (1 Corinthians 7:9), were regarded as concessions to human frailty, traditionally accompanied by penitential excommunication (*epitimia*) rather than festive nuptial crowning.

[^246]: Fol. 72v. Canonical Periods of Abstention for Second and Third Marriages. Nicephorus's rule prescribes a two-year abstention from Holy Communion for digamists (*двоже́нецъ*) and three years for trigamists (*триже́нецъ*), drawing upon the earlier penitential canons of St. Basil the Great (Canons 4 and 50) and the Council of Neocaesarea (Canon 3). In subsequent Byzantine and Slavic practice, these penitential timeframes were subject to the discretion and mitigation of the spiritual father.

[^247]: Fol. 72v. The Canonical Rescripts of Metropolitan Nicetas of Heraclea (*Ѡ ѿвѣща́нїи бл҃жнаго Ники́ты митрополи́та И҆раклїи́скаго...*). Nicetas, Metropolitan of Heraclea (late 11th century), authored celebrated canonical responsa to queries posed by Bishop Constantine. Here he distinguishes between strict canonical rigor (*ἀκρίβεια* / *ѡпа́сство*)—which strictly forbade the crowning of second unions—and the living customary practice of the Great Church of Constantinople (*вели́кыѧ цр҃кве ѡ҆бы́чай*), which permitted the crowning of digamists while maintaining the canonical penance regarding Eucharistic communion.

[^248]: Fol. 73r. The Council of Neocaesarea (c. 314–319 AD), Canon 7. Canon 7 of Neocaesarea explicitly forbids a presbyter from dining at the wedding banquet of digamists (*вече́рѧти съ ни́ми не оу҆законоположи́ша*): "A presbyter ought not to be present at the marriage feast of those who marry a second time; for, seeing that the digamist is in need of penance, what presbyter can he be who, by his presence at the feast, gives his sanction to the marriage?" The inclusion of this canon in the Balaban Trebnyk underscores the dual theological tension preserved in the Kyivan-Ruthenian recension between canonical discipline and pastoral mercy.

[^249]: Fol. 73v. The Order for a Second Marriage (*Послѣ́дованїе на двобра́чныѧ* / *Ἀκολουθία εἰς δίγαμον*). Unlike the rite of primary Crowning (Part IX), which begins with the solemn Eucharistic doxology (*"Blessed is the Kingdom..."*), the Order for Digamists opens with the simple sacerdotal blessing (*"Blessed is our God..."*) followed by the Trisagion and penitential prayers, reflecting the theological understanding of digamy as an accommodation to weakness rather than an unrepeatable sacrament of the mystical marriage of Christ and the Church.

[^250]: Fol. 73v. Introductory Trisagion and Troparion of the Day. The rubric prescribes the complete Ordinary Beginning (*Начало обычное*): the Trisagion prayers through the Lord's Prayer (*Our Father*), concluded by the Troparion of the current liturgical day or patron saint of the church, before initiating the litany.

[^251]: Fol. 73v. The Nuptial Litany for Digamists. The petitions are abbreviated to the essential cosmic and pastoral supplications, concluding with a petition specifically tailored to the second union: praying for God's divine protection (*по Бз҃ѣ покро́вѣ*) and peaceful cohabitation (*съжи́тельства и҆́хъ*).

[^252]: Fol. 74r. The Betrothal Prayer for Digamists (*Бж҃е вѣ́чный, и҆́же растоѧ́щаѧ събра́въ...*). Greek: *Ὁ Θεὸς ὁ αἰώνιος, ὁ τὰ διῃρημένα συναγαγὼν εἰς ἑνότητα...* The first prayer of betrothal from the primary marriage rite (cf. Part VIII) is here incorporated into the digamy sequence, imploring God to grant unity and the blessing bestowed of old upon Isaac and Rebecca (Genesis 24).

[^253]: Fol. 74v. Prayer of Head-Bowing at Betrothal (*Гдⷭ҇и Бг҃ъ на́шъ, и҆́же ѿ ꙗ҆зы́къ предъѡброучи́въ цр҃ковь...*). Greek: *Κύριε ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν, ὁ τὴν ἐξ ἐθνῶν προμνηστευσάμενος Ἐκκλησίαν παρθένον ἁγνήν...* A typology of Christ betrothing the Church from among the Gentiles, praying for humility (*въ смире́нїи*) and spiritual concord (*въ съєдине́нїи*) between the spouses.

[^254]: Fol. 74v. Rite of the Nuptial Rings for Digamists (*Прїе́мъ сщ҃енникъ пръ́стени...*). The rubric refers back to the Betrothal rite (cf. Part VIII, fol. 61v–62r), where the priest takes the rings, signs the spouses' foreheads thrice with them, places them on their right hands, and the friend of the bridegroom (*женихо́въ дроу́гъ* / *paranymphos*) exchanges them thrice.

[^255]: Fol. 75r. The First Solemn Penitential Prayer for Digamists (*Влⷣко Гдⷭ҇и Бж҃е на́шъ, и҆́же въсѣ́хъ щадѧ̀...*). Greek: *Δέσποτα Κύριε ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν, ὁ πάντων φειδόμενος...* This prayer embodies the distinct theology of the second-marriage rite, framing the union within an earnest plea for divine mercy and remission of sins (*проще́нїе съгрѣше́нїѡмъ*). It invokes Old and New Testament archetypes of divine forgiveness: Rahab the harlot (Joshua 2; Hebrews 11:31) and the Publican (Luke 18:13–14). The prayer also incorporates the penitential Psalter versicles: *"Remember not the sins of my youth, nor of mine ignorance"* (Psalm 24:7 LXX [MT 25:7]) and *"If Thou shouldst mark iniquities, O Lord, O Lord, who shall stand?"* (Psalm 129:3 LXX [MT 130:3]).

[^256]: Fol. 75v. The Triple Archetype of Evangelical Repentance in the Nuptial Rite. Citing three classic New Testament exemplars of saving repentance: the Publican's humility and justification (Luke 18:13–14), the sinful woman washing Christ's feet with her tears (Luke 7:37–48), and the Good Thief's dying confession on the cross (Luke 23:40–43). The prayer concludes with a Trinitarian doxology confessing God as the fashioner and ruler of the cosmos (*строи́тель всѧ́ческихъ* / *ὁ οἰκονόμος τῶν ἁπάντων*).

[^257]: Fol. 76r. Sacerdotal Prayer of Head-Bowing and the Pauline Theology of Second Marriage (*Гдⷭ҇и І҆и҃се Хрⷭ҇тѐ Сло́ве Бж҃їи...*). Greek: *Κύριε Ἰησοῦ Χριστέ, ὁ Λόγος τοῦ Θεοῦ...* This prayer synthesizes Christ's redemptive work upon the Cross—tearing up the handwriting of our sins (Colossians 2:14)—with the pastoral reality of human frailty. Quoting the Gospel parable of the laborers who could not endure "the burden and heat of the day" (Matthew 20:12) and St. Paul's pastoral counsel to the Corinthians ("It is better to marry in the Lord than to burn," 1 Corinthians 7:9, 39), the prayer justifies the second marriage as a therapeutic concession (*oikonomia*) granted to prevent spiritual ruin.

[^258]: Fol. 76v. Christ Taking Infirmities Upon His Shoulders and Universal Sinfulness. Evoking Isaiah 53:4 ("He hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows") and Luke 15:5 (the Good Shepherd placing the lost sheep upon His shoulders), and citing the Patristic aphorism derived from Job 14:4–5 LXX ("For none is clean from stain, even if his life on earth be but of one day"). The prayer confesses Christ as the sole sinless One who clothed Himself in human flesh without sin, and exalts Him as "the God of the penitent" (*Бг҃ъ ка́ющихсѧ*).

[^259]: Fol. 76v. Internal Cross-Reference to the Crowning Prayer (see fol. 66, physical leaf p149). The rubric directs the priest to read the classic third prayer of Crowning (*Бж҃е ст҃ы́и, и҆́же созда́вый ѿ пе́рсти чл҃ка...* / *Ὁ Θεὸς ὁ ἅγιος, ὁ πλάσας ἐκ χοὸς τὸν ἄνθρωπον...*), which appears earlier in the codex on fol. 66r (physical leaf p149), immediately preceding the Prokimenon and the reading of the Epistle.

[^260]: Fol. 77r. The Crowning of Digamists and Alignment with the Solemn Nuptial Office. Although strict canonical tradition (St. Nicephorus Canon 2; Council of Neocaesarea Canon 7) discouraged or barred nuptial crowning for second marriages, the pastoral practice of the Kyivan-Ruthenian Church, following the custom of the Great Church of Constantinople as expounded by Nicetas of Heraclea (cf. fol. 72v–73r), incorporates the sacramental crowning formula: *"The servant of God... is crowned in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit"* and the triple blessing *"O Lord our God, with glory and honor hast Thou crowned them"* (Psalm 8:5 LXX [MT 8:6]). The rubric directs that the remainder of the office—including the Epistle (Ephesians 5:20–33), Gospel (John 2:1–11), litanies, the Lord's Prayer, the Common Cup, and the dance of Isaiah around the tetrapod—is celebrated identically to the first marriage ("changing nothing"), followed by the dismissal.

[^261]: Fol. 78r. The Order of the Holy Oil (Holy Unction / Euchelaion) Chanted by Seven Priests (*Послѣ́дованїе ст҃го ма́сла пѣва́ємаго ѿ седьмѝ попѡ́въ* / Greek: *Ἀκολουθία τοῦ Ἁγίου Εὐχελαίου*). The Sacrament of Holy Unction, instituted according to the Apostolic injunction in James 5:14–15 ("Is any sick among you? Let him call for the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord..."). In Byzantine and Kyivan euchology, the full solemn office is celebrated by a college of seven presbyters (reflecting the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, Isaiah 11:2), though rubrics permit fewer if seven are unavailable. The rite opens with the preparation of the dish of wheat (*пшени́ца*), symbolizing new life and resurrection (John 12:24), holding a vessel filled with pure olive oil and red wine (commemorating the Good Samaritan, Luke 10:34), together with seven wands wrapped in cotton (*се́дмь па́личицъ*) for the sevenfold anointings.

[^262]: Fol. 78v. White Vestments, Paschal Symbolism, and the Censing at Holy Unction (*ѡ҆блъ́кшисѧ въ фело́ны бѣ́лы*). The rubrics prescribe that all ministering presbyters vest in white or bright phelonia (*λευκαῖς στολαῖς*), symbolizing the radiant joy, healing light, and spiritual resurrection bestowed through Christ's healing touch. The distribution of lit tapers to all seven presbyters and the initial circular censing around the analogion evoke the bridal and paschal character of the sacrament.

[^263]: Fol. 78v. Psalm 142 LXX [MT 143] as the Penitential Prologue to Holy Unction (*Ѱло́мъ рм҃в: Гдⷭ҇и оу҆слы́ши мл҃твоу мою̀...*). Psalm 142—the final Psalm of the Six Psalms of Matins—serves as the universal euchological opening for supplication in times of affliction and illness, pleading for divine mercy, guidance, and rescue from the spiritual and bodily snare of death.

[^264]: Fol. 79r. The Penitential Alleluia in Tone 6. In Byzantine and Slavonic liturgical tradition, chanting the Alleluia with penitential verses replaces the festive "God is the Lord" during Lenten services and rites of penitence and supplication, setting a somber, contrite tone for the unction office.

[^265]: Fol. 79r. Verses of Psalm 6:1–2 LXX [MT 6:1–2]. The Alleluia psalm-verses are drawn from Psalm 6, the first of the seven Penitential Psalms of the Psalter: *"O Lord, rebuke me not in Thine anger, neither chasten me in Thy wrath. Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak; heal me, O Lord, for my bones are troubled."* In liturgical medicine, bodily illness is directly approached within the sphere of divine chastening and spiritual restoration.

[^266]: Fol. 79v. The Classical Byzantine Theotokion of Compassion (*Мл҃рдїа двє́ри ѿвръзѝ на́мъ...* / *Τῆς εὐσπλαγχνίας τὴν πύλην ἄνοιξον ἡμῖν...*). This ubiquitous troparion, common to the Ordinary Beginning of many services, invokes the Mother of God as the portal of divine mercy and refuge from bodily and spiritual perils (*ѿ бѣ́дъ* / *ἐκ τῶν περιστάσεων*).

[^267]: Fol. 79v. Psalm 50 LXX [MT 51]. King David's great psalm of repentance (*"Have mercy on me, O God, according to Thy great mercy..."*) stands as the indispensable threshold before every liturgical canon, purifying the soul for sacramental supplication.

[^268]: Fol. 79v. The Canon of Holy Unction by Arsenios and its Acrostic (*Кано́нъ, є҆моу́же краегране́сїе: мл҃тва є҆ле́а, ѱало́мъ Арсе́нїевъ*). Greek: *Εὐχὴ ἐλαίου, ψαλμὸς Ἀρσενίου*. The canon of Holy Unction is the work of Arsenios (9th century, likely Arsenios of Corfu or a Studite hymnographer). In Greek, the initial letters of the troparia form the alphabetical acrostic: *Εὐχὴ ἐλαίου, ψαλμὸς Ἀρσενίου*. As typical in Church Slavonic translations, the acrostic title is faithfully transcribed and translated in the rubric even though the Slavonic poetic verses cannot sustain the literal Greek acrostic wordplay.

[^269]: Fol. 79v. Ode 1 Heirmos: *Мо́рѧ чръмна́го поучи́нꙋ немо́кръ[ными стопа́ми...]*; Greek: *Θαλάσσης τὸ ἐρυθραῖον πέλαγος ἀβρόχοις ἴχνεσιν...* Tone 4. The printer records the opening incipit, breaking off at *немо́кръ-* ("unwetted..."), directing the chanters to complete the familiar heirmos of the Passover through the Red Sea (Exodus 14).

[^270]: Fol. 80r. The Oil of Divine Compassion and the Parable of the Wise Virgins. Greek: *Μύρῳ τῷ τῆς σῆς εὐσπλαγχνίας, Δέσποτα...* The opening troparion of the canon connects the physical oil of unction (*ἔлαιον*) with divine mercy (*ἔλεος*), playing upon the classical Patristic paronomasia (*elaion / eleos*). The preservation of the oil of the faithful (*съхранѧ́ѧ ма́сло вѣ́рныхъ*) evokes the oil of good works and grace preserved in the lamps of the wise virgins (Matthew 25:1–13).

[^271]: Fol. 80r. The Mystical Anointing and the Universal Earthly Mercy. Greek: *Ἵλεων τῷ σῷ ἐλαίῳ, Δέσποτα...* Invoking Psalm 32:5 LXX [MT 33:5] ("The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord"), the hymn affirms that sacramental anointing mystically communicates that transcendent divine mercy which surpasses all human comprehension (Philippians 4:7).

[^272]: Fol. 80v. Apostolic Commission of Anointing and Remission of Sins. Concluding the *Glory* troparion from leaf 80r, which invokes Mark 6:13 ("And they anointed with oil many that were sick, and healed them") and James 5:15 ("And the prayer of faith shall save the sick... and if he have committed sins, they shall be forgiven him"). The sacred unction acts both as bodily medicine and spiritual absolution.

[^273]: Fol. 80v. The Theotokion of Ode 1: The Abyss of Peace (*Поучи́на ми́рови* / Greek: *Ἡ μόνη τὸν ἄβυσσον εἰρήνης κυήσασα*). A play on words between *μύρον* (myrrh/chrism) and *εἰρήνη* (peace) / *мир* (world/peace), honoring the Mother of God as the bearer of the Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6), who possesses an ocean of therapeutic healing for afflicted mortals.

[^274]: Fol. 80v. Ode 3 Heirmos: *Весели́тсѧ ѡ҆ тебѣ̀ цр҃кви твоѧ̀ Хрⷭ҇ѐ...*; Greek: *Εὐφραίνεται ἐπὶ σοὶ ἡ Ἐκκλησία σου, Χριστέ...* Tone 4. The familiar heirmos of Ode 3 celebrates the joy of the Church crying aloud: "Thou art my strength, O Lord, my refuge and my firm foundation."

[^275]: Fol. 80v. Christ Marvelous Among Men. Greek: *Σὺ μόνος ὑπάρχων θαυμαστός...* Confessing Christ as the sole source of divine healing and compassion, imploring Him to bestow His sanctifying and restorative grace from on high (*съвы́шше*) upon the suffering Christian.

[^276]: Fol. 80v. The Olive Branch of Noah as Typology of Sacramental Peace (*Ма́сличный сꙋ́чецъ...*). Greek: *Ἐλαίας τὸν κλάδον ποτέ...* Recalling the dove returning to Noah's Ark with an olive twig in its beak, signaling that the waters of the flood had subsided from off the earth (Genesis 8:11). In Christian typology, the olive branch prefigures the reconciliation of God with mankind and the pacification of bodily and spiritual storms through the oil of unction.

[^277]: Fol. 81r. The Radiant Lamp of Divine Light in Holy Oil (*Свѣ́щꙋ бж҃тве́наго свѣ́та...*). Greek: *Λαμπάδα φωτὸς θείου...* Continuing the imagery of the lamp burning before the holy icons and the analogion, beseeching Christ, the true Light of the world (John 8:12), to illuminate the bodily darkness and spiritual weakness of those anointed in faith.

[^278]: Fol. 81r. Maternal Intercession Dispersing Bitter Malady (*При́зри мл҃тивно, мт҃и всѧ́ческимъ тво́рцу...*). Greek: *Ἔπιδε ἵλεως, Μῆτερ τοῦ πάντων Ποιητοῦ...* Pleading for the maternal intercession of the Virgin Mary, the Mother of the Creator, to loose and dissolve the bitter affliction (*го́ркоую зло́боу* / *πικρὰν ὀδύνην*) weighing down the suffering person.

[^279]: Fol. 81r. Sessional Hymn (Kathisma) of Holy Unction and the River of Mercy (*Сѣда́лна, гла́съ д҃. По: Пасты́рскїи сопль вѣща́нїа твоє̀*). Model melody: Greek: *Ὁ ποιμενικὸς αὐλὸς τῆς θεολογίας σου...* (*The shepherd's pipe of thy theology / preaching*), the famous podoben in Tone 4 originally composed for hierarch-theologians (St. Gregory of Nazianzus, Jan 25; St. John Chrysostom, Nov 13). Here adapted to the euchological supplication of Unction, praising Christ as the boundless river of mercy (Psalm 45:5 LXX [MT 46:4]) and inexhaustible fountain of miracles (*и҆сто́чникъ неза́вистно* / *πηγὴν ἀφθόνως*) who cleanses and heals all believers.

[^280]: Fol. 81v. Conclusion of the Sessional Hymn. Concluding the earnest plea of the faithful that they ever have recourse to Christ's divine goodness (*бл҃гти молѧ́щесѧ*).

[^281]: Fol. 81v. Model Melody: *Tone 4, Podoben: "Thou Who wast lifted up upon the Cross" (Възнесы́йсѧ)*. Greek: *Ὁ ὑψωθεὶς ἐν τῷ Σταυρῷ ἑκουσίως...* The solemn Tone 4 podoben of the Feast of the Universal Exaltation of the Cross (Sept 14) and general troparion of the Holy Cross.

[^282]: Fol. 81v. Christ the Supreme Physician and Deliverer from Death (*Вра́чъ и҆ помо́щникъ болѧ́щимъ...*). Greek: *Ἰατρὸς καὶ βοηθὸς τῶν καμνόντων...* This sessional hymn evokes the core pastoral heart of Holy Unction: confessing Christ as the sole true Healer of soul and body, pleading that the sick servant be snatched from the jaws of impending bodily death to glorify God in the assembly of the living (Psalm 117:17–18 LXX [MT 118:17–18]).

[^283]: Fol. 81v. Ode 4 Heirmos: *Въздви́жена тѧ̀ ви́дѣвше цр҃кви...*; Greek: *Ἐπαρθέντα σε ἰδοῦσα ἡ Ἐκκλησία ἐπὶ Σταυροῦ...* Tone 4. Drawing upon the prophecy of Habakkuk (Habakkuk 3:11), the Church contemplates Christ elevated upon the Cross as the Sun of Righteousness, standing steadfast in her liturgical station.

[^284]: Fol. 81v. Christ as Incorruptible Myrrh Poured Forth (*Ꙗ҆́ко нетлѣ́нно му́ро є҆си Хрⷭ҇ѐ, и҆злива́емое бл҃гтїю...*). Greek: *Ὡς ἄφθαρτον μύρον, Χριστέ, ἐκκενωθὲν τῇ χάριτι...* Alluding to the Song of Songs 1:3 ("Thy name is as ointment [myrrh] poured forth"), identifying Christ Himself as the fragrant, heavenly unguent that cleanses the cosmos and soothes the festering ulcers and sores of fallen mortality.

[^285]: Fol. 82r. Ode 4 troparion 2 of the Canon of Holy Unction (attributed to Patriarch Arsenios of Corfu, 9th c.). Greek: *Τῷ τῆς πραότητος σημείῳ τοῦ ἐλαίου σου...*. The image of sealing the senses against demonic assault recalls the ancient baptismal and pre-sacramental sphragis.

[^286]: Fol. 82r. Ode 4 troparion 3. Direct allusion to the apostolic mandate of James 5:14: "Is any sick among you? Let him call for the elders of the church..." (*προσκαλεσάσθω τοὺς πρεσβυτέρους τῆς ἐκκλησίας*).

[^287]: Fol. 82r. Ode 4 theotokion. Traditional Marian architectural metaphors (*wall, haven, ladder, rampart*), alluding to Jacob's Ladder (Gen 28:12) and the defensive fortress imagery common in Byzantine hymnography.

[^288]: Fol. 82r. Ode 5 heirmos incipit (Tone 4): *Ты̀ ми Гдⷭ҇и свѣ́тъ въ ми́ръ прише́лъ єсѝ*. Greek: *Σὺ Κύριέ μου φῶς εἰς τὸν κόσμον ἐλήλυθας, φῶς ἅγιον ἐπιστρέφον, ἐκ ζοφώδους ἀγνοίας, τοὺς πίστει ἀνυμνοῦντάς σε* (John 12:46: "I am come a light into the world, that whosoever believes on Me should not abide in darkness").

[^289]: Fol. 82v. Ode 5 troparion 1. The printed witness reads *бе́зна* for *бе́здна* (abyss) and *бж҃твены ма́сло твои́мъ* (instrumental case with apocopated endings).

[^290]: Fol. 82v. Ode 5 troparion 2. The printed text reads *ѡс҃тивъ* (abbreviation for *освяти́въ*, having sanctified; Greek: *ἁγιάσας* or *καταυγάσας*), and *высѣ́хъ* for *всѣ́хъ*.

[^291]: Fol. 82v. Ode 5 troparion 3. Allusion to the sinful woman who anointed Christ's feet with myrrh (Luke 7:37-38, 47-48).

[^292]: Fol. 82v. Ode 5 theotokion. The Ruthenian recension reads *Бж҃твенымъ ти... ма́сломъ*, attributing the divine oil mediatingly through the Mother of God or as an objective genitive.

[^293]: Fol. 82v. Ode 6 heirmos incipit (Tone 4): *Пожрꙋ́ ти съ гла́сомъ хвале́нїа Гдⷭ҇и*. Greek: *Θύσω σοι, μετὰ φωνῆς αἰνέσεως Κύριε, ἡ Ἐκκλησία βοᾷ σοι, ἐκ δαιμόνων λύθρου κεκαθαρμένη, τῷ δι' οἶκτον, ἐκ τῆς πλευρᾶς σου ῥεύσαντι αἵματι* (Jonah 2:10; cf. Heb 13:15).

[^294]: Fol. 83r. Ode 6 troparion 1. Refers to the Old Testament anointing of prophets, kings, and high priests (cf. Exod 30:22-30; 1 Kgs 19:16), fulfilled through Christ's healing dispensation.

[^295]: Fol. 83r. Ode 6 troparion 2. The invocation acts as an apotropaic petition shielding the newly anointed sensory organs (*чю́вствомъ сп҃се зна́менанымъ*) against demonic affliction.

[^296]: Fol. 83r. Ode 6 troparion 3. Epiclesis-like petition over the oil (*ѡ҆стѝ є҆*, scribal contraction for *освяти́ є҆*).

[^297]: Fol. 83v. Completion of Ode 6 theotokion from fol. 83r. The imagery invokes Psalm 51:10 (LXX 51:8: "I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God").

[^298]: Fol. 83v. Model Melody: *Tone 4, Podoben: "Seeking the highest" (Вы́шниихъ)*. Greek: *Τὰ ἄνω ζητῶν*. In standard Church Slavonic and Greek editions this kontakion (*Πηγὴ ὑπάρχων ἐλέους...*) is appointed in Tone 2 (*Вышних ищя*). The Striatyn 1606 imprint uniquely specifies *Tone 4* (*глⷭ҇ · д҃*), while giving the model incipit in the genitive plural (*вы́шниихъ*), indicating either a typographic error for *Tone 2* (*в҃*) or an alternative local melodic adaptation.

[^299]: Fol. 83v. Kontakion of the Holy Oil. Greek: *Πηγὴ ὑπάρχων ἐλέους, ὑπεράγαθε...*.

[^300]: Fol. 83v. Ode 7 heirmos incipit (Tone 4): *Въ пе́щи а҆враа́мскыѧ*. Greek: *Ἐν τῇ καμίνῳ Ἀβραμιαῖοι Παῖδες τῇ Περσικῇ, πόθῳ εὐσεβείας μᾶλλον, ἢ τῇ φλογὶ πυρπολούμενοι, ἐκραύγαζον· Εὐλογημένος εἶ, ἐν τῷ ναῷ τῆς δόξης σου Κύριε* (Dan 3:24ff.).

[^301]: Fol. 83v. Ode 7 troparion 1. The printed text reads *высѣ́мъ* for *всѣ́мъ*.

[^302]: Fol. 84r. Completion of Ode 7 troparion 2 from fol. 83v.

[^303]: Fol. 84r. Ode 7 troparion 3. The liturgical sign of the Cross and holy oil is characterized as both a spiritual weapon (*Ѡроу́жїе*) and a purifying fire against demons and passions.

[^304]: Fol. 84r. Ode 7 theotokion. Alludes to Isaiah 40:12 ("Who hath measured the waters in the hollow of His hand...").

[^305]: Fol. 84r. Ode 8 heirmos incipit (Tone 4): *Роу́цѣ распросте́ръ данїи́лъ*. Greek: *Χεῖρας ἐκπετάσας Δανιήλ, λεόντων χάσματα ἐν λάκκῳ ἔφραξε* (Dan 6:16-23; Dan 14:31-42).

[^306]: Fol. 84v. Completion of Ode 8 troparion 1 from fol. 84r. The printed text reads *мно́жетво* for *мно́жество*, and *ма́сло сты́мъ* (instrumental *ма́сломъ святы́мъ*).

[^307]: Fol. 84v. Ode 8 troparion 2.

[^308]: Fol. 85r. Completion of Ode 8 troparion 3 from fol. 84v, concluding with the biblical canticle refrain of the Three Holy Children (Dan 3:57).

[^309]: Fol. 85r. Ode 8 theotokion. The printed text reads *є҆́стко* for *є҆стество̀* (nature / human nature; Greek: *ἡ φύσις*).

[^310]: Fol. 85r. Ode 9 heirmos incipit (Tone 4): *Ка́мень нерꙋкосѣ́чны[й] ·*. Greek: *Λίθος ἀχειρότμητος ὄρους, ἐξ ἀλαξεύτου σου Παρθένε, ἀκρογωνιαῖος ἐτμήθη, Χριστὸς συνάψας τὰς διεστώσας φύσεις...* (Dan 2:34, 45).

[^311]: Fol. 85r. Ode 9 troparion 1. The printed text reads *высѣ́мъ* for *всѣ́мъ*, and *за сщ҃е́нникъ ти* (through Thy priests).

[^312]: Fol. 85v. Completion of Ode 9 troparion 2 from fol. 85r. Alludes to Christ sending the Holy Spirit to the Apostles at Pentecost following His Ascension (Acts 1:9, 2:1-4; Eph 4:8). The printed text reads *то́же ѡ҆́бра радости* for *то́йжде ѡ҆́бразъ ра́дости*.

[^313]: Fol. 85v. Ode 9 troparion 3. Alludes to Psalm 91:5 (LXX 90:5: "Thou shalt not be afraid... for the arrow that flies by day") and Ephesians 6:16 ("the fiery darts of the wicked").

[^314]: Fol. 85v. Ode 9 theotokion.

[^315]: Fol. 85v. Incipit of the Megalynarion hymn to the Mother of God (*Ἄξιόν ἐστιν / Достойно есть*), chanted at the completion of the Ninth Ode before the Exapostilarion.

[^316]: Fol. 85v. Model Melody: *Exapostilarion, Podoben: "Thou hast visited us from on high" (Посѣти́лъ ны є́стъ свы́ше)*. Greek: *Ἐπεσκέψατο ἡμᾶς ἐξ ὕψους*. The printed text gives the abbreviated rubric: *свѣ́ , по́ , посѣти́лъ ны є́стъ съ ·* (abbreviating *свы́ше* / *съ высоты̀*).

[^317]: Fol. 86r. Exapostilarion text of Holy Unction. Greek: *Ἐλέους ὄμματι, Μόναχε / Ἀγαθέ, ἔπιδε ἐπὶ τὴν δέησιν ἡμῶν...*.

[^318]: Fol. 86r. Model Melody: *Tone 4, Podoben: "Thou hast given a sign" (Да́сть зна́менїе)*. Greek: *Ἔδωκας σημείωσιν*. In the Striatyn print, the model title is printed with the third-person *Да́сть зна́менїе* (He hath given a sign) instead of the standard second-person *Да́лъ є҆сѝ зна́менїе* (Thou hast given a sign).

[^319]: Fol. 86r. Sticheron 1 at the Praises / Aposticha of Holy Unction. Greek: *Ἔδωκας τὴν χάριν σου, διὰ τῶν σῶν Ἀποστόλων φιλάνθρωπε...*. The Ruthenian text reads *бл҃гопрїемѣни́телю* (benign acceptor / beneficent one; Greek *εὐεργέτα* or *ὑπεράγαθε*), and *высѧ́каго* for *вся́каго*.

[^320]: Fol. 86v. Completion of Sticheron 2 from fol. 86r (*Си́ждъ неѡбиме́нне всекро́ткыма си ѡ҆чи́ма...*). Greek: *Ἐπιβλέψας ἄσχετε, τοῖς πανοικτίρμοσιν ὄμμασι...*. The Slavonic witness exhibits *Си́ждъ* (calquing Greek *κατιδών* or *ἐπιδών*, having looked down) with *неѡбиме́нне* (uncircumscribed / unbounded; Greek: *ἀπεριγράπτως* or *ἀσχέτως*).

[^321]: Fol. 86v. Sticheron 3 at the Praises / Aposticha of Holy Unction. Greek: *Ἐλαίου χρίσει σου, καὶ ἱερέων ἐπιψαύσει...*.

[^322]: Fol. 87r. Theotokion following the Stichera of Holy Unction. Greek: *Σὲ τὴν τιμιωτάτην βασιλικὴν παστάδα, δυσωπῶ πολυύμνητε...*. The architectural-liturgical metaphor of the Mother of God as the "most honorable royal palace" (*цр҃скоу пола́тоу*) reflects Byzantine imperial Marian typologies. The text reads *сп҃се́* (here adverbial or participial for *спасенъ*, saved).

[^323]: Fol. 87r. Concluding Marian sticheron (*Ѿ въсѣ́хъ бѣ́дъ рабы̀ своѧ̀ съхранѧ́й...*). Greek: *Ἐκ παντοίων κινδύνων τοὺς δούλους σου φύλαττε, εὐλογημένη Θεοτόκε...*.

[^324]: Fol. 87r. Rubric prescribing the standard Trisagion Prayers through the Our Father (*Ѿче нашъ*), followed by the Troparion in Tone 4 (*Ско́ръ въ застоупле́нїи є҆ди́нъ сы́й Хрⷭ҇ѐ...*). In the Byzantine Rite, this troparion is appointed throughout healing services and the Visitation of the Sick.

[^325]: Fol. 87v. Completion of Troparion, Tone 4, from fol. 87r. The printed text reads *го́ркы҃ ра́нъ* with an abbreviated genitive plural *го́ркыхъ ра́нъ* (Greek: *πικρῶν πληγῶν* / bitter wounds).

[^326]: Fol. 87v. Rubric directing the first priest (or deacon, if one serves) to intone the Special Litany of Holy Unction (*дїа́конства* / *διακονικά*). In historical Slavonic Euchologia, the priest recites these petitions when serving without a deacon.

[^327]: Fol. 87v. Initial petitions of the Litany of Holy Unction, including the specific epiklesis petition over the oil (*Ѡ҆ бл҃ви́тисѧ ма́слоу семоу̀ си́лою и҆ дѣ́йствомъ и҆ прише́ствїемъ ст҃а́го дх҃а* / *Ὑπὲρ τοῦ εὐλογηθῆναι τὸ ἔλαιον τοῦτο τῇ δυνάμει, καὶ ἐνεργείᾳ, καὶ ἐπιφοιτήσει τοῦ Ἁγίου Πνεύματος*). The leaf concludes with the nominative petition for the sick person, leaving the name blank (*и҆́мⷶк* = *и҆́мⷬ҇къ*, *nomen proprium*).

[^328]: Fol. 88r. Completion of the Litany of Holy Unction from fol. 87v, concluding with the commemoration of the Theotokos and all the saints (*Пр҃тоую чⷭ҇тоую и҆ пребл҃же́ную влⷣчцоу на́шю...*).

[^329]: Fol. 88r. Rubric for the Priest's Prayer of the Oil, containing a historic typikon gloss: *Вѣ́домо же боу́ди ꙗ҆́ко въ вели́цѣй цр҃кви въ мѣ́сто воды̀ ви́но въ канди́ло маслопрїе́мца вълива́ютъ* ("Be it known that in the Great Church [Hagia Sophia / Constantinople], instead of water, they pour wine into the lamp of the oil-receiver"). In Byzantine practice, wine and oil were mingled in allusion to the Good Samaritan who poured oil and wine upon the wounds of the traveler (Luke 10:34), whereas Russian and northern Slavonic usage frequently substituted pure water or wine.

[^330]: Fol. 88v. The ancient consecratory Prayer of the Oil: *Гдⷭ҇и , и҆́же ми́лостїю и҆ щедрота́ми твои́ми и҆сцѣлѧ́ѧй съкроуше́нїа...*. Greek: *Κύριε, ὁ τῷ ἐλέει καὶ τοῖς οἰκτιρμοῖς σου ἰώμενος τὰ συντρίμματα τῶν ψυχῶν καὶ τῶν σωμάτων ἡμῶν, αὐτὸς Δέσποτα ἁγίασον τὸ ἔλαιον τοῦτο...*. In liturgical theology, this prayer constitutes the epiklesis of the Mystery of Holy Unction, asking that the oil become a medium of spiritual and bodily healing, remission of sins, and expulsion of demonic assaults.

[^331]: Fol. 88v. Rubric prescribing the chanting of healing troparia while the concelebrating priests sequentially recite the prayer of the oil. Tone 4: *Ско́ръ въ застꙋпле́нїи...*.

[^332]: Fol. 89r. Completion of Troparion 1 from fol. 88v.

[^333]: Fol. 89r. Troparion 2 (Kontakion of the Blind Man, Tone 4). Greek: *Τῆς ψυχῆς τὰ ὄμματα πεπηρωμένος, σοὶ Χριστὲ προσέρχομαι, ὡς ὁ Τυφλὸς ἐκ γενετῆς, ἐν μετανοίᾳ κραυγάζων σοι· Σὺ τῶν ἐν σκότει τὸ φῶς τὸ ὑπέρλαμπρον* (adapted here with the refrain *мл҃тикъ на́мъ бꙋ́ди є҆ди́не бл҃гопремѣни́телю*, "Be merciful unto us, O Thou Who alone art beneficent"). The printed form *мл҃тикъ* is an unusual hypocoristic/apocopated dialectal variant for *ми́лостивъ*.

[^334]: Fol. 89r. Troparion 3 (Kontakion of the Paralytic, Tone 4). Greek: *Τὴν ψυχήν μου Κύριε, ἐν ἁμαρτίαις παντοίαις, καὶ ἀτόποις πράξεσι, δεινῶς παραλελυμένην, ἔγειρον τῇ θεϊκῇ σου ἐπιστασίᾳ, ὥσπερ καὶ τὸν Πάραλυτον, ἤγειρας πάλαι...*.

[^335]: Fol. 89v. Troparion of Saint James, the Brother of the Lord and First Bishop of Jerusalem (Tone 4). Greek: *Ὡς τοῦ Κυρίου μαθητής, ἀνεδέξω Δίκαιε τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον· ὡς Μάρτυς ἔχεις τὸ ἀπαράτρεπτον· τὴν παρρησίαν ὡς Ἀδελφόθεος· τὸ πρεσβεύειν ὡς Ἱεράρχης...*. The Striatyn witness exhibits *показа́лъ є҆си* for *воспрїѧ́лъ є҆си* and *непрепи́санное* (uncontested / incontrovertible, calquing *ἀπαράτρεπτον*) for standard *неѡпи́санное*.

[^336]: Fol. 89v. Troparion (Kontakion) of Saint James (Tone 4). Greek: *Ὁ τοῦ Πατρὸς Μονογενὴς Θεὸς Λόγος, ἐπιδημήσας πρὸς ἡμᾶς ἐπ' ἐσχάτων τῶν ἡμερῶν, Ἰάκωβε θεσπέσιε, πρῶτόν σε ἀνέδειξε τῶν Ἱεροσολύμων Ποιμένα καὶ Διδάσκαλον...*. Saint James is commemorated specifically in the rite of Holy Unction as the author of the canonical New Testament mandate for the sacrament (James 5:14-15).

[^337]: Fol. 89v. Opening of the Kontakion of Saint Nicholas of Myra in Lycia (Tone 3, *Въ мѵ́рѣхъ ст҃е ст҃и́тель показа́сѧ...*). Greek: *Ἐν τοῖς Μύροις Ἅγιε, ἱερουργὸς ἀνεδείχθης· τοῦ Χριστοῦ γὰρ Ὅσιε, τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον πληρώσας...*.

[^338]: Fol. 90r. Completion of the Kontakion of Saint Nicholas from fol. 89v (*...сего̀ ра́ди ѡ҆ст҃и́сѧ ꙗ҆́коже ве́лїи тайнникъ Бж҃їи бл҃гти* / Greek: *διὰ τοῦτο ἡγιάσθης, ὡς μέγας μύστης τῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ χάριτος*).

[^339]: Fol. 90r. Troparion of the Holy Great-Martyr Demetrius of Thessalonica (Tone 3). Greek: *Μέγαν εὕρατο ἐν τοῖς κινδύνοις, σὲ ὑπέρμαχον ἡ οἰκουμένη, Ἀθλοφόρε τὰ ἔθνη τροπούμενον. Ὡς οὖν Λυαίου καθεῖλες τὴν ἔπαρσιν, ἐν τῷ σταδίῳ θαρρύνας τὸν Νέστορα...*. Demetrius is invoked as a patron of miraculous healing through the out-pouring of myrrh (*Myroblyte*).

[^340]: Fol. 90r. Troparion of the Holy Great-Martyr and Healer Panteleimon (Tone 3). Greek: *Ἀθλοφόρε Ἅγιε, καὶ ἰαματικὲ Παντελεῆμον, πρέσβευε τῷ ἐλεήμονι Θεῷ, ἵνα πταισμάτων ἄφεσιν, παράσχῃ ταῖς ψυχαῖς ἡμῶν*.

[^341]: Fol. 90v. Conclusion of the Troparion of the Holy Unmercenary Physicians (*Ст҃і́и безсре́бръници...*), citing the dominical commission of Matthew 10:8: *тоу́не прїѧ́сте, тоу́не и҆ дади́те* ("freely ye have received, freely give"; Greek: *δωρεὰν ἐλάβετε, δωρεὰν δότε*).

[^342]: Fol. 90v. Kontakion of Saint John the Apostle and Theologian (Tone 2). Greek: *Τὰ μεγαλεῖά σου Παρθένε τίς διηγήσεται; βρύεις γὰρ θαύματα, καὶ πηγάζεις ἰάματα...*. The Slavonic witness reads *на́шїи* for *на́шихъ*.

[^343]: Fol. 90v. Fervent Theotokion (*Мл҃тво те́пла, и҆ стѣ́но неѡ҆бори́ма...*), a celebrated supplication to the Mother of God frequently appended to healing offices and molebens (Greek: *Πρεσβεία θερμή, καὶ τεῖχος ἀπροσμάχητον...*).

[^344]: Fol. 90v. The First Prokeimenon of Holy Unction in Tone 4: Psalm 40:5 (LXX 40:4): *А҆́зъ рѣ́хъ: Го́споди, поми́луй мѧ̀, и҆сцѣлѝ ду́шу мою̀, ꙗ҆́кѡ согрѣши́хъ тебѣ̀* ("I said: Lord, have mercy on me, heal my soul; for I have sinned against Thee"), with verse Psalm 40:4 (LXX 40:3): *Го́сподь помо́жетъ є҆му̀ на ѻ҆́дрѣ болѣ́зни є҆гѡ̀* ("The Lord will help him on his bed of sickness"). Followed by the announcement of the Epistle reading from the General Epistle of James.

[^345]: Fol. 91r. The First Epistle of Holy Unction: James 5:10-14. The Slavonic text contains several archaic and recensional features: in verse 12, *да̀ не въ лицемиѣ́рїе въпа́дете* ("lest ye fall into hypocrisy") directly reflects the Byzantine manuscript tradition (*μὴ εἰς ὑπόκρισιν πέσητε*), found in early majuscules and the majority text, in contrast to later Byzantine printed editions reading *εἰς κρίσιν* ("into condemnation"). In verse 14, the Ruthenian print uses the vernacular-influenced term *пѡпы̀ цр҃кѡ́вныѧ* ("priests of the church") for standard *пресвѵ́теры церковныѧ* (Greek: *τοὺς πρεσβυτέρους τῆς ἐκκλησίας*).

[^346]: Fol. 91v. Conclusion of the First Epistle of Holy Unction: James 5:14-16. Verse 16: *мнѡ́го бо мо́же мл҃итва пра́веднаго поспѣ́шествоу́ема* translates the Greek *πολὺ ἰσχύει δέησις δικαίου ἐνεργουμένη* ("the prayer of a righteous man is of great power in its working").

[^347]: Fol. 91v. Alleluia of the First Gospel in Tone 2 with verse Psalm 100:1 (LXX 100:1): *Ми́лость и҆ сꙋ́дъ воспою̀ тебѣ̀, Го́споди* ("I will sing of mercy and judgment unto Thee, O Lord"). Followed by the liturgical announcement of the Gospel according to Luke.

[^348]: Fol. 91v. The First Gospel pericopa of Holy Unction: Luke 10:25-37 (the Parable of the Good Samaritan). The folio concludes with the opening words of verse 26: *Ѡ҆́нже речѐ къ не́моу · в̾ зако́нѣ* ("He said unto him: In the law..."), which continues onto fol. 92r (cohort 21): *что̀ пи́сано є҆́стъ; ка́кѡ чте́ши;* ("what is written? How readest thou?").

[^349]: Fol. 92r. Continuation of the First Gospel: Luke 10:26–31a (Greek: *τί ἐν τῷ νόμῳ γέγραπται; πῶς ἀναγινώσκεις;...*). In verse 27, the fourfold faculties of devotion from Deuteronomy 6:5 and Leviticus 19:18 are rendered: *срⷣца, дш҃а, крѣ́постїю, помышле́нїемъ* (*καρδίας, ψυχῆς, ἰσχύος, διανοίας*). In verse 30, the Ruthenian phrase *ѡ҆ста́вльше є҆́лѣ жи́ва сꙋ́ща* calques the Greek *ἡμιθανῆ τυγχάνοντα* ("leaving him half dead / scarcely alive").

[^350]: Fol. 92v. Continuation of the First Gospel: Luke 10:31b–36. In patristic exegesis (e.g., Saint John Chrysostom, Saint Ambrose), the Parable of the Good Samaritan is the primary locus for the sacramental theology of Holy Unction: Christ Himself is the Samaritan, the wounded traveler represents fallen humanity, the inn is the Church, and the oil and wine (*възлива́ѧ ма́сло и҆ вино̀* / *ἐπιχέων ἔλαιον καὶ οἶνον*) signify divine mercy and the restorative grace of the Mysteries. In verse 35, the Slavonic *прииждиве́ши* accurately translates the compound verb *προσδαπανήσῃς* ("spendest additionally / layest out over and above").

[^351]: Fol. 93r. Conclusion of the First Gospel: Luke 10:36b–37. The Lord's concluding injunction (*и҆дѝ и҆ ты̀ творѝ та́кожде* / *Πορεύου καὶ σὺ ποίει ὁμοίως*) establishes merciful visitation of the sick as a dominical imperative.

[^352]: Fol. 93r. The Augmented Litany (*є҆ктінїа̀* / *ἐκτενής*) of Holy Unction following the Gospel pericopa. The deacon or presiding priest recites the introductory petition of supplication: *Поми́лꙋй на́съ, Бж҃е...* (Greek: *Ἐλέησον ἡμᾶς, ὁ Θεός, κατὰ τὸ μέγα ἔλεός σου...*).

[^353]: Fol. 93r. Petition for the recovery of the sick candidate: *ѡ҆ мл҃ти ѡ҆ животѣ̀ ѡ҆ здра́вїи и҆ сп҃се́нїи, ѡ҆ посѣще́нїи и҆ ѡ҆ставле́нїи грѣхѡ́въ...* (Greek: *Ἔτι δεόμεθα ὑπὲρ ἐλέους, ζωῆς, εἰρήνης, ὑγείας, σωτηρίας, ἐπισκέψεως, συγχωρήσεως καὶ ἀφέσεως τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν τοῦ δούλου τοῦ Θεοῦ...*). The rubric provides the placeholder *и҆́мѧ ре́къ* (*nomen dicens*).

[^354]: Fol. 93r. Special petition for the absolution of all voluntary and involuntary sins: *ѡ҆ прости́ти сѧ є҆моу̀ всѧ́комоу прегрѣше́нїю во́лномоу и҆ нево́лномоу* (Greek: *Ἔτι δεόμεθα ὑπὲρ τοῦ συγχωρηθῆναι αὐτῷ πᾶν πλημμέλημα ἑκούσιόν τε καὶ ἀκούσιον*).

[^355]: Fol. 93r. Concluding petition of the Augmented Litany entreating the Lord God to send down the grace of deliverance (*бл҃гть и҆збавлє́нїа*) and raise the sufferer from the bed of pain (*ѿ ѻ҆́дра болѣ́зньнаго* / Greek: *ἐκ κλίνης ὀδύνης*), prompting the collective response: *рецѣ́мъ въсѝ: Гдⷭ҇и...* ("let us all say: O Lord...").

[^356]: Fol. 93v. Concluding ecphonesis of the Augmented Litany: *Ꙗ҆́ко мл҃тивый чл҃колю́бецъ Бг҃ъ є҆си...* (Greek: *Ὅτι ἐλεήμων καὶ φιλάνθρωπος Θεὸς ὑπάρχεις...*), sealed by the Father Paul Doxology standard: *нн҃ѣ и҆ прⷭ҇но и҆ въ вѣ́кы вѣкѡ́мъ · а҆ми́нь* ("now and ever, and unto ages of ages. Amen").

[^357]: Fol. 93v. The First Consecratory Prayer of the Priest: *Безна́чалне, неѡб̾име́нне, ст҃е ст҃ымъ...*. Greek: *Ἄναρχε, ἀτελεύτητε, Ἅγιε ἁγίων, ὁ τὸν μονογενῆ σου Υἱὸν ἐξαποστείλας, ἰώμενον πᾶσαν νόσον καὶ πᾶσαν μαλακίαν...*. The Ruthenian translation *неѡб̾име́нне* reflects the Greek *ἀπεριόριστε* or *ἀκατάληπτε* (uncircumscribed / incomprehensible), expressing the infinite nature of the Godhead.

[^358]: Fol. 94r. Critical rubrical typikon note: *Вѣ́домо же бꙋ́ди ꙗ҆́ко мл҃твꙋ сїю̀ нѣ́цїи доздѣ̀ то́чїю чтоу́тъ, съ възгла́сомъ: Твое́ бо є҆́стъ... нѣ́цїи же чтоу́тъ и҆ въсю̀ до конца̀*. In Byzantine and East Slavic Euchologia, two liturgical traditions existed regarding this prayer: one recension abbreviated it after the petition for the inheritance of the Kingdom of Heaven, proceeding directly to the ecphonesis, while the older and fuller recension preserved the expansive Eucharistic and covenantal anamnesis through fol. 95v.

[^359]: Fol. 94r. Continuation of the extended prayer: *Ты́ бо є҆си Бг҃ъ ве́лїи и҆ чю́денъ...* (Greek: *Σὺ γὰρ εἶ ὁ Θεὸς ὁ μέγας καὶ θαυμαστός...*). The prayer weaves together citations from Psalm 85:10 (LXX), the Covenant formula of Deuteronomy 7:9, and the Messianic liberation prophecy of Isaiah 61:1 and Isaiah 42:7 (*гл҃ѧ сꙋ́щимъ въ ꙋ҆́захъ: и҆зыдѣ́те...* / *λέγων τοῖς ἐν τοῖς δεσμοῖς· Ἐξέλθετε...*).

[^360]: Fol. 94v. Theological exposition of the Incarnation and divine sonship: *прїе́мши тебѐ да́лъ є҆си вла́сть ча́да Бж҃їа бы́ти...* directly alludes to John 1:12 (*ὅσοι δὲ ἔλαβον αὐτόν, ἔδωκεν αὐτοῖς ἐξουσίαν τέκνα Θεοῦ γενέσθαι*). The text asserts the abolition of bloody animal sacrifice in favor of the unction of holy oil imprinted with the sign of the Cross (*ѡ҆́бразъ крⷭ҇та твое́го* / *τύπον τοῦ Σταυροῦ σου*).

[^361]: Fol. 94v. Typological invocation of Moses and Samuel as biblical archetypes of consecratory ministry (cf. Exodus 30:22–33, 1 Samuel 16:13), requesting equal grace for the concelebrating Christian priests.

[^362]: Fol. 95r. The consecratory epiklesis and catalogue of divine gifts bestowed through the holy oil: *є҆ле́й ра́дости, є҆ле́и сщ҃е́нїа, ѡ҆дѣѧ́нїе цр҃ко, шле́мъ си́лы...* (Greek: *ἔλαιον ἀγαλλιάσεως, ἔλαιον ἁγιασμοῦ, ἔνδυμα βασιλικόν, θώρακα [or περικεφαλαίαν] δυνάμεως...*), recalling Psalm 44:8 (LXX 44:7) and Ephesians 6:14–17. The print reads *наводитъ* for the participle *наводи́маго* (about to be applied).

[^363]: Fol. 95v. Eschatological conclusion of the first prayer, petitioning that those anointed may receive the prize of the high calling (Philippians 3:14: *по́чть вы́шнѧго зва́нїа* / *τὸ βραβεῖον τῆς ἄνω κλήσεως*), concluding with the ecphonesis: *Твое́ бо є҆́стъ є҆́же ми́ловати, и҆ сп҃са́ти ны...*.

[^364]: Fol. 95v. Rubric prescribing the First Anointing: the priest dips the wand into the consecrated oil and anoints the sick person while reciting the prayer of healing (*пома́зоуетъ твора́щаго маслосщ҃е́нїе, гл҃ѧ мл҃твꙋ сїю̀*). The Ruthenian phrase *твора́щаго маслосщ҃е́нїе* ("the one performing / undergoing Holy Unction") denotes the recipient of the Mystery.

[^365]: Fol. 95v. The First Anointing Prayer of Holy Unction: *Ѽче ст҃ый вра́чю дꙋша́мъ и҆ тѣлесе́мъ...*. Greek: *Πάτερ ἅγιε, ἰατρὲ τῶν ψυχῶν καὶ τῶν σωμάτων, ὁ πέμψας τὸν μονογενῆ σου Υἱόν, τὸν Κύριον ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν, πᾶσαν νόσον ἰώμενον...*. This prayer represents the core sacramental formula repeated at each of the seven unctions in the Byzantine rite.

[^366]: Fol. 96r. Intercessory catalogue within the Anointing Prayer, invoking the Theotokos, the bodiless Heavenly Hosts, the Precious Cross, the Holy Forerunner, Apostles, Martyrs, God-bearing Fathers, and the Holy Unmercenary Healers Cosmas and Damian, Cyrus and John.

[^367]: Fol. 96v. Completion of the catalogue of healing saints: Saint Panteleimon, Saint Hermolaus, Saint Sampson the Hospitable, Saint Diomedes, Saints Photius and Anicetus, and the righteous Ancestors of God Joachim and Anna. The inclusion of Photius and Anicetus (*фо́тїа, и҆ а҆ники́ты*) is a characteristic Byzantine Euchologion witness (commemorated August 12).

[^368]: Fol. 96v. Rubric governing concelebration: *Сїа̀ мл҃тва гл҃етсѧ ѿ є҆ди́наго коего́ждо сщ҃енника, по прочита́нїи є҆ѵанге́лїй · и҆ по мл҃твѣ, коу́пно пома́зоующихъ є҆ле́омъ недꙋ́жнаго*. In the full seven-priest rite of Holy Unction, each priest sequentially recites an Epistle, Gospel, and Prayer of Anointing, anointing the sick person in turn.

[^369]: Fol. 96v. Second Prokeimenon in Tone 2: Psalm 117:14, 18 (LXX 117:14, 18): *Крѣ́пость моѧ̀ и҆ пѣ́нїе моѐ Го́сподь, и҆ бы́сть мнѣ̀ во спасе́нїе* ("The Lord is my strength and my song, and He is become my salvation"), with verse *Пока́зуѧ наказа́ мѧ Го́сподь, сме́рти же не предаде́ мѧ* ("Chasten me hath the Lord chastened, but He hath not given me over unto death"). Followed by the liturgical announcement of the Second Epistle reading from the Epistle to the Romans (*а҆пл҃ъ къ римлѧ́номъ* = Romans 15:1–7).

[^370]: Fol. 97r. Opening of the Second Epistle reading: Romans 15:1–3. The Apostle Paul establishes the duty of the strong to bear the infirmities of the weak, citing Psalm 68:10 (LXX 68:9): *поноше́нїа поносѧ́щихъ ти нападо́ша на мѧ̀* (Greek: *οἱ ὀνειδισμοὶ τῶν ὀνειδιζόντων σε ἐπέπεσον ἐπ' ἐμέ*), applied christologically to the suffering Savior.

[^371]: Fol. 97r. Continuation of the Second Epistle reading: Romans 15:4–7a. The Apostle emphasizes patience and comfort drawn from the Scriptures (*трѣпе́нїемъ и҆ оу҆тѣше́нїемъ писа́нїй* / *διὰ τῆς ὑπομονῆς καὶ διὰ τῆς παρακλήσεως τῶν γραφῶν*) that believers may with one mind and one mouth glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.

[^372]: Fol. 97v. Conclusion of the Second Epistle reading: Romans 15:7b (*прїемли́те дрꙋ́гъ дрꙋ́га, ꙗ҆́коже и҆ хс҃ъ прїѧ́тъ ва́съ въ сла́вꙋ бж҃їю* / Greek: *προσλαμβάνεσθε ἀλλήλους, καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς προσελάβετο ὑμᾶς, εἰς δόξαν τοῦ Θεοῦ*).

[^373]: Fol. 97v. Alleluia in Tone 5 with verse from Psalm 88:2 (LXX 88:1): *Мл҃ти твоѧ̀ гн҃и въ вѣ́кы въспою̀* (Greek: *Τὰ ἐλέη σου, Κύριε, εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα ᾄσομαι* — "Thy mercies, O Lord, will I sing unto ages").

[^374]: Fol. 97v. Opening of the Second Gospel reading: Luke 19:1–5. The encounter of Jesus with Zacchaeus (*закхе́й* / *Ζακχαῖος*) in Jericho, who climbed a sycamore tree (*ꙗ҆годи́чина* / *συκομορέα*) to see the Lord.

[^375]: Fol. 98r. Conclusion of the Second Gospel reading: Luke 19:5b–10. Zacchaeus's repentance and fourfold restitution (*възвращꙋ̀ четвери́цею* / *ἀποδίδωμι τετραπλοῦν*), culminating in Christ's declaration of salvation to his household and the saving mission of the Son of Man.

[^376]: Fol. 98r. The Augmented Litany (*є҆ктенїа̀* / *ἐκτενής*) of Holy Unction repeated after the Second Gospel reading, petitioning divine mercy, life, health, salvation, and visitation for the sick person.

[^377]: Fol. 98v. Petitions of the Augmented Litany for the sick candidate (*и҆́мѧ ре́къ* / *nomen dicens*), entreating the remission of all voluntary and involuntary transgressions and deliverance from the bed of pain (*ѿ ѻ҆́дра болѣ́зньнаго* / Greek: *ἐκ κλίνης ὀδύνης*).

[^378]: Fol. 98v. Concluding ecphonesis of the Augmented Litany: *Ꙗ҆́ко мл҃тивый чл҃колю́бецъ бг҃ъ є҆сѝ...* (Greek: *Ὅτι ἐλεήμων καὶ φιλάνθρωπος Θεὸς ὑπάρχεις...*), sealed by the canonical Trinitarian doxology.

[^379]: Fol. 98v. The Second Consecratory Prayer of the Priest: *Бж҃е вели́кїй и҆ вы́шнїй...* (Greek: *Ὁ Θεὸς ὁ μέγας καὶ ὕψιστος, ὁ ὑπὸ πάσης κτίσεως προσκυνούμενος, σοφίας πηγή, ἀγαθότητος ὄντως ἀνεξιχνίαστον πέλαγος, καὶ οἰκτιρμῶν ἀπεριόριστον ἄβυσσος...*).

[^380]: Fol. 99r. Continuation of the Second Consecratory Prayer, invoking God's transcendence before the ages (*пре́жде вѣ́къ и҆ чюдесе́мъ бг҃ъ*), citing Genesis 8:21 on human weakness from youth and Ezekiel 33:11 on God desiring repentance rather than the death of a sinner.

[^381]: Fol. 99v. Anamnesis of the Incarnation and dominical parables of mercy: Matthew 9:13 (calling sinners to repentance), Luke 15:4–10 (the Lost Sheep and the Lost Drachma), John 6:37 (not casting out him that comes), and Luke 7:36–50 (the penitent woman weeping at the Savior's feet).

[^382]: Fol. 99v. Quotation of the dominical agraphon on persistent repentance (*є҆ли́жды а҆́ще па́днеши, въста́ни и҆ сп҃се́шисѧ* — "As often as thou fallest, arise, and thou shalt be saved"; cf. Justin Martyr, *Dialogue with Trypho* 47) and Luke 15:7, 10 on heavenly joy over one repenting sinner.

[^383]: Fol. 100r. Epiklesis of the Second Consecratory Prayer: the priest entreats the descent of the grace of the All-holy Spirit (*блг҃отїю пр҃ста́го твое́го дх҃а*) upon the sick person (*и҆́мѧ ре́къ*), with complete absolution of sins in word, deed, or thought, and protection in the divine commandments.

[^384]: Fol. 100v. Eschatological conclusion of the Second Consecratory Prayer, frustrating the joy of the adversary (*врагоу̀ є҆го̀*), sealed by the solemn Trinitarian ecphonesis: *Твое́ бо є҆́стъ є҆́же ми́ловати и҆ сп҃ти ны́ Хе́ бг҃е...*.

[^385]: Fol. 100v. Third Prokeimenon in Tone 3: Psalm 26:1 (LXX 26:1): *Гдⷭь просвѣще́нїе моѐ и҆ сп҃ситель мо́й, кого́ сѧ оу҆бою̀...* (Greek: *Κύριος φωτισμός μου καὶ σωτήρ μου· τίνα φοβηθήσομαι;*).

[^386]: Fol. 100v. Announcement and opening of the Third Epistle reading: 1 Corinthians 12:27–28a (*вы̀ є҆сте тѣ́ло хв҃о и҆ оу҆́ди ѿ ча́сти...* / Greek: *Ὑμεῖς δέ ἐστε σῶμα Χριστοῦ καὶ μέλη ἐκ μέρους...*), outlining the diversity of charisms and offices in the Church.

[^387]: Fol. 101r. Continuation of the Third Epistle reading: 1 Corinthians 12:28b–13:2. The catalogue of spiritual gifts (*дарова́нїа и҆сцѣле́нїѡмъ, застꙋпле́нїа, и҆справле́нїе, ро́ди ꙗ҆зы́кѡмъ*) and the introduction to the Pauline Hymn to Love (*ἀγάπη* / *любы*).

[^388]: Fol. 101v. Conclusion of the Third Epistle reading: 1 Corinthians 13:2b–8a. The Apostle outlines the eternal qualities of Christian love. The 1606 Striatyn print renders *πάντα στέγει* as *всѧ̀ лю́битъ* ("loves all things") alongside *всемꙋ̀ вѣ́рꙋ є҆́млетъ, всѐ оу҆пова́етъ, всѧ̀ терпи́тъ*.

[^389]: Fol. 101v. Alleluia in Tone 2 with verse from Psalm 30:2 (LXX 30:1): *На тѧ̀ гн҃и оу҆пова́хъ, да непостыждꙋ́сѧ въ вѣ́кы* (Greek: *Ἐπὶ σοί, Κύριε, ἤλπισα, μὴ καταισχυνθείην εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα* — "In Thee, O Lord, have I hoped, let me not be put to shame unto ages").

[^390]: Fol. 101v. Liturgical announcement of the Third Gospel reading: the Gospel according to Saint Matthew (Matthew 10:1, 5–8), describing Christ sending forth the Twelve Apostles with power to heal the sick and cleanse lepers.

[^391]: Fol. 102r. Conclusion of the Third Gospel reading: Matthew 10:1, 5–8a. Christ commissions the Twelve Apostles, granting them authority over unclean spirits and commanding them to heal the sick, cleanse lepers, cast out demons, and preach that the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand (*тоу́не прїѧ́сте, тоу́не дади́те* / Greek: *δωρεὰν ἐλάβετε, δωρεὰν δότε*).

[^392]: Fol. 102r. Rubric indicating the repetition of the Augmented Litany: *Дїа́кѡнства пре́же пи́санїи* ("The diaconal petitions previously written"), with the opening petition from Psalm 50:3 (LXX 50:1).

[^393]: Fol. 102v. Petitions and concluding ecphonesis of the Augmented Litany (*Ꙗ҆́ко мл҃тивый чл҃колю́бецъ...*), followed by the rubrical introduction to the Third Consecratory Prayer.

[^394]: Fol. 102v. Opening of the Third Consecratory Prayer: *Влдко Гди вседержителю, Сты́й цр҃ю въ сла́вѣ...* (Greek: *Δέσποτα, Κύριε παντοκράτορ, ἅγιε Βασιλεῦ...*), addressing the Almighty King Who chastens without putting to death and asking the sanctification of the holy oil.

[^395]: Fol. 103r. Continuation and ecphonesis of the Third Consecratory Prayer: the priest prays for divine healing to descend from heaven upon the sick candidate (*и҆́мѧ ре́къ*), quenching fever, subduing passions, and raising him from the couch of suffering (*ѿ ѻ҆́дра ѡ҆злобле́нїа* / Greek: *ἐκ κλίνης ὀδύνης*) to glorify God in His holy Church, concluded by the ecphonesis *Твое́ бо є҆́стъ є҆́же ми́ловати...*.
