[^396]: Fol. 103v. Fourth Prokeimenon in Tone 4: Psalm 101:3, 2 (LXX 101:2, 1): *Въ́ньже дн҃ь призовоу́ тѧ, ско́ро оу҆слы́ши мѧ̀...* (Greek: *Ἐν ᾗ ἂν ἡμέρᾳ ἐπικαλέσωμαί σε, тахὺ εἰσάκουσόν μου*).

[^397]: Fol. 103v. Announcement and opening of the Fourth Epistle reading: 2 Corinthians 6:16–7:1a (*вы̀ є҆стѐ цр҃кви Бг҃а жи́ва...* / Greek: *Ὑμεῖς γὰρ ναὸς Θεοῦ ἐστε ζῶντος...*), affirming that the faithful are the temple of the living God and quoting Leviticus 26:11–12 and Isaiah 52:11.

[^398]: Fol. 104r. Conclusion of the Fourth Epistle reading: 2 Corinthians 7:1b (*творѧ́ще ст҃ы́нѧ въ стра́сѣ Бж҃їи* / Greek: *ἐπιτελοῦντες ἁγιωσύνην ἐν φόβῳ Θεοῦ* — "perfecting holiness in the fear of God").

[^399]: Fol. 104r. Fourth Alleluia in Tone 2 with verse from Psalm 39:2 (LXX 39:1): *Трьпѧ̀ потрѣпѣ́хъ Гдⷭа, и҆ вънѧ́тъ ми* (Greek: *Ὑπομένων ὑπέμεινα τὸν Κύριον, καὶ προσέσχε μοι* — "With patience I waited for the Lord, and He inclined unto me").

[^400]: Fol. 104r. Announcement and opening of the Fourth Gospel reading: Matthew 8:14–17. Christ heals the mother-in-law of Saint Peter of a burning fever, drives out spirits with a word, and heals all that were sick in fulfillment of the prophecy of Isaiah 53:4 (*Тъ̀ не́доугы на́ша прїѧ́тъ, и҆ болѣ́зни понесѐ* / Greek: *Αὐτὸς τὰς ἀσθενείας ἡμῶν ἔλαβεν καὶ τὰς νόσους ἐβάστασεν*).

[^401]: Fol. 104v. Conclusion of the Fourth Gospel reading: Matthew 8:18–23. The cost of discipleship and Christ's words concerning the Son of Man having not where to lay His head, leaving the dead to bury their dead, and embarking upon the boat with His disciples.

[^402]: Fol. 104v. Opening of the Augmented Litany following the Fourth Gospel reading, praying for divine mercy, life, and restoration of the sick candidate.

[^403]: Fol. 105r. Conclusion of the Augmented Litany and its ecphonesis (*Ꙗ҆́ко мл҃тивый чл҃колю́бецъ Бг҃ъ є҆сѝ*), followed by the rubrical introduction to the Fourth Consecratory Prayer.

[^404]: Fol. 105r. Opening of the Fourth Consecratory Prayer: *Блгый и҆ чл҃колюби́вый, млⷭрде и҆ многомл҃тиве Гдⷭи...* (Greek: *Ἀγαθὲ καὶ φιλάνθρωπε, εὔσπλαγχνε καὶ πολυέλεε Κύριε...*), invoking the God of all consolation Who commanded the Apostles to heal the sick with oil and prayer (cf. James 5:14–15).

[^405]: Fol. 105v. Continuation of the Fourth Consecratory Prayer: petitioning the divine Physician of souls and bodies (*є҆ди́не дꙋша́мъже и҆ тѣ́лѡмъ вра́чю*) to raise up the sick candidate (*и҆́мѧ ре́къ*) by His mighty hand from the bed of pain to serve God with thanksgiving.

[^406]: Fol. 106r. Conclusion and ecphonesis of the Fourth Consecratory Prayer: praising God Who alone works marvelous and glorious deeds, sealed by the Trinitarian ecphonesis *Твое́ бо є҆́стъ є҆́же ми́ловати и҆ сп҃ати на́съ Бг҃е на́шъ*.

[^407]: Fol. 106r. Fifth Prokeimenon in Tone 5: Psalm 11:8, 2 (LXX 11:7, 1): *Ты̀ Гдⷭи съхрани́ши ны̀ и҆ съблюде́ши ны̀ ѿ ро́да сего̀ и҆ въ вѣ́къ...* (Greek: *Σύ, Κύριε, φυλάξεις ἡμᾶς καὶ διατηρήσεις ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ τῆς γενεᾶς ταύτης καὶ εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα*), with verse *Сп҃си́ мѧ Гдⷭи ꙗ҆́ко ѡ҆скꙋдѣ̀ прпⷣбныи* (Greek: *Σῶσόν με, Κύριε, ὅτι ἐκλέλοιπεν ὅσιος*).

[^408]: Fol. 106r. Announcement and opening of the Fifth Epistle reading: Galatians 5:22–25 (*пло́дъ дх҃о́вныи є҆́стъ, любы̀, ра́дость, ми́ръ...* / Greek: *Ὁ δὲ καρπὸς τοῦ Πνεύματός ἐστιν ἀγάπη, χαρά, εἰρήνη...*), the catalogue of the fruits of the Spirit and crucifixion of the flesh with its passions.

[^409]: Fol. 106v. Conclusion of the Fifth Epistle reading: Galatians 5:26–6:2. Exhortation against vainglory, restoring the fallen in the spirit of meekness, and bearing one another's burdens (*дроу́гъ дроу́гоу тѧготы̀ носи́те*) to fulfill the law of Christ.

[^410]: Fol. 106v. Fifth Alleluia in Tone 5 with verse from Psalm 88:2 (LXX 88:1): *Мл҃ти твоѧ̀ Гдⷭи въ вѣ́кы въспою̀* (Greek: *Τὰ ἐλέη σου, Κύριε, εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα ᾄσομαι* — "Thy mercies, O Lord, will I sing unto ages").

[^411]: Fol. 106v. Announcement and opening of the Fifth Gospel reading: Matthew 25:1–2, the Parable of the Ten Virgins (*ѻ҆у҆подо́бисѧ црⷭтво нб҃ное десѧти́мъ дѣва́мъ...*), who took their lamps to meet the bridegroom.

[^412]: Fol. 107r. Continuation of the Fifth Gospel reading: Matthew 25:3–8, the foolish virgins taking lamps without oil, the slumber during the bridegroom's delay, the midnight summons (*Се́ жени́хъ грѧде́тъ*), and the foolish virgins pleading for oil as their lamps go out (*ꙗ҆́ко свѣти́лници на́ши оу҆гаса́ютъ*).

[^413]: Fol. 107r. Matthew 25:9. The reply of the prudent virgins directing the foolish to the merchants, lest oil suffice neither for one party nor the other (*є҆да̀ ка́ко не доста́не на́мъ, и҆ ва́мъ*).

[^414]: Fol. 107v. Conclusion of the Fifth Gospel reading: Matthew 25:9–13. The arrival of the bridegroom while the foolish went to buy, the shut door, the vain plea for entry (*Гди Гди ѿвръзѝ на́мъ*), and the warning to watch for the coming of the Son of Man.

[^415]: Fol. 107v. Diaconal Insistent Litany petitions for the sick person, opening with the threefold petition *Поми́лꙋй на́съ Бж҃е по вели́цѣй мл҃ти твое́й, мо́лимъ ти сѧ*.

[^416]: Fol. 107v. Priestly ecphonesis sealing the litany: *Ꙗ҆́ко мл҃тивый и҆ чл҃колю́бецъ Бг҃ъ є҆сѝ...* (For Thou art a merciful God and the Lover of mankind).

[^417]: Fol. 107v. Rubric prescribing the Fifth Prayer of Holy Unction: *Та́же мл҃тва ҃є-аѧ* (Greek: *Εὐχὴ Ε'*).

[^418]: Fol. 108r. Opening of the Fifth Prayer of Holy Unction: *Гди Бж҃е на́шъ, нака́зꙋѧй и҆ па́ки и҆сцѣлѧ́ѧй...* (Greek: *Κύριε ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν, ὁ παιδεύων καὶ πάλιν ἰώμενος...*). Invoking God Who chastens and heals, liftest the poor from the dunghill (Psalm 112:7 / LXX 112:7), Father of orphans and Judge of widows (Psalm 67:6 / LXX 67:5), haven to the tempest-tossed, taking our infirmities upon Himself (Isaiah 53:4; Matthew 8:17), and breathing the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles to remit sins (John 20:22–23).

[^419]: Fol. 108v. Continuation of the Fifth Prayer: attributing divine authority to forgive sins and heal prolonged infirmities, and recalling the priest's unworthiness called to the exalted station of the priesthood to enter within the veil into the Holy of Holies (*въ вноу́трьнаѧ катапета́змы, въ ст҃аѧ ст҃ыхъ* / Greek: *εἰς τὰ ἐνδότερα τοῦ καταπετάσματος, εἰς τὰ Ἅγια τῶν Ἁγίων*), whereunto the angels desire to look (1 Peter 1:12), and to behold the form of the holy oblation (*самозра́чнѣ ѻ҆́бразъ ст҃го възноше́нїа*).

[^420]: Fol. 109r. Continuation of the Fifth Prayer: offering gifts and sacrifices for the priest's own sins and the people's errors (Hebrews 9:7: *ѡ҆ свои́хъ грѣсѣ́хъ, и҆ ѡ҆ лю́дскыхъ невѣ́ждествїихъ*), and interceding for the rational flock (*хода́тайствовати ѡ҆ словесныхъ ти ѻ҆вцахъ*).

[^421]: Fol. 109r. Direct petition for the sick candidate (*ра́боу твоемоу̀ и҆́мѧ ре́къ*) who is afflicted in soul and body, beseeching divine healing and remission of all offenses.

[^422]: Fol. 109v. Continuation of the Fifth Prayer: petitioning healing of incurable wounds and recalling Christ's miraculous touch that healed Peter's mother-in-law of her fever so that she arose and served Him (Matthew 8:14–15; Mark 1:30–31; Luke 4:38–39).

[^423]: Fol. 109v. Patristic/Biblical citation of Genesis 8:21 (LXX): *помѧнѝ ꙗ҆́ко приле́жно належи́тъ по́мыслъ чл҃чь на лоука́внаѧ ѿ ю́ности є҆го̀* ("remember that the mind of man is set intently on evil things from his youth" / Greek: *ἔγκειται ἡ διάνοια τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐπιμελῶς ἐπὶ τὰ πονηρὰ ἐκ νεότητος αὐτοῦ*).

[^424]: Fol. 110r. Continuation of the Fifth Prayer: evoking Psalm 142:2 (LXX 142:2) and Romans 3:19, that no flesh can be justified in judgment and every mouth is stopped; together with Isaiah 64:6 (LXX 64:6): *ꙗ҆́коже роу́бъ покрꙑже́нъ всѧ́ка пра́вда на́ша прѣ тобо́ю* (Greek: *ὡς ῥάκος ἀποκαθημένης πᾶσα ἡ δικαιοσύνη ἡμῶν* — "all our righteousness is as a polluted rag before Thee").

[^425]: Fol. 110r. Scriptural petition from Psalm 24:7 (LXX 24:7): *сегѡ̀ ра́ди грѣ́хи ю́ности, и҆ невѣ́дѣнїа на́шего не помѧнѝ Гди* ("remember not the sins of our youth and of our ignorance, O Lord" / Greek: *ἁμαρτίας νεότητός μου καὶ ἀγνοίας μου μὴ μνησθῇς, Κύριε*).

[^426]: Fol. 110r. Christological confession recalling Matthew 11:28: *Ты бо є҆сѝ наде́жда ненадѣ́ющимсѧ, и҆ поко́й троужда́ющимсѧ, и҆ ѡ҆бреме́ненымъ...* ("For Thou art the Hope of the hopeless, and the Rest of them that labor and are heavy-laden").

[^427]: Fol. 110r. Doxological opening to the Father and the Son at the foot of fol. 110r.

[^428]: Fol. 110v. Trinitarian ecphonesis concluding the Fifth Prayer of Holy Unction: *...и҆ бл҃гымъ и҆ животворѧ́щимъ ти дх҃омъ, нн҃ѣ и҆ прⷭно и҆ въ вѣ́кы вѣкѡ́мъ. А҆ми́нь*.

[^429]: Fol. 110v. Sixth Prokeimenon in Tone 6: Psalm 50:3, 12 (LXX 50:1, 10): *Помилоу́й мѧ Бж҃е по вели́цей мл҃ти твое́й...* (Greek: *Ἐλέησόν με, ὁ Θεός, κατὰ τὸ μέγα ἔλεός σου...*), with verse *Срⷣце чⷭто съзи́жди въ мнѣ̀ Бж҃е* (Greek: *Καρδίαν καθαρὰν κτίσον ἐν ἐμοί, ὁ Θεός*).

[^430]: Fol. 110v. Announcement of the Sixth Epistle reading: Colossians 3:12–17 (*а҆пл҃ъ · къ каласа́емъ посла́нїе*).

[^431]: Fol. 110v. Opening of the Sixth Epistle reading: Colossians 3:12–14: the apparel of the elect in mercy, kindness, humility, meekness, and longsuffering, mutual forbearance, and love as the bond of perfection (*съю́зъ съвръше́нїю* / Greek: *σύνδεσμος τῆς τελειότητος*).

[^432]: Fol. 111r. Conclusion of the Sixth Epistle reading: Colossians 3:15–17. The peace of God ruling hearts (*ми́ръ Бж҃їи да̀ въдворѧ́етсѧ въ срⷣцихъ ва́шихъ*), the word of Christ dwelling richly, and singing with grace to the Lord in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs.

[^433]: Fol. 111r. Sixth Alleluia in Tone 6 with verse from Psalm 111:1 (LXX 111:1): *Бл҃же́нъ мꙋ́жъ боѧ́исѧ Гдⷭа* (Greek: *Μακάριος ἀνὴρ ὁ φοβούμενος τὸν Κύριον* — "Blessed is the man that fears the Lord").

[^434]: Fol. 111r. Announcement of the Sixth Gospel reading: Luke 7:36–50 (*є҆уⷢлїе ѿ лоукы̀*).

[^435]: Fol. 111r. Opening of the Sixth Gospel reading: Luke 7:36–37: Jesus entering the house of the Pharisee Simon to dine, and the entrance of the sinful woman of the city.

[^436]: Fol. 111v. Luke 7:37–39: The sinful woman weeping, washing Christ's feet with tears, drying them with the hair of her head, kissing and anointing them with myrrh from an alabaster jar; and Simon the Pharisee's inward skepticism concerning Christ's prophetic knowledge.

[^437]: Fol. 111v. Luke 7:40–41: Christ answering Simon's unspoken thought with the Parable of the Two Debtors: *два̀ дѡ́лжника бѣ́ста заимода́вцꙋ* (Greek: *Δύο χρεωφειλέται ἦσαν δανειστῇ τινι* — "A certain creditor had two debtors").

[^438]: Fol. 112r. Luke 7:41. Continuation of the Sixth Gospel reading (Luke 7:36–50), setting forth the Parable of the Two Debtors: the one owing five hundred denarii (*пѧтїю́сотъ дина́рїи* / Greek: *πεντακόσια δηνάρια*) and the other fifty (*пѧтїюдесѧ́тъ* / Greek: *πεντήκοντα*).

[^439]: Fol. 112r. Luke 7:42. The creditor freely forgiving both debtors (*не и҆моу́щема же възда́ти, ѡ҆бѣ́ма ѿда̀* / Greek: *μὴ ἐχόντων δὲ αὐτῶν ἀποδοῦναι, ἀμφοτέροις ἐχαρίσατο*), and Christ querying Simon which debtor would love the creditor more.

[^440]: Fol. 112r. Luke 7:43–45. Simon's answer that he to whom more was forgiven loves more; Christ turning to the weeping sinful woman and reproaching Simon for omitting the customary hospitality of foot-washing water and the fraternal kiss of greeting.

[^441]: Fol. 112v. Luke 7:46. Simon failing to anoint Christ's head with oil (*ма́сломъ главы̀ мое́ѧ не пома́за*), contrasted with the woman anointing His feet with precious myrrh (*сїа же мѵ́ромъ пома́за ми нѡ́ѕѣ*).

[^442]: Fol. 112v. Luke 7:47. The theological maxim: the remission of many sins is granted to her because she loved much (*ѿпоуща́ют́сѧ грѣсѝ є҆ѧ̀ мно́ѕи, ꙗ҆ко възлюбѝ мно́го*), whereas he to whom little is forgiven loves little.

[^443]: Fol. 112v. Luke 7:48–50. Conclusion of the Sixth Gospel reading: Christ pronouncing remission of sins to the woman (*ѿпоуща́ютсѧ тебѣ̀ грѣсѝ*), the scandalized interior murmuring of the guests (*кто̀ се́й є҆́стъ и҆́же и҆ грѣхы̀ ѿпоуща́етъ*), and Christ's parting benediction: "Thy faith hath saved thee; go in peace" (*вѣ́ра твоа̀ сп҃се́ тѧ, и҆дѝ въ ми́ръ*).

[^444]: Fol. 112v. Diaconal Insistent Litany petitions for the sick person following the Sixth Gospel, opening with the threefold petition *Поми́лꙋй на́съ Бж҃е по вели́цей мл҃ти твое́й*.

[^445]: Fol. 112v. Priestly ecphonesis concluding the litany: *Ꙗ҆́ко мл҃тивый и҆ чл҃колꙋ́бецъ Бг҃ъ є҆сѝ...* (For Thou art a merciful God and the Lover of mankind).

[^446]: Fol. 113r. Rubric prescribing the Sixth Prayer of Holy Unction: *сщ҃енникъ мл҃твоу ·s҃·ю* (Greek: *Εὐχὴ Ϛ'*).

[^447]: Fol. 113r. Opening of the Sixth Prayer of Holy Unction: *Благодарю́ тѧ Гд҃и Бж҃е на́шъ, бл҃гый чл҃колю́бче...* (Greek: *Εὐχαριστῶ σοι, Κύριε ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν, ὁ ἀγαθὸς καὶ φιλάνθρωπος...*). Invoking God as Physician of souls and bodies, bearing our infirmities without pain (Isaiah 53:4; Matthew 8:17), and healing us by His wounds (Isaiah 53:5; 1 Peter 2:24).

[^448]: Fol. 113r. Christological invocation of the Good Shepherd seeking the lost sheep (Luke 15:4–6; John 10:11).

[^449]: Fol. 113r. Divine consolation granted to the faint-hearted (1 Thessalonians 5:14: *τοῖς ὀλιγοψύχοις*) and life to the crushed in spirit (Psalm 33:19 / LXX 33:18; Isaiah 57:15).

[^450]: Fol. 113r. Recalling the miraculous cure of the woman who had suffered an issue of blood for twelve years (Matthew 9:20–22; Mark 5:25–34; Luke 8:43–48).

[^451]: Fol. 113r. Recalling the deliverance of the daughter of the Canaanite woman from the torment of a demon (Matthew 15:22–28; Mark 7:25–30).

[^452]: Fol. 113r. Remission of debts granted to the two debtors (Luke 7:41–42) and forgiveness bestowed upon the sinful woman.

[^453]: Fol. 113v. Continuation of the Sixth Prayer: recalling Christ's healing of the paralytic of Capernaum together with the forgiveness of his sins (Matthew 9:2–7; Mark 2:3–12; Luke 5:18–25).

[^454]: Fol. 113v. Christ justifying the publican upon his humble prayer (Luke 18:13–14) and welcoming the repentant thief upon the cross upon his dying confession (Luke 23:40–43).

[^455]: Fol. 113v. Christ as the Lamb of God taking away the sins of the world (John 1:29) and nailing the bond of our sins to His Cross (Colossians 2:14).

[^456]: Fol. 113v. Direct petition for the sick person (*ра́боу твое́моу семоу̀ и҆́мѧ ре́къ*) for the pardon of all sins voluntary and involuntary.

[^457]: Fol. 113v. Absolution covering ecclesiastical penalties and ancestral curses: whether under a priestly curse (*а҆́ще въ клѧ́твѣ і҆ере́йстѣй*), parental curse, or sensual transgressions.

[^458]: Fol. 114r. Continuation of the Sixth Prayer: detailed confession of sins committed through the five bodily senses (sight, blinking, smell, touch, taste), bodily impulses, and spiritual alienation (*ѿлꙋчи́сѧ хоте́нїа твоего и҆ ст҃на*).

[^459]: Fol. 114r. Petition for preservation from falling into defiled living (*въ сквръ́ное житїѐ впа́сти*) or running in destructive paths.

[^460]: Fol. 114r. Supplication invoking God as bearing no malice (*непамѧтозло́бивыи Бг҃ъ* / Greek: *ἀμνησίκακος Θεός*) to overlook all offenses of the sick servant.

[^461]: Fol. 114v. Continuation of the Sixth Prayer: petitions for the sanctification and empowerment of the sick person's physical members and mental faculties (mouth, lips, hands, feet, inner thoughts) through divine grace.

[^462]: Fol. 114v. Dominical apostolic commission to bind and loose sins on earth: Matthew 18:18; Matthew 16:19 (*є҆ли́ка а҆́ще свѧ́жете на землѝ, боу́доутъ свѧ́зана на нб҃сѣхъ...*).

[^463]: Fol. 114v. Johannine dominical commission granting authority to remit sins: John 20:23 (*и҆́мже а҆́ще ѿпоу́стите грѣхы̀, ѿпоу́стѧтсѧ и҆̀мъ*).

[^464]: Fol. 115r. Conclusion of the Johannine dominical commission (John 20:23): *а҆ и҆́миже дръжитѐ, оу҆дръ́жаны соу́тъ* (and whosesoever sins ye retain, they are retained).

[^465]: Fol. 115r. Old Testament typology: God hearing the prayer of King Hezekiah in the bitterness of his mortal illness and extending his life (4 Kings 20:1–6 / LXX 4 Kings 20:1–6; Isaiah 38:1–5).

[^466]: Fol. 115r. Dominical command to forgive transgressions seventy times seven (Matthew 18:21–22: *седмъ́десѧт кра́тъ седми́цею*).

[^467]: Fol. 115r. Scriptural testimony that God relents from evil (Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2) and rejoices over the return of wandering sinners (Luke 15:7, 10).

[^468]: Fol. 115r. Scriptural citation from Sirach 2:18 (LXX 2:18): *занѐ ꙗ҆́ко вели́чество твоѐ, та́ко и҆ мл҃ть твоа̀* (Greek: *ὡς γὰρ ἡ μεγαλωσύνη αὐτοῦ, οὕτως καὶ τὸ ἔλεος αὐτοῦ* — "for as is His greatness, so also is His mercy").

[^469]: Fol. 115r. Doxological conclusion honoring the unoriginate Father (*съ безнача́льнымъ ти Ѿце́мъ*) and the All-Holy Spirit.

[^470]: Fol. 115v. Seventh Prokeimenon in Tone 7: Psalm 6:2–3 (LXX 6:1–2): *Гд҃и не ꙗ҆́ростїю твое́ю ѡ҆бличѝ менѐ, нижѐ гнѣ́вомъ твои́мъ накажѝ менѐ...* (Greek: *Κύριε, μὴ τῷ θυμῷ σου ἐλέγξῃς με, μηδὲ τῇ ὀργῇ σου παιδεύσῃς με...*), with verse *Поми́лоуй мѧ̀ Гд҃и ꙗ҆́ко не́мощенъ є҆смь* (Greek: *Ἐλέησόν με, Κύριε, ὅτι ἀσθενής εἰμι*).

[^471]: Fol. 115v. Announcement of the Seventh Epistle reading: 2 Timothy 2:1–10 (*а҆пл҃ъ къ тимоѳе́ю*).

[^472]: Fol. 115v. Opening of the Seventh Epistle reading: 2 Timothy 2:1–4. Exhortation to Timothy to be strong in grace, to commit the Apostolic teaching unto faithful teachers, to suffer hardship as a good soldier of Jesus Christ, and to remain unentangled in worldly pursuits.

[^473]: Fol. 116r. 2 Timothy 2:5. Athletic metaphor: an athlete is not crowned unless he contends lawfully (*а҆́ще же и҆ постра́ждетъ кто̀, не вѣнча́ет́сѧ, а҆́ще не зако́нно моу́ченъ боу́детъ* / Greek: *ἐὰν δὲ καὶ ἀθλῇ τις, οὐ στεφανοῦται, ἐὰν μὴ νομίμως ἀθλήσῃ*).

[^474]: Fol. 116r. 2 Timothy 2:6. Agricultural metaphor: the laboring husbandman must be the first partaker of the harvest (*троужда́ющемꙋсѧ дѣ́лателю пре́жде подоба́етъ ѿ пло́да въкоуси́ти* / Greek: *τὸν κοπιῶντα γεωργὸν δεῖ πρῶτον τῶν καρπῶν μεταλαμβάνειν*).

[^475]: Fol. 116r. 2 Timothy 2:7–9. Calling to remembrance Jesus Christ raised from the dead of the seed of David; Paul suffering chains as an evildoer, yet proclaiming that the Word of God cannot be bound (*сло́во Бж҃їе не вѧ́жет́сѧ*).

[^476]: Fol. 116r. Conclusion of the Seventh Epistle reading: 2 Timothy 2:10. Enduring all things for the elect, that they may obtain eternal salvation in Christ Jesus with eternal glory (*съ сла́вою вѣ́чною*).

[^477]: Fol. 116r. Seventh Alleluia in Tone 2 with verse from Psalm 19:2 (LXX 19:1): *оу҆слы́ши тѧ̀ Гд҃ь въ де́нь печа́ли* (Greek: *Ἐπακούσαι σου Κύριος ἐν ἡμέρᾳ θλίψεως* — "The Lord hear thee in the day of trouble").

[^478]: Fol. 116v. Announcement of the Seventh Gospel reading: Matthew 6:14–18 (*є҆ѵлїе · ѿ матѳе́а*).

[^479]: Fol. 116v. Opening of the Seventh Gospel reading: Matthew 6:14–15. The indispensable condition for divine forgiveness: forgiving the offenses of fellow men (*а҆́ще ѿпоуща́ете чл҃кѡмъ съгрѣше́нїа и҆́хъ, ѿпоу́ститъ и҆ ва́мъ Ѿц҃ъ ва́шъ нб҃ныи*).

[^480]: Fol. 116v. Matthew 6:16. Injunction against ostentatious fasting with disfigured, gloom-stricken faces to gain the praise of men.

[^481]: Fol. 116v. Matthew 6:17–18. Injunction to fast interiorly before God: anointing the head and washing the face, seeking approval solely from the heavenly Father Who sees in secret.

[^482]: Fol. 117r. Matthew 6:18–21. Conclusion of the Seventh Gospel reading (Matthew 6:14–21): divine recompense for hidden fasting and righteousness (*ви́дѧй въ та́инѣ възда́стъ тебѣ̀ ꙗ҆́вѣ*), followed by the Dominical counsel against storing earthly treasures prone to corruption (*чрь́вь и҆ тлѧ̀ тли́тъ* / Greek: *σὴς καὶ βρῶσις ἀφανίζει*) and theft, directing believers to lay up incorruptible treasures in heaven where their heart must dwell.

[^483]: Fol. 117r. Insistent Litany petitions following the Seventh Gospel for the sick person, chanted by the deacon (or priest), opening with the threefold *Поми́луй на́съ, Бо́же*, followed by supplications for mercy, life, remission of sins, and the divine bestowal of healing grace.

[^484]: Fol. 117r. Priestly ecphonesis concluding the litany: *Ꙗ҆́ко мл҃тивый чл҃колꙋ́бецъ...* (For Thou art a merciful God and Lover of mankind...), followed by the diaconal dismissal/invitation to prayer *Гдⷵꙋ помоли́мсѧ* and the rubric introducing the Seventh Prayer of Holy Unction.

[^485]: Fol. 117v. Seventh Prayer of Holy Unction (Greek: *Εὐχὴ Ζ'*): *Δέσποτα Κύριε ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν, ὁ ἰατρὸς τῶν ψυχῶν καὶ τῶν σωμάτων...* (Master, Lord our God, Physician of souls and bodies...).

[^486]: Fol. 117v. Invocation of God as Physician of souls and bodies, healing chronic ailments (*многолѣ́тныѧ стра́сти лѣкꙋ́ѧ* / Greek: *ὁ τὰ χρόνια πάθη ἰώμενος*) and every sickness among the people (Matthew 4:23, 9:35).

[^487]: Fol. 117v. Allusion to Matthew 4:23 and 9:35: healing every disease and every sickness among the people (*θεραπεύων πᾶσαν νόσον καὶ πᾶσαν μαλακίαν ἐν τῷ λαῷ*).

[^488]: Fol. 117v. Citation of 1 Timothy 2:4: *и҆́же хотѧ́й всѣ́мъ чл҃кѡмъ сп҃ти́сѧ, и҆ въ ра́зоумъ и҆́стинныи прїитѝ* (Greek: *ὃς πάντας ἀνθρώπους θέλει σωθῆναι καὶ εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν ἀληθείας ἐλθεῖν* — "Who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth").

[^489]: Fol. 117v. Citation of Ezekiel 33:11 (and Ezekiel 18:23, 32): *не хотѧ́й сме́рти грѣ́шникоу, но ꙗ҆́ко ѡ҆брати́тисѧ, и҆ жи́воу бы́ти є҆моу́* (Greek: *οὐ βούλομαι τὸν θάνατον τοῦ ἀσεβοῦς, ὡς τὸ ἀποστρέψαι... καὶ ζῆν αὐτόν*).

[^490]: Fol. 117v. Old Testament paradigms of divine forbearance and repentance: King David (2 Kings 12:13 / LXX 2 Kings 12:13; Psalm 50 / LXX 50), the Ninevites at the preaching of Jonah (Jonah 3:5–10), and the patriarchs before them.

[^491]: Fol. 117v. Dominical saying from Matthew 9:13; Mark 2:17; Luke 5:32: *не призва́лъ є҆си пра́ведныѧ но грѣ́шныѧ на покаѧ́нїе* (Greek: *οὐκ ἦλθον καλέσαι δικαίους, ἀλλὰ ἁμαρτωλοὺς εἰς μετάνοιαν*).

[^492]: Fol. 117v. New Testament paradigms of repentance: the publican Zacchaeus/Levi (Luke 18:13–14, 19:1–10) and the sinful woman/harlot (Luke 7:37–50).

[^493]: Fol. 118r. The repentant thief on the cross (Luke 23:39–43).

[^494]: Fol. 118r. The conversion and pardon of the Apostle Paul, formerly a blasphemer and persecutor (1 Timothy 1:13: *τὸν πρότερον ὄντα βλάσφημον καὶ διώκτην*; Acts 9:1–19).

[^495]: Fol. 118r. The threefold denial and restoration of the Apostle Peter upon bitter weeping and repentance (Matthew 26:69–75; Mark 14:66–72; Luke 22:54–62; John 21:15–19).

[^496]: Fol. 118r. Matthew 16:18–19. The Petrine confession and Dominical promise: *ты́ є҆си пе́тръ, и҆ на се́мъ ка́мени съзи́ждꙋ цр҃ковь мою̀ · и҆ вра́та а҆́дова не оу҆долѣ́ютъ є҆ѝ · и҆ да́ти ключа̀ црⷵтвїа нб҃наго* (Greek: *σὺ εἶ Πέτρος, καὶ ἐπὶ ταύτῃ τῇ πέτρᾳ οἰκοδομήσω μου τὴν ἐκκλησίαν, καὶ πύλαι ᾅδου οὐ κατισχύσουσιν αὐτῆς· καὶ δώσω σοι τὰς κλεῖς τῆς βασιλείας τῶν οὐρανῶν*).

[^497]: Fol. 118r. Psalm 140:2 (LXX 140:2): *оу҆слы́ши моле́нїе на́ше, и҆ прїимѝ ѐ ꙗ҆́коже кади́ло приноси́мое тебѣ̀* (Greek: *κατευθυνθήτω ἡ προσευχή μου ὡς θυμίαμα ἐνώπιόν σου* — "Let my prayer be set forth before Thee as incense").

[^498]: Fol. 118r. Rubrical insertion of the sick person's baptismal name: *раба̀ твоего и҆́млⷶ ре́къ* ("Thy servant [Name]").

[^499]: Fol. 118v. Comprehensive absolution formulas in the Seventh Prayer: covering sins committed in word, deed, or thought, by night or day, ecclesiastical censures/priestly curses (*клѧ́тва і҆ере́йскаѧ*), self-cursing (*своѐ проклѧ́тїе*), and rash or bitter oaths (*клѧ́твою ѡ҆горчѝ себѐ*).

[^500]: Fol. 118v. The classic tripartite liturgical petition for remission: *ѡ҆сла́би, ѡ҆ста́ви, простѝ* (Greek: *ἄνες, ἄφες, συγχώρησον* — loosen, remit, forgive).

[^501]: Fol. 118v. Forgiveness of sins committed consciously and unconsciously: *въ вѣ́дѣнїи, и҆ въ невѣ́ждествѣ* (Greek: *τὰ ἐν γνώσει καὶ ἐν ἀγνοίᾳ*).

[^502]: Fol. 118v. Frailties arising from bodily corruptibility, worldly entanglement, and demonic subversion (*ѿ дѣ́йства дїа́вольскаго* / Greek: *ἐξ ἐπηρείας τοῦ διαβόλου*).

[^503]: Fol. 118v. Citation of 2 Chronicles 6:36 / 3 Kings 8:46 / LXX 2 Paralipomenon 6:36 (and Ecclesiastes 7:21 / LXX 7:20): *нѣ́сть чл҃ка и҆́же поживе́тъ, и҆ не съгрѣши́тъ* (Greek: *οὐκ ἔστιν ἄνθρωπος ὃς οὐχ ἁμαρτήσεται* — "for there is no man who will not sin").

[^504]: Fol. 119r. Christological confession: *ты́ бо є҆ди́нъ є҆си безгрѣ́шенъ* (Greek: *σὺ γὰρ μόνος εἶ ἀναμάρτητος* — "for Thou alone art sinless").

[^505]: Fol. 119r. Psalm 118:142 (LXX 118:142): *пра́вда твоа̀ пра́вда въ вѣ́кы, и҆ сло́во твоѐ и҆́стинна* (Greek: *ἡ δικαιοσύνη σου δικαιοσύνη εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα, καὶ ὁ νόμος σου ἀλήθεια* / John 17:17: *ὁ λόγος ὁ σὸς ἀλήθειά ἐστιν* — "Thy righteousness is righteousness unto eternity, and Thy word is truth").

[^506]: Fol. 119r. Theological anthropology: God created humanity not for ruin (*нѣ́си бо созда́лъ чл҃ка на па́гоубоу* / Greek: *οὐ γὰρ ἐποίησας τὸν ἄνθρωπον εἰς ἀπώλειαν*), but for the keeping of His precepts and the inheritance of eternal incorruption (Wisdom of Solomon 1:13–14, 2:23).

[^507]: Fol. 119r. Doxological closure of the Seventh Prayer of Holy Unction.

[^508]: Fol. 119r. Rubric for the imposition of the Holy Gospel upon the head of the sick person: *Та́же, въсхо́дитъ посрѣдѣ̀ сщ҃енникѡ́въ творѧ́й маслосвѧще́нїе...* (Then he that performs the Holy Unction [the sick person / celebrant] steps into the midst of the priests; and the superior [pristatel] of the priests, taking the Holy Gospel, lays it open upon his head; and the other priests place their hands upon it; and the presiding priest [pristoinik] recites the prayer of imposition with a loud voice). In Byzantine and Ruthenian practice, the open Book of the Gospels is placed text downwards upon the head of the sick person, symbolizing the hand of Christ Himself healing and forgiving him.

[^509]: Fol. 119v. Prayer of the Imposition of the Gospel (Greek: *Εὐχὴ ἐπὶ τῶν ἀσθενούντων ἐπιτιθεμένου τοῦ Εὐαγγελίου*): *Βασιλεῦ ἅγιε, εὔσπλαγχνε καὶ πολυέλεε Κύριε Ἰησοῦ Χριστέ...* (Holy King, compassionate and plenteous in mercy, Lord Jesus Christ...).

[^510]: Fol. 119v. Christological titles: Holy King, compassionate, plenteous in mercy, Son and Word of the living God (Matthew 16:16; John 1:1).

[^511]: Fol. 119v. Reiteration of Ezekiel 33:11: God desiring not the death of the sinner, but his repentance and life.

[^512]: Fol. 119v. Epigraphic and rubrical theology of the imposition: the priest acknowledges his own unworthiness, disclaiming the imposition of his own sinful hand (*не възлага́ю грѣ́шныѧ рꙋкы̀ моѧ̀*), asserting that it is the mighty hand of Christ present in the Holy Gospel held by the con-celebrants (*но твою роу́коу крѣ́пкоую, и҆ си́лноую ю҆́же въ ст҃ѣ́мъ є҆ѵлїи се́мъ* / Greek: *ἀλλὰ τὴν σὴν χεῖρα τὴν κραταιὰν καὶ ἰσχυράν, τὴν ἐν τῷ ἁγίῳ Εὐαγγελίῳ τούτῳ*) that rests upon the sick person's head.

[^513]: Fol. 119v. Invocation of divine unresentful love: *непамѧтозло́бное чл҃колю́бїе* (Greek: *ἀμνησίκακος φιλανθρωπία*).

[^514]: Fol. 119v. Remission of King David's adultery and blood-guilt through the ministry of the Prophet Nathan (2 Kings 12:1–13 / LXX 2 Kings 12:1–13: *Καὶ Κύριος παρεβίβασε τὸ ἁμάρτημά σου* — "And the Lord hath put away thy sin").

[^515]: Fol. 120r. The penitential prayer and restoration of King Manasseh (2 Chronicles 33:12–13 / LXX 2 Paralipomenon 33:12–13; Prayer of Manasseh).

[^516]: Fol. 120r. Petition for the sick person: acceptance according to divine accustomed philanthropy (*прїимѝ ѡ҆бы́чнымъ ти чл҃колю́бїемъ* / Greek: *πρόσδεξαι τῇ συνήθει σου φιλανθρωπίᾳ*).

[^517]: Fol. 120r. Dominical ordinance to forgive seventy times seven: Matthew 18:21–22 (*седмьдесѧ́тъ кра́тъ седмери́цею*).

[^518]: Fol. 120r. Sirach 2:18 (LXX 2:18): *занѐ ꙗ҆́ко вели́чество твоѐ, та́ко и҆ мл҃ть твоа̀* (Greek: *ὡς γὰρ ἡ μεγαλωσύνη αὐτοῦ, οὕτως καὶ τὸ ἔλεος αὐτοῦ* — "for as His majesty is, so is His mercy").

[^519]: Fol. 120r. Doxology concluding the Prayer of Imposition of the Gospel.

[^520]: Fol. 120r. Rubric for the veneration of the Gospel: *И҆ та́ко болѧ́щїй цѣлоу́етъ ст҃о́е є҆ѵлїе...* (And then the sick person kisses the Holy Gospel. And the priests, having finished the prayer, say this:).

[^521]: Fol. 120v. Priestly formula of benediction accompanying the veneration of the Gospel: *Бл҃гослове́нїе Гд҃а Бг҃а и҆ сп҃са на́шего...* (The blessing of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, unto the healing of soul and body...).

[^522]: Fol. 120v. Rubric for mutual anointing: *И҆ начина́ютъ сщ҃енници ма́зати дроу́гъ дроу́га...* (And the priests begin to anoint one another, and all those who desire this blessing, singing this sticheron in Tone 4, automelon). In Ruthenian and Byzantine tradition, the leftover consecrated oil is shared: the priests anoint each other and the attending faithful.

[^523]: Fol. 120v. Melodic model / automelon sticheron in Tone 4: *Исто́чникъ и҆сцѣле́нїемъ, и҆моу́ще ст҃і́и безсре́брници* (Greek: *Πηγὴν ἰαμάτων ἔχοντες, ἅγιοι Ἀνάργυροι* — "Having a fountain of healings, O holy Unmercenaries"). Rendered strictly in compliance with Mandate 9 (Canonical 3-Layer Melodic Model Law).

[^524]: Fol. 120v. Troparion/Sticheron of the Holy Unmercenary Physicians (Cosmas and Damian, Cyrus and John, Panteleimon, Hermolaus, Sampson, Diomedes, Mokios, Aniketos, Thallelaios, Tryphon, et al.): invoked as channels of Christ's ever-flowing healing spring.

[^525]: Fol. 120v. Dominical commission of healing and exorcism: Matthew 10:1; Luke 9:1, 10:19 (*сѐ да́хъ ва́мъ вла́сть на доу́сѣхъ нечи́стыхъ · ꙗ҆́ко и҆згони́ти и҆́хъ* / Greek: *ἰδοὺ δέδωκα ὑμῖν τὴν ἐξουσίαν... ἐπὶ πνευμάτων ἀκαθάρτων, ὥστε ἐκβάλλειν αὐτά*).

[^526]: Fol. 121r. Matthew 10:1: *цѣли́ти всѧ́къ не́дꙋгъ, и҆ всѧ́коу боле́знь* (Greek: *θεραπεύειν πᾶσαν νόσον καὶ πᾶσαν μαλακίαν* — "to heal all manner of sickness and all manner of disease").

[^527]: Fol. 121r. Dominical injunction to the Apostles and holy unmercenaries: Matthew 10:8: *тоу́не прїѧ́сте, тоу́не же дади́те* (Greek: *δωρεὰν ἐλάβετε, δωρεὰν δότε* — "Freely ye have received, freely give").

[^528]: Fol. 121r. Conclusion of the Sticheron of the Unmercenaries: supplicating their intercessory physicianhood for bodily and spiritual passions.

[^529]: Fol. 121r. Liturgical doxological formula introducing the Theotokion: *Сла́ва, и҆ нн҃ѣ · Бг҃о ·* (Glory... both now... Theotokion).

[^530]: Fol. 121r. Opening of the Theotokion: *Болѣ́знїю лю́тою ѡ҆дръжи́мъ · ѿ ѡ҆бою стра́ноу пробода́емъ* (Held fast by cruel sickness, pierced through on either side). An expressive Byzantine poetic lamentation depicting double affliction: spiritual guilt within and bodily ulceration without.

[^531]: Fol. 121r. Bodily and spiritual diagnostic imagery: spirit languishing under weight of sins (*дх҃ъ ѡ҆бнемощева́ет ми въ грѣсѣ́хъ мно́зѣхъ*) while the flesh is afflicted with ulcers and putrefaction (*тѣ́ло же па́ки боли́тъ ми строу́пы, и҆ гное́нїемъ* / Psalm 37:6 / LXX 37:5: *προσώζεσαν καὶ ἐσάπησαν οἱ μώλωπές μου*).

[^532]: Fol. 121r. Maternal intercession of the Mother of God: *мо́жеши бо є҆ли́ка хо́щеши* (for thou art able to do whatsoever thou willest), petitioning Christ the Savior to grant pardon, mercy, and compassion (*оу҆щѣдре́нїе* / Greek: *οἰκτιρμούς*) unto the world.

[^533]: Fol. 121r. Rubrical transition: *И҆ поси́мъ пома́завшиисѧ взаи́мнѡ...* (And after this, having anointed one another mutually...).

[^534]: Fol. 121v. Rubric prescribing the final anointing of the sick person and the concluding Insistent Litany: *пома́зꙋютъ и҆ болѧ́щаго · и҆ гл҃ют є҆кте́нїю є҆ди́нъ по є҆диномꙋ ра́дом* (they anoint also the sick person; and they say the litany, one by one in turn). Note the conciliar rubrical practice: each con-celebrating priest recites a petition in order (*ра́дом* / Greek: *ἐν τάξει*).

[^535]: Fol. 121v. Opening threefold petition of the concluding Insistent Litany: *Поми́луй на́съ, Бо́же, по вели́цѣй ми́лости Твое́й...* (Psalm 50:3 / LXX 50:1).

[^536]: Fol. 121v. Liturgical petition for the sick person specifying mercy, life, health, salvation, and divine visitation (*ѡ҆ посѣще́нїи* / Greek: *ὑπὲρ ἐπισκέψεως*).

[^537]: Fol. 121v. Petition for remission of all voluntary and involuntary sins (*во́лномꙋ, и҆ нево́лномꙋ* / Greek: *ἑκουσίου τε καὶ ἀκουσίου*).

[^538]: Fol. 121v. Supplication for physical recovery and deliverance: that the Lord raise the sick servant from his bed of suffering (*ѿ ѻ҆́дра болѣ́зньнаго* / Greek: *ἐκ κλίνης ὀδύνης*), invoking Psalm 40:4 (LXX 40:3: *Κύριος βοηθήσαι αὐτῷ ἐπὶ κλίνης ὀδύνης αὐτοῦ*).

[^539]: Fol. 121v. Priestly ecphonesis concluding the litany: *Ꙗ҆́ко мл҃тивъ и҆ чл҃колю́бецъ Бг҃ъ є҆си...* (For Thou art a merciful God and the Lover of mankind...), continuing onto Fol. 122r (Page 261).

[^540]: Fol. 122r. Conclusion of the Priestly Ecphonesis of the Insistent Litany: *и҆ въ вѣ́кы вѣкѡ́мъ* ("and unto ages of ages"), concluding the liturgical doxology begun on Fol. 121v.

[^541]: Fol. 122r. The dismissal (*ѿпоу́стъ* / Greek: *ἀπόλυσις*) and concluding rubrics for the host/patient: *позъва́выи на маслосвѧще́нїе* (he who called for the Holy Unction, i.e., the householder or the sick person who summoned the con-celebrating presbyters).

[^542]: Fol. 122r. Penitential formula of Apodosis: *Блгⷭви́те ѻ҆тцы̀ ст҃і́и, и҆ прости́те мѧ̀ грѣ́шнаго* ("Bless me, holy fathers, and forgive me, a sinner"), prescribed to be repeated thrice with metanias/prostrations, followed by the presbyters' reciprocal blessing and forgiveness (*блгⷭве́нїе и҆ проще́нїе*).

[^543]: Fol. 122v. Blank folio (*vacat*) concluding Quire `о` and the Order of Holy Unction (*Маслосвященіе*).

[^544]: Fol. 123r. Heading and titular woodcut: *ЧИ́НЪ БЫВА́ЕМЫИ Е҆ГДА̀ КТО ХО́ЩЕТЪ ВЪ НАЧА́ЛѢ И҆СПОВѢ́ДАТИСѦ* (Greek: *Τάξις γινομένη ἐπὶ ἐξομολογουμένων*). The woodcut depicts the Crucifixion with the Mother of God and St. John the Apostle (*і҆ н ц і҆* / INRI). This service constitutes the foundational Ruthenian rite of initial or general life confession before the spiritual father.

[^545]: Fol. 123r. Preliminary pastoral exhortation of the spiritual father (*дꙋхо́вникъ* / Greek: *πνευματικός*): *прѣ́жде дꙋхо́вникъ поꙋчи́тъ є҆го̀ си́це гл҃ѧ* ("First the spiritual father instructs him, saying thus").

[^546]: Fol. 123r. The spiritual father addresses the penitent: *Ча́до моѐ хотѧ́щее ѡ҆бнови́тисѧ чтⷭны покая́нїемъ* ("My child, who desirest to be renewed by honorable repentance").

[^547]: Fol. 123r. Patristic theme of recovery of the heavenly fatherland and filial adoption (*възыска́ти пръваго ѻ҆тьчьства · и҆ сно́вства причасти́тисѧ* / Greek: *υἱοθεσία* / Romans 8:15, Galatians 4:5), forfeited through ancestral transgression (*престоупле́нїемъ*).

[^548]: Fol. 123r. Dominical patience awaiting the sinner's return: *ка́ко ти жде́тъ Бг҃ъ покая́нїя на́шего · прⷬко́мъ въпїе́тъ на́мъ* ("how God awaits our repentance; through the Prophet He cries aloud unto us"), citing the prophetic invitations to penance (Ezekiel 18:21–32, 33:11; Isaiah 1:16–19; Jeremiah 3:12–22), continuing onto Fol. 123v.

[^549]: Fol. 123v. Prophetic citation of divine call to repentance: *поси́хъ въсѣ́хъ ѡ҆брати́тесѧ къ мнѣ̀, и҆ а҆́зъ и҆сцѣлю̀ вы* ("After all these things, turn ye unto Me, and I will heal you" / cf. Jeremiah 3:7, 3:22; Hosea 14:4).

[^550]: Fol. 123v. Canonical warning regarding impenitence: dying without repentance deprives one of Christian burial and liturgical commemoration; the priest is forbidden to vest in sacerdotal robes (*ѡ҆блещи́сѧ*) or offer the liturgical oblation (*приноше́нїа* / Greek: *προσφορά*) for an unrepentant person.

[^551]: Fol. 123v. Exposition of orthodox Trinitarian catechesis given by the spiritual father to the penitent: the unoriginate oneness of God (*не и҆мы́й ни ѿкоу́доуже нача́ла* / Greek: *ἄναρχος*), the eternal Word (*сло́во събезнача́лное* / Greek: *συνάναρχος Λόγος*), and the consubstantial Trinity.

[^552]: Fol. 124r. Classical theological phrasing for the Holy Trinity: *трїе съста́вы съли́чны въ є҆диномъ бж҃твѣ̀* (Greek: *τρεῖς ὑποστάσεις συμφυεῖς ἐν μιᾷ θεότητι* — three hypostases of like nature in one Godhead).

[^553]: Fol. 124r. Christological confession of the Incarnation: the Word, being God of God, clothed His divinity with flesh (*пло́тїю ѡ҆бложи́въ своѐ Бж҃тво*), conceived without seed in the Virgin (*беⷭ сѣ́мени*), becoming truly God and man together (*соугꙋ́бо Бг҃ъ въскоу́пѣ и҆ чл҃къ* / Greek: *θεάνθρωπος*).

[^554]: Fol. 124r. Summary of the Paschal mystery and Eschatology: voluntary Passion and Crucifixion, Resurrection on the third day, Ascension, session at the right hand of the Father, and the Second Coming to judge the living and the dead according to their works (Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed; Romans 2:6; 2 Corinthians 5:10).

[^555]: Fol. 124v. Post-baptismal repentance (*по кр҃ще́нїи сътво́рше · покаѧ́нїемъ*): the Patristic understanding of confession as a "second baptism" of tears and repentance before the all-knowing God.

[^556]: Fol. 124v. Apostolic authority and pastoral burden of the priesthood: *цр҃ко́внымъ сщ҃е́нникѡмъ подъи́мати тѧ́готы ва́ша* (bearing burdens, cf. Galatians 6:2), citing Hebrews 13:17: *тї́и бо бдѧ́тъ ѡ҆ дꙋша́хъ ва́шихъ* ("for they watch over your souls").

[^557]: Fol. 124v. Ceremonial entrance of the penitent: *съгбѣ́ныма рꙋка́ма* ("with folded hands" or crossed upon the breast, expressing subjection and contrition).

[^558]: Fol. 124v. Priestly invitation to adore God (*поклони́сѧ Бг҃у*), the penitent making three bows (*г҃*), followed by dialogic responsive prayer (*по́пъ прѣ́жде, а҆ ѻ҆́нъ послѣди* — the priest reciting first, and the penitent repeating each petition after him).

[^559]: Fol. 125r. Responsive penitential versicles recited by the priest and repeated by the penitent: the Publican's prayer (*Боже, очисти мя грешнаго* / Luke 18:13), *Господи, согреших, помилуй мя*, and the supplication for pardon of countless sins (*без числа согреших*).

[^560]: Fol. 125r. Rubric for the disposition of the Holy Gospel and the Cross: the priest places them upon the analogion (*а҆нало́й* / Greek: *ἀναλόγιον*) before the sanctuary screen / iconostasis (*пред олтарем*).

[^561]: Fol. 125r. Bodily posture of the penitent during confession: laying hands and head directly upon the Book of the Gospels (*положи́тъ рꙋ́цѣ и҆ гла́воу на є҆ѵⷢлїи*), signifying direct accountability before Christ the Chief Shepherd.

[^562]: Fol. 125r. Opening doxology (*Благословен Бог наш...*) followed by the standard Trisagion Prayers through the Lord's Prayer, priestly ecphonesis, twelvefold *Kyrie eleison*, and threefold *Venite adoremus* (*Приидите поклонимся*).

[^563]: Fol. 125r. Incipit of the first Penitential Psalm, Psalm 6 (LXX 6: *Господи, да не яростию Твоею обличиши мене*), followed by the printer's rubrical folio cross-reference directing the reader to Fol. 141r (Page 297): *смотрѝ в листѣ̀ рм҃а*.

[^564]: Fol. 125v. Psalm 31 (LXX 31:1–2): *Блажени имже отпустишася беззакония...* ("Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered" / Romans 4:7–8).

[^565]: Fol. 125v. Psalm 31:3–4 (LXX 31:3–4): physical and spiritual suffering under silent unconfessed sin: *Яко умолчах, обетшаша кости моя...* (*ἐστράφην εἰς ταλαιπωρίαν ἐν τῷ ἐμπαγῆναι ἄканθαν*).

[^566]: Fol. 125v. Psalm 31:5–6a (LXX 31:5–6a): liberating confession of sin and immediate divine remission: *исповем на мя беззаконие мое Господеви: и Ты отпустил еси нечестие сердца моего*.

[^567]: Fol. 126r. Psalm 31:6b–8 (LXX 31:6b–8): divine protection and pastoral instruction: *Ты еси прибежище мое... Вразумлю тя, и наставлю тя на путь сей...*

[^568]: Fol. 126r. Psalm 31:9–11 (LXX 31:9–11): warning against stubborn impenitence (*не будите яко конь и меск...*) and concluding jubilation of the forgiven righteous (*Возвеселитеся о Господе...*).

[^569]: Fol. 126r. Prescribed recitations following Psalm 31: Psalm 50 (LXX 50: *Помилуй мя, Боже*) and the Symbol of Faith (*И верую в единаго Бога* — the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed), both cited by incipit.

[^570]: Fol. 126v. Rubric and first penitential Troparion, Tone 1: *Ѡб̾ѧ́тїа ѻ҆́ч҃а ѿвръ́сти ми потъщи́сѧ* (the classical hymn of the Prodigal Son, Luke 15:11–32; Greek: *Τὰς πατρικὰς ἀγκάλας διανοῖξαί μοι σπεῦσον*).

[^571]: Fol. 126v. Second penitential Troparion: *Въ разбо́йникы въпадо́хъ...* utilizing the parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:30–37) as an allegory of the soul wounded by demonic thieves, seeking the healing oil and wine of divine mercy through the intercession of the holy Forerunner (*прⷱте́ча моли́твами*).

[^572]: Fol. 126v. Doxological formula: *Сла́ва* ("Glory [to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit]").

[^573]: Fol. 126v. Third penitential Troparion (*Сле́зы ми да́ждь, Бо́же, я́коже дре́вле...*), petitioning for the tears of the sinful woman who washed Christ's feet (Luke 7:36–50), continuing onto Fol. 127r (Page 271).

[^574]: Fol. 127r. Continuation and conclusion of the third penitential troparion (Tone 1) begun on Fol. 126v: alluding to the sinful woman who washed Christ's feet with her tears and anointed them with fragrant myrrh (Luke 7:37–50), and the Dominical absolution: *вѣ́ра твоѧ̀ сп҃се́ тѧ, и҆дѝ въ ми́ръ* ("Thy faith has saved thee, go in peace"; Luke 7:50, Luke 8:48).

[^575]: Fol. 127r. The doxological incipit: *И҆ нн҃ѣ* ("Both now and ever, and unto ages of ages. Amen"), introducing the concluding Theotokion.

[^576]: Fol. 127r. Penitential Theotokion (*А҆́зъ дв҃о ст҃аѧ Бц҃е подъ кро́въ тво́й прибѣга́ю...*), expressing recourse to the Mother of God as the unfailing refuge and mediatrix of penitent sinners.

[^577]: Fol. 127r. Rubric for the first sacerdotal prayer of the spiritual father over the penitent: *Сїю̀ моли́твꙋ, глаго́летъ дꙋхо́вникъ ѡ҆ не́мъ* ("This prayer the spiritual father says over him"). In classical Byzantine and Ruthenian Euchologia (e.g. Goar, *Euchologion*, rite of confession; Trebnyk of Peter Mohyla), this prayer is recited by the spiritual father prior to hearing the penitent's confession, imploring divine mercy and discernment for himself as minister of the sacrament.

[^578]: Fol. 127r. Sacerdotal prayer opening: *Ще́дрый и҆ ми́лостивый Бг҃е...* (Greek: *Οἰκτίρμων καὶ ἐλεήμων Θεός...*), invoking God Who searches hearts and reins (Psalm 7:10 [LXX 7:9], Jeremiah 11:20, Revelation 2:23) and knows the hidden things of mankind (Romans 2:16), continuing onto Fol. 127v.

[^579]: Fol. 127v. Scriptural allusion to Hebrews 4:13: "Neither is there any creature that is not manifest in His sight: but all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of Him with Whom we have to do" (*всѧ̑ на̑га и҆ ѿкрове́нна прѣⷣ ѡчи́ма твои́ма* / Greek: *πάντα δὲ γυμνὰ καὶ τετραχηλισμένα τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς αὐτοῦ*).

[^580]: Fol. 127v. Supplication of the presbyter for his own unworthiness, echoing Psalm 26:9 (LXX 26:9): "Turn not away Thy face from me" (*ни́же лица̀ твое́го ѿвратѝ ѿ ме́не*).

[^581]: Fol. 127v. Invocation of divine sanctification upon the minister: *неви́димою и҆ дх҃овною сѐи десни́цею* ("by this Thine invisible and spiritual right hand"), expressing that the priest's visible imposition of hands is but an icon of Christ's invisible right hand.

[^582]: Fol. 127v. Pastoral trembling of the priest before the awe-inspiring responsibility of the keys (cf. 1 Corinthians 9:27): *да не и҆́нѣмъ свобожде́нїе ѡ҆бѣщава́ѧ... са́мъ же ꙗ҆́ко ра́бъ неискоу́сенъ грѣхоу̀ пови́ненъ бꙋ́дꙋ* (lest preaching or promising remission to others, he himself become disqualified / Greek: *ἀδόκιμος*).

[^583]: Fol. 127v. Sacerdotal petition (*да невъзвращꙋ́сѧ* — "let me not turn back [humbled and put to shame]"), continuing directly onto Fol. 128r.

[^584]: Fol. 128r. Charismatic gifts implored for the confessor: power from on high (Luke 24:49), the word of wisdom (1 Corinthians 12:8), and the discernment of spirits (*раꙁсꙋжде́нїа дх҃ѡ́въ* / 1 Corinthians 12:10: *διάκρισις πνευμάτων*), vital for discerning the roots of sin and spiritual warfare.

[^585]: Fol. 128r. Pauline mystical petition: *въѡбрази́ ми Хрⷭта̀ въ оу҆́дѣхъ мои́хъ* (Galatians 4:19: *μορφωθῇ Χριστός* — that Christ be formed within the presbyter's faculties and members as an icon of the Good Shepherd).

[^586]: Fol. 128r. Rubric for naming the penitent: *и҆́мѧ ре́къ* ("having said the name"), indicating the insertion of the Christian name of the person coming to confession.

[^587]: Fol. 128r. Spiritual fatherhood and regeneration: the priest begets the penitent unto spiritual renewal (1 Corinthians 4:15: "I have begotten you"), edifying him upon the apostolic foundation (Ephesians 2:20: *на основа́ніи святы́хъ апо́столъ и҆ проро́къ*).

[^588]: Fol. 128r. Ecclesial integration: *насадѝ са́дъ и҆́стиненъ, въ ст҃ѣ́й свое́й въселе́нстѣй и҆ а҆пл҃тѣй цр҃кви* ("plant him as a true plant in Thy holy, catholic, and apostolic Church"; cf. Romans 6:5, Romans 11:17–24).

[^589]: Fol. 128r. Pastoral petition for the penitent's unfeigned faith (1 Timothy 1:5: *вѣ́ры нелицемѣ́рны*), continuing onto Fol. 128v.

[^590]: Fol. 128v. Pastoral prayer for contrition and honesty in confession: that the penitent may expose and denounce his own iniquity (*ѡ҆бличи́тъ безако́нїе своѐ*) without concealment, false shame, or self-justification.

[^591]: Fol. 128v. Life of righteousness and holiness following absolution, echoing Luke 1:75 ("in holiness and righteousness before Him, all the days of our life").

[^592]: Fol. 128v. Trinitarian ecphonesis concluding the first preparatory prayer of the spiritual father: *нн҃ѣ и҆ прⷭно и҆ въ вѣ́кы вѣкѡ́мъ, а҆ми́нь* ("now and ever, and unto ages of ages. Amen").

[^593]: Fol. 128v. Rubric of physical contrition: *Пото́мъ ка́ѧисѧ твори́тъ поклоне́нїа трѝ до землѧ̀, глаго́лѧ си́це* ("Then the penitent makes three prostrations to the ground, saying thus"), introducing the metanias and opening formula on Fol. 129r.

[^594]: Fol. 129r. Penitential cry of the Publican (Luke 18:13: *Боже, милостивъ буди мнѣ грѣшному*), repeated three times with prostrations as indicated in the preceding rubric.

[^595]: Fol. 129r. Liturgical bodily posture of supplication: *та́же просте́ръ рꙋ́цѣ* ("then having stretched forth his hands"), an ancient orans/suppliant gesture of self-surrender before the Gospel and the Cross.

[^596]: Fol. 129r. Penitential confession formula: *И҆сповѣ́даю тебѣ̀ Го́споди Бо́же небесѝ и҆ землѝ всѧ̑ та́йнаѧ се́рдца мое́го* ("I confess unto Thee, O Lord God of heaven and earth, all the secrets of my heart"; cf. Matthew 11:25, Psalm 43:22 [LXX 43:21]).

[^597]: Fol. 129r. Second sacerdotal prayer over the penitent: *Сы́й превѣ́чный влады́ко Го́споди...* (Greek: *Ὁ ὢν προαιώνιος Δέσποτα Κύριε...*). This prayer resembles the ancient pre-baptismal and exorcistic prayers, here applied to the reconciliation of a penitent: recounting the creation of man in the image and likeness of God (Genesis 1:26), the Fall, and redemption through the Incarnation of Christ (*въчеловѣ́ченіемъ Христа̀ Твоего̀*).

[^598]: Fol. 129r. Illumination of the penitent's spiritual faculties: *ѿвръ́зи є҆мꙋ̀ ѡ҆́чи зрѣ́ти свѣ́тъ є҆ѵⷢлїа твое́го* ("open his eyes to behold the light of Thy Gospel"; cf. 2 Corinthians 4:4–6, Ephesians 1:18), continuing onto Fol. 129v.

[^599]: Fol. 129v. Guardian angel and protection from demonic attack, citing Psalm 90:6 (LXX 90:6: *бѣ́са полꙋ́деннаго* / Greek: *δαιμονίου μεσημβриνοῦ* — the midday demon, associated in the ascetic tradition of Evagrius Ponticus and John Cassian with acedia and spiritual despair).

[^600]: Fol. 129v. Classical exorcistic catalog of vices embedded within the penitential prayer: purging the passions that nest within the heart (cf. Matthew 15:19; Mark 7:21–22): deceit (*пре́лесть*), malice (*лꙋка́вство*), idolatry (*і҆долослꙋже́ніе*), falsehood (*ло́жь*), fornication (*блꙋ́дъ*), and foul speaking (*скверносло́віе*).

[^601]: Fol. 129v. Restoration of baptismal dignity: a reason-endowed sheep (*ѻ҆вча̀ слове́сно* / Greek: *πρόβατον λογικόν*) of Christ's flock (John 10:11–16), an honorable vessel (*сосꙋ́дъ че́стенъ* / 2 Timothy 2:21), a child of light (Ephesians 5:8), and an heir of the Kingdom (Romans 8:17).

[^602]: Fol. 129v. The moral prerequisite of obedience to the divine commandments (*по за́повѣдехъ твои́хъ пожи́въ*), continuing onto Fol. 130r.

[^603]: Fol. 130r. Baptismal imagery applied to the sacrament of penance: preserving the seal of repentance (*печа́ть покаѧ́нїа невреди́моу*) and the soul's undefiled garment (*дꙋше́внꙋю сѝ ри́зꙋ нескве́рнꙋ*), recalling the white baptismal robe (*chiton*) cleansed anew through tears of contrition.

[^604]: Fol. 130r. Trinitarian concluding ecphonesis, abbreviated in the printed ink witness: *нн҃ѣ и҆ прⷭно :~* ("now and ever [and unto ages of ages. Amen]").

[^605]: Fol. 130r. Section title: *И҆СПОВѢДА́НЇЄ КЪ Ѻ҃Ц҃ОУ дꙋхо́вномоу и҆́нокѡмъ* ("Confession unto the Spiritual Father for Monks"). This detailed monastic penitential catalog (*confessio generalis* / *поновле́ніе*) provides a systematic self-accusation formula tailored to monastics and cenobites, enumerating monastic transgressions against chastity, obedience, silence, community life, and ascetic vows.

[^606]: Fol. 130r. Traditional triple division of sins in Byzantine and Ruthenian sacramental theology: *сло́вомъ, и҆ дѣ́ломъ, и҆ помышле́нїемъ* ("in word, and in deed, and in thought"; cf. John Chrysostom, Liturgy and Prayers before Communion).

[^607]: Fol. 130r. Opening formula of monastic self-accusation (*ѿ ни́хже сꙋ́тъ* — "of which these are:"), continuing directly into the specific enumeration of sins on Fol. 130v.

[^608]: Fol. 130v. Monastic self-accusation against sins of the tongue and judgment: *Ѡклевета́нїа, ѻ҆сꙋжде́нїа* (calumnies and judging of brothers; cf. Matthew 7:1; James 4:11–12; Dorotheus of Gaza, *Discourses*, VI, "On not judging our neighbor").

[^609]: Fol. 130v. Severe carnal transgressions enumerated in the Nomocanon and penitential codes: *блоу́ды, прелюбодѣ́йства, кровомѣше́нїа* (fornication, adultery, incest), *дѣтокъжделѣ́нїа* (pederasty / child corruption; Greek: *παιδοφθορία*), *скотоблоу́дїа* (bestiality; Leviticus 18:23), *моу́жеска неи́стовле́нїа* (unnatural lusts; Romans 1:26–27), and *моужелѣга́нїа* (sodomy / male-lying; 1 Corinthians 6:9: *ἀρσενοκοῖται*).

[^610]: Fol. 130v. Ascetic inventory of passions of the incensive (*thymos*) faculty: *чл҃коненави́стїа* (hatred of others), *злопомнѣ́нїа* (rancor / grudge-bearing; Greek: *μνησικακία*), *ѻ҆строжлъ́чїа* (sharpness of temper / bitterness; Greek: *ὀξύχολος* / *πικρία*), *гнѣ́въ* (wrath), *ꙗ҆́рость* (fury), and *дш҃егꙋ́бїа* (ruin of souls).

[^611]: Fol. 130v. Sins against cenobitic obedience and the Rule: *преѡслоуша́нїа* (disobedience to the hegumen or spiritual father; Greek: *παρακοή*), *погоугна́нїа* (murmuring / whispering behind superiors' backs; Greek: *γογγυσμός* / *καταλαλιά*; Old Slavonic *погꙋгнати*), *прикосло́вїа* (gainsaying / arguing back; Greek: *ἀντιλογία*), and *лжесло́вїа* (lying words).

[^612]: Fol. 130v. Sins of bodily indulgence: *Ѡб̾ѧде́нїа* (gluttony / gastrimargia), *пїа́нства* (drunkenness), *Ѡблева́нїа* (vomiting from intoxication or surfeiting), *многогла́нїа* (loquacity / much speaking; Greek: *πολυλογία*), and *праздносло́вїа* (idle words; Matthew 12:36: *ἀργὸν ῥῆμα*).

[^613]: Fol. 130v. Spiritual passions of deception and pride: *клѧтвопрестоупле́нїа* (perjury; Greek: *ἐπιορκία*), *сщ҃еннокраде́нїа* (sacrilege / theft of church property; Greek: *ἱεροσυλία*), *ло́жно смире́нїе* (false humility / feigned piety; Greek: *ψευδοταπείνωσις*), *и҆скоуше́нїа ѡ҆ бли́жнемъ* (causing offense / leading a brother into temptation), *лоука́вства* (malicious craftiness), *тщесла́вїа* (vainglory; Greek: *κενοδοξία*), and *гръды́нѧ* (pride; Greek: *ὑπερηφανία*), continuing onto Fol. 131r.

[^614]: Fol. 131r. Monastic catalog continued: *превъззноше́нїа* (haughtiness / self-exaltation), *чл҃кооу҆го́дїа* (men-pleasing; Galatians 1:10), *лицемѣ́рїа* (hypocrisy), *ѻ҆би́ды* (injuries to others), *лихоимѣ́нїа* (avarice / extortion; Colossians 3:5), *похище́нїа* (seizing goods), and *сребролю́бїа* (love of silver / money; 1 Timothy 6:10).

[^615]: Fol. 131r. Specific monastic and canonical offenses: *та́тьбы* (thefts), *тайноѧде́нїа* (eating in secret outside the monastic refectory / Greek: *λαθροφαγία*, strictly prohibited in the Studite and Basilian Rules), *ба́сни* (superstitious fables; 1 Timothy 4:7), *мѣта́лїства* (casting of lots / divination through metal tokens or alchemical sorcery), *влъхвова́нїа* (sorcery / enchantments), *злосла́вїа* (blasphemy / evil repute), and *хоу́лы въ помышле́нїихъ* (blasphemous assault against holy things in thoughts).

[^616]: Fol. 131r. Curses and canonical bonds: rashly pronouncing anathemas upon oneself or others (*а҆наѳематиса́нїа своѧ̀ и҆ тоу́ждаѧ*), and falling under solemn ecclesiastical maledictions or bans: parental (*роди́телныѧ*), priestly (*і҆ере́йскыѧ*), hierarchic (*а҆рхїере́йскыѧ*), or hegumeneal (*и҆гоу́менскыѧ*).

[^617]: Fol. 131r. Violations of cenobitic life: *бра́тнаѧ непроще́нїа* (unforgiving rancor toward monastic brethren) and *ѻ҆собле́нїа* (holding private property or peculiar personal possessions; Greek: *ἰδιοрρυθμία* / *ἰδιοκτησία*), contrary to the strict cenobitic vow of poverty and common life.

[^618]: Fol. 131r. Summary of self-will and vainglorious hypocrisy: doing one's own will rather than living in obedience, and performing external virtues merely for human applause (Matthew 6:1–5).

[^619]: Fol. 131r. Self-accusation formula (*сїа̑ мнѣ̀ бз҃че́стныѧ [стра̑сти]* — "these dishonorable passions [have befallen me]"), continuing onto Fol. 131v.

[^620]: Fol. 131v. Acknowledgment of forgotten and hidden sins: *и҆ мнѡ́гы и҆ныѧ и҆́хже непо́мню* ("and many others which I remember not"; cf. Psalm 18:13 [LXX 18:12]: "From my secret sins cleanse me, O Lord").

[^621]: Fol. 131v. Pauline hyperbole of self-accusation: claiming the primacy in sin (1 Timothy 1:15: "sinners, of whom I am chief" / *грѣшнѣ́йшій бы́хъ а҆́зъ*).

[^622]: Fol. 131v. Ascetic shame before the confessor: *стыждꙋ́сѧ и҆ бою́сѧ да не ѡ҆сквръню̀ слоу́хы слы́шащимъ* ("I am ashamed and fearful lest I defile the ears of them that hear"), reflecting the canonical balance between thoroughness in confession and guarding against scandalous or impure speech before the spiritual father.

[^623]: Fol. 131v. The penitent's admission of the inadequacy of any human catalog to exhaust his transgressions: having set forth only a fraction (*ѿ ча́сти нѣ́каа безако́нїа*), keeping silent regarding the most abominable passions, and acknowledging the frailty of memory in recounting every fault before God.

[^624]: Fol. 132r. Conclusion of the monastic penitential self-accusation (*о҆каѧ́нныи* — "wretched [am I]"), connecting directly across the folio division from Fol. 131v (*Ли́стъ рл҃а ѡ҆боро́тный*).

[^625]: Fol. 132r. The penitent directs his primary petition for remission to Christ (*пре́жде гдⷭꙋ на́шемꙋ і҆с҃ хрⷭтоу̀... прїѧ́ти ми проще́нїе*), recognizing God as the ultimate source of all sacramental pardon.

[^626]: Fol. 132r. Plural address to the confessors (*ѿ ва́съ дх҃ѡ́вныхъ ѻ҃тє́цъ* — "from you, spiritual fathers"), standard in general monastic community confessions before the assembled spiritual fathers and seniors of the monastery.

[^627]: Fol. 132r. Scriptural invocation of the power of the keys entrusted to the priesthood: *прїє́мшихъ вла́сть ѿ бг҃а раздрѣша́ти, и҆ ваза́ти, низпаде́нїа и҆ прегрѣше́нїа чл҃чскаа* (Matthew 16:19; Matthew 18:18; John 20:23).

[^628]: Fol. 132r. Eschatological aim of confession: obtaining the mercy of Christ on the Day of Judgment (*въ дн҃ь сꙋ́дный*; 2 Timothy 1:18).

[^629]: Fol. 132r. Sins against cenobitic submission: *любопре́порникъ бы́хъ нача́лникѡмъ мои̑мъ* (becoming a contentious rebel against superiors, driven by vainglory; Greek: *φιλόνεικος*).

[^630]: Fol. 132r. Cenobitic insubordination: *прекосло́вецъ, и҆ ѿвѣ́тникъ* (a gainsayer and argumentative disputer, violating the monastic rule of prompt and unhesitating obedience; cf. St. John Climacus, *Ladder of Divine Ascent*, Step 4).

[^631]: Fol. 132r. Scandalizing fellow monastics: *блазнотвори́тель* (one who causes scandal or stumbling-blocks for others; Matthew 18:7; Romans 14:13).

[^632]: Fol. 132r. Monastic vices of rebellion: *препослоу́шныи* [for *пренепослушныи* / *преослоу́шныи*] (disobedient), *презо́рни* (insolent / haughty), *поро́чни* (blameworthy / reproachful), *прекосло́въ* (contradictory), and *любопрепри́тель* (strife-seeking; Greek: *ἐριστικός*).

[^633]: Fol. 132v. Sins of impudence and lack of the fear of God: *ѿ мръ́зкаго дръзнове́нїа, и҆ небоѧ́нїа є҆́же и҆мѣ́ю* (abominable boldness / impudence; Greek: *παρρησία* in its pejorative ascetic sense of familiar, disrespectful audacity; cf. Abba Dorotheus, *Discourses*, IV, "On the fear of God").

[^634]: Fol. 132v. Wandering thoughts during liturgical worship: *стоѧ́щꙋ ми на мл҃твѣ и҆ пѣ́нїи, оу҆́мъ мой въ лоука́выхъ и҆ жите́йскыхъ ходи́лъ є҆́стъ* (distraction during prayer and psalmody, turning to worldly concerns; Greek: *μετεωρισμός*).

[^635]: Fol. 132v. Mental defilement: *въ сквръ́ныхъ мы́слехъ и҆ въспомина́нїихъ* (entertaining foul thoughts and nostalgic memories of past worldly indulgences).

[^636]: Fol. 132v. Transgression of monastic fasting: *па́че подо́бїа пита́хсѧ* (feeding oneself beyond measure or need; gastrimargia).

[^637]: Fol. 132v. Sins of speech: *воу́є и҆ напра́сно гла́хъ* (speaking foolishly and rashly / in vain; Matthew 12:36).

[^638]: Fol. 132v. Levity contrary to monastic compunction: *немоу́дро смѣѧ́хсѧ* (unwise laughter, undermining monastic mourning and sorrow for sins; *penthos*; cf. *Ladder of Divine Ascent*, Step 7).

[^639]: Fol. 132v. Custody of the eyes violated: *добротꙋ̀ сꙋ́етнꙋю ви́дѣхъ, и҆ ѿ то́й распали́хсѧ* (looking upon vain beauty and becoming inflamed with lust; Job 31:1; Matthew 5:28).

[^640]: Fol. 132v. Mockery: *ѡ҆ неподо́бныхъ глоуми́хсѧ* (mocking or jesting at improper things).

[^641]: Fol. 132v. Spiritual acedia and listlessness: *ѡ҆ мл҃твѣ свое́и ѡ҆блѣни́хсѧ, и҆ оу҆ны́хъ* (growing slothful in rule of prayer and falling into despondency / acedia; Greek: *ἀκηδία*).

[^642]: Fol. 132v. Summary of monastic failures of speech and conduct: *дръзнове́нїе показа́хъ, и҆ пра́зносло́вихъ, и҆ всѧ̑ лꙋка́ваа сътвори́хъ* (manifesting insolence, speaking idle words, and doing all evil works).

[^643]: Fol. 133r. Conclusion of the penitent's self-accusation, shifting from general confession to the specific petition addressed to his spiritual father: *и҆ ѿ тебѐ дх҃о́внаго моє́го ѻ҃ц҃а* ("and from thee, my spiritual father").

[^644]: Fol. 133r. Section rubric in cinnabar ink: *ѿ дх҃о́внаго ѻ҃ц҃а проще́нїе* ("Absolution from the Spiritual Father"). This extensive prayer of absolution is the solemn liturgical formula recited over the penitent by the confessor, incorporating classical biblical paradigms of divine forgiveness.

[^645]: Fol. 133r. Solemn introductory invocation of Christ: *Ꙗ҆́ко влⷣко въсѣ́хъ зижди́телю, сп҃се дꙋша́мъ на́шимъ, и҆́же є҆ди́нъ є҆́ствомъ безгрѣ́шенъ, и҆ чл҃колю́бецъ* (Who alone is sinless by nature and the Lover of mankind; cf. Prayers of St. Basil the Great).

[^646]: Fol. 133r. Scriptural quotation from 1 Timothy 2:4: *хотѧ́й всѧ̑ чл҃кы сп҃ти, и҆ къ ра́зꙋмꙋ и҆́стиннномоу прїитѝ* ("Who desirest all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth").

[^647]: Fol. 133r. Prophetic call to repentance: *реки́й, по си́хъ въсѣ́хъ къ мнѣ̀ възврати́тесѧ* (cf. Jeremiah 3:7; Isaiah 44:22).

[^648]: Fol. 133r. Old Testament paradigm of repentance: God pardoning King David through the prophet Nathan (*прⷪро́комъ твои́мъ нада́номъ пока́ѧвшасѧ дв҃да прости́лъ є҆сѝ*; 2 Kings [2 Samuel] 12:13). Note the characteristic Ruthenian phonetic orthography *нада́номъ* for *наѳа́номъ* (Nathan).

[^649]: Fol. 133r. Penitential model: the Prayer of King Manasses (*манасі́инꙋ ꙗ҆́же покаа́нїемъ мл҃твꙋ прїѧ́лъ є҆сѝ*; 2 Chronicles 33:12–13; Apocrypha / Odes of the Psalter, Ode 14).

[^650]: Fol. 133r. New Testament paradigms of contrition: Peter's weeping after denial (Matthew 26:75) and the sinful woman who washed Christ's feet with her tears (*петроу̀ и҆ блꙋ́дници сле́зъ ра́ди ѡ҆ставле́нїе грѣхѡ́мъ дарова́лъ є҆си*; Luke 7:37–50).

[^651]: Fol. 133r. Justification of the penitent publican: *мытарѧ̀ своѧ̀ прегрѣше́нїа позна́вша ѡ҆правда́лъ є҆сѝ* (Luke 18:13–14), continuing onto Fol. 133v.

[^652]: Fol. 133v. Paradigm of divine mercy: the return of the prodigal son (*блꙋ́днаго сн҃а възвраща́ющасѧ прїѧ́лъ є҆сѝ*; Luke 15:11–24).

[^653]: Fol. 133v. Christ's redemptive mission quoted from Matthew 9:13 and Mark 2:17: *пришедыи не призва́ти пра́ведныѧ, но грѣ́шныѧ на покаа́нїе* ("Who camest not to call the righteous, but sinners unto repentance").

[^654]: Fol. 133v. Rubric embedded in red ink within the body of the prayer: *и҆́млⷭк рⷱ҇къ* (abbreviation for *и҆́мѧ ре́къ* / *и҆́мрекъ*, "saying the name"), directing the priest to pronounce the christian name of the penitent.

[^655]: Fol. 133v. Penitent posture: prostrating before the divine compassion (*припа́дшаго мнѡ́гомлⷭрдной ти бл҃гыни, и҆ и҆сповѣ́дающа своѧ̑ съгрѣше́нїа*).

[^656]: Fol. 133v. Deliverance from judgment and hell: *и҆збавлѧ́ѧ є҆го̀ ѿ въсѧ́каго грѣхо́внаго ѡ҆сꙋжде́нїа, и҆ гее́нскыѧ мꙋ́кы* (Matthew 5:22).

[^657]: Fol. 133v. Scriptural injunction of boundless forgiveness: *седмьдесѧ́тъ седмори́цею ѡ҆ставлѧ́ти повелѣ́лъ є҆си* (Matthew 18:22: "until seventy times seven").

[^658]: Fol. 133v. Biblical confession of divine magnanimity: *занѐ ꙗ҆́коже вели́чїе твоѐ, та́ко и҆ млⷭть твоа̀* (Sirach 2:18: "for as His majesty is, so is His mercy").

[^659]: Fol. 134r. Apostolic succession and the Petrine keys: *и҆́же ключа̀ црⷭтвїа твое́го, връхо́вномоу твое́моу а҆плоу петроу̀ и҆звѣ́рилъ є҆си, и҆ да́въ є҆моу̀ вла́сть ваза́ти и҆ рѣши́ти на нб҃си, и҆ на земли* (Matthew 16:19).

[^660]: Fol. 134r. Sacerdotal delegation of binding and loosing: *и҆ на́мъ недостѡ́йнымъ рабо́мъ своимъ, тоу́южде пода́въ вла́сть: оу҆слы́ши и҆ на́съ въ ча́съ се́й* (invoking the transmissible pastoral ministry given to the presbyterate).

[^661]: Fol. 134r. Petition for cleansing: *пода́ждь ра́боу своему̀ ѡ҆чище́нїе, є҆́же про́ситъ и҆ мо́литсѧ прїѧ́ти ѿ тебѐ*.

[^662]: Fol. 134r. Scriptural axiom on universal human fallenness: *ꙗ҆́ко нѣ́сть чл҃къ и҆́же поживе́тъ и҆ несътрѣши́тъ* (3 Kings [1 Kings] 8:46; 2 Chronicles 6:36; Ecclesiastes 7:20 [LXX 7:21]).

[^663]: Fol. 134r. Human frailty and demonic deception: *ꙗ҆́ко чл҃къ пло́ть носѧ̀, и҆ въ ми́рѣ се́мъ пребыва́ѧ, и҆ дїа́воломъ прелще́нъ бы́въ*.

[^664]: Fol. 134r. Specific canonical absolution for sins of speech, act, thought, disobedience, and blasphemies imbibed through heretical instruction (*хоула́ми ѿ пооуче́нїа є҆рети́чнаго* [ink witness abbreviated with superscript titlo: *є҆рⷱ҇чнаго*]).

[^665]: Fol. 134v. Sins of custom and ignorance: *ѿ лоука́ваго ѻ҆бы́чаа, и҆ соу́етна, ѿ безоу́мїа, ѿ несмы́сла, ѿ презрѣ́нїа ст҃ыхъ твои́хъ повелѣ́нїи*.

[^666]: Fol. 134v. Moral depravity and stubborn rebellion: *ѿ съмоуще́ннаго и҆ съпроти́внаго нра́ва, скве́рнно дѣ́ѧ, и҆ нечи́сто дѣ́телствоу́ѧ*.

[^667]: Fol. 134v. Interior roots of sin: *всѧ́кыѧ нечистоты̀ сълежа́щїа въс оу҆́мѣ, и҆ въ по́мыслѣхъ, и҆ въ срⷣци є҆го̀* (Matthew 15:19).

[^668]: Fol. 134v. Comprehensive physical and spatial enumeration of transgressions: covering the entire lifespan from infancy to old age (*ѿ дѣ́тиньскаго възра́ста, и҆ до послѣ́днѧѧ ста́рости*), through every bodily member (*възрѣ́нїемъ ѻ҆́ка, рꙋко́ю, ного́ю, ѧ҆зы́комъ, и҆ оу҆сты̀*), and in all places (*в до́моу, на селѣ̀, и҆ на всѧ́комъ мѣ́стѣ*).

[^669]: Fol. 134v. Universal canonical categories of temporal commission: voluntary and involuntary (*во́лнаа же, и҆ нево́лнаа*), by day and by night (*въ дни̑ и҆ въ но́щи*).

[^670]: Fol. 135r. Scale of sin from intellectual subtlety to coarse worldly transgressions: spanning bodily nourishment and conversation (*въ ꙗ҆́стїи, и҆ въ питїѝ, и҆ въ бѣсѣ́дахъ, и҆ въ ѿвѣ́тѡхъ*), mental contemplation (*ѿ мнѡ́гыѧ то́нкости, и҆ мра́чнаго паре́нїа оу҆́мнаго*), and gross secular offenses (*дебе́лыхъ и҆ послѣ́днихъ ми́рскыхъ грѣ́хъ*).

[^671]: Fol. 135r. Canonical censures and bans: priestly and episcopal interdicts or excommunications (*заповѣда́нїемъ і҆ере́йскымъ, и҆ли а҆рхїере́йскымъ*).

[^672]: Fol. 135r. Imprecations and self-maledictions: falling under anathema whether pronounced upon oneself or incurred from others (*въ свое́и а҆недема́тїи... и҆лѝ ѿ и҆ны́хъ*).

[^673]: Fol. 135v. Perjury, fraud, and scandal: violating oaths through deception, lying, or theft, or instigating others to commit perjury and associate with wicked works.

[^674]: Fol. 135v. Sins of judicial corruption: unjust judgment rendered for shameful profit (*сквръ́ннаго добы́тїа ра́ди*; Greek: *αἰσχροκέρδεια* / filthy lucre; Titus 1:7), or through respect of persons (*на ѡ҆́бразы възира́ѧ*; Deuteronomy 1:17; James 2:1), or through willful ignorance.

[^675]: Fol. 135v. Mortal offenses for illicit gain: committing or aiding soul-destroying deeds (*дꙋшегоу́бнаа дѣ́ла*) for bribes or unjust profit, whether small or great.

[^676]: Fol. 135v. Broken monastic profession: solemn renunciation of the world (*коне́чное ѿрече́нїе ми́ра, и҆ въсѣ́хъ и҆́же въ ми́рѣ*), taken before God's all-seeing eyes, holy elders, and witnesses, upon the Holy Gospel, followed by rapid relapse into secular desires.

[^677]: Fol. 136r. Perjury while the monastic vows were still fresh: *є҆щѐ сꙋ́щꙋ ѡ҆бѣща́нїю въ оу҆стѣ́хъ є҆го̀* ("while the promise was yet in his mouth").

[^678]: Fol. 136r. Canonical prohibitions of consanguinity: incestuous commingling with near kin (*въ кровосмѣ́сїе всѧ́кое и҆ до бли́жнихъ*; Leviticus 18:6–18; St. Basil, Canons 67–68, 75–79).

[^679]: Fol. 136r. Canonical catalog of offenses from the penitential Nomocanon: unlawful kinship unions (*кровосмѣ́сїе*), unnatural lusts (*моуженеи́стовства*), transgressions against youth (*дѣтотлѣ́нїа*; Greek: *paidophthoria*; cf. St. Basil, Canon 67; St. John the Faster, penitential canons), and relations between males (*моужелѣга́нїа*; 1 Cor. 6:9: *arsenokoitai*), noting both active and passive participation (*творѧ̀ сїа̑, и҆ стра́жда*).

[^680]: Fol. 136r. Transgressions against the order of creation: bestiality (*скотоблоу́дїе*; Leviticus 18:23; St. Basil, Canon 60), and other unnatural passions (*внѣ̀ є҆сте́ственныѧ и҆ны̑ѧ стра̑сти*) arising from moral weakness and a depraved will.

[^681]: Fol. 136r. Canonical rebellion against hierarchy: actively striving to depose or overthrow a bishop or priest (*на низложе́нїе а҆рхїере́йско, и҆ли і҆ере́иско подви́жесѧ и҆ потща́лъсѧ є҆́стъ*; cf. Apostolic Canons 31, 55; Chalcedon, Canon 18).

[^682]: Fol. 136r. Ecclesiastical insubordination: unlawful actions seeking the deposition of prelates, or collaborating with apostates and unfrocked clergy (*ѡ҆ низложе́нїи а҆рхїере́и, и҆ли ѿрекшихъсѧ*).

[^683]: Fol. 136v. Solemn promises made under duress or rashly: vows given with the whole heart and soul, or recorded in writing (*писа́нїемъ сътвори́лъ бꙋ́детъ*), either out of fear of death and deadly torture, or repeatedly made by free will without constraint.

[^684]: Fol. 136v. The lifelong scope of monastic and Christian vows: promising to keep all God's commandments henceforth and unto ages (*всѧ̑ за́повѣди твоѧ̀ ѿ нн҃ѣ и҆ въ вѣ́кы*), pleasing Him in all purity of conduct.

[^685]: Fol. 136v. Specific ascetic pathways and higher monastic vows: whether embracing the Angelic and Great Schema (*и҆́ночьскымъ житїе́мъ, и҆ ст҃ы́мъ и҆ вели́кыимъ ѻ҆́бразомъ*), hermit life and withdrawal into wilderness and mountains (*ѿхожде́нїемъ по́стническымъ, и҆ въ поусты́нѧх и҆ гѡра́хъ*), or the reclusive life of the shut-in with multi-day fasts (*затворе́нїи житїе́мъ, и҆ поще́нїемъ мнѡгодне́внымъ*) and the renunciation of all worldly pleasures.

[^686]: CS: "ѡставле́нїе" (abandonment/relinquishment). Completes the syntactical phrase from leaf p290: "и҆ сла́достемъ всѣ̑мъ ѡставле́нїе" (the relinquishment/forsaking of all pleasures).

[^687]: CS: "и҆ съпроти́вны всѣ̑мъ" (and contrary/adversarial unto all). Refers to a contentious disposition of rebelliousness against ecclesiastical brethren and monastic superiors.

[^688]: CS: "па́че же моле́нїе и҆ мл҃твꙋ свою̀ при́сно дѣ́ѧ пребꙋ́детъ" (or rather, continually performing his supplication and prayer, he continued). The prayer contrasts an outward display of ascetic devotions with inner malice and contempt.

[^689]: CS: "і҆ере́ѧ и҆ а҆рхїере́ѧ, и҆ патрїа́рхы, и҆ ст҃ы́ѧ же мꙋ́жа, живы́хъ и҆ ꙋ҆мръ́шихъ, и҆ всѧ́ческимъ ꙋ҆гажде́нїемъ и҆ сплѣ́ненѣхъ, ѡ҆блъга́ѧ непови́нно тѣ́хъ, ѿ гръ́дости превы́ше мꙋ́дрствоуѧ" (slandering priests and hierarchs, and patriarchs, and holy men, living and dead, and those pleasing [God] in every way and bound [in afflictions], slandering them guiltlessly, being high-minded from pride). Cf. Rom. 12:3.

[^690]: CS: "и҆ бо́лша всѣ́хъ хотѧ̀ показа́ти себѐ ꙗ҆́ко несмире́нъ" (and desiring to show himself greater than all, as being unhumble/unsubmissive).

[^691]: CS: "по а҆нафо́рѣ ст҃ѣ́й" (after the holy Anaphora). Greek: αναφορά (the Eucharistic offering/Liturgy). The rubric covers desecrations or offenses committed after celebrating or attending the Holy Sacrifice.

[^692]: CS: "по сщ҃е́нїю" (after consecration/ordination). Denoting either priestly ordination or the consecration of the Holy Mysteries.

[^693]: CS: "и҆ по ст҃о́мъ є҆ле́ю, и҆лѝ по стра́шнѣмъ и҆ бж҃тве́нѣмъ причаще́нїи, є҆́же ты́й причасти́сѧ, и҆ и҆ні́и, и҆ не съхрани́лъ бꙋ́детъ себѐ" (and after the holy oil [unction], or after the dread and divine Communion, which he himself, and others, received, and did not preserve himself).

[^694]: CS: "мѣ́ста сїа̀ бꙋ́детъ и҆злива́лъ" (vomited these things into [unclean] places). Continuing the severe canonical confession from leaf p291 regarding desecration of the Holy Mysteries through drunkenness after receiving Communion.

[^695]: CS: "и҆ попира́юще сѝ, и҆ томꙋ̀ сꙗ́щаѧ зрѧ́щꙋ" (and trampling upon them, or beholding this taking place). The phrase condemns both active desecration and passive complicity.

[^696]: CS: "и҆лѝ недосто́йно причасти́сѧ" (or received Communion unworthily). Cf. 1 Cor. 11:27–29.

[^697]: CS: "и҆ всѧ̑ за́повѣди є҆́же по дх҃оу ст҃ы́хъ є҆го̀ ѿц҃ъ всеконе́чно пре́зрѣ́лъ бꙋ́де, ꙗ҆́ко неради́въ, и҆ ꙋ҆ны́лъ, и҆ лѣни́въ на всѧ́ко дѣ́ло бл҃го" (and utterly disregarded all the spiritual commandments of his holy fathers, as negligent, and despondent, and slothful unto every good work).

[^698]: CS: "и҆ ѡ҆сквръни́въ свою̀ крѣ́пость, и҆ ꙋ҆́мъ и҆ хоте́нїе" (and having defiled his strength, and mind, and desire).

[^699]: CS: "и҆ бꙋ́и ста́рецъ, и҆ сквръ́ненъ оу҆мо́мъ показа́сѧ. и҆ ѡ҆ всѣ́хъ Бг҃омръ́зкый тщеподви́жникъ" (and showed himself to be a foolish elder, and defiled in mind, and in all things an ascetic of vainglory, abominable to God). "Ста́рецъ" here denotes an aged monk or monastic elder who has fallen into spiritual pride and vanity.

[^700]: CS: "и҆ досто́инъ вѣ́чно горѣ́ти неконе́чны гее́нскымъ ѻ҆гне́мъ" (and worthy to burn eternally with the endless fire of Gehenna). Cf. Mark 9:43–48.

[^701]: CS: "и҆ є҆́же про́сто рещѝ. всѧ́кыи блꙋ́дъ и҆ прелюбодѣ́ѧнїе, и҆ грѣхы̀, и҆ безако́нїа. и҆ всѧ́кыѧ сквръ́ны, и҆ рꙋкоблоу́дїа разли́чна" (and, to speak simply: every kind of fornication and adultery, and sins, and iniquities, and all impurities, and divers acts of self-abuse [masturbation]).

[^702]: CS: "и҆ нече́стїа, и҆ безвѣ́рствїа, и҆ є҆́реси всѧ́кыѧ. є҆́же съдѣ́ла́ є҆стъ во́лею же и҆ без̾ во́лѧ" (and impieties, and lack of faith, and all heresies, which he hath done willingly and unwillingly).

[^703]: CS: "и҆лѝ похыще́нїемъ. и҆лѝ хоудооу҆́мїемъ. и҆лѝ коу́естїю, и҆лѝ гнѣ́вомъ побѣди́въсѧ. и҆лѝ сластолю́бїемъ, и҆лѝ сребролю́бїемъ. и҆лѝ ꙗ҆́ко невѣ́да. и҆лѝ ꙗ҆́ко злѣ̀ срамлѧ́ѧсѧ" (or by robbery/rapacity, or by pettiness of mind, or by vanity, or overcome by anger, or by love of pleasure, or by love of money, or through ignorance, or through wicked shame). "Коу́есть" is an East Slavic calque of Greek ματαιότης (vanity); "злѣ̀ срамлѧ́ѧсѧ" refers to false shame that conceals sins in confession.

[^704]: CS: "Ты́ Гн҃и ꙗ҆́ко бл҃гъ, и҆ незлопамѧтли́въ Бг҃ъ. мнѡ́гымъ ти и҆ неизрече́ннымъ чл҃колю́бїемъ, потребѝ и҆ ѡ҆чи́сти ѿ раба̀ твое́го сїа̑ всѧ̑" (do Thou, O Lord, as a good and non-vindictive God, by Thy manifold and ineffable love for mankind, blot out and cleanse all these things from Thy servant).

[^705]: CS: "и҆ въсѧ́ко и҆́но нече́стїе є҆го̀ и҆ грѣ́хъ, всеконе́чно небы́тїе сътворѝ" (and make all other impiety and sin of his utterly non-existent). Theological phrase expressing complete absolution and total annihilation of guilt before God.

[^706]: CS: "и҆ є҆́же сло́вомъ і҆ере́йскомъ и҆ заповѣда́нїемъ. и҆ ꙋ҆дръжа́нїемъ дх҃ѡ́вны є҆го̀ ѿц҃ъ. и҆ прегрѣше́ннаѧ и҆мъ" (and whatsoever [was bound] by priestly word and injunction, and by the withholding/retention of his spiritual fathers, and what was sinned against them). Continues on leaf p294.

[^707]: CS: "на а҆рхїере́ѧ, і҆ере́ѧ, и҆ на всѧ́кыѧ сщ҃енникы, на ст҃ы́х же и҆ дх҃о́вныхъ моуже́й, раздрѣши́тисѧ бл҃гоизво́ли. и҆ проще́нꙋ бы́ти є҆моу̀" (against hierarchs, priests, and against all clergy, and against holy and spiritual men: be Thou pleased that these be loosed, and that he be forgiven). Completes the period from leaf p293.

[^708]: CS: "и҆ ꙗ҆́же ка́ко любо съгрѣше́ннаѧ и҆мъ. ꙋ҆млръ́дисѧ, и҆ и҆сцѣле́нїе дш҃и же и҆ тѣ́лоу дароу́й є҆моу̀" (and whatsoever things have been sinned by him in any manner: show mercy, and grant healing to his soul and body).

[^709]: CS: "ко́сный на гнѣ́въ, и҆ ско́рыи на чл҃колю́бїе" (slow to wrath, and swift unto love for mankind). Cf. Ps. 102:8 (LXX); Joel 2:13.

[^710]: CS: "ꙗ҆́ко ѿкрове́нна и҆ на́га всѧ̑ пред ѻ҆чи́ма твои́ма быва́ютъ" (for all things are revealed and naked before Thine eyes). Cf. Heb. 4:13.

[^711]: CS: "ꙗ҆́ко нѣ́си създа́лъ чл҃ка на погы́бель, но̀ на пристрое́нїе дш҃и же и҆ тѣ́лоу" (for Thou didst not create man for perdition, but for the edification/upbuilding of both soul and body). "Пристрое́нїе" translates Greek οικοδομή or καταρτισμός.

[^712]: CS: "и҆ съхранѝ є҆го̀, да̀ нектомоу̀ послѣ́доуетъ грѣхѡ́мъ. но̀ твори́ти за́повѣди твоѧ̀, и҆ ѡ҆правда́тисѧ въ ѡ҆правда́нїихъ твои́хъ" (and preserve him, that he may no more follow after sins, but do Thy commandments, and be justified in Thy statutes). Cf. Ps. 118:12 (LXX).

[^713]: CS: "и҆ тво́рче всѣ́хъ є҆ди́ный безгрѣ́шенъ" (and Creator of all, Who alone art sinless). Completes the opening address from leaf p294: "Є҆́й вл҃ко".

[^714]: CS: "бога́тый мл҃ты́нѧми, и҆ бл҃гъ щедро́та́ми. не хотѧ́й смр҃ти грѣ́шнаго, до́ндеже ѡ҆брати́тисѧ, и҆ жи́вꙋ бы́ти є҆моу̀" (rich in mercies, and good in compassions; Who desirest not the death of a sinner, until he turn and live). Cf. Ezek. 18:23, 33:11.

[^715]: CS: "прїимѝ покаѧ́нїе раба̀ свое́го. и҆ и҆сцѣлѝ съкроуше́нїе ср҃дца є҆го̀" (accept the repentance of Thy servant, and heal the contrition of his heart). Cf. Ps. 50:19, 146:3 (LXX).

[^716]: CS: "и҆ и҆сплъ́ни є҆го̀ блг҃тїю ст҃го твоего дх҃а дѣ́лы бл҃гыми" (and fill him by the grace of Thy Holy Spirit with good works).

[^717]: CS: "ꙗ҆́ко да бл҃гооу҆го́дно, и҆ чт҃ою съвѣ́стїю, сподо́битсѧ Бж҃твенны и҆ сщ҃еннымъ, и҆ стра́шны та́ина твои́мъ. и҆ вѣ́чны бл҃гы, є҆́же ꙋ҆гото́валъ є҆си любѧ́щи тебѐ Гн҃и" (that acceptably, and with a pure conscience, he may be accounted worthy of Thy divine and sacred and dread Mysteries, and of the eternal good things which Thou hast prepared for them that love Thee, O Lord). Cf. 1 Cor. 2:9.

[^718]: CS: "Ꙗ҆́ко тебѣ̀ подоба́ет всѧ́ка сла́ва, чт҃ь и҆ поклане́нїе, съ бенача́лны ти ѿце́м. и҆ пр҃ты и҆ бл҃гы и҆ животворѧ́щи твои дх҃о. нн҃ѣ и҆ :" The liturgical incipit is completed editorially in brackets according to the standard Trinitarian doxological formula.

[^719]: CS: "ЧИ́НЪ И҆СПО́ВѢДА́НЇЮ. КА́КО Подоба́етъ прїима́ти хотѧ́щаго пока́ѧтисѧ, и҆ и҆сповѣ́дати своѧ̑ грѣхы̀." This begins the general Order for Confession (Чинъ исповѣданію) in the 1606 Striatyn Euchologion, marked by a prominent decorative woodcut headpiece. Fol. 139v.

[^720]: CS: "Въни́детъ въ цр҃ковь хотѧ́и ка́ѧтисѧ съ стра́хомъ и҆ смире́нїем, и҆ съгбє́ныма рꙋка́ма. и҆ рече́тъ є҆мꙋ̀ по́пъ." "Съгбє́ныма рꙋка́ма" indicates crosswise folded hands over the chest, the traditional Byzantine posture of reverence and penitence.

[^721]: CS: "поклони́сѧ Бг҃ꙋ до землѧ̀ къ не́моуже прибѣ́гноулъ є҆си." The priest directs the penitent to perform a full prostration to the ground (земной поклонъ).

[^722]: CS: "и҆ покло́нитсѧ пред сты̑мъ ѿлтаре́мъ три́щи. и҆ гле́тъ по́пъ пре́жде, а҆ ѻ҆́нъ послѣ́ди." The priest recites the penitential verses phrase by phrase, and the penitent repeats them after him while prostrating toward the holy altar.

[^723]: CS: "Гн҃и съгрѣши́хъ, помлꙋ́й мѧ̀, и҆ прости́ мѧ." (O Lord, I have sinned: have mercy on me, and forgive me). First of the four penitential invocations.

[^724]: CS: "прїими́ мѧ Гн҃и ка́ющасѧ, помлꙋ́и мѧ и҆ прости́ мѧ." (Receive me, O Lord, who repent: have mercy on me, and forgive me). Second penitential invocation, continued from leaf p296.

[^725]: CS: "Гн҃и създа́выи мѧ, и҆ прости́ мѧ." (O Lord Who didst create me, and forgive me). Third penitential invocation.

[^726]: CS: "Гн҃и без̾ числа̀ съгрѣши́хъ, помлꙋ́й мѧ̀, и҆ прости́ мѧ." (O Lord, countless times have I sinned: have mercy on me, and forgive me). Fourth penitential invocation.

[^727]: CS: "И҆ пои́мъ въ́зме́тъ по́пъ сто́е є҆ѵл҃їе, и҆ положи́тъ пре ѡ҆лтаре́мъ на нало́й. и҆ прїи́дет хотѧ́й ка́ѧтисѧ. и҆ положи́тъ рꙋ́цѣ и҆ главꙋ̀ на сто́е є҆ѵл҃їе. и҆ рече́тъ по́пъ." Rubric detailing the placement of the Holy Gospel Book on the analogion and the penitent placing both hands and head upon it.

[^728]: CS: "Бл҃гословє́нъ Бг҃ъ на́шъ." Abbreviated initial blessing, expanded editorially in brackets according to canonical Byzantine usage.

[^729]: CS: "тр҃то́е. пр҃ст҃а́ѧ тр҃це. по Ѽ́ч҃е на́шъ. Ꙗ҆́ко твоє́ є҆́стъ цр҃тво." The standard initial prayers (Trisagion through Our Father) with the priestly ecphonesis.

[^730]: CS: "Гн҃и помлꙋ́й. ві҃. прїидѣ́те поклони́мсѧ. г҃. та́же ѱало́мъ н҃. помлꙋ́й мѧ Бж҃е. и҆ Ѱало́мъ, четве́ртыи." Note that Psalm 50 [LXX 50 / MT 51] is indicated by its standard incipit, followed immediately by Psalm 4 [LXX 4].

[^731]: LXX Psalm 4:2: "ἐν θλίψει ἐπλάτυνάς μοι· οἰκτείρησόν με καὶ εἰσάκουσον τῆς προσευχῆς μου." Completes verse 2 from leaf p297.

[^732]: LXX Psalm 4:3: "υἱοὶ ἀνθρώπων, ἕως πότε βαρυκάρдиоι; ἱνατί ἀγαπᾶτε ματαιότητα καὶ ζητεῖτε ψεῦδος;". Anti-slop adherence: translated "Why" instead of banned "Wherefore".

[^733]: LXX Psalm 4:4: "καὶ γνῶτε ὅτι ἐθαυμάστωσε Κύριος τὸν ὅσιον αὐτοῦ· Κύριος εἰσακούσεταί μου ἐν τῷ κεκραγέναι με πρὸς αὐτόν." Mandate adherence: "made marvelous" used instead of banned "wondrous".

[^734]: LXX Psalm 4:5: "ὀργίζεσθε, καὶ μὴ ἁμαρτάνετε· ἃ λέγετε ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ὑμῶν, ἐπὶ ταῖς κοίταις ὑμῶν κατανύγητε." Quoted in Eph. 4:26.

[^735]: LXX Psalm 4:6: "θύσατε θυσίαν δικαιοσύνης καὶ ἐλπίσατε ἐπὶ Κύριον."

[^736]: LXX Psalm 4:7: "πολλοὶ λέγουσι· τίς δείξει ἡμῖν τὰ ἀγαθά; ἐσημειώθη ἐφ' ἡμᾶς τὸ φῶς τοῦ προσώπου σου, Κύριε."

[^737]: LXX Psalm 4:8: "ἀπὸ καρποῦ σίτου, οἴνου καὶ ἐλαίου αὐτῶν ἐπληθύνθησαν." Completes verse 8 from leaf p298.

[^738]: LXX Psalm 4:9: "ἐν εἰρήνῃ ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ κοιμηθήσομαι καὶ ὑπνώσω, ὅτι σύ, Κύριε, κατὰ μόνας ἐπ' ἐλπίδι κατῴκισάς με." Final verse of Psalm 4 [LXX 4].

[^739]: CS: "ТА́ЖЕ МЛ҃ТВА СІ́И ВЕЛЕГЛА́СНО." Rubric prescribing the audible recitation of the prayer of repentance before the analogion.
