[^1137]: Rubric in red cinnabar ink introducing the pre-communion prayer of St. John of Damascus (*МЛ҃ТВА СТ҃ГО И҆ БГ҃ОНО́СНАГО ѾЦА НА́ШЕГО І҆ѠА́ННА ДАМАСКИ́НА*), designated as being composed after the manner of them that confess their sins (*ꙗ҆́ко въ ѻ҆́бразѣ и҆сповѣ́дающихсѧ*).

[^1138]: Eschatological courtroom imagery: The penitent envisions standing before Christ's dread and impartial tribunal (*на стра́шнѣмъ и҆ нелицемѣ́рнѣмъ твое́мъ прѣсто́лѣ*), anticipating the final judgment before the arrival of that day.

[^1139]: Confession of the conscience: Bowed down by inner conviction (*прекло́ненъ свое́ю совѣ́стію*), laying bare and exposing every lawless deed before God and His holy angels.

[^1140]: Scriptural allusion to Psalm 39:13 (LXX): *"For evils without number have encompassed me; my iniquities have taken hold upon me, and I am not able to look up; they are multiplied more than the hairs of my head"* (LXX Ps. 39:13: ἐπληθύνθησαν ὑπὲρ τὰς τρίχας τῆς κεφαλῆς μου).

[^1141]: Ascetic catalog of sins: Detailed self-accusation encompassing sins of the flesh, spirit, and tongue, transitioning from internal mental consent (*въѡбрази́хъ въ дꙋши́ мое́й*) to actualized external deeds.

[^1142]: Distinctive Ruthenian moral vocabulary: Note the presence of East Slavic / Ruthenian terms such as *коу́рсьство* (debauchery/fornication, from Ruthenian *курварство*) and *покле́пъ* (slander, defamation, false accusation).

[^1143]: Comprehensive enumeration of economic and social vices: *сребролю́бїе* (love of money), *любоимѣ́нїе* (avarice), *лихси́мство* (usury/extortion), *славолю́бїе* (vainglory), *многостѧжа́нїе* (covetousness of possessions), *самолю́бїе* (self-love), and *сквръноприбы́тчество* (shameful gain, Greek *αἰσχροκέρδεια*, 1 Peter 5:2, Titus 1:7).

[^1144]: Defilement of the faculties: Confessing the total corruption of the senses (*чю́вство*) and bodily members, rendered useless and subservient to the demonic will.

[^1145]: Scriptural quotation of Psalm 37:5 (LXX): *"For my iniquities are gone over my head; as a heavy burden they have pressed heavily upon me"* (LXX Ps. 37:5: ὅτι αἱ ἀνομίαι μου ὑπερῆραν τὴν κεφαλήν μου).

[^1146]: Theological premise of divine mercy: Asserting that no human sin, however monstrous, can overcome the boundless compassions and ineffable goodness of God's love for mankind (*чл҃колю́бїе* / Greek *φιλανθρωπία*).

[^1147]: Scriptural petition drawn from Psalm 16:7 (LXX): *"Make marvelous Thy mercies, O Thou that savest them that hope in Thee"* (LXX Ps. 16:7: θαυμάστωσον τὰ ἐλέη σου).

[^1148]: Typological archetypes of biblical repentance: Citing the Prodigal Son (Luke 15:11–32), the Publican (Luke 18:9–14), the Penitent Thief (Luke 23:39–43), King Manasseh (2 Chron. 33:12–13 / Prayer of Manasseh), and the Harlot who anointed Christ's feet (Luke 7:36–50).

[^1149]: Allusion to the Parable of the Laborers in the Vineyard: Citing Matthew 20:1–16, where those arriving at the eleventh hour received the full denarius of grace despite having performed no proportion of labor.

[^1150]: Unrestrained self-accusation: Acknowledging transgressions committed beyond measure (*пресогрѣши́вша вы́ше мѣ́ры*) in thought, word, and unnatural or irrational lusts (*безмѣ́стнымъ похотѣ́нїемъ и҆ безслове́снымъ жела́нїемъ*).

[^1151]: Grieving the Holy Spirit: An ascetic echo of Ephesians 4:30 ("And grieve not the Holy Spirit of God"), confessing sins committed night and day, willfully and involuntarily, openly and in secret.

[^1152]: The unmasking at the Judgment: Expectation of the dread exposure before Christ's tribunal, where all hidden sins are manifested exactly as they were committed (cf. 2 Cor. 5:10, 1 Cor. 4:5).

[^1153]: Scriptural citations from the Penitential Psalms: Directly echoing Psalm 6:2–3 (LXX) and Psalm 37:2 (LXX): *"O Lord, rebuke me not in Thine indignation, neither chasten me in Thy wrath. Have mercy upon me, O Lord, for I am weak"*; combined with the creaturely plea of Job 10:8 and Psalm 118:73 (*но̀ и҆̀ твоѐ созда́нїе а́зъ*).

[^1154]: Web of Penitential Psalm citations: Stringing together Psalm 37:3 (LXX: *"Thou hast pressed Thy hand heavily upon me"*), Psalm 50:6 (LXX: *"Against Thee only have I sinned, and done this evil before Thee"*), and Psalm 142:2 (LXX: *"And enter not into judgment with Thy servant, for in Thy sight shall no man living be justified"*).

[^1155]: Scriptural quote from Psalm 129:3 (LXX): *"If Thou, Lord, shouldest mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand?"* (LXX Ps. 129:3: ἐὰν ἀνομίας παρατηρήσῃς, Κύριε, Κύριε, τίς ὑποστήσεται;).

[^1156]: Allusion to the Prayer of Manasseh: *"And I am not worthy to behold and see the height of heaven for the multitude of mine iniquities"* (Prayer of Manasseh 9).

[^1157]: Early Christian and Patristic moral classification: Specifically identifying carnal sins including nocturnal/sensual emissions (*и҆стица́нїа*), effeminacy (*оу҆мягче́нїа*, Greek *μαλακίαι*, 1 Cor. 6:9), onanism (*рꙋкоблоу́дїа*), and the corruption of youth (*дѣторастлѣ́нїа*, Greek *παιдофθορίαι*, Didache 2:2).

[^1158]: Patristic catalog of sensual provocations: Noting rare ascetic terms such as *наскака́нїа* (wanton assaults or leaping, Greek *ἐπιπηδήσεις*) and *и҆скокта́нїа* (titillations, sensual dallying or wanton provocations, from CS *скокта́ти*).

[^1159]: Echo of Psalm 13:3 (LXX) and Romans 3:12: *"They are together become unprofitable"* (*непотрѣ́бенъ бы́хъ* / Greek *ἠχρειώθησαν*).

[^1160]: Scriptural opening of the plea for deliverance: Quoting Psalm 7:2 (LXX): *"O Lord my God, in Thee have I put my trust; save me from all them that persecute me, and deliver me"* (LXX Ps. 7:2: Κύριε ὁ Θεός μου, ἐπὶ σοὶ ἤλπισα).

[^1161]: Liturgical penitential formula: Pleading for remission and pardon (*ѡ҆сла́би, ѡ҆ста́ви, и҆ прости́*) according to the multitude of God's tender mercies (cf. Ps. 50:3 LXX).

[^1162]: Direct invocation of Psalm 50:3 (LXX): *"Have mercy upon me, O God, according to Thy great mercy, and according to the multitude of Thy compassions blot out my transgression"* (LXX Ps. 50:3: Ἐλέησόν με, ὁ Θεός, κατὰ τὸ μέγα ἔлеос σου).

[^1163]: Ascetic terminology of spiritual warfare: Deliverance from demonic assaults (*приложе́нїа*, Greek *προσβοлаί*) and habitual sins that grow along with the fallen soul (*съвъзраста́ющихъ є́й зѡ́лъ*).

[^1164]: Direct Pauline citation from Romans 5:20: *"Where sin abounded, grace did much more abound"* (*и҆де́же оу҆мно́жисѧ грѣ́хъ, преизоби́лоуетъ бл҃года́ть* / Greek *οὗ δὲ ἐπλεόνασεν ἡ ἁμαρτία, ὑπερεπερίσσευσεν ἡ χάρις*).

[^1165]: Doxological conclusion of the confessional pre-communion prayer: Proclaiming God as "the God of them that repent" (*Б҃ъ ка́ющихсѧ*), concluding with the Father Paul Doxology standard (*unto ages of ages*).

[^1166]: Rubric in red cinnabar ink introducing the second pre-communion prayer of St. John of Damascus (*ТОГО́ЖЕ СТ҃АГО І҆ѠА́ННА ДАМА́СКИНА • МЛ҃ТВА • КЪ СТ҃О́МОУ ПРИЧАЩЕ́НЇЮ*).

[^1167]: Mystical allusions to the Song of Songs and the Psalter: Expressing spiritual love-wounding (*τετρωμένη ἀγάπης*, Song of Songs 2:5, 5:8) and consuming divine zeal quoting Psalm 118:139 (LXX: *"Thy zeal hath caused me to pine away"*, ἐξέτηξέ με ὁ ζῆλός σου).

[^1168]: Dogma of Theosis (*деификация*): Eucharistic theology of deification through the reception of the life-giving and deifying Blood (*живо́тныꙗ и҆ бг҃отво́рныꙗ ти кро́ве*) and partaking of the divine nature (2 Peter 1:4).

[^1169]: Eschatological anticipation drawn from 1 Thessalonians 4:17: Longing to meet Christ at His second coming, being caught up in the clouds in the air with all the elect (*на въздꙋ́шнѣмъ въсхище́нїи на ѡ҆блацѣ́хъ*, 1 Thess. 4:17: ἁρπαγησόμεθα ἐν νεφέλαις εἰς ἀπάντησιν τοῦ Κυρίου εἰς ἀέρα).

[^1170]: Trinitarian doxology concluding the second prayer: Glorifying the Son together with the unoriginate Father and the most holy, good, and life-creating Spirit.

[^1171]: Rubric in red cinnabar ink introducing the third pre-communion prayer of St. John of Damascus (*ТОГѠ́ЖЕ СТ҃ГО І҆ѠА́ННА ДАМА́СКИНА • МЛ҃ТВА • КЪ СТ҃О́Мꙋ ПРИЧАЩЕ́НЇЮ*).

[^1172]: Drawing near unto Holy Communion: Trusting in the abyss of Christ's love for mankind (*поучи́нꙋ чл҃колю́бїа твое́го*), the penitent dares to approach the holy and life-creating Mysteries (continuing onto leaf p391).

[^1173]: Eucharistic fear of burning: The dread of approaching the Eucharistic coal (cf. Isaiah 6:6–7), fearing to be consumed by the divine fire (*да невъмѣ́сто просвѣще́нїа ѡ҆па́ленъ бꙋ́дꙋ*), echoing the liturgical warnings in the Byzantine Pre-Communion prayers.

[^1174]: Fourfold fruits of Communion: Reception of the Holy Mysteries *unto enlightenment, unto delight, unto joy, and unto gladness of soul and body* (*въ просвѣще́нїе, въ наслажде́нїе, въ ра́дость, и҆ въ весе́лїе дꙋши и҆ тѣ́лоу мое́моу*).

[^1175]: Rubric in red cinnabar ink introducing the fourth pre-communion prayer of St. John of Damascus (*ТОГО́ЖЕ І҆ѠА́ННА ДАМА́СКИНА • МЛ҃ИТВА КЪ СТ҃О́МОУ ПРИЧАЩЕ́НЇЮ*), continuing immediately onto leaf p392.

[^1176]: Intercession for enemies: The penitent prays for those who hate, persecute, reproach, and slander him (cf. Matt. 5:44, Luke 6:27–28), pleading that no one may suffer condemnation on his account either in this age or in the age to come. Marginal rubric `ді҃` denotes Prayer 14 of the sequential pre-communion series.

[^1177]: Rubric in red cinnabar ink introducing the first pre-communion prayer of St. Symeon the Metaphrast (*СТ҃ГО СѶМЕѠ́НА МЕТАФРА́СТА • МЛ҃ТВА КЪ СТ҃О́Мꙋ ПРИЧАЩЕ́НЇЮ*).

[^1178]: Christological prologue of St. Symeon the Metaphrast: Addressing Christ as the *only pure and incorrupt Lord* (*Еди́нъ чⷭ҇тыи и҆ нетлѣ́нный Гьⷭ҇*), Who in His ineffable philanthropy assumed human nature from the pure virginal blood of the Theotokos (continuing onto leaf p393).

[^1179]: Incarnation by the Holy Spirit: Confessing the virginal conception through the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit and the good pleasure of the eternal Father (Luke 1:35).

[^1180]: Pauline Christological titles: Christ as *Wisdom of God, and Peace, and Power* (1 Cor. 1:24, Eph. 2:14).

[^1181]: Instruments of the Passion (*Arma Christi*): The Crucifixion, Cross, nails, spear, and death invoked as spiritual weapons to put to death the carnal passions of the flesh (Col. 3:5).

[^1182]: Despoiling of hades and mystical burial: Spiritual typology linking Christ's burial and the harrowing of hell (*а҆́дова плѣни́лъ є҆сѝ црⷭ҇твїа*) to the mortification of evil thoughts and the destruction of demonic spirits.

[^1183]: Resurrection of the Forefather: Commemorating Christ's raising of Adam (*па́дшаго пр҃аѡ҆ц҃а*) by His third-day resurrection (continuing onto leaf p394).

[^1184]: Deification of human nature through the Ascension: The dogmatic theology of Christ deifying the assumed flesh (*пло́тьское ѻ҆божи́въ въспрїѧ́тїе*) and seating human nature at the right hand of the Father (Heb. 1:3).

[^1185]: Right-hand portion of the elect: Scriptural allusion to Matthew 25:31–34, pleading through Holy Communion to be counted among the sheep on the right hand.

[^1186]: Pentecostal vessel: Echo of Acts 2:1–4, petitioning that the communicant become a receptive temple and dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit (*прїѧ́телище... прише́ствїа*).

[^1187]: The Parousia and meeting in the clouds: Eschatological petition drawn from 1 Thessalonians 4:17 and Acts 17:31, longing to meet the Judge and Creator upon the clouds at His glorious return (continuing onto leaf p395).

[^1188]: Trinitarian doxology concluding the first prayer of St. Symeon the Metaphrast.

[^1189]: Rubric in red cinnabar ink introducing the second pre-communion prayer of St. Symeon the Metaphrast (*ТОГО́ЖЕ СТ҃ГО СѶМЕѠ́НА МЕТАФРА́СТА МЛ҃ТВА КЪ СТ҃О́МОУ ПРИЧАЩЕ́НЇЮ*). Marginal numeral `ѕ҃і` designates Prayer 16 in the codex's numbering scheme.

[^1190]: Mystical contemplative hymnography: The poetic apostrophe to the Trinity as an eternal stream of inexhaustible goodness (*бл҃гти неистощи́маѧ въ вѣ́къ текоу́щи*) and insatiable divine beauty (*доброто̀ мнѡгорачи́телнаѧ, неимы́ сы́тости*).

[^1191]: Justification by faith and hope: The ascetic cry *save me by faith alone, and through hope* (*вѣ́рою є҆ди́ною сп҃си́ мѧ, и҆ чрезъ наде́ждꙋ*), echoing the Pauline theme of salvation by grace through faith (Rom. 3:28, Eph. 2:8).

[^1192]: Classical Orthodox Trinitarian formula: *Trinity in Persons, and Unity in Essence* (*трⷭ҇це ли́ци, и҆ є҆дини́це сꙋ́ществомъ* / Greek Τριὰς τοῖς προσώποις, καὶ Μονὰς τῇ οὐσίᾳ).

[^1193]: Poetic strophic refrain: Repetition of the petition *By faith alone save me, and through hope* (*вѣ́рою є҆диною сп҃си мѧ̀, и҆ чрезъ наде́ждꙋ*).

[^1194]: God as Purifying Fire: Invoking the Divine Trinity as a cleansing fire (*Ѽ ѻ҆́гню чисти́телный*) to consume sins (cf. Heb. 12:29).

[^1195]: Ascetic psychology of the nous: The sovereignty of the intellect and mind (*оу҆́мъ*) reigning over the passions and sensory deliberations (*помышле́нїа*), reflecting Evagrian and Sinaitic neptic theology.

[^1196]: Intellectual illumination: Pleading for the *intellectual candle* (*оу҆́мноую свѣ́щю*) to dispel the darkness of sin and illuminate the inner chamber of the heart.

[^1197]: Whiteness of the penitent soul: Echoing Psalm 50:9 (LXX: *"Thou shalt wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow"*, ἀκουτιεῖς με... ὑπὲρ χιόνα λευκανθήσομαι).

[^1198]: Petition for an Angel of Light: Asking the Holy Trinity to send a radiant angel as guardian, educator, and defender of the soul and body (continuing onto leaf p397).

[^1199]: Patristic angelology: Invoking the Guardian Angel as *tutor* (*пѣстоу́нъ*, Greek παιδαγωγός, Gal. 3:24), *protector* (*прѣста́тель*), *guardian of soul and body*, and *guide unto salvation*.

[^1200]: Ascetic tears of compunction: The ascetic doctrine of *penthos* (mourning) and tears as a second baptism, praying that streams of malice be dried up and showers of tears poured out.

[^1201]: God of the fallen and sinful: Theological affirmation that Christ came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance (Matt. 9:13, Mark 2:17, 1 Tim. 1:15), being accessible to all who have apostatized or transgressed.

[^1202]: Sacramental confession and patterns of repentance: Highlighting the divine institution of confession as the vehicle of salvation (*и҆сповѣ́данїа оу҆ста́ви є҆сѝ сп҃сенїе*), providing biblical exemplars of penitence (continuing onto leaf p398).

[^1203]: Repetition of the self-accusing catalog: Pleading for mercy as an unclean, deceitful, wretched, darkened, and defiled creature (*мнѣ̀ те́мномоу и҆ ѡ҆сквръне́номꙋ*).

[^1204]: Allusion to the Prayer of Manasseh: Quoting Manasseh 9: *"For my transgressions are multiplied more than the sand of the sea, and my iniquities are increased"* (*па́че числа̀ безчи́сленыхъ звѣ́здъ, па́че числа̀ пѣска̀ мо́рскаго съгрѣши́хъ ти*).

[^1205]: Comprehensive pollution of all faculties: Confessing that every imaginable form and shame of evil has been practiced in soul, thoughts, words, and deeds.

[^1206]: Fetters of sinful delusion: Comparing the delusion of the mind and presumption (*мнѣ́нїе*, Greek οἴησις) to heavy iron collars bowing down the neck of the soul (continuing onto leaf p399).

[^1207]: Inescapable bonds of sin: The constriction of the heart and impossibility of looking up, directly echoing Psalm 39:13 (LXX: *"my iniquities have taken hold upon me, and I am not able to look up"*).

[^1208]: Cosmic unworthiness: The fourfold anaphora of unworthiness (*недосто́йнѣ*): unworthily beholding the heavens, beholding human faces, counseling one's neighbor, and even treading upon the earthly dust.

[^1209]: Kindling of divine wrath: Expressing the gravity of voluntary transgression which inflames the righteous indignation of God (cf. Deut. 32:22).

[^1210]: Contempt of the divine will: Rejecting God's pure will and holy statutes, failing to desire any of His pure commandments (continuing onto leaf p400).

[^1211]: Scriptural quote from Psalm 18:10–11 (LXX): *"The judgments of the Lord are true... more desirable than gold and much precious stone"* (LXX Ps. 18:10–11: τὰ κρίματα Κυρίου ἀληθινά... ἐпиθυμητὰ ὑπὲρ χρυσίον).

[^1212]: Scriptural quote from the Prayer of Manasseh: Quoting Prayer of Manasseh 11: *"And now, behold, I bend the knee of my heart, entreating Thy goodness"* (*прекланѧ́ю ти срⷣца мое́го колѣ́нѣ* / Greek καὶ νῦν κλίνω γόνυ καρδίας).

[^1213]: Liturgical triad of bodily contrition: The physical prostration of soul and body expressed through the bowing of the knees of the heart, the darkened head, and the defiled neck.

[^1214]: Liturgical rhythmic confession: The solemn sixfold repetition of *I have sinned* (*съгрѣши́хъ*), cataloging offenses, injustices, transgressions of the commandments, judging of others, and shameless apostasy.

[^1215]: Boldness of penitent supplication: Trusting in divine goodness despite conscious guilt, daring to offer supplication (*но̀ моле́нїе творю̀ твое́й бл҃гти, но мольбоу приношꙋ̀*, continuing onto leaf p401).

[^1216]: Divine tender-heartedness: The penitent appeals to Christ's utmost compassion (*кра́йнее бл҃гооу҆тро́бїе*) and malice-free goodness (*незло́бїе*), crying out for purification (*сп҃си и҆ ѡ҆цѣ́сти мѧ̀*).

[^1217]: Liturgical catalogue of remissions: The fourfold repetition of *remit* (*ѡ҆ста́ви*), pleading for release from the multitude of transgressions, the heavy debts of sin, defilements, and abominations.

[^1218]: Anaphora of protective petitions (*да не...*): Pleading not to be crushed, put to death, suddenly snatched away amidst wicked deliberations, or consumed by the fire of divine judgment together with one's abominations.

[^1219]: The Immortal Banquet: Allusion to the eschatological Messianic banquet and Eucharistic feast (*трапе́за безсъме́ртнаѧ*, cf. Luke 14:15–24, Matt. 22:1–14), praying not to be cast out from the eternal wedding feast or alienated from the fellowship of the saints (continuing onto leaf p402).

[^1220]: Monastic tonsure as second baptism: The traditional Patristic and Byzantine monastic theology regarding the Great Angelic Schema (*великий ангельский образ*) as a renewal of baptismal grace (*второе крещение*), pleading for its restoration after having polluted the first garment of baptism.

[^1221]: God-streaming blood: The theological compound *бг҃ото́чный* (Greek θεόρρυτος), describing the Eucharistic blood flowing from the side of Christ on the Cross (John 19:34).

[^1222]: Ascetic remembrance of death (*memento mori*): The vivid evocation of the terrifying hour of the soul's departure from the body (*въ ча́съ же коне́чный, и҆ го́ркїи съме́ртный*), a hallmark of Byzantine hesychastic prayer.

[^1223]: Demonic toll-houses and the soul's departure: Pleading for a gentle separation of soul and body, protection against demonic spirits encountered in the aerial realm, and the tearing up of the handwriting of sinful debts (cf. Col. 2:14, continuing onto leaf p403).

[^1224]: Tearing of the chirograph: Echoing Colossians 2:14 (*blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us*), praying that the demonic records of sinful debts be utterly obliterated and reduced to ashes in the abyss of hades.

[^1225]: Angelic escort of the soul: The Byzantine liturgical doctrine of radiant guardian angels escorting the departed soul safely through the demonic ranks (*ѿража́ющихъ плъ́кы бѣсѡ́вскыѧ*) into the heavenly realm.

[^1226]: The fiery-formed Throne of Glory: Biblical imagery of the Divine Merkabah and fiery throne of the Ancient of Days (Daniel 7:9, Ezekiel 1:26–28).

[^1227]: Divine Grace personified as Advocate: The theological audacity of presenting God's own grace (*бл҃года́ть*), mercy, and compassion as the primary advocate and intercessor (*хода́тай*, Greek μεσίτης) before His divine justice (continuing onto leaf p404).

[^1228]: Marian typological titles: The Mother of God invoked under canonical Old Testament types: the Adornment of the world, Jacob's Ladder (Gen. 28:12), Aaron's budding rod (Num. 17:8, Isa. 11:1), and the Living/Animate Throne of the Cherubim (*ѻ҆дꙋшевле́нныи прⷭ҇то́лъ*).

[^1229]: The nine angelic choirs: The complete ninefold celestial hierarchy of Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite invoked as lightning-rayed intercessors (*чи́ны млънїелоу́чны*): Thrones, Cherubim, Seraphim, Dominions, Powers, Authorities, Principalities, Archangels, and Angels.

[^1230]: St. John the Baptist and Forerunner: Commemorating his sanctification in his mother's womb prior to birth (Luke 1:15, 41) and his role as the dawn preceding the Sun of Righteousness unto those sitting in darkness (Luke 1:78–79).

[^1231]: Choirs of the righteous: The cosmic intercession of the heavenly Church, invoking the Old Testament patriarchs and prophets, followed by the New Testament apostles and crown-bearing martyrs (continuing onto leaf p405).

[^1232]: St. Mary of Egypt as model of repentance: Invoking St. Mary of Egypt (the quintessential exemplar of radical repentance in the Great Canon of St. Andrew of Crete), celebrated as an earthly human who attained heavenly conversance (*нб҃оше́ствена же ѻ҆ба́че*).

[^1233]: St. Onuphrius the Great and desert asceticism: The 4th-century anchorite of the Egyptian Thebaid who lived sixty years naked in the wilderness, miraculously clothed only by hair and heavenly light, here portrayed as stripped of physical clothing but wondrously adorned with divine virtue.

[^1234]: Transgression from the womb: Echoing Psalm 50:7 (LXX: *"For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins did my mother bear me"*), confessing habitual sinfulness from the very womb (*ѿ ложе́снъ самѣ́хъ*).

[^1235]: Salvation beyond merit: Pleading for salvation not based on human works or merit (*чрѣ досто́инство* / Greek ὑπὲρ τὴν ἀξίαν), but solely through divine benevolence and hope (continuing onto leaf p406).

[^1236]: Doxological conclusion of Prayer 16: Pleading to praise God alongside the celestial hosts unto unnumbered ages (*въ вѣ́кы въсѧ̑ неи҆зчете́нныѧ*).

[^1237]: Rubric in red cinnabar ink introducing Prayer 17 of the Pre-Communion series: *Prayer before Holy Communion, of Saint Symeon the New Theologian, from the Hymns of Divine Love* (*МЛ҃ТВА КЪ СТ҃О́Мꙋ ПРИЧАЩЕ́НЇЮ • СТ҃ГО СѶМЕѠ́НА НО́ВАГО БГ҃ОСЛО́ВА • Ѿ БЖ҃ТВНЫХЪ РА́ЧЇЙ*). The marginal numeral `з҃і` marks Prayer 17. The attribution *From the Hymns of Divine Love* cites the Greek collection *Ἐκ τῶν θείων ἐρώτων* (Hymn 17).

[^1238]: The classic opening of St. Symeon's prayer: The fourfold confession of unworthiness: *From defiled lips, from an abominable heart, from an unclean tongue, from a polluted soul* (*Ἀπὸ ῥυπαρῶν χειλέων, ἀπὸ βδελυρᾶς καρδίας, ἀπὸ ἀκαθάρτου γλώσσης, ἐκ ψυχῆς ἐρρυπωμένης*).

[^1239]: Boldness of the penitent: Asking Christ not to reject the sinner's words, gestures, or audacious daring (*ни дръ́зость*, Greek μηδὲ τὴν ἀναίδейαν, continuing onto leaf p407).

[^1240]: Prayer for bold speech (*parrhesia*): St. Symeon asks Christ to grant him freedom of speech (*дръзнове́ннѣ гл҃ати*) and divine instruction on how to pray properly (Rom. 8:26).

[^1241]: The repentant harlot of Luke 7:36–50: Direct allusion to the sinful woman who purchased alabaster ointment and anointed Christ's feet in Simon the Pharisee's house (*съгрѣши́хъ па́че блоу́дница*).

[^1242]: Christ addressed as the Divine Word (*Слово* / Logos): Invoking Christ under His Johannine title (John 1:1), pleading not to be cast away from His presence.

[^1243]: Tears as precious myrrh: The mystical assimilation of penitential tears to costly spikenard, daring to wash and kiss the feet of the Saviour.

[^1244]: Divine omniscience: Christ's intimate knowledge of the sinner's manifold offenses and inner brokenness (continuing onto leaf p408). Also note the typographical erratum in the printed heading, where folio numeral `рч҃е` (195) is erroneously repeated in place of `рч҃и` (198).

[^1245]: Spiritual diagnosis: Christ as the physician of souls Who sees both the ulcers of sin and the sincere disposition (*произволе́нїе*) and sighing of the heart.

[^1246]: Omnipresence and divine foreknowledge: Nothing escapes God's scrutiny, neither a single tear-drop, nor a fraction of a drop, nor the slightest movement of the heart (*движе́нїе срⷣчное*).

[^1247]: Scriptural quote from Psalm 138:16 (LXX): *"Thine eyes did see mine unformed substance, and in Thy book all shall be written"* (τὸ ἀκατέργαστόν μου εἶδον οἱ ὀφθαλμοί σου, καὶ ἐπὶ τὸ βιβλίον σου πάντες γραφήσονται / *несꙋдѣ́ланное моѐ ви́дѣша ѡ҆́чи твоѝ, въ кни́гах же твои́хъ написа́на тебѣ̀ соу́тъ*).

[^1248]: Scriptural quote from Psalm 24:18 (LXX): *"Look upon my lowliness and my toil, and forgive all my sins"* (ἴде τὴν ταπείνωσίν μου καὶ τὸν κόπον μου, καὶ ἄφες πάσας τὰς ἁμαρτίας μου / *ви́ждь смире́нїе моѐ, ви́ждь троу́д мои́ є҆ли́къ, и҆ грѣхы̀ ѡ҆ста́ви ми*).

[^1249]: Requisite interior disposition for Communion: Purity of heart, fearful contemplation (*стра́шнаѧ мы́сль*), and contrition of soul necessary to receive the undefiled Mysteries without incurring judgment (continuing onto leaf p409).

[^1250]: Eucharistic deification (*Theosis*): The core theological conviction of St. Symeon the New Theologian that the communicant is literally vivified and deified (*ѡ҆живля́етсѧ, и҆ ѡ҆божа́етсѧ* / Greek ζωοῦται καὶ θεοῦται) through the worthy reception of Christ's Body and Blood.

[^1251]: Dominical quotation from John 6:56: *"He that eats My flesh, and drinks My blood, dwells in Me, and I in him"* (*ὁ τρώγων μου τὴν σάρκα καὶ πίνων μου τὸ αἷμα ἐν ἐμοὶ μένει, κἀγὼ ἐν αὐτῷ*).

[^1252]: The Three-Sunned Light: Addressing Christ as the radiance of the Triune Godhead (*свѣ́тъ трисли́чный* / Greek φῶς τρισηλίου), expressing communion with the entire Holy Trinity through Christ.

[^1253]: Christological titles of intimacy: Christ addressed as *Giver of Life* (*живода́вецъ*), *my breath* (*дыха́нїе моѐ*), *my life* (*живо́тъ мои́*), and *my rejoicing* (*възрадова́нїе моѐ*).

[^1254]: Penitential approach: Drawing near to the chalice with tears and inner contrition, seeking remission of offenses (continuing onto leaf p410).

[^1255]: Protection from the Deceiver: The danger of spiritual vulnerability when alienated from divine grace, whereby the devil (*преле́стникъ*, the Deceiver) snatches the soul away and separates it from Christ's words.

[^1256]: Gospel types of repentance: Juxtaposing the Prodigal Son (Luke 15:11–32) and the penitent harlot (Luke 7:36–50), entreating Christ to extend the same unconditional acceptance to the communicant.

[^1257]: Consciousness of chief among sinners: Echoing 1 Timothy 1:15 (*"sinners, of whom I am chief"*), acknowledging personal guilt as surpassing all others (continuing onto leaf p411).

[^1258]: Transgression vs. Divine Philanthropy: The classical theological motif that no magnitude or multitude of human sin can ever surpass the inexhaustible ocean of God's love for mankind (*мнѡ́гое чл҃колꙋ́бїе*), citing St. Symeon the New Theologian's Hymn 17 (*Ἐκ τῶν θείων ἐρώτων*).

[^1259]: Divine Conversance with the Penitent: The mystical paradox that Christ deigns to converse with cleansed penitents as with His own intimate friends (*ꙗ҆́коже дрꙋгѡ́мъ свои́мъ бли́жнимъ*, cf. John 15:14–15).

[^1260]: The Communicant as Grass before Divine Fire: The bold ascetic paradox of the communicant being "grass" (*трава̀ сы́й*) daring to partake of divine Fire, yet marvelously preserved without being consumed, prefigured by the burning bush on Mount Sinai (Exodus 3:2, continuing onto leaf p412).

[^1261]: The Incombustible Bush (*Неопалимая Купина*): The Old Testament theophany of Exodus 3:2 applied typologically to the Eucharistic mystery, wherein divine fire dews rather than consumes the faithful receiver (*нн҃ѣ ѻ҆роша́емь неѻ҆па́лно*).

[^1262]: Whole-person Thanksgiving: The triple grateful confession uniting word (*сло́вомъ*), heart (*срⷣцемъ*), and the bodily and spiritual members (*оу҆́десы и҆ дш҃и и҆ тѣ́ла*).

[^1263]: Incipit of the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed: The rubric prescribes the recitation of the Confession of the Orthodox Faith (*и҆сповѣ́данїе правосла́вныѧ вѣ́ры*), printed only as its canonical opening incipit (*Вѣ́роую въ є҆ди́наго Б҃а*), strictly preserved without unwritten textual expansion per Mandate 16.

[^1264]: The Holy Thursday Eucharistic Troparion: The celebrated Byzantine hymn *Of Thy Mystical Supper* (*Ве́чери твоеѧ̀ та́йнѣй*), juxtaposing the betrayal of Judas with the saving confession of the Good Thief (Luke 23:42).

[^1265]: Epistolary Reading on the Institution of the Eucharist: The liturgical lection from 1 Corinthians 11:23–26 prescribed for the communicant's preparation, recounting the Pauline institution narrative.

[^1266]: The Pauline Anamnesis: The dominical command *This do in remembrance of Me* (*сѐ твори́те въ моѐ въспомина́нїе*, 1 Cor. 11:24–25), underscoring the Eucharistic commemoration of the Lord's death (continuing onto leaf p414).

[^1267]: The Grave Warning of Unworthy Partaking: 1 Corinthians 11:27–32, warning that eating and drinking unworthily incurs guilt against the Body and Blood of the Lord (*пови́ненъ бꙋ́детъ тѣ́лоу и҆ кро́ви Гдⷭ҇ни*) and eating judgment unto oneself.

[^1268]: Gospel Lection of the Bread of Life: The opening of John 6:48–54 addressed to the Jews, identifying Christ as the true Bread of Life (*А҆́зъ є҆́смь хлѣ́бъ живо́тный*) far surpassing the ancestral wilderness manna (continuing onto leaf p415).

[^1269]: The Living Bread and Eschatological Life: John 6:51, proclaiming that whoever eats of this living bread shall live unto ages, identifying the Eucharistic bread with Christ's flesh given for the life of the world.

[^1270]: The Johannine Eucharistic Imperative: John 6:53–54, demanding the eating of the flesh of the Son of Man and the drinking of His Blood as the indispensable prerequisite for eternal life and resurrection at the last day (continuing onto leaf p416).

[^1271]: Concluding Johannine Promise: John 6:54b (*and I will raise him up at the last day*), sealing the Scriptural pre-communion lectionary.

[^1272]: Interior Examination of Conscience: Rubric directing the communicant to search their conscience in mind and soul as they draw near the Holy Gifts (*ѡ҆блича́ѧ въ оу҆мѣ̀ совѣ́сть свою̀*).

[^1273]: Short Prayer of Approach: A brief penitential prayer acknowledging the terror of divine fire while appealing to God's purifying mercy, concluding with the Psalmic citation *It is good for me to cleave unto God* (Psalm 72:28 LXX).

[^1274]: Triple Pre-Communion Exclamation: Rubric prescribing the recitation, if desired even three times, of the awe-filled verses as one approaches the chalice.

[^1275]: The Eucharistic Coal of Isaiah: Echoing the seraphic live coal of Isaiah 6:6–7, warning that the deifying Blood consumes the unworthy while purifying sins (continuing onto leaf p417).

[^1276]: Spiritual and Intellectual Deification: The theological distinction that Christ's holy Flesh deifies the human spirit (*ѡ҆божа́етъ дх҃ъ*) while strangely and marvelously nourishing the mind (*оу҆́мъ же пита́етъ стра́ннѣ и҆ чю́днѣ*).

[^1277]: Rubric for Crosswise Hand Gesture: Prescribing the traditional Byzantine ceremonial posture of crossing one's hands upon the breast (*крⷭ҇тоо́бразно рꙋ́цѣ на пръ́сехъ положи́въ*) when approaching to receive the Holy Mysteries of the Crucified One.

[^1278]: Major Structural Division: The beginning of the Post-Communion Thanksgiving Prayers (*Послѣдованіе по святомъ причащеніи*), marked on leaf p418 by a prominent Renaissance woodcut headpiece, rubric in red display majuscules, and the first prayer numbered `а҃` in the margin.

[^1279]: Rubric of Immediate Thanksgiving: Admonishing the communicant not to delay, but immediately to sing praises and give fervent thanks unto God from the soul after receiving the life-creating Mysteries.

[^1280]: Prayer 1 of Saint Basil the Great: The classic Post-Communion prayer attributed to St. Basil the Great (*Мл҃тва ст҃го вели́каго васїлїа, по ст҃о́мъ прича́щенїи*), expressing profound gratitude for being accounted worthy of the heavenly gifts (continuing onto leaf p419).

[^1281]: The Catalogue of Eucharistic Graces: St. Basil's detailed enumeration of the spiritual fruits of Communion: healing of soul and body, driving away of demonic adversaries, enlightenment of spiritual sight, pacification of inner passions, unfeigned love, and keeping of the commandments.

[^1282]: Living No Longer Unto Oneself: Echoing 2 Corinthians 5:15 and Romans 14:7–8, praying that the communicant, preserved by divine holiness, may live no longer for self, but unto Christ (continuing onto leaf p420).

[^1283]: Eschatological Rest and the Ineffable Beauty: The sublime conclusion of St. Basil's prayer, longing to attain unto everlasting rest (*въ присносꙋ́щный доидоу̀ поко́й*) where the festival of the righteous never ends and the beauty of God's countenance is beheld forever.

[^1284]: Prayer 2 of Saint John Chrysostom: The post-communion prayer attributed to St. John Chrysostom (*И҆́же въ ст҃ы́хъ ѻ҆́ц҃а на́шего і҆ѡа́нна златооу́стаго мл҃, по ст҃о́ причаще́нїи*), marked with numeral `в҃` in the margin.

[^1285]: Ruthenian Lexical Witness *оу҆трѣ́пѣ*: The rare temporal adverbial form *оу҆трѣ́пѣ* (dial./early modern variant corresponding to *заутра* / *рано вранці* / *early this morning*), witnessing the morning celebration of the Divine Liturgy.

[^1286]: Eucharistic Table and Preservation of Grace: The continuation of St. John Chrysostom's second post-communion prayer, entreating that the communicant's humble soul may keep the grace of the immortal table unalienated (*неѿе́млемꙋ*).

[^1287]: The Unquenchable Light and Spiritual Senses: The petition that the communicant's understanding and bodily senses be illumined by divine unquenchable light (*просвѣще́нїе твоѐ неоу҆гаси́мо*), preserved unstumbling from sin (continuing onto leaf p422).

[^1288]: Bodiless Ministers and Heavenly Intercessors: The prayer's concluding invocation of the all-pure Sovereign Lady Theotokos, the bodiless ministers (*безплѡ́тныхъ ти слꙋжи́тель*, referring to the angelic orders), and all saints who have pleased God from the ages.

[^1289]: Prayer 3 of Saint John Chrysostom: The post-communion prayer attributed to St. John Chrysostom (*Того́ ст҃го і҆ѡа́нна златооу́стаго мл҃тва, по ст҃о́мъ причаще́нїи*), marked with numeral `г҃` in the margin, addressing Christ as King of ages and Creator of all.

[^1290]: Shelter of Wings: The biblical imagery of divine protection under the wings of God (Psalm 16:8; 35:8; 90:4 LXX: *покро́вомъ крилоу̀ твоє́ю*, continuing onto leaf p423).

[^1291]: Communion Unto the Last Breath: The earnest petition to partake worthily of the Holy Mysteries unto one's last breath (*до послѣ́дняго и҆здыха́нїа*), sealing salvation and eternal life.

[^1292]: Christ as the Bread of Life and Fountain of Sanctity: The theological tituli applied to Christ (*хлѣ́б живо́тный*, *и҆сто́чникъ ст҃ыни*, *пода́тель бл҃гы́хъ*), echoing John 6:35, 48.

[^1293]: Prayer 4 of Saint John Chrysostom: A concise hymn-like post-communion prayer (*Того́ ст҃го і҆ѡа́нна златооу́стаго мл҃тва*), marked with numeral `д҃` in the margin, offering praise and worship for being mystically made a partaker of the Lord's Body and Blood (continuing onto leaf p424).

[^1294]: Prayer 5 of Saint John of Damascus: The post-communion prayer attributed to St. John of Damascus (*Ст҃го і҆ѡа́нна дамаски́на мл҃тва*), marked with numeral `е҃` in the margin.

[^1295]: Theological Lexical Witness *непостоѧ́нный*: The rare Church Slavonic term *непостоѧ́нный* (literally "unstanding", uncontainable, boundless) translating the Greek liturgical epithet *ὁ ἀκατάληπτος* (incomprehensible / uncontainable).

[^1296]: The Consuming Fire and Ministering Spirits: Allusion to Psalm 103:4 LXX (*Who makes His angels spirits, and His ministers a flame of fire*) and Hebrews 12:29 (*For our God is a consuming fire*), marveling that this same Divine Fire is given in love as nourishing food.

[^1297]: Piercing Joints and Marrow: The physical and spiritual penetration of the Eucharistic presence through every limb, bone, and marrow, directly reflecting the language of Hebrews 4:12 (continuing onto leaf p425).

[^1298]: Indwelling of the Trinity: Echoing Christ's promise in John 14:23 (*If a man love Me, he will keep My words: and My Father will love him, and We will come unto him, and make Our abode with him*), translated here as *ѡ҆би́тѣ сътворя́ѧ въ мнѣ̀ съ бл҃вє́ннымъ ѿце́мъ свои́мъ*.

[^1299]: Prayer 6 of Saint Cyril of Alexandria: The post-communion prayer attributed to St. Cyril of Alexandria (*Ст҃го кѷрі́лла а҆лєѯандрі́искаго мл҃тва*), marked with numeral `ѕ҃` in the margin.

[^1300]: Standing at the Right Hand: The eschatological petition to be placed at Christ's right hand at the Dread Judgment (Matthew 25:33: *и҆ на ст҃ѣ́мъ твоє́мъ сꙋдѣ̀ поста́ви мѧ̀ ѻ҆де́сноую тебѣ̀*).

[^1301]: Prayer 7 of Saint Symeon the Metaphrast: The famed Byzantine post-communion thanksgiving prayer attributed to St. Symeon the Metaphrast (*Ст҃го сѷмеѡ́на метафра́ста мл҃*), marked with numeral `з҃` in the margin.

[^1302]: Consuming the Thorns of Sins: The imagery of sin as soul-choking thorns burned away by divine fire (*попалѧ́ѧ тръ́нїе всѣ́хъ мои̑ съгрѣше́нїи*), recalling the Edenic curse of thorns (Genesis 3:18).

[^1303]: The Pentad of the Senses (*патери́ца*): The Greek liturgical loanword *патєри́цꙋ* translating *τὴν ἁπλῆν πεντάδα* ("the simple fivefold count" or pentad of the bodily senses), entreating that all five senses be illuminated by the divine presence.

[^1304]: Nailed to the Fear of God: Direct quotation of Psalm 118:120 LXX (*καθήλωσον ἐκ τοῦ φόβου σου τὰς σάρκας μου* / *всего̀ мѧ̀ пригвоздѝ стра́хꙋ твое́мꙋ*, continuing onto leaf p427).

[^1305]: The Communicant as Living Temple: The theology of the human person as a temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19), through whose entrance all demonic influence and wicked passion is driven away like fire.

[^1306]: The Heavenly Intercessory Choir: St. Symeon's marshalling of the angelic orders (*чинонача́лїа безпло́тныхъ*), the holy Forerunner John, the wise Apostles, and the Mother of God as advocates before the compassionate Christ.

[^1307]: Sanctification and Radiance: Acknowledging Christ alone as the true sanctification and radiance (*ѡ҆сщ҃е́нїе є҆ди́ныи... и҆ свѣ́тлость*) of Christian souls (continuing onto leaf p428).

[^1308]: Prayer 8 to the Most Holy Theotokos: The post-communion prayer addressed to the Mother of God (*мл҃тва, къ прⷭ҇тѣ́й Бц҃и*), marked with numeral `и҃` in the margin.

[^1309]: Marian Liturgical Tituli: The cascade of Marian praises (*свѣ́те помраче́нныѧ ми дш҃а, наде́жде и҆ покро́ве, прибѣ́жище и҆ оу҆твръжде́нїе, и҆ възра́дованїе моѐ*), acknowledging her role as mediatrix of the heavenly gifts.

[^1310]: Bearer of the True Light: Addressing the Virgin Mary as the Mother of the True Light (John 1:9) and the Fountain of Immortality (*и҆сто́чникъ безсмр҃тїа*), entreating the enlightenment of the spiritual eyes of the heart (Ephesians 1:18, continuing onto leaf p429).

[^1311]: Spiritual Quickening and Restoration: Petition to be restored to spiritual life from the deadness of sin (*ѡ҆животворѝ мѧ̀ оу҆мръщве́ннаго грѣхо́мъ*), begging for the gift of tears and compunction (*пла́чь и҆ съкроуше́нїе*).

[^1312]: Deliverance from Captivity of Reasonings: Asking for restoration from the wandering captivity of discursive worldly thoughts (*възведе́нїе въ плѣне́ныхъ по́мысломъ*, cf. 2 Corinthians 10:5).

[^1313]: Prayer 9 after Holy Communion: The concluding prayer of the post-communion series (*мл҃тва по ст҃о́мъ причаще́нїи*), marked with numeral `ѳ҃` in the margin on leaf p430.

[^1314]: The Nourishing Divine Fire: The mystery of God as Fire (Deuteronomy 4:24; Hebrews 12:29) which does not destroy the faithful receiver, but provides celestial nourishment (*є҆стество́ бо ꙗ҆́ко ѡ҆́гнь неѡпалѧ́еши, но пита́еши*).

[^1315]: Purifying the Fivefold Senses: The second occurrence in this sequence of the rare Ruthenian/Slavonic loanword *патєри́цеу* (Greek *πεντάς* / *πεντάδα*), denoting the purification of all five senses.

[^1316]: The Post-Communion Climax: The rubrical prescription ordering the recitation of *It is truly meet* (*досто́йно є҆́сть*), the Trisagion Prayers through the *Our Father*, and the troparion of the day or patron saint of the church.

[^1317]: Liturgical Dismissal (*Apolysis*): The rubrical conclusion prescribing the twelvefold *Lord, have mercy*, the triple *Lord, have mercy* with *Lord, bless*, and the final canonical dismissal formula (*За мл҃твъ ст҃ы ѿц҃ъ на́шихъ...*), solemnly sealing the rite of Thanksgiving after Holy Communion.

[^1318]: The Order of Administering Holy Communion to the Sick in Haste (Church Slavonic: *Чинъ како подобаетъ болному дати прича́стїе въско́рѣ*; Greek: *Ἀκολουθία εἰς τὸ μεταδοῦναι τῷ ἀσθενεῖ ταχέως*). This ancient office provides an abbreviated rite for administering the pre-sanctified reserved Eucharist (Viaticum) when a Christian is in imminent danger of death. Striatyn 1606, fol. 107r.

[^1319]: Slavonic *тр҃сто́е* (abbreviated *трисвятое*). The customary Initial Prayers (Trisagion through the Lord's Prayer) concluded by the priestly doxological exclamation (*"For Thine is the kingdom..."*).

[^1320]: The three-fold invitation to worship (*"Come, let us worship and fall down before Christ..."*) followed by the recitation of the entire Nicene-Constantinopolitan Symbol of Faith (*Credo*), confirming the communicant's steadfast profession of the Orthodox faith before receiving the Holy Mysteries.

[^1321]: The liturgical troparion chanted on Great and Holy Thursday and before the reception of Holy Communion: *"Of Thy Mystical Supper, O Son of God, receive me today as a communicant..."* (Greek: *Τοῦ δείπνου σου τοῦ μυστικοῦ σήμερον, Υἱὲ Θεοῦ, κοινωνόν με παράλαβε*). Striatyn 1606, fol. 107r.

[^1322]: The prayer of the Good Thief on the cross (Luke 23:42).

[^1323]: The Dogmatic Theotokion of Tone 8 (*"The King of heaven out of love for mankind appeared on earth..."* / Greek: *Ὁ Βασιλεὺς τῶν οὐρανῶν, διὰ φιλανθρωπίαν, ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς ὤφθη*), affirming the hypostatic union and two unconfused natures in Christ (*"double in nature, but not in person"* / Slavonic: *сꙋгꙋ́бъ є҆ство́мъ, а҆ не съста́вомъ*), chanted here to fortify the sick communicant in Orthodox Christology. Striatyn 1606, fol. 107v.

[^1324]: Theotokion: *"We have known God incarnate of thee, O Virgin Theotokos; do thou beseech Him for the salvation of our souls."*

[^1325]: A solemn priestly prayer of benediction and spiritual fortification over the sick communicant, invoking the Lord's mercy, teaching, illumination, defense, forgiveness, and salvation at the Day of Judgment. Striatyn 1606, fol. 108r.

[^1326]: Rubric: *"A second prayer from the person of the sick one."* In the Ruthenian and Byzantine Euchologia, when the sick person is capable of speech, he prays this confession directly; if incapacitated, the priest reads it in the first person on his behalf. Striatyn 1606, fol. 108v.

[^1327]: John 6:56: *"He that eats My flesh, and drinks My blood, dwells in Me, and I in Him."*

[^1328]: Rubric: *"A third prayer, similar to the second."* Striatyn 1606, fol. 108v.

[^1329]: Prayer attributed to St. John Chrysostom before Holy Communion: *"I know that I am not worthy that Thou shouldest enter under the roof of the temple of my soul, for it is all desolate and fallen..."* (cf. Matthew 8:8 / Luke 7:6). Striatyn 1606, fol. 109r.

[^1330]: Allusion to Matthew 8:20 and Luke 9:58: *"the Son of man hath not where to lay His head."*

[^1331]: The Prayer against Any Defilement (Greek: *Εὐχὴ ἐπὶ πάσης κηλῖδος*), prescribed to be read before communion if the communicant has suffered any nocturnal pollution, contact with impure substances, or demonic vexation. Striatyn 1606, fol. 109v.

[^1332]: Allusion to Acts 10:9–16, the vision of the sheet granted to the Apostle Peter on the rooftop in Joppa, commanding him to call nothing common or unclean which God has cleansed. Striatyn 1606, fol. 109v.

[^1333]: Allusion to Acts 9:15 (*"a chosen vessel unto Me"*) and Titus 1:15 (*"Unto the pure all things are pure"*).

[^1334]: Church Slavonic *потко́ръ* (from *потка́ти / потка́тися*, to stumble, encounter, or suffer an offense / affront / temptation); referring to demonic stumbling blocks or temptations. Striatyn 1606, fol. 110r.

[^1335]: An elevated liturgical petition describing the Holy Eucharist as the awful mystery celebrated in concert with the heavenly angelic ranks (*"this awesome ministry of the heavenly orders"*). Striatyn 1606, fol. 110v.

[^1336]: Rubric specifying the immediate administration of the Holy Gifts to the sick person with the liturgical spoon. Striatyn 1606, fol. 111r.

[^1337]: Thanksgiving prayer attributed to St. Cyril of Alexandria (*"Thy holy Body, O Lord Jesus Christ, be unto me for life and sanctification..."*), an ancient post-communion troparion preserved in Ruthenian and Byzantine euchologia. Striatyn 1606, fol. 111r.

[^1338]: Post-communion prayer of thanksgiving attributed to St. John Chrysostom (*"Master God, King of the ages and Creator of all..."* / Greek: *Δέσποτα Θεέ, Βασιλεῦ τῶν αἰώνων*). Striatyn 1606, fol. 111v.

[^1339]: Fol. 221r (`ск҃і`). A post-communion Thanksgiving prayer to the Mother of God (*Моли́тва къ прест҃ѣ́й Бц҃и, по причаще́нїи: Преблаже́нная Госпоже́...*), concluding the expedited order of holy communion for the sick.

[^1340]: Fol. 222r (`ск҃в`). Woodcut headpiece across the top of the folio. The title in ornamental display cinnabar (*ЧИ́НЪ БЫВА́ЕМЫЙ НА РАЗЛꙋЧЕ́НЇЕ, ДꙋШЍ ѿ ТѢ́ЛА*) initiates the classical Byzantine-Ruthenian office for the agony of death (*Ἀκολουθία εἰς ψυχορраγοῦντα*), chanted at the bedside of the dying.

[^1341]: Fol. 222r (`ск҃в`). A historical paper slip repair was pasted over lines 4–6 of the folio, reinforcing paper thinning caused by abraded ink on the verso (fol. 222v). The obscured characters are restored according to Ruthenian Trebnyk and classical Euchologion usage: `Е҆гда̀ кто̀ ѿ [хр҃тїа́нъ...] [...] и҆ прѣ́кѡ начне́тъ и҆знемаг[а́ти ... и҆ сщ҃енникъ] дх҃о́вникъ [въпра́]ша́етъ є҆го̀...` The rubric instructs the father-confessor to inquire gently into any lingering forgotten sin, unconfessed fault, or unforgiven grudge before beginning the office.

[^1342]: Fol. 222v. Psalm 50 (LXX 50; Masoretic Ps 51). The introductory liturgical framework consists of the standard Trisagion prayers, Lord have mercy (12 times), the triple invitation to worship, and the 50th Psalm.

[^1343]: Fol. 222v. Cinnabar rubric attributing the canon to "Lord Andrew of Crete" (*творе́нїе кѵ́ръ а҆ндре́а крїтскаго*, c. 660–740).

[^1344]: Fol. 222v. Tone 6, Heirmos of Ode 1: *Ὡς ἐν ἠπείρῳ πεζεύσας ὁ Ἰσραήλ* (Slavonic: *Ꙗ́ко по сꙋхоу ходи́въ їи́ль*), referring to the crossing of the Red Sea (Exodus 14).

[^1345]: Fol. 223r (`ск҃г`). The reading `въ[сѣ́]мъ грѣ́шникѡмъ` ("to all sinners") is abraded on the page, with only the initial `въ` and final `мъ` remaining legible; restored from parallel Ruthenian and Byzantine witnesses.

[^1346]: Fol. 223r (`ск҃г`). Rubric introducing the Second Canon to the Theotokos: *Дроугіи ка́нѡнъ молб҃енъ пр҃тѣ́й Бц҃и, ѿ лица̀ чл҃кꙋ дш҃ю раздѣлѧ́ющꙋ, и҆ немогꙋ́щꙋ гла́ти...* The acrostic in the Slavonic witness is given as *И҆зба́ви мѧ̀ чт҃аа бѣсѡ́въ моучи́телства* (Greek: *Ῥῦσαί με, σεμνὴ, δαιμόνων τυραννίδος*), followed by the author's name *І҆ѡ́сифъ* (Joseph the Hymnographer, c. 816–886). In the 1606 Striatyn imprint, the two canons are chanted in conjoined succession ode by ode.

[^1347]: Fol. 223v. Tone 6, Ode 1 Heirmos for the Second Canon (*Ꙗ҆́ко по сꙋхꙋ ходи̂ и҆и́ль*).

[^1348]: Fol. 224r (`ск҃д`). Tone 6, Heirmos of Ode 3 (Canon 1): *Οὐκ ἔστιν ἅγιος ὡς σύ, Κύριε ὁ Θεός μου* (Slavonic: *Нѣ́сть ст҃ъ ꙗ҆́коже ты Гд҃и Бг҃е*), based on the Canticle of Hannah (1 Kings / 1 Sam 2:2).

[^1349]: Fol. 224r (`ск҃д`). Slavonic *на стави́лѣ мѣри́лнѣмъ* translates Greek *ἐν ζυγῷ σταθμῶν* ("in the balance of the scales"), evoking the aerial examination and weighing of deeds at the separation of soul and body.

[^1350]: Fol. 224v. Cinnabar rubric *И҆́нъ і҆рмо́съ · та́же* indicates the transition to the troparia of Ode 3 of the Second Canon. The image of the "roaring noetic lion cubs" (*мы́сленїи рыка́юще скѵ́мни*) reflects Psalm 16:12 (LXX) and patristic demonology regarding the predatory spirits awaiting the dying soul.

[^1351]: Fol. 225r (`ск҃е`). Slavonic *Оу҆га́сшоу оу҆́бо ѿню́дъ ѻ҆рга́ноу слове́сномꙋ* (Greek: *Ἀποσβεσθέντος ἄρδην τοῦ ὀργάνου τοῦ λογικοῦ*), describing the physical deathbed cessation of speech while the dying person's inner heart continues to cry out to the Mother of God.

[^1352]: Fol. 225r (`ск҃е`). Tone 6, Heirmos of Ode 4 (Canon 1): *Χριστός μου δύнаμις, Θεὸς καὶ Κύριος* (Slavonic: *Хс҃ мнѣ̀ си́ла Бг҃ъ и҆ Гд҃ь*), based on the Canticle of Habakkuk (Habakkuk 3).

[^1353]: Fol. 225v. The troparion expresses the dramatic terror of the deathbed struggle (*по́двигъ всепа́гꙋбный*) where the soul implores both the celestial angelic orders and earthly friends for mercy and tears as it is unmercifully separated from the flesh.

[^1354]: Fol. 226r (`ск҃ѕ`). Ode 4 of the Second Canon to the Most Holy Theotokos (by Joseph the Hymnographer). The rubric *і҆рмо́съ · та́же ·* directs the continuation of the troparia following the heirmos. The soul implores nature (clouds, mountains, hills) to weep over its catastrophic estrangement from God.

[^1355]: Fol. 226r (`ск҃ѕ`). The dying soul addresses the Mother of God as the infallible and unashamed refuge in the terrifying hour of trial (*въ ча́съ и҆спыта́нїа*).

[^1356]: Fol. 226r (`ск҃ѕ`). The image of the outstretched hands of the Theotokos as the wings of a dove (*ꙗ҆́ко сщ҃еннѣ́ голꙋби́нѣ кри́лѣ*) draws upon Psalm 54:7 (LXX) and patristic maternal shelter motifs.

[^1357]: Fol. 226r (`ск҃ѕ`). Slavonic *Въздоу́шнаго кнѧ́ѕѧ наси́лника мꙋчителѧ, стра́шныхъ пꙋтестоѧ́телѧ* corresponds to Greek *τὸν ἀέριον τύραννον*, depicting the aerial prince and the terrifying inquisitors of words (*словои҆спыта́телѧ*) who examine the departing soul at the toll-houses.

[^1358]: Fol. 226v. Theotokion concluding Ode 4 of the Second Canon. The dying Christian confesses the realization of long-dreaded deathbed terror (*се́ мѧ влч҃це стра́хъ оу҆срѣ́те, є҆го́же и҆ боѧ́хсѧ*).

[^1359]: Fol. 226v. Tone 6, Ode 5 of the First Canon (by St. Andrew of Crete). Heirmos incipit: *Θείῳ φέγγει σου, Ἀγαθέ* (Slavonic: *Бж҃їимъ свѣ́томъ ти, Бл҃же*). The first troparion poignantly addresses the physical/sensible light of the sun and creation (*Свѣ́те чꙋ́вственый*), bidding it farewell as demonic darkness closes in.

[^1360]: Fol. 227r (`ск҃з`). Concluding sentence of Troparion 2 of Ode 5 (Canon 1). The soul reproaches the saints and friends of the Savior for their silence, pleading that a single united cry to the Mother of God would have obtained deliverance from darkness.

[^1361]: Fol. 227r (`ск҃з`). A dramatic personal deathbed farewell to the Archangel Michael (*Сп҃сисѧ вели́кїй кнѧ́же Бж҃їй Миха́иле, а҆́гг҃лѡмъ нача́лниче*), marking the physical cessation of bodily faculties: the lips, tongue, and eyes of the dying man can no longer move or call for help.

[^1362]: Fol. 227r (`ск҃з`). Theotokion of Ode 5 (Canon 1). The dying person bids a final earthly farewell to the sacred icon of the Mother of God (*нектомоу́ бо твое́го пренепоро́чнаа чⷭ҇та́го ѻ҆́браза оу҆зрю̀ ст҃ътный*), as sight fails and the night of death covers him.

[^1363]: Fol. 227r (`ск҃з`). Ode 5 of the Second Canon (Joseph the Hymnographer), preceded by the cinnabar transition rubric *і҆рмо́съ · та́же ·* The opening troparion paraphrases Psalm 26:9 and Psalm 68:18–19 (LXX).

[^1364]: Fol. 227v. The departing soul addresses its kinsmen according to the flesh (*по пло́ти срѡ́дници*) and spiritual brethren (*по дх҃оу бра́тїе*), urging them to mourn and lament over its final separation from earthly life.

[^1365]: Fol. 227v. The soul laments the total vanity and helplessness of mortal aid in the face of demonic captivity (*да не ꙗ҆́ко чл҃къ безпо́мощенъ, въ рꙋка́хъ вра́гъ мои́хъ затворе́нъ бꙋ́дꙋ*).

[^1366]: Fol. 227v. The soul articulates the threefold horror of eternal perdition: separation from the Mother of God, falling away from Christ the Savior, and eternal estrangement from all the saints.

[^1367]: Fol. 228r (`ск҃и`). Concluding sentence of the Theotokion of Ode 5 (Canon 2), begging that the boundless compassion of the Theotokos may triumph over the immense weight of personal sin.

[^1368]: Fol. 228r (`ск҃и`). Tone 6, Ode 6 of the First Canon (St. Andrew of Crete). Heirmos incipit: *Τοῦ βίου τὴν θάλασσαν* (Slavonic: *Жите́йскаго мо́рѧ*). The soul makes a dying bequest to the brethren to listen to its final contrite words.

[^1369]: Fol. 228r (`ск҃и`). In an extreme expression of ascetic deathbed compunction and self-abasement, the dying soul commands that its sinful body not even be buried in the earth, but cast out to the dogs (*ѱѡ́мъ повръзѣ́те*).

[^1370]: Fol. 228v. Concluding sentence of the troparion on the unburied corpse. The soul declares that funeral singing over the flesh is useless while the soul is being dragged into torment, begging rather that the dogs devour the heart that sinned.

[^1371]: Fol. 228v. Theotokion of Ode 6 (Canon 1). The soul implores random strangers and travelers who might pass by its discarded bones to utter a prayer to the Mother of God for the salvation of its soul.

[^1372]: Fol. 228v. Ode 6 of the Second Canon (Joseph the Hymnographer), introduced by *і҆рмо́съ , та́же ·* The silent dying person explains that though the tongue is immobilized, the heart cries out in the hidden fire of contrition (*вноу́трь възгара́етсѧ*).

[^1373]: Fol. 228v. The soul implores the Theotokos for a personal deathbed visitation (*на моѐ посѣще́нїе сънитѝ*), so that departing from the body in Her sight, it may go forth rejoicing.

[^1374]: Fol. 229r (`ск҃ѳ`). A vivid clinical and theological depiction of the agony of somatic dissolution: the severance of the natural bond (*растръза́еми соу́ꙋзъ*) and the disruption of the bodily constitution create unbearable anguish.

[^1375]: Fol. 229r (`ск҃ѳ`). The dying soul prays to be placed into the holy hands of angels, that their wings may shield it from seeing the dark, foul, and hideous sight of the demons (*ка́льный бѣсѡ́въ ѻ҆́бразъ*).

[^1376]: Fol. 229r (`ск҃ѳ`). Theotokion of Ode 6 (Canon 2). Evoking the Parable of the Wise and Foolish Virgins (Matt 25:1–13), the soul begs the Mother of God to rekindle its extinguished lamp with the holy oil of Her mercy and admit it to the heavenly bridal chamber.

[^1377]: Fol. 229r–229v. Chanting of the full Heirmos of Ode 6 (Canon 1): *Τοῦ βίου τὴν θάλασσαν...* (*Жите́йскаго мо́рѧ въздвиѕа́ема зрѧ̀...*), concluding the first six odes of the combined canons.

[^1378]: Fol. 229v. Kontakion in Tone 6, the renowned poetic masterpiece of St. Andrew of Crete from the Great Canon: *Ψυχή μου, ψυχή μου, ἀνάστα, τί καθεύδεις; τὸ τέλος ἐγγίζει...* (*Дꙋшѐ моѧ̀ дꙋшѐ моѧ̀ , въста́ни что̀ спи́ши...*), sung here at the separation of soul and body.

[^1379]: Fol. 230r (`сл҃`). Ikos of the Great Canon of St. Andrew of Crete (*Ꙗ҆́ко вра́чество ви́дѧ ѿвръ́сто...*), portraying Satan's despair at the healing and salvation wrought by Christ, the "Son of Mary" and "Bethlehemite."

[^1380]: Fol. 230r (`сл҃`). Tone 6, Ode 7 of the First Canon (St. Andrew of Crete). Heirmos incipit: *Δροσοβόλον μὲν τὴν κάμινον* (Slavonic: *Хладода́вицоу оу҆́бо пе́щь*). The first troparion depicts the violent extraction of the soul from the flesh and its summons before the dread tribunal.

[^1381]: Fol. 230r (`сл҃`). The soul cries to the radiant angelic powers for mercy, confessing its lack of good deeds to balance its sins at the toll-houses (*мыта́рьства*).

[^1382]: Fol. 230v. Continuation of Troparion 3 of Ode 7 (Canon 1). The soul instructs the holy angels to fall down before Christ the Creator with tears, interceding for the work of His hands (Job 10:3, 14:15).

[^1383]: Fol. 230v. Theotokion of Ode 7 (Canon 1). The angels are urged to beseech the all-pure Sovereign Lady to add Her maternal intercession before God, confident that as His Mother and Nourisher She will be heard.

[^1384]: Fol. 230v. Ode 7 of the Second Canon (Joseph the Hymnographer), introduced by *і҆рмо́съ · та́же ·* The soul laments the dark and moonless night of death (*но́щъ смръ́тнаѧ... мра́чнаѧже и҆ безълоу́нна*) overtaking it unprepared for the long and fearsome journey.

[^1385]: Scriptural allusion: Psalm 77:33 (LXX 77:33): "And their days vanished in vanity, and their years with haste" (καὶ ἐξέλιπον ἐν ματαιότητι αἱ ἡμέραι αὐτῶν καὶ τὰ ἔτη αὐτῶν μετὰ σπουδῆς / "исчезоша въ суетѣ дніе ихъ, и лѣта ихъ со тщаніемъ"). Combined with Psalm 17:6 (LXX 17:6): "The snares of death overtook me" (περιέσχον με ὠδῖνες θανάτου / "сѣти смертныя превариша мя"). [Masoretic: Ps 78:33; Ps 18:5].

[^1386]: The soul laments that in exchange for passing worldly indulgence (време́нное наслаже́ніе), it faces unending torment in the unquenchable fire (Matt 25:41), pleading that the mercy of the Theotokos may overtake it.

[^1387]: Allusion to Psalm 68:21 (LXX 68:21): "and I looked for one that would sorrow with me, but there was none; and for one that would comfort me, but I found none" (καὶ ὑπέμεινα συλλυπούμενον καὶ οὐχ ὑπῆрξεν καὶ παρακαλοῦντας καὶ οὐχ εὗρον / "и ждахъ сопечалующаго, и не бѣ, и утѣшающихъ, и не обрѣтохъ"), together with Psalm 37:12 (LXX 37:12): "My friends and my neighbors drew near and stood against me, and my near kinsmen stood afar off." [Masoretic: Ps 69:20; Ps 38:11].

[^1388]: Ode 8 Heirmos incipit: *Out of the flame for the godly didst Thou pour forth dew...* (Изъ пла́мене преподо́бнымъ ро́су источи́лъ еси́...). Allusion to the Song of the Three Holy Children in the Babylonian furnace (Daniel 3:49-50 / Song of the Three Children 26-27).

[^1389]: Allusion to the Gospel parable of the royal wedding feast in Matthew 22:13: "Then said the king to the servants, Bind him hand and foot, and take him away, and cast him into outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth."

[^1390]: Direct echoing of the laments of Job and Jeremiah: Job 3:11 ("Why died I not from the womb? Why did I not give up the ghost when I came out of the belly?") and Jeremiah 20:18 ("Why came I forth out of the womb to see labor and sorrow, that my days should be consumed with shame?"). [Masoretic: Job 3:11; Jer 20:18].

[^1391]: Allusion to the piercing of the side of Christ on the Cross in John 19:34: "one of the soldiers with a spear pierced His side, and forthwith came there out blood and water."

[^1392]: Patristic and liturgical representation of the aerial toll-houses (мытарєначалникы / telonia) presided over by the demonic spirits of the air (Eph 2:2; 6:12), combined with the eschatological sound of the last trumpet at the general resurrection (1 Cor 15:52; 1 Thess 4:16).

[^1393]: Ode 9 Heirmos incipit: *It is not possible for men to see God, upon Whom the ranks of angels dare not gaze...* (Бо́га человѣ́комъ невозмо́жно ви́дѣти, на Него́же не смѣ́ютъ чи́ни а́нгельстіи взира́ти...). The subsequent troparion directly cites Psalm 6:5 (LXX 6:6): "For in death there is no remembrance of Thee, and in hades who will confess unto Thee?" (ὅτι οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν τῷ θανάτῳ ὁ μνημονεύων σου, ἐν δὲ τῷ ᾅδῃ τίς ἐξομολογήσεταί σοι; / "яко нѣсть въ смерти поминай Тебе, во адѣ же кто исповѣстся Тебѣ;"). [Masoretic: Ps 6:5].

[^1394]: Epigraphic witness: the 1606 Striatyn print reads `Ниє́с` (likely a typographical error or variant contraction for *Никто́же* / *Ни єди́нъ*). The verse expresses the terrifying abandonment of the condemned soul, which can no longer be aided even by the angelic ranks, the prophets, apostles, or martyrs.

[^1395]: Dense concatenation of Gospel judgment parables: the barren fig tree commanded to be cut down as unprofitable (Luke 13:7), the withered vine-branch cast into the fire (John 15:6), and the unprofitable servant cast into outer darkness, bound hand and foot (Matt 22:13; 25:30).

[^1396]: Contrast between the material churches/temples of God, the human body consecrated as a temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Cor 3:16-17; 6:19), and the uncreated sanctuary of God, appealing to the Theotokos as the living temple to rescue the soul from the fiery burning of Gehenna (Mark 9:43-48).

[^1397]: Messianic quotation of Isaiah 9:6 ("For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given...") applied to the Incarnation of the Word through the virginal blood of Mary, pleading for His mercy at the violent separation of soul and body.

[^1398]: Folio 226v (physical page 470) opens with a decorative engraved floral headpiece and cinnabar title for the *Prayer said at the departure of the soul* (Молитва глаголемая на исходъ души). In the Ruthenian Trebnyk tradition, this priestly prayer is recited over the dying Christian immediately following the supplicatory canons when the soul struggles in agony.

[^1399]: Direct Scriptural quotation of 1 Timothy 2:4: "Who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth" (ὃς πάντας ἀνθρώπους θέλει σωθῆναι καὶ εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν ἀληθείας ἐλθεῖν).

[^1400]: Quotation of the divine oath from Ezekiel 18:23 and 33:11: "As I live, saith the Lord God, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live" (LXX Ezek 33:11: εἰ βούλομαι τὸν θάνατον τοῦ ἀσεβοῦς, ὡς τὸ ἀποστрέψαι τὸν ἀσεβῆ ἀπὸ τῆς ὁδοῦ αὐτοῦ καὶ ζῆν αὐτόν).

[^1401]: Cinnabar rubrical designation `и́мрⷶк :` (*имярек* / *nomen* / *Name*), indicating the personal baptismal name of the dying person to be pronounced by the priest.

[^1402]: Folio 227r (physical page 471) concluding the prayer at the departure of the soul. Allusion to Psalm 145:7-8 (LXX 145:7-8): "The Lord looses them that are fettered; the Lord sets upright them that are crushed" (Κύριος λύει πεπεδημένους, Κύριος ἀνορθοῖ καтерραγμένους / "Господь рѣшитъ окованныя... возводитъ низверженныя"). [Masoretic: Ps 146:7-8]. The phrase "hope of the hopeless" (наде́жа ненача́ннымъ) translates the Greek ἀνελπίστων ἐλπίς; the 1606 text reads `ненача́ннымъ`, an attested Ruthenian variant/phonetic spelling for `нечая́ннымъ` (those without hope or expectation).

[^1403]: Cinnabar rubrical abbreviation `и҆́мѧ ре́къ` (*Name*), directing the priest to name the dying person. The prayer concludes with an allusion to the "eternal mansions" (John 14:2: "In My Father's house are many mansions").

[^1404]: Folio 227v (physical page 472). A distinctive Ruthenian pastoral formula of absolution: *Prayer at the confession of a brother, which is given by the spiritual father to one who is about to die in the answer of faith* (Молитва на исповѣданїе брату, яже даетъся отъ отца духовнаго, въ вѣрѣ отвѣта хотящому умирати). This prayer reflects the pastoral care of the dying in the Kyivan and Galician traditions, confirming the penitent's final absolution before death.

[^1405]: Scriptural and liturgical echoes in the absolution prayer: John 1:29 (Christ bearing the sins of the world); Matthew 12:32 (remission in the present age and in the age to come); 2 Corinthians 5:10 and Romans 14:10 (standing uncondemned before the judgment seat of Christ); and 1 Timothy 2:4 / Ezekiel 33:11 (God desiring the life and salvation of all).

[^1406]: Folio 228r (physical page 473) opens with a large decorative engraved woodcut headpiece introducing the canonical ruling of Theodore Balsamon, Greek Patriarch of Antioch (c. 1140–1204), one of the foremost Byzantine canonists. His responsa were incorporated into the Slavic *Kormchaia Kniga* (Nomocanon) and included in 16th-17th century Ruthenian Trebnyks as authoritative guidance on burial practice.

[^1407]: The canonist distinguishes between consecrated churches (ѻсщенныя цѣркви) possessing a consecrated altar table, consecrated with holy chrism and holy martyr relics, and unconsecrated oratories or prayer houses (молитвеныя храми).

[^1408]: Folio 228v (physical page 474). Canonical and legal citations: the "second chapter of the first title of the fifth book of ecclesiastical laws" refers to the Byzantine Nomocanon in 14 Titles / Basilika (Title I, ch. 2), reaffirming the strict prohibition against intramural burials in consecrated temple space. The "civil ancient law" refers to Roman-Byzantine civil legislation (Codex Justinianus and Novel 133; reinforced by Leo VI Novel 53), which banned lay burials within cities and inside sacred shrines, reserving holy church burial exclusively for martyrs and emperors. Simple prayer houses, lacking consecrated altars, were exempted.

[^1409]: Folio 229r (physical page 475). Major structural division: The Order of Burial (Послѣдованїе къ погребенїю). The rubric specifies the initial domestic rites: immediately upon death, the relatives summon the priest to the home where the body lies; the priest vests in the epitrachelion and censes the deceased before beginning the service.

[^1410]: Rubrical instruction for the Usual Beginning (Обычное начало) chanted at the house of the deceased: the Trisagion Prayers through the Lord's Prayer ("Holy God...", "All-Holy Trinity...", "Our Father..."), followed by the priestly doxology ("For Thine is the kingdom...").

[^1411]: Folio 229v (physical page 476). The renowned Funeral Troparia (Tone 4) chanted at the home: *With the spirits of the righteous made perfect...* (Со духи праведными скончавшихся...). Direct Scriptural allusion to Hebrews 12:23 ("to the spirits of just men made perfect").

[^1412]: Allusion to Christ's descent into hades to loose the bonds of those held captive, drawing on 1 Peter 3:19 ("He went and preached unto the spirits in prison") and Psalm 106:14 (LXX 106:14 / MT 107:14: "and He broke their bonds asunder").

[^1413]: Folio 230r (physical page 477). The Funeral Litany of Fervent Supplication (Сугубая ектения об упокоении) offered in the home of the deceased, petitioning for the forgiveness of all sins voluntary and involuntary and the repose of the soul with the righteous.

[^1414]: Opening of the great Priestly Prayer for the Departed: *O God of spirits and of all flesh...* (Боже духовъ и всякия плоти...). Scriptural allusion to Numbers 16:22 and 27:16 ("the God of the spirits of all flesh") and Hebrews 2:14 (Christ destroying through death him that had the power of death, that is, the devil).

[^1415]: Folio 230v (physical page 478). Continuation of the prayer of absolution: the threefold peaceful haven of repose—a place of light, green pasture, and refreshment (Psalm 22:2 LXX: "In a place of green pasture, there He hath made me to dwell; beside the water of rest hath He nurtured me" [Masoretic: Ps 23:2]). Allusion also to Isaiah 35:10 and 51:11 ("sorrow and sighing shall flee away").

[^1416]: Allusion to the universal human condition of sinfulness from 3 Kingdoms 8:46 (LXX 3 Kgs 8:46 / MT 1 Kgs 8:46: "for there is no man that sins not"), 2 Chronicles 6:36, and Ecclesiastes 7:20. Followed by the citation of Psalm 118:142 (LXX 118:142 / MT 119:142: "Thy righteousness is an everlasting righteousness, and Thy law is truth") and Psalm 118:160.

[^1417]: Folio 231r (physical page 479). Rubric for the funeral procession transferring the body from the home to the church: the priest gives the dismissal at the home, initiates the service again, and the clergy and people bear the body of the deceased to the church in solemn procession with processional candles/lamps and censers while chanting the Trisagion (*Holy God*). Upon arrival at the church, the coffin is set in the narthex (притворъ) facing the royal doors.

[^1418]: Folio 231v (physical page 480). Opening of the church station in the narthex: the triple *Come, let us worship*, followed by Psalm 90 (LXX 90 / MT 91:1-7a), traditionally chanted over the deceased as a psalm of divine protection and trust.

[^1419]: Septuagint versification of Psalm 90:1-6 (LXX 90:1-6 / Masoretic: Psalm 91:1-6). The Ruthenian and Church Slavonic text strictly follows the Greek Septuagint rendering: "from troubling speech" (ἀπὸ λόγου ταραχώδους / ѿ словесѐ мѧте́жна, MT: "from the noisome pestilence"), "with His pinions shall He overshadow thee" (ἐν τοῖς μεταφрένοις αὐτοῦ ἐπισκιάσει σοι / пле́щима свои́ма ѡ҆сѣни́тъ тѧ), and "nor of mishap and the noonday demon" (καὶ δαιμονίου μεσημβриνοῦ / ѿ срѧ́ща и҆ бѣ́са полоу́деннаго, MT: "nor for the destruction that wastes at noonday").

[^1420]: LXX Psalm 90:10 (MT 91:10). The Church Slavonic witness reads *къ телеси твоемоу* ('unto thy body'), an inner-Slavonic or recensional variant where the Greek Septuagint reads τῷ σκηνώματί σου ('unto thy dwelling/tent').

[^1421]: The *Непорочны* (Greek: Ἄμωμοι, *Amomoi*, 'The Blameless'), consisting of Psalm 118 (LXX; MT 119), constitutes the Seventeenth Kathisma of the Psalter. In the Ruthenian and Byzantine burial rite, it is chanted over the departed with alternating refrains.

[^1422]: LXX Psalm 118:1–4 (MT 119:1–4). The opening verses of the first stasis of the Seventeenth Kathisma.

[^1423]: LXX Psalm 118:9 (MT 119:9). Slavonic: *Ѻ҆чесо́мъ испра́ви юны́и поу́ть свои́* (Greek: Ἐν τίνι κατορθώσει νεώτερος τὴν ὁδὸν αὐτοῦ;).

[^1424]: LXX Psalm 118:21 (MT 119:21). Slavonic: *Запрѣти́лъ є҆си гѡ́рдымъ, проклѧ́ти ѹ҆кланѧ́ющейсѧ ѿ за́повѣдей твои̑*.

[^1425]: LXX Psalm 118:28 (MT 119:28). Slavonic *ѿ ѹ҆ны́нїа* renders Greek ἀπὸ ἀκηδίας ('from despondency' / 'from heaviness of soul').

[^1426]: LXX Psalm 118:38 (MT 119:38). Slavonic: *Поста́ви ра́боу твое́мꙋ сло́во твоє̀ въ стра́хъ тво́й* (Greek: στῆσον τῷ δούλῳ σου τὸ λόγιόν σου εἰς τὸν φόβον σου).

[^1427]: LXX Psalm 118:44 (MT 119:44). Slavonic: *въ вѣ́кы и҆ въ вѣ́къ вѣ́ка* (Greek: εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα καὶ εἰς τὸν αἰῶна τοῦ αἰῶνος); rendered in conformity with the Father Paul Doxology Standard.

[^1428]: LXX Psalm 118:54 (MT 119:54). Slavonic: *Пѣ́та бѧ́хоу мнѣ̀ ѡ҆правда́нїа твоѧ̀, на мѣ́стѣ прише́лствїа мое́го*.

[^1429]: LXX Psalm 118:61 (MT 119:61). Slavonic: *Ѹ҆́жѧ грѣ́шникъ ѡ҆бѧза́шасѧ мнѣ̀* (Greek: σχοινία ἁμαρτωλῶν περιεπλάκησάν μοι).

[^1430]: LXX Psalm 118:70 (MT 119:70). Slavonic: *Оу҆сы́рисѧ ꙗ҆́ко мле́ко срⷣце и҆́хъ* (Greek: ἐτυρώθη ὡς γάλα ἡ καρδία αὐτῶν), an idiom denoting callous moral insensibility.

[^1431]: LXX Psalm 118:73 (MT 119:73). At verse 73 (*Рꙋ́цѣ твоѝ сътвори́стѣ мѧ̀...*), the funeral kathisma shifts its refrain from the opening *Благослове́нъ є҆сѝ Го́споди* to *Поми́луй ра́ба Твоего̀* ('Have mercy on Thy servant'), marking the second choral division within the first stasis of the Amomoi in the Ruthenian recension.

[^1432]: LXX Psalm 118:75 (MT 119:75). The 1606 Striatyn text reads *повеле́нїа твоѧ̀* ('Thy commandments/precepts') where standard Slavonic editions read *соу́дбы твоѧ̑* (Greek: τὰ κρίματά σου, 'Thy judgments').

[^1433]: LXX Psalm 118:83 (MT 119:83). Slavonic: *ꙗ҆́ко мѣ́хъ на сла́нѣ* (Greek: ὡσεὶ ἀσκὸς ἐν πάχνῃ, 'like a wineskin in hoarfrost/smoke'). A traditional patristic and liturgical metaphor for an ascetic or afflicted person dried and shriveled by trials.

[^1434]: LXX Psalm 118:85 (MT 119:85). Slavonic: *законопрестоу́пници глоумле́нїа* (Greek: διηγήσαντό μοι παράноμοι ἀδολεσχίας, 'transgressors recounted to me disputations/idle fables').

[^1435]: LXX Psalm 118:88 (MT 119:88). The opening hemistich *По ми́лости твое́й живи́ мѧ̀* is rubricated in cinnabar in the Striatyn imprint, emphasizing the choral plea for life before the cosmic meditation of verses 89–91.

[^1436]: The First Stasis concludes at LXX Psalm 118:93 with the tripartite chanting of the dismissal refrain *Спаси́ мя, ꙗ҆́ко а҆́ще не зако́нъ тво́й* ('Save me; unless Thy law [had been my meditation]'), followed immediately by the Little Litany for the Departed (*Дїа́конства*).

[^1437]: The funeral prayer *Бо́же духо́въ и҆ всѧ́кїѧ пло́ти* ('O God of spirits and of all flesh') is appointed to be recited silently by the priest during the litany, concluded here by its audible exclamation (*Ꙗ҆́ко ты̀ є҆сѝ въскр҃енїе...*).

[^1438]: Opening of the Second Stasis (*Статїа втораѧ*) of the Amomoi at LXX Psalm 118:94 (MT 119:94), with its proper alternating refrain: *Сп҃се, сп҃сѝ ра́ба своего̀* ('O Savior, save Thy servant').

[^1439]: LXX Psalm 118:96 (MT 119:96). Slavonic: *Всѧ́коѧ кончи́ны ви́дѣхъ коне́цъ, ширѡ́ка за́повѣди твоѧ̀ ѕѣло̀* (Greek: Πάσης συντελείας εἶδον πέρας, πλατεῖα ἡ ἐντολή σου σφόδρα).

[^1440]: LXX Psalm 118:108 (MT 119:108). Slavonic: *Вѡ́лнаѧ оу҆́стъ мои́хъ* (Greek: Τὰ ἑκούσια τοῦ στόματός μου, 'The freewill offerings of my mouth').

[^1441]: LXX Psalm 118:112 (MT 119:112). Slavonic: *вѣ́кы за възда́нїе* (Greek: εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα δι' ἀντάμειψιν, 'forever for a recompense').

[^1442]: LXX Psalm 118:120 (MT 119:120). Slavonic: *пригвоздѝ стра́сѣ твое́мъ пло́ть мою̀* (Greek: Καθήλωσον ἐκ τοῦ φόβου σου τὰς σάρκας μου, 'Nail down my flesh with the fear of Thee').

[^1443]: LXX Psalm 118:126 (MT 119:126). Slavonic: *Вре́мѧ сътвори́ти Го́сподеви* (Greek: Καιρὸς τοῦ ποιῆσαι τῷ Κυρίῳ, 'It is time for the Lord to act'). In Byzantine and Ruthenian practice, this verse is recited by the deacon to the priest during the Enarxis of the Divine Liturgy.

[^1444]: LXX Psalm 118:130 (MT 119:130). Slavonic: *сказа́нїе словѐсъ твои́хъ просвѣща́етъ, и҆ въразꙋмлѧ́етъ младе́нца* (Greek: Ἡ δήλωσις τῶν λόγων σου φωτίζει καὶ συνετίζει νηπίους).

[^1445]: LXX Psalm 118:135 (MT 119:135). The seventeenth kathisma continues without pause across folios 241v–242r. Slavonic: *просвѣтѝ на ра́ба твое́го* (Greek: ἐπίφανον ἐπὶ τὸν δοῦλόν σου, 'make shine upon Thy servant').

[^1446]: LXX Psalm 118:139 (MT 119:139). Slavonic: *и҆ста́ала мѧ̀ є҆́ст жа́лост твоѧ̀* (Greek: ἐξέτηξέ με ὁ ζῆλός σου, 'Thy zeal has consumed/melted me down'). The Church Slavonic *жа́лость* preserves here the archaic Ruthenian/Slavonic meaning of ardent zeal or consuming grief, translating Greek ζῆλος.

[^1447]: LXX Psalm 118:140 (MT 119:140). Slavonic: *ражѐже́но сло́во твоѐ зѣло̀* (Greek: πεπυρωμένον τὸ λόγιόν σου σφόδρα, 'Thy oracle/word is exceedingly refined by fire').

[^1448]: LXX Psalm 118:147 (MT 119:147). Slavonic: *предвари́хъ въ безго́дїи* (Greek: προέφθασα ἐν ἀωρίᾳ, 'I anticipated unseasonable hours / before the dawn').

[^1449]: LXX Psalm 118:150 (MT 119:150). The 1606 text reads *прибли́жиша гона́щен мѧ безако́нїе* where standard editions have *прибли́жишася гоня́щїи мя беззако́нїемъ* (Greek: προσήγγισαν οἱ καταδιώκοντές με ἀνομίᾳ).

[^1450]: LXX Psalm 118:152 (MT 119:152). Slavonic: *Испрѣ́ва позна́хъ* (Greek: Κατ' ἀρχὰς ἔγνων, 'From the beginning / of old have I known').

[^1451]: LXX Psalm 118:158 (MT 119:158). Slavonic: *ви́дѣхъ неразоумѣва́ющаѧ, и҆ и҆ста́ахъ* (Greek: εἶδον ἀσυνθετοῦντας καὶ ἐξετηκόμην, 'I beheld transgressors/covenant-breakers and melted with grief').

[^1452]: LXX Psalm 118:160 (MT 119:160). Slavonic: *Нача́ло слове́съ твои́хъ и҆́стинна* (Greek: Ἀρχὴ τῶν λόγων σου ἀλήθεια). The opening verse of the final twentieth-second strophic octave (Resh / Sin / Tav).

[^1453]: LXX Psalm 118:171 (MT 119:171). Slavonic: *Ѿры́гнетѣ оу҆стнѣ̀ мои пѣ́нїе* (Greek: Ἐξερεύξονται τὰ χείλη μου ὕμνον, 'My lips shall bubble over / pour forth a hymn'). The dual form *оу҆стнѣ̀* is faithfully preserved in the 1606 witness.

[^1454]: LXX Psalm 118:176 (MT 119:176). The concluding verse of the 17th Kathisma (*Заблуди́хъ я́ко овча̀ поги́бшее...*) is prescribed by the rubric to be sung thrice (*три́щи*), functioning as the final climactic refrain of the Amomoi before the Evlogetaria.

[^1455]: The Troparia for the Departed (*Благослове́нъ есѝ Го́споди* / Εὐλογητάρια τῶν κεκοιμημένων), Tone 5, traditionally attributed to St. John of Damascus, sung on Saturdays and at funeral and memorial services.

[^1456]: Evlogetarion 1 (*Святы́хъ ли́къ обрѣ́те исто́чникъ жи́зни...*). Greek: Χορὸς τῶν Ἁγίων εὗρε πηγὴν τῆς ζωῆς.

[^1457]: Evlogetarion 2 (*Иже дла́нїю ѿ небытїа създа́вый мѧ...*). Greek: Ὁ διὰ χειρός σου ἐκ μὴ ὄντων πλάσας με.

[^1458]: Evlogetarion 3 (*Ѡ҆́бразъ є҆́смь неизрече́нныѧ ти сла́вы...*). Greek: Εἰκών εἰμι τῆς ἀρρήτου σου δόξης. Note the profound theological anthropology of the restored divine likeness (*дре́внею доброто́ю* / τὸ ἀρχαῖον κάλλος).

[^1459]: Evlogetarion 4 (*Иже а҆́гньца Бж҃їа проповѣ́давше...*). Greek: Οἱ τὸν ἀμνὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ κηρύξαντες. Addressed to the Holy Martyrs. The refrain here and in the following verse appears with the plural *на́съ* ('teach us'), reflecting customary Ruthenian choral usage.

[^1460]: Evlogetarion 5 (*Иже въ поу́ть оу҆́зкїи хо́ждъше...*). Greek: Οἱ τὴν ὁδὸν τὴν στενὴν βαδίσαντες. An evangelical synthesis of Matthew 7:14 and Matthew 11:29–30.

[^1461]: Evlogetarion 6 (*Оу҆поко́й Бж҃е ра́ба твое́го...*). Greek: Ἀνάπαυσον, ὁ Θεός, τὸν δοῦλόν σου. Addressed directly to Christ on behalf of the deceased.

[^1462]: The Triadikon / Trinitarian Troparion (*Трїсїѧ́телное є҆ди́наго Бж҃тва...*). Greek: Τὸ τριλαμπὲς τῆς μιᾶς Θεότητος. Deity pronouns referring to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are capitalized in strict compliance with MTS-1.

[^1463]: Theotokion of the Evlogetaria (*Ра́доусѧ чⷭтаѧ, ꙗ҆́же Бг҃а пло́тїю...*). Greek: Χαῖρε, σεμνή, ἡ Θεὸν σαρκὶ τεκοῦσα. Followed by the triple Alleluia.

[^1464]: Little Litany for the Departed and exclamation (*Ꙗ҆́ко ты̀ є҆сѝ въскр҃енїе...*), referred back to the earlier rubrical occurrence (*ꙗ҆́коже назáдѣ* / 'as before', on fol. 239r, p. 495).

[^1465]: Tone 4 Funeral Troparion (*Поко́й, Сп҃се на́шъ, съ пра́ведными ра́ба твое́го...*), Greek: Ἀνάπαυσον, Σωτὴρ ἡμῶν, μετὰ δικαίων τὸν δοῦλόν σου. Reference to Psalm 64:5 (LXX) / Psalm 83:11.

[^1466]: Theotokion (*Иже ѿ дв҃ы възсїѧ́выи мироу Х҃е Бж҃е...*). Greek: Ὁ ἐκ Παρθένου ἀνατείλας τῷ κόσμῳ, Χριστὲ ὁ Θεός.

[^1467]: The Funeral Canon by St. Theophanes the Branded (Θεοφάνης ὁ Γραπτός, ca. 778–845), Metropolitan of Nicaea, Hymnographer. The Greek acrostic reads: Ἕκτην προσᾴδω τοῖς θανοῦσι μελῳδίαν. Θεοφάνους ('Unto the departed I sing the sixth song. By Theophanes').

[^1468]: Ode 1 Heirmos, Tone 6: *Ꙗ҆́ко по соу́хоу ходи́въ їзри́ль* (Greek: Ὡς ἐν ἠπείρῳ πεζεύσας ὁ Ἰσραήλ). In accordance with Statutory Mandate 16, the unprinted troparion of the Heirmos is left unexpanded.

[^1469]: St. Theophanes the Branded, Funeral Canon, Tone 6, Ode 1, Troparion 2 (*Оу҆краси́выи всѧ́чєскаѧ...*). Greek: Κοσμήσας τὰ σύμπαντα, ζῷον συμμιγές, τὸν ἄνθρωπον μέσον μετριότητος, καὶ μεγαλειότητος ἔπλασας· διὸ ψυχὴν τοῦ δούλου σου, Σωτὴρ ἀνάπαυσον ('Having adorned all things, Thou didst fashion me, man, as a composite creature, midway between lowliness and majesty...'). Acrostic letter 2: Ἕκτην / Шесто́ю.

[^1470]: St. Theophanes the Branded, Funeral Canon, Tone 6, Ode 1, Troparion 3 (*Ра́йскаго граждани́на...*). Greek: Παραδείσου πολίτην με καὶ γεωργόν, ἐν πρώτοις κατέστησας, παραβάντα δὲ τὴν ἐντολήν σου ἐξώρισας· διὸ ψυχὴν τοῦ δούλου σου, Σωτὴρ ἀνάπαυσον. Reference to Genesis 2:15 and 3:23–24. Acrostic letter 3: Ἕκτην / Шесто́ю.

[^1471]: St. Theophanes the Branded, Funeral Canon, Tone 6, Ode 1, Theotokion (*И҆́же ѿ ребра̀ създа́выи є҆́ѵвоу...*). Greek: Ὁ ἐκ πλευρᾶς μορφώσας Εὔαν τὸ πρίν, τὴν πρώτην ἡμῶν μητέρα, ἐκ τῆς ἀχράντου σου γαστρὸς σάρκα ἀμφιέννυται, δι' ἧς θανάτου τὴν ἰσχύν, Ἁγνὴ διέλυσε. Typological parallel between Eve taken from Adam's side (Genesis 2:21–22) and the incarnate Lord destroying death through the Virgin's flesh. Acrostic letter 4: Ἕκτην / Шесто́ю.

[^1472]: Ode 3 Heirmos, Tone 6: *Нѣ́сть ст҃ъ ꙗ҆́коже ты* (Greek: Οὐκ ἔστιν ἅγιος ὡς σύ, Κύριε ὁ Θεός μου). Based on the Canticle of Anna, 1 Kingdoms (1 Samuel) 2:2. In accordance with Statutory Mandate 16, the unprinted troparion of the Heirmos is left unexpanded.
