[^2955]: Third Elevation (facing West) and Station to the North: following the third centenary, the priest turns northward to intone the fourth petition for all afflicted Christian souls (`Є҆щѐ мо́лимсѧ ѡ҆ всѧ́кой дꙋши хрⷭтїа́нстѣй...`).

[^2956]: Fourth Elevation (facing North): the choir chants the fourth centenary as the Cross is bowed and raised toward the north in the same manner as the previous stations.

[^2957]: Fifth Elevation (facing East): the priest returns to the eastward orientation for the final petition (for the monastery and serving clergy) and fifth centenary. At every station, the rubric requires the priest to bless the faithful thrice cruciformly with the basil-adorned Cross (`крⷭто́мъ къ наро́домъ , г҃ , крⷭта ѡ҆бра́зно`).

[^2958]: Kontakion of the Exaltation of the Cross: *Tone 4: "Thou Who wast lifted up upon the Cross of Thine own will..."* (`Възнесы́йсѧ на крⷭтъ во́лею` / Greek: *Ὁ ὑψωθεὶς ἐν τῷ Σταυρῷ ἑκουσίως*). The text in the Balaban Trebnyk reflects the received Byzantine/Ruthenian recension.

[^2959]: Ceremony of Veneration: the priest and superior (*престатель*, hegumen) make two bows, kiss the Precious Cross upon the analogion, make one metania, and bow to both monastic choirs. The brethren then venerate two by two while chanting the liturgical troparion *Кресту Твоему покланяемся Владыко* (Greek: *Τὸν Σταυρόν σου προσκυνοῦμεν, Δέσποτα*).

[^2960]: Folio cross-reference: the rubric notes *Ихже смотри на задѣ на листѣ то҃з* ("which look behind on folio 377"), referring back to physical leaf p783 in the codex for the full hymnographic text of the aposticha stichera *Tone 2: "Come, ye faithful, let us venerate the life-giving wood..."* (`Прїидѣ́те вѣ́рнїи , животворѧ́щему дре́вꙋ поклони́мсѧ`).

[^2961]: Woodcut emblem: fol. 488r opens with a Renaissance strapwork headpiece featuring a pelican in her piety in an oval cartouche, piercing her breast to feed her chicks with her own blood. In Christian iconology, this is a prominent Eucharistic and Christological symbol, with the motto *СПЛА ЖИВОТ* ("The Savior is Life").

[^2962]: Division title: *On Stauropegia* (`Ѡ҆ СТАѪРОПИГІ́АХЪ` / Greek: *Περὶ σταυροπηγίων*). This canonical chapter codifies the juridical and liturgical procedure for establishing a patriarchal stauropegion—a monastery or church enjoying extraterritorial immunity from the local diocesan bishop and placed directly under the jurisdiction of the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople. In the late 16th and early 17th centuries, the status of stauropegion was of vital ecclesiological importance in the Ruthenian Church (e.g. the Lviv Dormition Brotherhood).

[^2963]: Inscriptional protocol: the Patriarch sends an official decree authorizing his Exarch or a designated hierarch to lay the foundation and consecrate the church, accompanied by a wooden patriarchal cross inscribed on both faces by patriarchal scribes.

[^2964]: Reverse inscriptional formula: the inscription on the reverse face records the civil and imperial dating formula (`При црⷭтвѣ̀ бл҃гочти́вѣйшихъ цр҃ехъ на́шихъ и҆́мѧ ре́къ...`) alongside the day, month, and year.

[^2965]: Rubric: at the consecration of a stauropegial church, the patriarchal cross is erected directly behind the Holy Table (`въдрꙋжа́етъ и҆ крⷭтъ съза́ди ст҃ыѧ трапе́зы`) within an elevated, ornamental structure or holder made of stone, iron, or bronze, explicitly modeled after the liturgical arrangement in the Great Church of Constantinople (Hagia Sophia).

[^2966]: Conclusion of the rubric from leaf p1006 (`...въ велицѣй цр҃кви`).

[^2967]: Codicological note: physical folio 489v (leaf p1008) is an unprinted blank verso (*vacat*) concluding Gathering `ѡ̃ ѡ̃` (Gathering 52) of the 1606 imprint. In this exemplar, later 17th-century East Slavic cursive (*skoropis'*) hands inscribed ownership and donation records: *Сїа Книга глаголемая Служебникъ... монастыра...* ("This book, called the Sluzhebnik... of the monastery...").

[^2968]: Gathering mark and headpiece: leaf p1009 marks the start of Gathering 53 (`цц` / *Ts ts*, fol. 490r), embellished with an elaborate Renaissance headpiece featuring two vases brimming with flowers and scrolling acanthus foliage.

[^2969]: Major division heading: *Prayers for Every Need* (`МЛ҃ТВЫ НА ВСІА́КОУ ПОТРЕ́БОУ` / Greek: *Εὐχαὶ εἰς διαφόρους περιστάσεις*). This heading introduces the comprehensive compendium of occasional prayers and minor benedictions within the Euchologion.

[^2970]: Penitential benediction: *Prayer over one who has eaten defiled meats of the pagans* (`Мл҃тва над̾ ꙗ҆доу́щимъ сквръ́наѧ мяса̀ ѿ поганъ` / Greek: *Εὐχὴ ἐπὶ τῶν φαγόντων μιαρόν τι*). In historical Ruthenian and Byzantine liturgical life, this prayer was read over Christians who had inadvertently, under duress, or during Ottoman/Tatar captivity eaten meat sacrificed to idols or forbidden by canonical dietary norms (Acts 15:29).

[^2971]: Prayer petition: the prayer asks that the penitent, having unknowingly or under compulsion tasted unclean food, be absolved and deemed worthy to receive the Holy Mysteries of Christ's Body and Blood without condemnation.

[^2972]: Doxology formula: the closing exclamation in the Slavonic text reads `ꙗ҆́ко Твое́ є҆́стъ црⷭтво и҆ си́ла и҆ сла́ва въ безъконе́чныѧ вѣ́кы , а҆ми́нь` ("unto endless ages, Amen"), an ancient liturgical variant of the eternal doxology.

[^2973]: Pastoral and canonical context: *Prayer over a youth who has apostatized, defiled himself, and is repenting* (`Мл҃тва , ѡ҆тро́чищꙋ ѿвръ́гшꙋсѧ , и҆ поганившꙋ . и҆ кающусѧ` / Greek: *Εὐχὴ ἐπὶ παιδὸς ἀρνησαμένου καὶ μιανθέντος καὶ μετανοοῦντος*). This pastoral office was appointed for young Christians who, having fallen into the hands of non-Christians (Tatars, Ottomans, or pagans) through capture, abduction, or slavery, or having succumbed to coercion or youthful frailty, had apostatized or participated in defiling pagan/Islamic rites, and subsequently escaped or returned desiring reconciliation with the Church. Fol. 491r is marked in the outer margin as `уч҃а` (491) and signed at the foot as Gathering 53, sheet 2 (`цц в҃`).

[^2974]: Scriptural citations: the prayer opens with the Pauline formulation of 1 Timothy 2:4 (`хотя́й всѣ̑мъ чл҃кѡмъ сп҃тисѧ , и҆ въ позна́нїе и҆́стинны прїитѝ` / Greek: *ὁ πάντας ἀνθρώπους θέλων σωθῆναι καὶ εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν ἀληθείας ἐλθεῖν*), joined to the parable of the lost sheep (Matt. 18:12, Luke 15:4) and the restoration of the divine image in humanity (Gen. 1:26–27).

[^2975]: Patristic and Scriptural allusions: fol. 491v. The prayer invokes the parable of the Prodigal Son (Luke 15:11–32: `ꙗ҆́ко блꙋ́днаго к тебѣ̀ Бг҃ꙋ и҆ ѿц҃ꙋ̀ възвраща́ющасѧ`), and asks that the restored youth be made a partaker with the faithful of God's "most pure priesthood" (`прчⷭты̑мъ ст҃е́нствомъ твои̑мъ` / Greek: *τῷ παναγίῳ ἱερατείῳ σου*), an allusion to the royal priesthood of all believers (1 Peter 2:9: *βασίλειον ἱεράτευμα*).

[^2976]: Doxology and prayer of head-bowing dialogue: fol. 492r (`уч҃в`, Gathering 53, sheet 3: `цц г҃`). The first prayer concludes with the standard Trinitarian doxology (`ны́нѣ и҆ при́сно и҆ въ вѣ́кы вѣкѡ́мъ , а҆ми́нь`), followed by the rubrical dialogue introducing the prayer of head-bowing (*κεφαλοκλισία*): the priestly blessing of peace (`Іере́й . Ми́ръ всѣ̑мъ`) and the bidding to bow before the Lord (`Гла́вы ва́ша Гв҃и приклони́те`).

[^2977]: Scriptural citations: fol. 492v. The prayer of head-bowing integrates Psalm 143:5 [LXX] (`Приклони́вый нб҃са̀ , и҆ съше́дъ` / *Κύριε, κλῖνον οὐρανοὺς καὶ κατάβηθι*), redemption from the ancestral curse (Gal. 3:13), angelic joy over one repenting sinner (Luke 15:7, 10: `ра́дости бы́ти на нб҃сѣхъ ѡ҆ є҆ди́номъ грѣ́шницѣ ка́ющемсѧ`), and Christ's promise of authority over adversarial powers (Luke 10:19: *ἰδοὺ δίδωμι ὑμῖν τὴν ἐξουσίαν τοῦ πατεῖν ἐπάνω ὄφεων καὶ σκορπίων, καὶ ἐπὶ πᾶσαν τὴν δύναμιν τοῦ ἐχθροῦ*).

[^2978]: Foliation anomaly: fol. 493r is misnumbered in the outer margin as `ф҃` (500) rather than `уч҃г` (493), jumping eight folios ahead due to a compositor's error in Gathering 53 (`цц д҃`). The erroneous 500-series foliation persists through folios 494r (`ф҃а` = 501) and 495r (`ф҃в` = 502).

[^2979]: Reconciliatory Chrismation rubric: the rubric directs the priest to take the Holy Myron and sign the returning penitent cruciformly upon the sensory gateways—the forehead, hands, and feet (`И҆ взе́мъ ст҃о́е му́ро зна́менаетъ и҆ на челѣ̀ , и҆ на рꙋка́хъ , и҆ на нога́хъ` / Greek: *Καὶ λαβὼν τὸ ἅγιον μύρον, σφραγίζει αὐτὸν εἰς τὸ μέτωπον, καὶ τὰς χεῖρας, καὶ τοὺς πόδας*). In Eastern canonical jurisprudence (Canon 7 of the Second Ecumenical Council and Canon 95 of the Council in Trullo), apostates who had received valid Trinitarian baptism are reconciled through the re-sealing of the gift of the Holy Spirit via Chrismation rather than re-baptism.

[^2980]: Initiation office: *Prayer when thou wishest to catechize a pagan* (`Мл҃тва є҆гда̀ хо́щеши ѡ҆гласи́ти ꙗ҆зы́чника` / Greek: *Εὐχὴ ἡνίκα βούλει κατηχῆσαι Ἕλληνα*). This ancient Byzantine euchological rite marks the formal admission of a pagan or non-Christian convert into the order of catechumens. The rubric prescribes that the candidate kneel outside the threshold before the church doors (`пре́дъ две́рьми` / Greek: *πρὸ τῶν πυλῶν*), signifying his status outside the ecclesial body prior to illumination. The priest signs him thrice cruciformly with the initial prayer quoting Titus 2:14 (`лю́ди прⷭносоу́щныѧ , ревни́телѧ блага́ымъ дѣ́лѡмъ` / Greek: *λαὸν περιούσιον, ζηλωτὴν καλῶν ἔργων*).

[^2981]: Illuminative prayer of the Catechumenate: fol. 494r (Gathering 53, sheet 5: `цц є҃`, numbered `ф҃а` = 501). The prayer petitions for the interior illumination of the candidate's senses (Ps. 118:18 [LXX]) and his preparation for baptismal rebirth ("the font of regeneration," Titus 3:5). Following the prayer, the priest repeats the triple cruciform blessing over the catechumen before intoning the second prayer of illumination (*Σύ, Δέσποτα, ἐπὶ σωτηρίᾳ τοῦ κόσμου ἐξαπέστειλας τὸν ἅγιόν σου Λόγον...*).

[^2982]: Canonical office of reconciliation: *Prayer over a Christian who was seduced into pagan error, and has returned again, and fled unto the Church of God* (`Мл҃тва хрⷭтїа́ниноу прельсти́вшоусѧ въ ꙗ҆зы́ческое прельще́нїе . и҆ па́ки възврати́вшоусѧ , и҆ цр҃кви Бж҃їи прибѣ́гшоу` / Greek: *Εὐχὴ ἐπὶ χριστιανοῦ ἀπατηθέντος εἰς ἑλληνικὴν ἀπάτην, καὶ πάλιν ἐπιστρέψαντος, καὶ τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ τοῦ Θεοῦ προσδραμόντος*). This comprehensive penitential office addresses adult baptized Christians who lapsed into paganism, Islam, or heresy and subsequently returned seeking reconciliation. The opening invocation quotes 1 Timothy 4:10 (`сп҃се всѣ̑мъ чл҃кѡмъ , па́че же вѣ́рнымъ` / Greek: *ὅς ἐστι σωτὴρ πάντων ἀνθρώπων, μάλιστα πιστῶν*).

[^2983]: Historical context of captivity and epigraphic reading: fol. 495r (numbered `ф҃в` = 502). The text describes the concrete historical reality of Ruthenian and Byzantine Christians held in captivity by "godless enemies" (`ѿ плѣне́нїа безъбѡ́жныхъ вра̑гъ`), where lapse into error occurred either through lack of instruction or under torturous coercion (`и҆лѝ нꙋ́ждею томле́на`). At the start of line 16, the physical ink reads `чтѝ .`, which translates the Greek imperative *καθάρισον* ("cleanse [him]"), representing an abbreviated or reduced Slavonic imperative form of *чистити* (or compositor's omission of the prefix in *[ѡ҆]чистѝ*).

[^2984]: Theology of the baptismal character: fol. 495v (502v). The prayer contains one of the most vivid patristic metaphors for the indelible seal (*печатлѣ́нїе* / *σφραγίς*) of Holy Baptism. Though obscured during apostasy, the spark of baptismal grace (*и҆́скры сп҃снаго кр҃ще́нїа* / *ὁ... σπινθὴρ τοῦ σωτηρίου βαπτίσματος*) is never extinguished; fanned by the breeze of divine grace (*въздоу́хы бл҃гти твоеѧ̀* / *ταῖς τῆς σῆς χάριτος αὔραις*), it is noetically rekindled into a spiritual flame (*въ пла́мень дх҃о́венъ оу҆́мно распали́сѧ* / *εἰς φλόγα πνευματικὴν νοερῶς ἀναφθῇ*). The prayer continues across the gathering break onto physical leaf p1021 in Cohort 103.

[^2985]: Ecclesiological and liturgical reconciliation: conclusion of the *Prayer over a Christian who was seduced into pagan error, and has returned again, and fled unto the Church of God* (`Мл҃тва хрⷭтїа́ниноу прельсти́вшоусѧ въ ꙗ҆зы́ческое прельще́нїе...` / Greek: *Εὐχὴ ἐπὶ χριστιανοῦ ἀπατηθέντος εἰς ἑλληνικὴν ἀπάτην...*), continued from physical leaf p1020. The prayer petitions for the complete uprooting from the penitent's heart of every custom of pagan godlessness (`всѧ́къ ѡ҆бы́чай ꙗ҆зы́чнаго безбо́жїа` / *πᾶν ἔθος τῆς ἑλληνικῆς ἀθεότητος*), restoration to blameless walking in God's commandments, and worthy, uncondemned communion of the Holy Mysteries. The prayer concludes with the truncated liturgical doxology incipit `нн҃ѣ и҆ прⷭно и҆ въ вѣ́кы :~` ("now and ever, and unto ages."). Fol. 496r continues the compositor's foliation anomaly initiated on fol. 493r (`ф҃` = 500), being numbered in the outer margin as `ф҃г` (503).

[^2986]: Canonical and euchological context of lustral purification: *Prayer over anything, if something unclean falls into a vessel: into wine, or into oil, or into a well, or into anything else; and it is fresh, not having decayed* (`Мл҃тва въ всѧ́комꙋ , а҆́ще впа́детъ что сквръ́но въ съсоу́дъ , въ ви́но , и҆ли въ є҆ле́й , и҆ли въ кла́денецъ , и҆ли въ и҆́но что̀ • и҆ бꙋ́детъ ново не разгнило́сѧ` / Greek: *Εὐχὴ ἐπὶ παντὸς μολυσθέντος σκεύους, οἴνου, ἢ ἐλαίου, ἢ μέλιτος, ἢ ἄλλου τινός*). In Byzantine and Slavic canonical jurisprudence (cf. the Nomocanon in the Kormchaia Kniga and the canonical responsa of Patriarch Luke Chrysoberges and Matthew Blastares), a rigorous distinction is drawn regarding unclean animals (mice, reptiles, insects) falling into liquid food vessels: if discovered immediately while the creature is whole and fresh (`ново не разгнило́сѧ`), the creature is cast out, the vessel is cleansed and censed, and the liquid is sanctified with holy water and prayer; if the carcass has decomposed, the liquid is deemed permanently defiled and must be poured out.

[^2987]: Rubrical movements and Scriptural theology of ritual purity: fol. 496v. The rubric directs that the contaminating object be cast out (`въ́врещи во́нъ`), another clean vessel washed both inside and outside (`и҆ внꙋ́трь , и҆ внѣоу́дꙋ`), and censed within and without (`покади́въ вноу́трьꙋдꙋ , и҆ внѣ́ꙋдꙋ`). The prayer opens with an illuminated initial `[С]` (`[С]ты́и вл҃ко Г҃и Іс҃ Х҃е Бг҃е на́шъ` / *Holy Master, Lord Jesus Christ our God*). The prayer grounds the purification of foods in Christ's teaching on true spiritual purity in Matthew 15:11 ("not that which goes into the mouth defiles a man"), the apostolic doctrine of Titus 1:15 ("Unto the pure all things are pure"), and invokes Saint Paul as God's "chosen vessel" (Acts 9:15: `съсоу́домъ и҆збра́ннымъ` / *σκεῦος ἐκλογῆς*).

[^2988]: Scriptural citations: fol. 497r (misnumbered `ф҃д` = 504). The prayer quotes 1 Timothy 4:4–5 (`ничи́мже ѿмѣ́тнымъ • найпа́че же Бж҃їемъ сло́вомъ , и҆ мо-ли́твою ѡ҆сщ҃е́нномъ` / *οὐδὲν ἀπόβλητον μετὰ εὐχαριστίας λαμβανόμενον, ἁγιάζεται γὰρ διὰ λόγου Θεοῦ καὶ ἐντεύξεως*). The text petitions God, Who graciously looks down upon human infirmity (`ты̀ нн҃ѣ ѡ҆склабля́ѧй не́мощь на́шю` / Greek: *ὁ διαμειδιῶν τὴν ἀσθένειαν ἡμῶν*), to banish all psychological scrupulosity and demonic anxiety from the conscience of the faithful concerning the creature that fell into the vessel (`ѿженѝ ѿ съвѣ́сти ра́бъ твои́хъ`).

[^2989]: Epiphany water purification and priestly testing rubric: fol. 497v. Following the doxology, the rubric prescribes that the Priest pour holy water from the Feast of the Holy Theophany (`влива́етъ во́дꙋ ѿ ст҃ы́хъ Бг҃оѧвле́нїи`, the Great Agiasma) into the liquid cruciformly thrice (`крⷭтоѡбра́зно г҃`). Crucially, after the dismissal, the Priest is commanded to taste of the purified liquid first (`въкꙋсѝ прѣ́ждѣ іере́й`), thereby tangibly demonstrating to the faithful that the liquid is purified of all demonic pollution and fit for consumption. If the liquid has already decayed, it must be discarded (`а҆́ще ли бꙋ́детъ и҆згни́ло , да̀ пролїе́тсѧ`).

[^2990]: Codicological transition, Gathering 54 (`чч`), and Old Testament typologies of water purification: fol. 498r marks the beginning of Gathering 54, signed at the foot as `чч` and misnumbered in the outer margin as `ф҃є` (505). The office is entitled *Prayer over a well defiled by an unclean thing falling into it* (`Мл҃тва на ѡ҆сквръ́ньшимсѧ стоу́денце ѿ и҆здръже́нїи впа́дшаго нечи́стаго` / Greek: *Εὐχὴ ἐπὶ φρέατος μιανθέντος*). The preparatory rubric prescribes a substantial physical cleansing—drawing forty buckets of water from the well (`подоба́етъ пре́жде и҆злїа́ти и҆з̾ него м҃ , вѣ́дръ воды̀`)—prior to liturgical sanctification with three kindled candles and circular censing. The prayer opens with an illuminated initial `[Б]` (`[Б]е вели́кый и҆ ди́вный` / *O God, great and marvelous*), citing two major Old Testament prefigurations of water transformation: the sweetening of the bitter waters of Marah through the wood cast in by Moses (Exod. 15:23–25), and the healing of the barren waters of Jericho through salt cast in by the Prophet Elisha (4 Kings [2 Kings] 2:19–22).

[^2991]: Apostolic vision and apotropaic petition: fol. 498v. The prayer recalls Peter's vision at Joppa of the sheet let down from heaven containing all manner of beasts and reptiles, wherein divine voice proclaimed: "What God hath cleansed, call not thou common" (Acts 10:9–16), coupled again with Saint Paul's maxim in Titus 1:15. The petition asks for deliverance from every harmful thing, venomous reptile (`га́да ꙗ҆дови́таго`), uncleanness, and demonic sorcery or phantom deception (`потво́ра` / Greek: *γοητείας* / *φαρμακείας* / *φαντασίας*), followed by the rubric instructing the Priest to pour holy water into the well.

[^2992]: Healing office and Christological healing typologies: fol. 499r (Gathering 54, sheet 2: `чч в҃`, misnumbered `ф҃ѕ` = 506). Following the tasting of the well-water by the Priest and bystanders, a major therapeutic office opens: *Prayer over Every Manner of Infirmity* (`Мл҃тва на всѧкоѡ҆́бразнѣй не́мощи` / Greek: *Εὐχὴ ἐπὶ πάσης ἀσθενείας* or *Εὐχὴ ἐπὶ παντοίας νόσου*). The text begins with an illuminated initial `[С]` (`[С]ла́венъ Бг҃ъ бл҃гїи вра́чь дꙋша́мъ и҆ тѣ́лѡмъ на́шимъ` / "Glorious is God, the good Physician of our souls and bodies"). The prayer systematically gathers the central evangelical testimonies of Christ's healing power: Isaiah's prophecy of the Suffering Servant Who bore our infirmities and by Whose wound we were healed (Isa. 53:4–5; Matt. 8:17; 1 Pet. 2:24), the harrowing of Hades and granting of life to those in the graves (Paschal Troparion allusion), the resurrection of four-days-dead Lazarus (John 11), the healing of the fever of Peter's mother-in-law (Matt. 8:14–15; Mark 1:30–31; Luke 4:38–39), and the forgiveness of the two debtors (Luke 7:41–43).

[^2993]: Demonological and therapeutic petitions: fol. 499v. The prayer continues with Christ's forgiveness of the sinful woman (Luke 7:36–50) and appeals to God's patient repentance over human evils (Jonah 4:2; Joel 2:13: *μετανοῶν ἐπὶ ταῖς κακίαις τῶν ἀνθρώπων*). It petitions for specific relief from cephalalgia / headache (`гла́вноую боле́знь`), envious oppression (`зави́стную тѧготоу̀`), terrors, chills, fevers (`ѻ҆гнѧ̀`), the evil day and hour, the evil eye of malicious persons (`ѻ҆́чїю злы́хъ чл҃къ` / *ὀφθαλμῶν πονηρῶν* / *βασκανίας*), and the noon-day demon of Psalm 90:6 [LXX] (`бѣ́са полоу́деннаго` / *δαιμονίου μεσημβρινοῦ*). It culminates in David's prayer of repentance from Psalm 50:1 [LXX] (`помл҃уй мѧ Бг҃е по вели́цей мл҃ти твоей`).

[^2994]: Linguistic and codicological witness: fol. 500r (Gathering 54, sheet 3: `чч г҃`, misnumbered `ф҃з` = 507). Line 2 preserves the distinct Old Ruthenian / Church Slavonic verb form `ѡ҆цѣстѝ ѿ него̀ вьсѧ́ко безако́нїе` ("cleanse from him all lawlessness") from the root *cist-* (attesting to second palatalization morphology *цѣстити* / *ѡ҆цѣсти́ти* alongside standard *ѡ҆чи́стити*), translating Psalm 50:1 [LXX] (*ἐξάλειψον τὸ ἀνόμημά μου*). Following the priestly exclamation (`въꙁгла́съ`), the title of the second healing office appears in red cinnabar: *Second Prayer, for the Same* (`Мл҃тва в҃ , томоу́же`). The prayer opens with an illuminated initial `[В]` (`[В]лко Вседръжителю вра́чю дꙋша́м и҆ тѣ́лѡмъ` / *Master Almighty, Physician of souls and bodies*), invoking 1 Kings [1 Sam.] 2:6–7 and Job 5:18 (`смирѧ́ѧ и҆ възносѧ̀ • пока́зоуѧ и҆ па́ки и҆сцѣлѧ́ѧ` / *ὁ ταπεινῶν καὶ ἀνυψῶν, ὁ παιδεύων καὶ πάλιν ἰώμενος*).

[^2995]: Pneumatological and Christological restoration: fol. 500v. The prayer implores God to stretch forth His invisible healing arm (Ps. 135:12 [LXX]), raise the sick from the bed of infirmity, rebuke the spirit of disease (Luke 13:11–12), and cast out every affliction, burning fever (`ѻ҆гньницꙋ` / *πυреτόν*), and shaking ague / chills (`трѧса́вицоу` / *ῥῖγος*). It petitions for the remission of all deliberate and involuntary transgressions, concluding with an impassioned plea to spare God's own creation in Christ Jesus our Lord, sealed with the Trinitarian doxology unto ages of ages.

[^2996]: Church Slavonic rubric: *Егда кр҃тъ творитъ їерей надъ страстїю недꙋга съ ст҃ымъ копїемъ* ("When the Priest makes the sign of the cross over the suffering of an infirmity with the holy spear"). In Ruthenian and Byzantine Euchologia, the liturgical spear (*kopie*, λόγχη)—customarily employed during the Proskomedia to extract the Lamb and commemorative particles from the prosphora—is utilized as an instrument of blessing over those suffering acute physical afflictions, tumors, or localized pain, making cruciform signs over the afflicted member while chanting troparia honoring the Cross and Christ's side pierced by the lance (John 19:34).

[^2997]: The troparion *Искоупилъ ны єси ѿ клѧтвы законныѧ* ("Thou hast redeemed us from the curse of the law") is the classical Troparion of Great and Holy Friday (Galatians 3:13), here prescribed together with the Troparion of the Pierced Side (*Копїемъ въ ребро твоѐ ѡ х҃е мой прободе́ бысть*) to invoke the healing stream of blood and water that flowed from Christ's pierced side for the life and incorruption of mankind.

[^2998]: Church Slavonic heading: *Мл҃тва, на бо́лимымъ и неспѧ́щымъ* ("Prayer for the Ailing and Sleepless"). This corresponds to the Byzantine Euchologion office *Εὐχὴ ἐπὶ ἀσθενοῦντος καὶ μὴ ὑπνοῦντος*, appointed for those suffering severe illness accompanied by intractable insomnia or delirium.

[^2999]: The prayer invokes an extensive litany of intercessors renowned for healing, monastic discipline, and victorious confession, including the three Great Hierarchs (Basil, Gregory, John Chrysostom), Cyril and Athanasius of Alexandria, Nicholas of Myra, Spyridon of Trimythous, Stephen the Protomartyr, the great military martyrs (George, Demetrius, Theodore the Stratelates), and the anchorites of the Egyptian and Palestinian deserts (Antony, Euthymius, Sabbas, Theodosius, Onuphrius).

[^3000]: Church Slavonic: *а҆вимеле́ха слоугꙋ своего въ хра́мѣ а҆гри́ппы* ("Abimelech Thy servant in the estate of Agrippa"). This refers to the narrative in the pseudepigraphical *Paralipomena of Jeremiah* (4 Baruch 5:1–34), wherein Ebed-melech (Abimelech) the Ethiopian (cf. Jeremiah 38:7–13) is sent by Jeremiah to gather figs from the estate of Agrippa, falls asleep under a tree, and sleeps undisturbed for 66 years through the Babylonian destruction and exile of Jerusalem, waking with the figs still fresh and dripping milk. In Eastern Christian Euchologia, this miraculous slumber is invoked as the archetype of peaceful, restorative, and providential sleep.

[^3001]: A reference to the Seven Sleepers of Ephesus (Maximian, Malchus, Martinian, Dionysius, John, Serapion, and Constantine), who were sealed in a cave on Mount Celion/Pion under Emperor Decius (c. 250 AD) and awoke during the reign of Emperor Theodosius II. The duration of 372 years (*три́ста и седмьдесѧ́тъ и двѣ лѣ́тѣ*) reflects the standard chronological figure preserved across Byzantine and Slavonic Euchologia and synaxaria, presented as an empirical pledge of the General Resurrection.

[^3002]: An explicit quotation of James 1:17: *всѧ́ко даа́нїе бл҃го, и въсѧ́къ да́ръ съвръше́нъ* ("Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights"), which also serves as the foundation of the Prayer behind the Ambo in the Divine Liturgy.

[^3003]: Church Slavonic heading: *Въ ст҃ꙋю пѧтидесѧ́тницꙋ мл҃тва надъ коливомъ* ("On Holy Pentecost, Prayer over the Kolyvo"). In the Ruthenian typikon tradition witness of the Striatyn Euchologion, this unique blessing is formulated specifically for Pentecost, directly invoking the historical descent of the Holy Spirit in fiery tongues (*ѡ҆гньными ꙗзы́кы сꙋще́ственнѣ посла́въ всест҃ыи дх҃ъ твой*) upon the Apostles, while sanctifying boiled wheat (*kolyvo*) offered in thanksgiving and in memory of all sanctified souls.

[^3004]: Daniel 1:11–16: Daniel and the three holy youths (Ananias, Azarias, and Misael) requested pulse (seeds/vegetables) and water rather than defiling themselves with the meat and wine from the table of King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon; after ten days, their countenances appeared fairer and fatter in flesh than all the youths who ate the portion of the king's delicacies.

[^3005]: Church Slavonic heading: *Мл҃тва на гдⷭ҇кыѧ пра́здники надъ коливомъ* ("Prayer on Feasts of the Lord, over the Kolyvo"). In traditional Byzantine and Ruthenian practice, *kolyvo* (boiled wheat decorated with honey, nuts, and raisins) is offered not only at memorials for the departed, but also on major Feasts of the Lord (*Dominical / Despotic Feasts*) and patronal celebrations, symbolizing the seed that falls into the earth and bears much fruit (John 12:24) in the resurrection.

[^3006]: Church Slavonic heading: *Мл҃тва глаго́лемаѧ надъ коутї́ю на па́мѧти ст҃ыхъ* ("Prayer Said over the Kutia on the Memory of the Saints"). Note the appearance of the East Slavic/Ruthenian term *kutiya* (*коутї́ѧ*) alongside *kolyvo* (*ко́ливо*), demonstrating recensional vernacular realia in the 1606 Striatyn print.

[^3007]: The prayer explicitly links the commemoration of the saint of the day (*ст҃го и́мѧ реⷦ҇, є҆го́же и҆ па́мѧть съвръша́емъ*) with prayer for the departed faithful (*и҆ въ па́мѧть и҆же въ бл҃гоче́стїи, и҆ вѣ́рѣ сконча́вшихсѧ*), continuing across the foliation boundary onto leaf p1041.

[^3008]: Church Slavonic rubric: *Бл҃годаре́нїе на ко́ливо на трапе́зѣ* ("Thanksgiving over the Kolyvo at the Trapeza"). In traditional Byzantine and Ruthenian practice, following the Divine Liturgy or memorial service, the *kolyvo* (boiled wheat with honey) is brought from the church into the monastic refectory (*trapeza*) or common dining hall, where it is elevated, blessed with thanksgiving, and distributed among the brethren while chanting festive or memorial acclamations.

[^3009]: The proclamation commemorates the civil and political authorities: *благочести́вымъ, и҆ дръжа́внымъ ст҃ы́мъ госпѡда́ремъ на́шимъ, и҆ цр҃емъ, и҆ кнѧѕе́мъ* ("our pious and sovereign holy rulers, and tsars, and princes"). This composite formula reflects the recensional context of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and neighboring Ruthenian/Slavic lands, combining the title of *hospodar* (ruler/prince in Ruthenia and the Danubian principalities of Moldavia and Wallachia) with imperial (*tsar*) and princely (*kniaz*) titulature.

[^3010]: Church Slavonic heading: *Въ соубѡ́тоу* ("On Saturday"). Saturday is liturgically consecrated throughout the Byzantine rite to the memory of the departed, martyrs, and all reposed righteous ancestors, concluding the refectory kolyvo blessing with the solemn singing of *Eternal Memory* (*Вѣ́чнаѧ и҆̀мъ па́мѧть*).

[^3011]: Church Slavonic heading: *пра́здникѡмъ Госпо́дьскымъ* ("On Feasts of the Lord"). Variable commemorations insert the specific salvation-historical mystery of the feast: the Nativity (*ро́ждшемусѧ*), Theophany/Baptism (*кр҃ти́вшемусѧ*), Transfiguration (*преѡбрази́вшемусѧ*), or Ascension (*възне́сшемусѧ*), followed by corresponding commemorations for the Great Feasts of the Theotokos (Annunciation, Nativity of the Theotokos, Entry into the Temple, and Dormition).

[^3012]: The rubrics provide distinct health and salvation proclamations for ecclesiastical dignitaries: a bishop (*преѡсщ҃е́нномꙋ є҆пⷭ҇пꙋ*), an elder hegumen designated as *прпⷡ҇номꙋ въ є҆рмона́сѣхъ* ("venerable among hieromonks"), or any monastic brother, to which the choir/people respond thrice: *Сп҃си бж҃е... три́щи*.

[^3013]: Church Slavonic heading: *Мл҃тва на ѡ҆чїще́нїе цр҃кви, ѡ҆скверненно́й ѿ є҆рети́къ* ("Prayer for the Cleansing of a Church Defiled by Heretics"). Corresponding to the Byzantine Euchologion rite *Εὐχὴ ἐπὶ καθαρισμῷ ναοῦ μιαнθέντος ὑπὸ αἱρετικῶν*, this prayer was appointed for cases where a consecrated church or altar had been occupied, celebrated in, or profaned by heretics or schismatics, purging the sanctuary through invocations of the Holy Spirit and aspersion with holy water prior to the celebration of the Holy Mysteries.

[^3014]: Church Slavonic heading: *Мл҃тва ю҆́же гл҃етъ а҆рхїере́й, и҆ли дх҃о́вникъ проще́нноу • за грѣхы̀ всѧ̑ во́лныѧ и҆ нево́лныѧ...* ("Prayer of Absolution Said by a Hierarch or Spiritual Father for All Sins, Voluntary and Involuntary..."). Known across Slavic Euchologia by its running title *Праща́лнаѧ* (*Praščal'naja molitva*), this monumental prayer of absolution—traditionally ascribed to Patriarch John the Faster or ancient Byzantine patriarchal practice—is read over penitents, monastics at tonsure or death, or during times of public penance, functioning as an exhaustive liturgical absolution covering every canonical transgression, secret sin, and occult involvement.

[^3015]: The prayer anchors its petition in three gospel exemplars of divine mercy: the creditor who freely forgave two debtors of five hundred and fifty denarii (Luke 7:41–43); the penitent sinful woman whose many sins were forgiven because she loved much (Luke 7:36–50); and the paralytic at Capernaum whose physical healing was united to the remission of his sins (Matthew 9:1–8; Mark 2:1–12).

[^3016]: The catalogue of sins begins with spiritual and ecclesiastical censures: falling under curses, excommunication by a hierarch or priest, rash self-anathematization, violation of oaths made in the name of God, and cursing fellow Christians in anger (cf. Matthew 5:22; Apostolic Canons 25, 27; Basil the Great, Canons 28, 64).

[^3017]: Denunciation of magical, occult, and divinatory practices: consulting sorceresses (*чародѣ́ицы*), magi/soothsayers (*влъхвы*), and potion-makers (*ѻ҆тра́вницы*, makers of philtres and poisons) who perform illusions and enchantments (*ѡ҆бва́нїа*), strictly forbidden under Canons 61 and 65 of the Council in Trullo (Quinisext).

[^3018]: Systematic enumeration of carnal transgressions and sexual aberrations, distinguishing fornication, adultery, masturbation (*роу́чный блоу́дъ*), corruption of youth (*ѻ҆троча̀ растли́лъ*), sodomy (*содо́мскаа дѣ́ла*), and bestiality (*скотоло́жество*, copulation with quadrupeds or birds), closely adhering to the canonical penitential categories of John the Faster and the Nomokanon.

[^3019]: Ascetical and monastic failures: distraction of the mind during psalmody and divine worship (*стоѧ́щꙋ є҆мꙋ̀ на мл҃итвѣ, и҆ на пѣ́нїи, оу҆́мъ є҆го въ лоука́ваѧ и҆ жите́йскаа ѻ҆бхожда́аше*), secret eating (*скрѡ́вно ꙗ҆дѐ*, Greek λαθροφαγία, eating outside established hours or violating fasts surreptitiously), and nocturnal/bodily pollutions (*и҆стица́нїе*).

[^3020]: Sins of the heart and interpersonal faults: judging a brother's small speck while blind to one's own transgressions (Matthew 7:3–5), disobedience to one's spiritual father, acedia or spiritual despondency (*оуны̀*), and spiritual pride (*възвели́чисѧ ꙗ҆́ко цѣломоу́дренъ є҆́стъ мнѧ̀ себѐ*), continuing onto leaf p1051.

[^3021]: The conclusion of the exhaustive absolution prayer (*Праща́лнаѧ*) begun on leaf p1045 (Fol. 515v), wherein the confessor petitions the divine goodness on behalf of the penitent (*за ра́ба твоего̀ и҆́мѧ ре́къ*), beseeching that his acknowledged and confessed transgressions be overlooked and remitted.

[^3022]: Church Slavonic: *и҆ съжи́телѧ сътворѝ є҆го̀ твои́хъ вѣ́чныхъ бла̑гъ* (literally, "and make him a fellow-dweller / co-inhabitant of Thine eternal good things"), reflecting the Byzantine patristic conception of salvation as eternal citizenship in the Kingdom of Heaven (cf. Ephesians 2:19, συμπολῖται τῶν ἁγίων καὶ οἰκεῖοι τοῦ Θεοῦ).

[^3023]: Scriptural citation of Matthew 18:18 (cf. Matthew 16:19): the apostolic authority to bind and loose committed by Christ to His Church, forming the canonical and theological foundation of sacramental absolution.

[^3024]: Rubric in red cinnabar: *Разрѣше́нїе прѡсщ҃еннаго патрїарха коньстантина града, кѵръ михаила, рекомаго аѱалона • мл҃тва и҆сповѣда́нїю* ("Absolution of the Most Sacred Patriarch of Constantinople, Kyr Michael, Surnamed Apsalon; a Prayer at Confession"). In Byzantine and South Slavic Euchologia (Goar, *Euchologion*, pp. 544–545; Dmitrievsky, *Opisanie*, II, pp. 278, 412), this personal absolution prayer is attributed to Patriarch Michael II Kourkouas (Oxeites, 1143–1146) or Michael III of Anchialos (1170–1178), transmitted under the epithet *Apsalas* / *Apsalon* (Greek: τοῦ Ἀψαλᾶ). In the Ruthenian Trebnik tradition, it constitutes an intimate pastoral absolution addressed directly to the penitent (*Бра́те, ꙗ҆́ко съкроуше́нно срⷣце мно́го показа́лъ є҆си...*).

[^3025]: Church Slavonic: *и҆ є҆ли́ка помѧноу́лъ є҆си, и҆ и҆списа́въ прише́лъ є҆си* ("and whatsoever things thou hast remembered, and having written them down hast come"). This explicit reference to the penitent bringing a written catalogue of sins (*исписавъ*) provides vital pastoral evidence for Early Modern Ruthenian penitential practice, wherein the faithful were encouraged to prepare for confession by conducting an examination of conscience and noting their sins in writing before approaching the spiritual father.

[^3026]: Church Slavonic rubric: *Мл҃тва на кле́ншихсѧ де́рзостїю* ("Prayer over Those Who Have Sworn Rashly/Audaciously"). Greek: *Εὐχὴ ἐπὶ τῶν ἐξ ἀπονοίας ἢ προπετείας ὀμοσάντων* (Goar, *Euchologion*, p. 556). In canonical jurisprudence (Matthew 5:34–37; James 5:12; St. Basil, Canons 10, 29, 64), taking rash, imprudent, or thoughtless oaths was considered a perilous spiritual transgression binding the conscience (*темне́нїе кла́твы*, "the darkening/bond of an oath"); this prayer looses the penitent from the spiritual burden and censure incurred by hasty swearing.

[^3027]: Church Slavonic rubric: *Мл҃тва въ по́стъ въходѧ́щимъ* ("Prayer for Those Entering upon a Fast"). Greek: *Εὐχὴ ἐπὶ τῶν εἰсеρχομένων εἰς τὴν ἁγίαν τεσσαρακοστήν* (Goar, *Euchologion*, p. 558), appointed to be read at the onset of Great Lent (or the seasonal fasts of the Nativity, Apostles, or Dormition) to invoke divine protection, angelic companionship, and bodily endurance for the ascetical journey.

[^3028]: Scriptural citation of Psalm 64:6 (LXX 64:5): *Надѣѧ́нїе всѣ̑мъ кѡ́нцемъ землѝ, и҆ сѫ́щимъ въ мо́ри дале́че* ("O Hope of all the ends of the earth, and of those that are far off upon the sea").

[^3029]: Church Slavonic rubric: *Мл҃, на рожⷣтво хв҃о дѣ́темъ дх҃овнымъ* ("Prayer on the Nativity of Christ for Spiritual Children"). In 16th- and 17th-century Ruthenian parish and monastic usage, spiritual fathers assembled their penitents (*дѣти духовні*) on major feasts—particularly following the Nativity fast—to bestow an official pastoral blessing, reconcile penitents, and prepare them for Holy Communion.

[^3030]: Gospel commemoration of Christ's Nativity in Bethlehem of Judea (Matthew 2:1; Luke 2:4–7), weaving festal imagery into the prayer of pastoral reconciliation.

[^3031]: John 1:29: *взъє́млющаго грѣхы̀ всего̀ ми́ра* ("Who takest away the sins of the whole world").

[^3032]: Evocation of the Apostle Peter: his distress while walking upon the waves and rescue by the Savior (Matthew 14:28–31), followed by his threefold denial and bitter weeping of repentance (Matthew 26:69–75; John 21:15–19).

[^3033]: Gospel models of penitence: the humble contrition of the tax collector in the Temple (Luke 18:13) and the repentant sinful woman who washed Christ's feet with her tears and dried them with her hair (Luke 7:37–38).

[^3034]: Luke 23:42–43: the confession of the Wise Thief crucified alongside Christ (*Помѧни́ мѧ, Го́споди, є҆гда̀ прїи́деши во Ца́рствїи Твое́мъ*) and Christ's assurance of salvation (*Дне́сь со Мно́ю бо́удеши въ раи́*).

[^3035]: Luke 2:8–20 and Matthew 2:1–12: the adoration of the Magi with offerings of gold, frankincense, and myrrh; the angels chanting the heavenly hymn (*Сла́ва въ вы́шнихъ Бо́гоу...*); and the Judean shepherds playing upon their reed-pipes (*па́стыремъ свѣрѧ́ющимъ*, from *свирѣ́ль*, the rustic pastoral flute).

[^3036]: Cf. Matthew 2:3: King Herod and all Jerusalem were troubled (*і҆ю́дѣ матѧ́щесѧ*) at the arrival of the Magi and the tidings of the birth of the Messiah.

[^3037]: The opening incipit of the First Heirmos of the Canon of the Nativity of Christ by St. Cosmas of Maiuma (*Хрїсто́съ ражда́етсѧ, сла́вите; Хрїсто́съ съ небе́съ, срѧ́щите; Хрїсто́съ на земли́, возноси́тесѧ*), based on the famous Nativity Oration (Oration 38) of St. Gregory the Theologian.

[^3038]: In the printed imprint on Fol. 522r (p1059), the word *д҃шю* ("with soul") is interlineated above *срⷣце* by the Striatyn typographers to supply the complete liturgical triad: praising God with soul, heart, and lips (*похвалимъ д҃шею, срⷣцемъ, и҆ оу҆стна́ми*).

[^3039]: Cf. John 1:29; 1 Peter 1:19; Revelation 5:6, 12: Christ the spotless and unblemished Lamb slain for the redemption and life of the world.

[^3040]: Church Slavonic rubric: *Мл҃ • въ нл҃ю цвѣ́тноую на клѡ́нїа* ("Prayer on Flowery [Palm] Sunday over the Branches/Boughs"). Greek: *Εὐχὴ εἰς τὸ εὐλογῆσαι τὰ βάϊα* / *τῶν κλάδων* (Goar, *Euchologion*, p. 586). In Ukrainian and Ruthenian practice, Palm Sunday is called *Цвѣ́тнаѧ недѣ́лѧ* ("Flowery Sunday", modern *Квітна неділя* or *Вербна неділя*), on which willow boughs and palm or olive branches (*клѡ́нїа*, Greek κλάδοι) are solemnly blessed with this prayer.

[^3041]: Genesis 8:11: the dove returning to Noah in the ark bearing an olive branch in its beak, interpreted in patristic and liturgical typology as an image of the Holy Spirit, the mystery of the Church, and the peace of the New Covenant fulfilled by the children of Jerusalem greeting Christ with palm branches (Matthew 21:8–9; John 12:12–13).

[^3042]: Conclusion of the Palm Sunday blessing of branches (*ва́їа* / *клѡ́нїа*, Greek: κλάδοι / βαΐα) begun on leaf p1060 (Fol. 522v), commemorating the festal entry of Christ into Jerusalem when the multitude and children went out to meet Him with olive and palm boughs (Matthew 21:8–9; John 12:12–13).

[^3043]: Scriptural acclamation: Matthew 21:9; Mark 11:9–10; Luke 19:38; John 12:13 (cf. Psalm 117:25–26 LXX): *Ѡ҆са́нна въ вы́шнихъ* (Ὡσαννὰ ἐν τοῖς ὑψίστοις, "Hosanna in the highest").

[^3044]: Psalm 117:26 (LXX 117:26): *Благослове́нъ грѧды́й во и҆́мѧ Госпо́дне* ("Blessed is He that comes in the name of the Lord"), expanded dogmatically in the liturgical text to encompass both Christ's First Coming in the flesh and His Second Coming in righteousness to judge the world (*бл҃венъ прише́дый, и҆ па́ки грѧды́й сꙋди́ти пра́вдою*).

[^3045]: Church Slavonic rubric in red cinnabar: *И҆́же въ ст҃ы́хъ ѻ҆ц҃а на́шего і҆ѡа́нна а҆рхїепⷭ҇па константинопо́лѧ златоу́стаго • Сло́во оу҆тѣши́телно въ ст҃ый и҆ вели́кїй четвръто́къ • Бл҃ви ѻ҆́ч҃е* ("Of our Father among the Saints, John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople: A Consoling Word on Holy and Great Thursday. Bless, father:"). In Byzantine and Old Cyrillic liturgical codices (Goar, *Euchologion*, pp. 586–587; Mansvetov, *Tserkovnyi Ustav*, p. 312), this homiletic exhortation to communicants is traditionally read by the spiritual father or deacon before the reception of Holy Communion on Great and Holy Thursday, the feast commemorating the Mystical Supper (*Cena Domini*), warning penitents against approaching the Holy Mysteries without sincere repentance, confession, and reconciliation.

[^3046]: Luke 1:74–75: *въ прпⷣбїи и҆ пра́вдѣ* (ἐν ὁσιότητι καὶ δικαιοσύνῃ, "in holiness and righteousness before Him all the days of our life").

[^3047]: The fear and trembling requisite for partaking of the Holy Mysteries, reflecting 1 Corinthians 11:27–29 and the Chrysostomic liturgy's communion call: *Со стра́хомъ Бо́жїимъ и҆ вѣ́рою пристоупи́те* ("With fear of God and faith draw near").

[^3048]: In the printed imprint on Fol. 523v (p1062), the text reads *не бо а҆́зъ є҆́смь гл҃ѧни оу҆ча́й ва́съ*, where *гл҃ѧни* is an epigraphic crasis or typesetting corruption for *глаго́лѧй и҆* ("speaking and"). The preacher disclaims personal authority, attributing the words of instruction to the grace of the Holy Spirit (cf. Matthew 10:20: "For it is not ye that speak, but the Spirit of your Father which speaks in you").

[^3049]: Church Slavonic: *є҆ще́же и҆ ѿ своеѧ̀ ѻ҆глоуче́мъ съвѣ́сти*, where *ѻ҆глоуче́мъ* represents a printer error / contamination of *обличаемъ* (Greek: ἐλεγχόμενος ὑπὸ τοῦ ἰδίου συνειδότος, "convicted by his own conscience", cf. John 8:9) or *отлученъ* ("separated/excluded").

[^3050]: Scriptural citation of Hebrews 12:29 and Deuteronomy 4:24: *Бг҃ъ бо на́шъ ѻ҆́гнь поѧда́ѧй є҆́стъ* (καὶ γὰρ ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν πῦρ καταναλίσκον, "For our God is a consuming fire"). In Byzantine Eucharistic theology, the divine Fire of the Eucharist either purifies and illumines the contrite heart or burns and condemns the unrepentant (cf. St. Symeon Metaphrastes, Eucharistic Thanksgiving: "Consuming my sins as fire, yet enlightening my soul").

[^3051]: Scriptural quotation of 1 Corinthians 11:30: *сего ра́ди въ ва́съ мнѡ́ѕи не́мощни и҆ бѡ́лни, и҆ спѧ́тъ дово́лни* ("For this cause many among you are weak and sickly, and many sleep").

[^3052]: St. John Chrysostom's patristic exegesis on 1 Corinthians 11:30, explaining that the Apostle's word "sleep" (*спятъ*) euphemistically signifies physical death without sacramental absolution (*си́рѣчь оу҆мира́ютъ мнѡ́ѕи неи҆сповѣ́давшесѧ, и҆ безъ покаѧ́нїа*).

[^3053]: A comprehensive canonical catalogue of sins and spiritual impediments precluding reception of the Holy Mysteries, synthesizing the Pauline catalogues (1 Corinthians 6:9–10; Galatians 5:19–21; 1 Timothy 1:9–10) with Nomocanonical penances (e.g. Canons of St. Basil and St. John the Faster).

[^3054]: Church Slavonic: *манихе́й* (Manichaean), designating adherents of dualist heresy who denied the physical incarnation and the reality of Christ's Body and Blood, applied broadly in East Slavic canonical jurisprudence to heretics who reject Orthodox Eucharistic doctrine.

[^3055]: Scriptural quotation of Hebrews 10:31: *стра́шно бо впа́сти въ роу́цѣ Бг҃а жи́ва* (φοβερὸν τὸ ἐμπεσεῖν εἰς χεῖρας Θεοῦ ζῶντος, "It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God").

[^3056]: Scriptural quotation of Hebrews 4:12: *Ѻ҆стрѣ́йше бо є҆́стъ сло́во Бж҃їе па́че меча̀ ѻ҆бою́доу ѻ҆́стра • проходѧ́щее да́же до члѣ́нѡвъ и҆ мо́згѡвъ, и҆ кѡсті́й, и҆ мы́слїи, и҆ срⷣцъ* (τομώτερος ὑπὲρ πᾶσαν μάχαιραν δίστομον... ἄχρι μερισμοῦ ψυχῆς καὶ πνεύματος, ἁρμῶν τε καὶ μυελῶν).

[^3057]: Scriptural quotation of Deuteronomy 32:39: *а҆́зъ є҆́смь, и҆ нѣ́сть Бг҃ъ ра́звѣ менѐ • а҆́зъ оу҆бїю̀, и҆ жи́ти сътворю̀, и҆ нѣ́сть и҆́же и҆зме́тъ вы и҆зъ роу́къ мои́хъ* (ἴδετε ἴδετε ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι, καὶ οὐκ ἔστι Θεὸς πλὴν ἐμοῦ· ἐγὼ ἀποκτενῶ, καὶ ζῆν ποιήσω... καὶ οὐκ ἔστιν ὃς ἐξελεῖται ἐκ τῶν χειρῶν μου).

[^3058]: Church Slavonic rubric: *Мл҃, на па́схꙋ дѣ́темъ дх҃о́внымъ* ("Prayer on Pascha for Spiritual Children"). Parallel to the Nativity prayer on leaf p1056 (Fol. 520v), this prayer was recited by the spiritual father or parish priest over his spiritual children following the Paschal Liturgy, recapitulating the liturgical cycle of the Great Fast and Holy Week.

[^3059]: The biblical archetype of the Holy Great Fast: the forty days of prayer and fasting undertaken by Christ in the Judean wilderness (Matthew 4:1–2; Luke 4:1–2), prefigured by Moses on Mount Sinai (Exodus 34:28) and Elijah on Mount Horeb (1 Kings 19:8).

[^3060]: Commemoration of the Third Sunday of Great Lent, the Sunday of the Veneration of the Precious and Life-Giving Cross (*Крестопоклонная неделя*), marking the midpoint of the ascetical journey.

[^3061]: The raising of the four-days-dead Lazarus of Bethany (John 11:1–44), celebrated on Lazarus Saturday immediately preceding Palm Sunday as the assurance of the universal resurrection.

[^3062]: Commemoration of Palm Sunday: Christ's triumphal entry into the holy city of Jerusalem, greeted by the children of the Hebrews bearing branches and chanting *Hosanna in the highest* (Matthew 21:8–9; John 12:12–13).

[^3063]: The Instruments of the Passion (*arma Christi*) and the stations of Great and Holy Friday: the Crucifixion, the piercing with the Spear (John 19:34), the Sponge soaked with vinegar and gall offered on the Reed (Matthew 27:48), the Deposition from the Cross (*сънѧ́тїе*), and the Burial of the Lord by Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus (Matthew 27:57–60).

[^3064]: The Paschal celebration: the Resurrection of Christ on the third day according to the Scriptures, heralded by the angel at the empty sepulchre (Matthew 28:1–7).

[^3065]: Luke 7:37–48: the penitent woman weeping at Jesus' feet in the house of Simon the Pharisee, an enduring model of contrition and forgiveness in Byzantine hymnography (e.g. the Troparion of Kassiani).

[^3066]: Matthew 26:75; Luke 22:62; John 21:15–19: the Apostle Peter's bitter weeping following his threefold denial, and his subsequent threefold restoration and commissioning by the risen Lord.

[^3067]: Church Slavonic rubric in red cinnabar: *Мл҃твы, надъ бра́шномъ бра́шенъ мѧ́съ, въ ст҃оую и҆ вели́коую недѣ́лю па́схи* ("Prayers over the Meat of Meat Foods on the Holy and Great Sunday of Pascha"). Greek: *Εὐχὴ εἰς τὸ εὐλογῆσαι κρέα τῇ ἁγίᾳ καὶ μεγάλῃ κυριακῇ τοῦ Πάσχα* (Goar, *Euchologion*, p. 587). This benediction marks the canonical cessation of the Lenten abstinence from meat and animal products.

[^3068]: Rubric in red cinnabar: *Твори́тъ і҆ере́й нача́ло • С х҃съ въскр҃се • г҃ • та́же, Гдⷭ҇у помоли́мсѧ •* The red capital *С* before *х҃съ* stands for *Свяще́нникъ:* ("Priest:") or *Спѣва́етъ:* ("He sings:"). The priest initiates the blessing rite by chanting the Paschal troparion *Christ is risen from the dead* thrice.

[^3069]: Genesis 22:13: the ram caught by its horns in the thicket, offered by the Patriarch Abraham as a burnt offering in place of his son Isaac on Mount Moriah, universally interpreted as a type of the Lamb of God sacrificed for mankind.

[^3070]: Genesis 4:4: Abel bringing of the firstlings of his flock and of the fat thereof, acceptable unto the Lord as a whole burnt offering (*на всепло́дїе*, Greek εἰς ὁλοκάρπωσιν).

[^3071]: Luke 15:23–30: the parable of the Prodigal Son, wherein the compassionate father commands the fatted calf (*те́лецъ оу҆пита́нный*, τὸν μόσχον τὸν σιτευτόν) to be slaughtered and feasted upon at the return and repentance of his lost child.

[^3072]: Church Slavonic: *си́це и҆ ѡ҆сщ҃е́нныхъ тобо́ю, нелѣ́нныхъ наслади́мсѧ въ пи́щꙋ въсѣ́хъ на́съ*. In Greek euchologia (Goar, p. 587), the text reads: οὕτω καὶ τῶν παρὰ σοῦ ἡγιασμένων καὶ εὐλογηθέντων ἀπολαύσωμεν ("so also may we enjoy those things sanctified and blessed by Thee"). The Slavonic reading *нелѣ́нныхъ* (from *нелѣ́ный*, "unstinting, generous, ungrudging") expresses the unreserved divine munificence bestowed upon creation.

[^3073]: Church Slavonic rubric: *Мл҃тва • въ тоу́южде недѣ́лю надъ бл҃ве́нїемъ сы́ра, и҆ ꙗ҆и́цъ* ("Prayer on the Same Sunday over the Blessing of Cheese and Eggs"). Greek: *Εὐχὴ εἰς τὸ εὐλογῆσαι τυρὸν καὶ ᾠά* (Goar, *Euchologion*, p. 588). In Ruthenian and wider Slavic custom, dairy products, butter, hard cheeses, and dyed Easter eggs (*крашанки* / *писанки*) are blessed with this prayer immediately after the Paschal midnight Liturgy.

[^3074]: Church Slavonic: *бл҃ви млѣ́ко оу҆сыре́нное, съ ни́мже и҆ ꙗ҆йца* ("bless the curdled milk, and with it the eggs"), translating Greek τὸ γάλα τὸ τετυρωμένον (from τυρόω, to coagulate, curdle, or make cheese; cf. Psalm 67:16 LXX: ὄρος τετυρωμένον, *гора усыренная*).

[^3075]: Concluding petition of the prayer of blessing over cheese and eggs begun on fol. 527v (p1070). The phrase "независтно подателныя дары" ("gifts unbegrudgingly bestowed") reflects the Byzantine liturgical idiom referring to God's generous provision of food at the Paschal feast following the Great Fast.

[^3076]: The Greek Euchologion prayer (*Εὐχὴ ἐπὶ μεταλήψεως τυροῦ καὶ ᾠῶν*) concludes with this identical doxological clause acknowledging God's sovereignty over all creation.

[^3077]: Fol. 528r (p1071). Title in cinnabar: "Мл҃тва третїа. надъ сыромъ, и масы, и прочими брашны" (*A Third Prayer: Over Cheese, and Meat, and Other Foods*). This prayer synthesizes the blessing of all foods permitted after the Great Fast, linking bodily nourishment with spiritual renewal.

[^3078]: Refers to the biblical archetypes of forty-day fasts: Moses on Mount Sinai (Exodus 34:28), Elijah on Mount Horeb (1 Kings 19:8 / 3 Kingdoms 19:8 LXX), and Christ in the wilderness (Matthew 4:2, Luke 4:2).

[^3079]: Evokes the miraculous feeding of the five thousand with five loaves and two fish recorded in Matthew 14:15–21, Mark 6:35–44, Luke 9:12–17, and John 6:5–14.

[^3080]: Cf. Deuteronomy 32:13 ("He made him suck honey out of the rock, and oil out of the flinty rock") and Psalm 80:17 LXX (81:16 MT: "and with honey out of the rock should He have satisfied thee").

[^3081]: Fol. 528v (p1072). Title in cinnabar: "Мл҃ . на основанїе церкви" (*Prayer at the Foundation of a Church*). Appointed to be recited by the priest at the laying of the cornerstone or first foundation logs of a new church building.

[^3082]: An explicit quotation of the eucharistic and dedicatory formula: "твоя ѿ твоихъ тебѣ приносящихъ" ("offering Thee Thine own of Thine own"), rooted in King David's prayer at the preparation for building the Temple in 1 Chronicles 29:14: "For all things come of Thee, and of Thine own have we given Thee."

[^3083]: Rubric in cinnabar providing the liturgical alternative formula when the church is dedicated to a particular patron saint: "или въ имѧ ст҃го его имѧ рцы̀ твоего угодника" (*or in the name of the Saint [name him], Thy well-pleasing servant*).

[^3084]: Fol. 529v (p1074). Title in cinnabar: "Мл҃тва на основанїе домоу" (*Prayer at the Foundation of a House*). Recited at the groundbreaking or commencement of construction for a new family residence.

[^3085]: Echoes Psalm 135:5–6 LXX (136:5–6 MT): "To Him that by understanding made the heavens... To Him that stretched out the earth above the waters."

[^3086]: Allusion to Christ's parable of the wise builder in Matthew 7:24–25, who founded his house upon a rock, so that when the rains descended and the winds blew, it fell not.

[^3087]: Fol. 530r (p1075). Title in cinnabar: "Мл҃, на бл҃гословенїе дому и храму нову" (*Prayer over the Blessing of a New House and Habitation*). In Ruthenian liturgical usage, "храмъ" in conjunction with "домъ" designates the domestic chambers or rooms of the new residence.

[^3088]: Direct citation of the narrative of Zacchaeus the publican in Luke 19:1–10, specifically Christ's declaration: "Today salvation is come to this house" (Luke 19:9).

[^3089]: Fol. 530v (p1076). Title in cinnabar: "Мл҃тва вкратцѣ ѡст҃ити воду" (*A Brief Prayer to Sanctify Water*). A condensed formula of the Lesser Blessing of Waters (*Μικρὸς Ἁγιασμός*) used for domestic visits and household blessings.

[^3090]: Citation of Job 5:9 and 9:10: "Who does great things and unsearchable; marvelous things without number."

[^3091]: Fol. 531r (p1077). Title in cinnabar: "Мл҃тва надъ домомъ ѡблазнаемымъ ѿ злыхъ мѣчтокъ" (*Prayer over a House Troubled by Evil Phantasms*). Appointed to be read in households suffering from demonic harassment, nightly apparitions, or spiritual disturbances. "Мѣчта" corresponds to Greek φαντασία (*phantasia*), referring to illusory sensory deceptions produced by evil spirits.

[^3092]: Scriptural imagery drawn from Psalm 17:11 LXX (18:10 MT) and Psalm 79:2 LXX (80:1 MT): "Thou that sittest upon the Cherubim."

[^3093]: Pauline phraseology from Ephesians 1:21: "Far above all principality, and power, and might, and dominion, and every name that is named."

[^3094]: Cf. Psalm 88:8 LXX (89:7 MT): "God is greatly to be feared in the assembly of the saints, and to be had in reverence of all them that are about Him."

[^3095]: Allusion to Isaiah 40:22 LXX: "Who established heaven as a vault [ὡς καμάραν / ꙗко камару], and stretched it out as a tent to dwell in."

[^3096]: Cf. Jeremiah 10:12 and 51:15: "He hath made the earth by His power, He hath established the world by His wisdom."

[^3097]: Job 9:6: "Who shakes the earth out of her place, and the pillars thereof tremble."

[^3098]: Job 9:7: "Who commands the sun, and it rises not; and seals up the stars."

[^3099]: Nahum 1:4: "He rebukes the sea, and makes it dry, and dries up all the rivers."

[^3100]: Nahum 1:6: "His fury is poured out like fire, and the rocks are thrown down by Him."

[^3101]: Psalm 106:16 LXX (107:16 MT) and Isaiah 45:2: "For He hath broken the gates of brass, and cut the bars of iron in sunder," traditionally applied to the Harrowing of Hades.

[^3102]: Allusion to Matthew 12:29 and Mark 3:27: binding the strong man and plundering his house.

[^3103]: Patristic motif rooted in Job 40:20 LXX (41:1 MT: "Canst thou draw out Leviathan with a hook?"): the Incarnation of the Word conceived as a divine baited hook (*hamus divinitatis*), wherein Christ's human flesh served as bait concealing His Godhead, capturing the primordial serpent. See Gregory of Nyssa (*Catechetical Oration*, 24) and John Chrysostom (*Homily on the Paschal Triduum*).

[^3104]: Cf. 2 Peter 2:4 ("cast them down to hell [ταρταρώσας], and delivered them into chains of darkness") and Jude 1:6 ("reserved in everlasting chains under darkness").

[^3105]: Reference to the exorcism of the Gerasene demoniac in Mark 5:1–20 and Luke 8:26–39.

[^3106]: Allusion to the healing of the boy possessed by a deaf and dumb spirit in Mark 9:25: "Thou dumb and deaf spirit, I charge thee, come out of him, and enter no more into him."

[^3107]: Quotation of Luke 10:19: "Behold, I give unto you power to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy: and nothing shall by any means hurt you."

[^3108]: Quotation of Psalm 90:5–6 LXX (91:5–6 MT): "Thou shalt not be afraid for the terror by night; nor for the arrow that flies by day; nor for the pestilence that walks in darkness; nor for the mishap and the noonday demon."

[^3109]: Cf. Psalm 33:8 LXX (34:7 MT): "The angel of the Lord encamps round about them that fear Him, and delivers them."

[^3110]: Quotation of Psalm 117:6 LXX (118:6 MT): "The Lord is my helper, and I will not fear what man shall do unto me," paired with Psalm 22:4 LXX (23:4 MT: "I will fear no evil, for Thou art with me") which continues onto fol. 533r (p1081).

[^3111]: Psalm 22:4 (LXX 22:4): "For though I should walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for Thou art with me."

[^3112]: Isaiah 9:6 (LXX 9:6): "Mighty Ruler, Prince of Peace, Father of the age to come."

[^3113]: Psalm 144:13 (LXX 144:13): "Thy kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and Thy dominion endures throughout all generations."

[^3114]: Title rubric: *Prayer over the Planting of a Vineyard* (Слав. *Мл҃, насажде́нїемъ виногра́да*; Greek *Εὐχὴ ἐπὶ καταφυτεύσει ἀμπέλου*).

[^3115]: Allusion to John 15:1 ("I am the true vine, and My Father is the vinedresser") and John 15:5 ("I am the vine, ye are the branches").

[^3116]: Allusion to Psalm 79:9-10 (LXX 79:9-10): "Thou hast brought a vine out of Egypt: Thou hast cast out the heathen, and planted it." Here typologically applied to the calling of the Gentiles.

[^3117]: Marginal gloss printed in cinnabar: the main text reads *оу҆глубѝ* ("deepen / sink deeply"), while the margin supplies *вкоренѝ* ("root / plant firmly").

[^3118]: Slav. *ледѧ́ница ноу́жно носи́маго*—literally, "violently driven freezing rain / ice / rime."

[^3119]: Slav. *вѣ́тръ съжеже́нїа*—the parching, scorching wind (Greek καύσων; cf. James 1:11, Jonah 4:8).

[^3120]: Psalm 79:15-16 (LXX 79:15-16): "Look down from heaven, and behold, and visit this vine; and the vineyard which Thy right hand hath planted."

[^3121]: Liturgical intention of the vineyard: specifically that the wine produced from its vintage may be offered at the holy altar to be transformed by the Holy Spirit into the Precious Blood of Christ (*въ є҆́же претвори́тисѧ є҆моу̀ въ кро́вь х҃а твое́го*).

[^3122]: Title rubric: *Prayer over the Gathering of a Vineyard* (Слав. *Мл҃тва, надъ бра́нїемъ виногра́да*; Greek *Εὐχὴ ἐπὶ τρύγης ἀμπέλου*).

[^3123]: Slav. *безсмр҃тїа вино́венъ показа́въ*—Greek *καὶ τὸν καρπὸν αὐτῆς ἀθανασίας πρόξενον ἀναδείξας* ("and having manifested its fruit as the dispenser/cause of immortality"). In Church Slavonic, *виновенъ* preserves the etymological Greek sense of αἴτιος / πρόξενος ("author", "cause", "dispenser").

[^3124]: Epigraphic textual note: The printed Slavonic witness reads *и҆ съз́ка́вшаго на,*, which collates against the Byzantine Euchologion archetype *τὸν δὲ συγκαλέσαντα ἡμᾶς* ("and him who hath called us together / invited us"). The form *съз́кавшаго* represents a printed corruption of *съзвавшаго* (or *съискавшаго*), while *на,* is a truncated witness for *насъ* (*ἡμᾶς*).

[^3125]: Title rubric: *Prayer over the Blessing of Wine:* (Слав. *Мл҃тва, на бл҃венїемъ вина:*).

[^3126]: Scriptural allusions to Jacob's well (Genesis 33:18-19, John 4:6), the pool of Siloam (John 9:7), and the Eucharistic cup given to the Holy Apostles at the Mystical Supper (Matthew 26:27-28).

[^3127]: Scriptural citation of the Marriage at Cana of Galilee and the turning of water into wine (John 2:1-11).

[^3128]: Title rubric: *A Second Prayer, over the Blessing of Wine* (Слав. *Мл҃тва вто́раѧ, на бл҃венїе виноу́*).

[^3129]: Slav. *растворе́нїе бл҃го*—temperate mixture / wholesome moderation (Greek εὔκρατον / κρᾶσιν ἀγαθήν), referring both to the temperate mingling of wine and water, and to physical health and spiritual sobriety without drunkenness.

[^3130]: Slav. *без всѧ́коѧ непрїѧ́зньныѧ дѣ́тели*—"without any diabolic / hostile operation" (*неприязнь* = the adversary, Satan; *дѣтель* = operation, energy).

[^3131]: Title rubric: *Prayer over Sowing* (Слав. *Мл҃тва, надъ сѣ́ѧнїемъ*; Greek *Εὐχὴ ἐπὶ σπόρου*).

[^3132]: Slav. *сѣ́менъ подда́нїе*—the presentation / offering of seeds (Greek τὴν τῶν σπερμάτων παράθεσιν).

[^3133]: Isaiah 55:10: "...and make it bring forth and bud, that it may give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater."

[^3134]: Scriptural citations of Deuteronomy 28:12 ("The Lord shall open unto thee His good treasure, the heaven to give the rain unto thy land") and Malachi 3:10 ("and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it").

[^3135]: Scriptural allusion to Malachi 3:11: "And I will rebuke the devourer for your sakes, and he shall not destroy the fruits of your ground" (Слав. *и҆ ражденѝ [=разжени] ѿ на́съ всѧ снѣда́ющаѧ пло́дъ на́шъ зе́мный*).

[^3136]: Title rubric: *Prayer over the Blessing of a Herd* (Слав. *Мл҃, надъ бл҃венїемъ ста́да*).

[^3137]: Scriptural allusion to Genesis 30:29-43 and 31:4-12, recounting the miraculous multiplication and preservation of the flocks of the Patriarch Jacob.

[^3138]: Rubrical formula printed in cinnabar: *и҆́мѧ ре́къ* ("naming the name" / [Name]).

[^3139]: Slav. *възду́ха съмр҃тнаго, и҆ гоуби́телнаго недꙋ́га*—pestilential murrain and deadly air, accompanied by demonic afflictions and sorceries (*чародѣ́йства, и҆ влъше́бства*).

[^3140]: Title rubric: *Prayer for the Rebuking of Thunders and Lightnings* (Слав. *Мл҃тва, на запрѣще́нїе гро́мовъ, и҆ млъ́нїй*; Greek *Εὐχὴ ἐπὶ ἀπειλῆς βροντῶν καὶ ἀστραπῶν*).

[^3141]: Allusion to the confession of the disciples in Luke 17:10: "We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do."

[^3142]: Allusion to Psalm 84:5-6 (LXX 84:5-6): "Turn us, O God of our salvation, and cause Thine anger toward us to cease. Wilt Thou be angry with us unto ages?"

[^3143]: Scriptural allusion to Amos 4:13 (LXX 4:13): "He that establishes the thunder, and creates the spirit..."

[^3144]: Scriptural citation of Psalm 17:14-15 (LXX 17:14-15): "The Lord also thundered from heaven, and the Highest gave His voice; hailstones and coals of fire. Yea, He sent out His arrows, and scattered them; and He multiplied lightnings, and discomfited them."

[^3145]: Slav. *въ ти́хїи є҆ди́ръ въздꙋ́ха*—the Greek loanword *αἰθήρ* (ether, clear bright sky), corrupted or dialectally rendered in the 1606 imprint as *єдиръ*. The prayer continues onto leaf p1091 (*...преложѝ* / "...turn it into a calm ether of the air").

[^3146]: Slav. *въ ти́хость претворѝ*—conclusion of the *Prayer for the Rebuking of Thunders and Lightnings* (begun on leaf p1089).

[^3147]: Title rubric: *Prayer against the Evil Turbulence of Winds, and a Tempest of the Sea* (Слав. *Мл҃, на злорастворе́нїе вѣ́трѡвъ, и҆ бꙋ́рю мо́рскыѧ*; Greek *Εὐχὴ ἐπὶ δυσαερίας ἀνέμων καὶ ζάλης θαλάσσης*).

[^3148]: Scriptural allusions to the hypostatic Word and Spirit creating all things ex nihilo (Genesis 1:1-2, John 1:1-3), setting the sand as the bound of the sea (Jeremiah 5:22; Job 38:8-11), and meting out heaven with the span and the mountains in a balance (Isaiah 40:12).

[^3149]: Slav. *проти́воу нестрада́телномꙋ же и҆ нераздрꙋ́шномꙋ оу҆правлѧ́ѧ*—Greek *πρὸς τὸ ἀπαθὲς καὶ ἀδιάλυτον ἰθύνων* ("directing [all things] toward the impassible and indissoluble").

[^3150]: Slav. *преесте́венымъ и҆ ѡ҆бы́чнымъ твои́мъ чловеколю́бїемъ*—Greek *τῇ ὑπερφυεῖ καὶ συνήθει σου φιλανθρωπίᾳ* ("by Thy supernatural and accustomed love for mankind").

[^3151]: Allusions to the ransom paid through Christ (1 Peter 1:18-19, 1 Timothy 2:6) and the ineffable communion of the Holy Spirit (2 Corinthians 13:13).

[^3152]: Liturgical and cosmic theology: nature's catastrophic disturbance is viewed as the reverberation of human disorder (*безъчи́нїе*), lawless deformity (*безъ ѻ҆́бразїе*), and sinful life (*зла́го житїа́ на́шего*); divine mercy restores creation to its natural harmony and cosmic order (*къ є҆стве́номоу съли́чествꙋ и҆ чи́нꙋ*).

[^3153]: Scriptural citation of Psalm 106:23-24 (LXX 106:23-24): "They that go down to the sea in ships, that do business in great waters; these see the works of the Lord, and His wonders in the deep."

[^3154]: Scriptural account of Christ sleeping in the boat and rebuking the winds and the sea (Matthew 8:23-27, Mark 4:35-41, Luke 8:22-25).

[^3155]: Marginal gloss: The main text reads *пла́вати* ("to sail"), while the outer margin provides the Early Modern Ruthenian (*prosta mova*) synonym *пло́вїти*.

[^3156]: Title rubric: *Prayer over the Offered Fruit of Every Kind of Produce* (Слав. *Мл҃тва, надъ приноси́мымъ плодомъ въсѧ́кого ѡ҆во́щїа*; Greek *Εὐχὴ ἐπὶ προσφερόντων ἀπαρχὰς ὀπωρῶν*). In Ruthenian and Church Slavonic usage, *ѡ҆во́щїе* encompasses tree fruits, garden vegetables, and cultivated edible produce.

[^3157]: Title rubric: *A Second Prayer for the Same* (Слав. *Мл҃тва втора́ѧ томоу́ждє*).

[^3158]: Liturgical offering formula: *твоѧ̑ ѿ твои́хъ приноси́ти тебѣ̀* ("offering unto Thee Thine own of Thine own"), echoing 1 Chronicles 29:14 and the Eucharistic Anaphora.

[^3159]: Scriptural allusion to the poor widow's offering of two mites (Mark 12:41-44, Luke 21:1-4).

[^3160]: Rubrical formula printed in cinnabar: *и҆́мѧ ре́къ* ("naming the name" / [Name]).

[^3161]: Major headpiece and Title Rubric: *Order Performed in Fields, or in a Vineyard, or in a Garden, if it Chance that they be Harmed by Creeping Things, or by Other Species [of Pests]* (Слав. *ЧИ́НЪ быва́емый на ни́вахъ, и҆ли въ виногра́дѣ, и҆ли въ врътогра́дѣ, а҆́ще слꙋ́читсѧ врежда́тисѧ и҆́мъ ѿ га́дъ, и҆ли ѿ и҆ныхъ ви́дъ*; Greek *Ἀκολουθία γενομένη εἰς χωράφιον, ἢ ἀμπελῶνα, ἢ κῆπον, εἰ τύχοι βλάπτεσθαι ὑπὸ ἑρπετῶν, ἢ ἄλλων εἰδῶν*).

[^3162]: Patrons invoked against agricultural pests: St. Tryphon of Campsada in Phrygia (commemorated Feb. 1), St. Eustathius Placidas (Sept. 20), and St. Julian of Tarsus / Cilicia (June 21).

[^3163]: Liturgical practice: The priest takes sanctified oil from the saint's vigil lamp (*є҆ле́й ѿ канди́ла*) and Great Sanctification Theophany water (*во́доу сты́хъ Бг҃оѧвле́нїи*), sprinkling the threatened plot crosswise while reciting the prayers.

[^3164]: Hexaemeron creation narrative: Genesis 1:1, 1:11-12 (vegetation, herb yielding seed, and fruit tree yielding fruit), and 1:14-18 (sun, moon, and stars).

[^3165]: Marginal gloss: The main text reads *ѻ҆пла́зньства лоука́ваго* ("the snare / assault of the deceitful one"), while the left margin supplies the vernacular Ruthenian gloss *проны́ри* ("guile, cunning deceit, machinations").

[^3166]: Title rubric: *Exorcistic and Commendatory Prayer of the Holy Martyr Tryphon, spoken in a garden, or in a vineyard, or in a field* (Слав. *Мл҃тва повѣ́тна и҆ заклина́телнаѧ ст҃го мч҃нка трѵ́фона, гл҃емаѧ въ врътогра́дѣ, и҆ли виногра́дѣ, и҆ли на ни́вѣ*; Greek *Εὐχὴ ἐξορκισμοῦ τοῦ ἁγίου ἐνδόξου μάρτυρος Τρύφωνος*). The prayer text continues onto leaf p1101.

[^3167]: Rubric continuation: *...in a garden, or in a vineyard, or in a field* (Слав. *...врътогра́дѣ, и҆ли виногра́дѣ, и҆ли на ни́вѣ*). Campsada (Слав. *Кампсада*, Greek *Καμψάδα* or *Κάμψαδα*) was the native village of the Holy Martyr Tryphon (commemorated February 1), located near Apamea in Phrygia. The narrative introduction recites the hagiographical account of the saint's youthful pastoral life pasturing geese (*го́уси па́сꙋщꙋ ми*), when a plague of agricultural pests descended upon the region.

[^3168]: Slav. *гнѣ́въ съни́де ѿ Бг҃а вседръжи́телѧ не то́кмо на мѣ́сто ѻ҆́но, но̀ и҆ въ ѻ҆́кр҃тныѧ предѣ́лы*—Greek *ὀργὴ κατῆλθεν ἀπὸ Θεοῦ παντοκράτορος οὐ μόνον ἐπὶ τὸν τόπον ἐκεῖνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ εἰς τὰ περικείμενα ὅρια*. The pestilence is depicted as a manifestation of divine chastisement (*гнѣ́въ*) affecting the entire ecosystem.

[^3169]: The text references the lake adjoining the village of Campsada (*па́че же и҆́же въ ве́си ѻ҆́ной живꙋ́щихъ прилежа́щаго є҆́зера*), traditionally identified with Lake Apamea / Aulocrene in Phrygia. The villagers approached Tryphon seeking his intercession before God.

[^3170]: The exhaustive catalogue of agricultural vermin, insects, and venomous pests reflects both classical Greek entomological vocabulary (*Εὐχολόγιον*) and East Slavic / Ruthenian zoological terms: caterpillar (*гꙋ́сѣница* / *κάμπη*), cankerworm (*чр҃вь* / *σκώληξ*), locust / wingless grasshopper (*прꙋ́гы* / *βροῦχος*), beetle / cockchafer (*хроу́стъ* / *κάνθαρος*), mole-cricket (*щꙋ́ры* / *γρυλλοτάλπη*), snout-beetle / grub (*връпела*), mole (*крыти́ца* / *ἀσπάλαξ*), mice (*мы́ши* / *μύες*), diverse midges (*мꙋ́шица* / *κωνώπιον*), grain-weevil (*гъгрі́нца* / *σιτόφιλος*), cloth/grain moths (*мо́лїе* / *σῆτες*), lice/gnats (*скни́пы* / *σκνῖπες*), destructive flies (*тлетво́рныѧ моу́хи* / *μυῖαι*), ants (*мра́вїе* / *μύρμηκες*), horseflies / gadflies (*ѡ҆́вады* / *οἶστροι*), wasps (*ѡ҆́сы* / *σφῆκες*), and venomous reptiles and arthropods (*ꙗ҆́звъ скорпі́а, ѕмі́а, мнѡгоно́жна*).

[^3171]: Slav. *зла́ца же, лькы̀, є҆́жеве, сла́ны, за́висти, лю́тости*—technical terminology for parasitic crop blights, fungal rusts (*зла́ца* / *ἐρυσίβη*), weeds/dodder (*лькы̀*), mildew/hail-rot (*є҆́жеве*), rime/frost damage (*сла́ны* / *πάχνη*), and atmospheric blastings (*за́висти*, *лю́тости*).

[^3172]: Title rubric: *And the exorcism is as follows* (Слав. *Заклина́нїе же си́цеко є҆́сть*; Greek *Ὁ δὲ ἐξορκισμὸς οὕτως ἔχει*). Here the celebrant shifts from narrative recollection to direct epigraphic adjuration (*Заклина́ю ва́съ* / *Ὁρκίζω ὑμᾶς*).

[^3173]: Angelic hierarchy and the Thrice-Holy Hymn: Allusions to the Cherubim and Seraphim crying "Holy, Holy, Holy is the Lord of Sabaoth" (Isaiah 6:2-3; Revelation 4:8) and the myriads of heavenly hosts ministering before the divine glory (Daniel 7:10; Revelation 5:11).

[^3174]: Scriptural and exorcistic motif: Banishment of destructive powers to wild mountains and unfruitful trees (*на ди́выѧ гѡ́ры на непло́днаа дре́ва*), mirroring Christ's authority over demons cast out into the wilderness or into swine (Matthew 8:28-32), while affirming God's providence providing nourishment even for wild creatures (Psalm 103:27-28 / LXX 103:27-28).

[^3175]: Patristic invocation of the covenantal God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Exodus 3:6; Matthew 22:32) and the eschatological reality of Christ returning to judge the living and the dead (2 Timothy 4:1; 1 Peter 4:5).

[^3176]: Slav. *но̀ и҆ воро́бїи посыла́емїи мое́ю мл҃твою поꙗдѧ́тъ вы*—a specific miracle attributed to Saint Tryphon in his hagiography, wherein flocks of sparrows and birds descended at his prayer to devour the swarms of destructive insects.

[^3177]: Allusion to the ineffable divine Tetragrammaton and Psalm 67:3 (LXX 67:3 / Masoretic 68:2): "as wax melts before the face of fire, so let the wicked perish at the presence of God" (Слав. *ꙗ҆́ко во́скъ ѿ лица̀ ѻ҆гню̀*).

[^3178]: Liturgical rubric and prayer: *Prayer of Bowing of Heads* (Слав. *Главы̀ ва́шѧ Гд҃ви приклони́те*; Greek *Τὰς κεφαλὰς ὑμῶν τῷ Κυρίῳ κλίνατε*). Typological commemoration of God's blessing upon holy places: Bethlehem (birthplace of Christ, Micah 5:2; Matthew 2:1), Gethsemane (site of Christ's prayer, Matthew 26:36), and the blessing of the patriarch Jacob, renamed Israel (Genesis 32:28).

[^3179]: Divine blessing upon the house of David (2 Samuel 7:29) applied to the agrarian possession (*стѧжа́нїе*). Slav. *ѡ҆блѣ́нїи плодоноси́ти* is an archaic syncopated spelling for *ѡ҆би́льнїи* / *ѡ҆би́льнѣ* ("in abundance", Greek *ἐν εὐθηνίᾳ*). Intercessory invocation includes the three patron saints of agriculture and pests: Great-Martyr Tryphon, Great-Martyr Eustathius Placidas, and Great-Martyr Julian.

[^3180]: Title rubric: *Prayer over a Threshing Floor* (Слав. *Мл҃тва, надъ гоумно́мъ*; Greek *Εὐχὴ ἐπὶ ἅλωνα*). In traditional agrarian liturgy, the threshing floor (*гоумно́*, Greek *ἅλως*) was consecrated before winnowing to protect the grain harvest from decay, theft, and vermin, invoking Deuteronomy 28:8 and Psalm 103:15 (LXX 103:15 / Masoretic 104:15: "wine that makes glad the heart of man, oil to make his face to shine, and bread that strengthens man's heart").

[^3181]: Title rubric: *Prayer over the Blessing of Nets* (Слав. *Мл҃тва . надъ бл҃венїемъ сѣ́тей*; Greek *Εὐχὴ εἰς τὸ εὐλογῆσαι δίκτυα*). Commemoration of the miraculous multiplication of the five loaves and two fishes feeding the five thousand (Matthew 14:15-21) and the invocation of Saint Peter the Apostle, the Galilean fisherman and leader of the Apostles (*пръвовръхо́внаго а҆плсо́м петра̀*, Greek *τοῦ πρωτοκορυφαίου τῶν ἀποστόλων Πέτρου*), for safety, abundant catch, and bodily health.

[^3182]: Title rubric: *Prayer at the Construction of a Ship, or a Boat* (Слав. *Мл҃тва · на съѻ҆рꙋже́нїе кораблѧ̀, и҆ли ло́дьи*; Greek *Εὐχὴ ἐπὶ κατασκευῇ πλοίου*). This Euchological blessing consecrated newly constructed maritime vessels—both seagoing ships (*кора́бль*, Greek *πλοῖον*) and river craft or boats (*ло́дьꙗ*, Greek *λέμβος* / *σκάφη*)—before launching, placing the vessel under divine and angelic guardianship.

[^3183]: Allusion to Noah building the Ark (Genesis 6:14-22). The printer supplies an explicit marginal gloss in the right margin: *кїѡ́тъ* (from Greek *κιβωτός*, "ark/chest"), explaining the Slavonic word *ковче́гъ* (*съѻ҆рꙋжи́ти ковче́гъ на сп҃сенїе ми́ра*). The theology of the prayer contrasts the multiplicity of wooden planks joined into a single unified hull (*ѿ мнѡ́гихъ дре́въ... є҆ди́нѣмъ дре́вомъ бы́ти, и҆ съчета́тисѧ*) with God's sovereign governance over inanimate creation, typologically prefiguring the Church as the Ark of salvation navigating the turbulent waters of the world.

[^3184]: Title rubric: *Prayer over Salt* (Слав. *Мл҃тва, надъ со́лью*; Greek *Εὐχὴ ἐπὶ ἅλατος*). In Byzantine and Ruthenian domestic liturgy, salt was formally blessed as a staple of sustenance, a preservative against decay, and an agent of purification, recalling Christ's word: "Ye are the salt of the earth" (Matthew 5:13) and Saint Paul's exhortation: "Let your speech be always with grace, seasoned with salt" (Colossians 4:6).

[^3185]: Scriptural typology: The healing of the poisonous and barren spring at Jericho by the Prophet Elisha through casting salt into a new cruse (2 Kings 2:19-22 / LXX 4 Kingdoms 2:19-22: "Thus saith the Lord: I have healed these waters; there shall not be from thence any more death or barren land").

[^3186]: Slav. *преложѝ ю҆ въ жръ́твоу радова́нїа*—Greek *ποίησον αὐτὸ θυσίαν ἀγαλλιάσεως* ("make it a sacrifice of exultation/joy"), echoing Psalm 26:6 (LXX 26:6: "And I offered in His tabernacle a sacrifice of joy").

[^3187]: Title rubric: *Prayer over a Woman when She Has Miscarried* (Слав. *Мл҃, на[д] жено́ю є҆гда̀ и҆звръ́жетъ*; Greek *Εὐχὴ ἐπὶ γυναικὶ ὅταν ἐκτρώσῃ* or *Εὐχὴ ἐπὶ γυναικὶ ἀποβαλούσῃ*). In Eastern Christian canon law and pastoral theology, miscarriage or stillbirth—whether caused by maternal trauma, physical infirmity, involuntary accident, or intentional intervention—was treated as a profound bereavement and spiritual crisis requiring formal prayers of physical healing, consolation, purification, and reconciliation.

[^3188]: Introductory liturgical rubric: The priest begins with the customary Trisagion prayers (*Тр҃тое* = Trisagion, *пр҃таа тр҃це* = All-Holy Trinity, *Ѿч҃е на́* = Our Father, *Ꙗ҆́ко твоѐ є҆́стъ цр҃тво* = priestly doxological exclamation "For Thine is the kingdom"), followed by the Troparion of the current day (*Тро · дню*), and the deacon's/priest's invitation to prayer: "Let us pray to the Lord" (*Гд҃ꙋ помоли́мсѧ*).

[^3189]: Incarnational invocation: The opening address of the prayer commemorates Christ's Nativity and His reclining as a newborn babe in the manger at Bethlehem (Luke 2:7, 12, 16), juxtaposing Christ's holy infancy with the lost life of the miscarried child.

[^3190]: Canonical and pastoral terminology: Slav. *въпа́дшоую грѣхмѝ въ оу҆бїи́ство во́лное* (Greek *περιπεσοῦσαν ἁμαρτίαις εἰς φόνον ἑκούσιον ἢ ἀκούσιον*). Ancient canonical tradition (e.g. Saint Basil the Great, Canons 2 and 8; Ancyra, Canon 21; Trullo, Canon 91) categorizes the destruction of a fetus—whether procured through abortifacients (*во́лное* / voluntary) or resulting from bodily trauma, distress, or involuntary mishap (*нево́лное* / involuntary)—under the broader juridical heading of homicide (*φόνος* / *оу҆бїи́ство*), requiring canonical absolution, physical healing, and spiritual restoration. On leaf p1115, the text explicitly adds the balanced phrase: *во́лею, и҆ли нево́лею зача́тое въ не́й и҆звръ́гшей* ("whether by will or against her will having cast forth that which was conceived within her").

[^3191]: Rubrical and pastoral prayer for physical recovery: Slav. *възста́ви ю҆ ѿ ло́жа нане́мже ѡ҆бложе́на є҆́стъ*—Greek *ἀνάστησον αὐτὴν ἀπὸ τῆς κλίνης ἐν ᾗ περίκειται*. The woman experiencing a miscarriage was typically bedridden from hemorrhage, shock, and weakness; the prayer asks Christ, the Physician of souls and bodies, to raise her up as He did the mother-in-law of Saint Peter (Matthew 8:14-15) and the paralytic (Mark 2:11).

[^3192]: Penitential quotation from Psalm 50:7 (LXX 50:7 / Masoretic 51:5: "For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins did my mother bear me") and Isaiah 64:6 ("we are all become as an unclean thing").

[^3193]: Intercession for the attendants and midwives: Slav. *и҆ всѣ́хъ ѡ҆брѣта́ющих́сѧ, и҆ прикосноу́вшихсѧ є҆́й*—Greek *καὶ πάντων τῶν εὑρεθέντων καὶ ἁψαμένων αὐτῆς*. Under ancient ritual purity canons derived from Levitical law (Leviticus 15:19-30), touching a person during active postpartum flux or after contact with stillbirth was considered ritual defilement requiring priestly blessing and prayer before approaching the Holy Mysteries.

[^3194]: Title rubric: *Prayer, Said before Prayer, and over Those Who Have Been Tempted in Sleep* (Слав. *Мл҃тва, гл҃емаѧ прѣ́жде мл҃[итвы] · и҆ на съблазни́вшихсѧ во снѣ̀*; Greek *Εὐχὴ λεγομένη πρὸ τῆς εὐχῆς, καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν σκανδαλισθέντων καθ' ὕπνους*). This prayer belongs to the classical monastic and sacerdotal euchological corpus (cf. the Canon of Preparation for Holy Communion and the Rule against Nocturnal Defilement, *Канонъ молебный ѡ҆ ѡ҆скверне́нїи во снѣ̀*). It is prescribed for a priest or deacon before celebrating the Divine Liturgy, or for any Christian prior to standing in prayer or receiving the Holy Mysteries, after suffering nocturnal emissions or deceptive dreams caused by demonic assault or bodily incontinence.

The Eucharistic gifts are designated "dread and fearful" because of the holy presence of Christ's Body and Blood, demanding moral purity and spiritual sobriety (1 Corinthians 11:27-29).

The Ruthenian noun *скра́пїа* / *кра́пїа* (from the root *krap-* / *skrap-*, cf. Old East Slavic *краплꙗ*, Ukrainian *крапля*, Polish *kropla*, "drop, droplet, oozing, discharge") translates the Greek concept of seminal defilement (*καταρρύπανσις*, *μολυσμός*), specifically referring to involuntary nocturnal discharge or emissions provoked by demonic fantasy (*блоу́дъ*, fornication/lust). The rubric introduces an exorcistic and reconciliatory prayer restoring the believer to Eucharistic communion.

The prayer seeks to sever any spiritual entanglement (*прича́стїе*) contracted through demonic nocturnal deception.

[^3202]: Liturgical restoration to the Altar and Holy Communion: Slav. *прѣста́ви ст҃омꙋ твое́мꙋ жръто́вникꙋ · и҆ нб҃ных твои́хъ животворѧ́щихъ та́инъ сподобѝ*—Greek *παράστησον τῷ ἁγίῳ σου θυσιαστηρίῳ, καὶ τῶν ἐπουρανίων σου καὶ ζωοποιῶν μυστηρίων ἀξίωσον*. This formula demonstrates that the prayer functioned as an absolution and cleansing for clergy and communicants barred by canon law from the Holy Altar following a defiling occurrence.

Patriarch Kallistos I of Constantinople (Ecumenical Patriarch 1350–1353, 1355–1363), renowned hesychast writer, disciple of St. Gregory of Sinai, and author of numerous liturgical prayers.

[^3618]: Editorial continuation marker: text spans physical leaf p1202 (fol. 593v) to p1203 (fol. 594r).

[^3624]: Editorial continuation marker: text spans physical leaf p1203 (fol. 594r) to p1204 (fol. 594v).

[^3662]: Concluding troparion of Ode 8 of the Supplicatory Canon for the Overcoming of the Pestilential Sickness.

[^3663]: Theotokion of Ode 8, beseeching the Mother of God for alleviation from the deadly plague.

[^3665]: Troparion of Ode 9 invoking Christ's boundless miracles (Job 5:9 LXX) and the intercession of the Theotokos and martyrs (побѣдоно́сцы, trophy-bearers).

[^3667]: Cf. Eph. 2:4: "God, Who is rich in mercy."

[^3668]: Troparion of Ode 9 addressed to Christ the divine Physician.

[^3669]: Concluding Theotokion of the Supplicatory Canon for the Overcoming of the Pestilential Sickness.
