[^3670]: Rubric heading for the concluding prayers of intercession against pestilence and infectious mortality.

[^3671]: The rubrical cross-reference directs the priest back to fol. 410r (physical leaf p835), where this prayer against sudden and fearful death ("O Master, Lord our God, inexhaustible Fountain of compassions...") is printed in full.

[^3672]: Rubric heading for the second prayer in time of pestilence.

[^3673]: The rubric directs the reader back to fol. 412v (physical leaf p840), where the third prayer of St. Philotheus for general distress and repentance ("We have sinned, we have committed iniquity...") is printed in full.

[^3674]: Rubric heading introducing the comprehensive supplicatory prayer in time of pestilential plague ("O Almighty Master, Long-suffering, Plenteous in mercy..."), corresponding to the classic Greek Euchologion prayer of penitence in epidemic disease (Εὐχὴ ἐπὶ λοιμοῦ).

[^3675]: Beginning of the long penitential prayer, reciting the history of salvation from creation through the Fall, the Law, and the Prophets.

[^3676]: Gen. 2:7: "And the Lord God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul."

[^3677]: Patristic theology of primordial communion in Eden prior to the ancestral transgression.

[^3678]: Heb. 1:1: "God, Who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets."

[^3679]: The theological narrative of the prayer continues onto fol. 600v (leaf p1216).

[^3680]: Traditional Byzantine angelology of the Guardian Angel as educator and spiritual pedagogue (cf. Ex. 23:20; Ps. 90:11 LXX).

[^3681]: Classic Patristic soteriology of the Cappadocians and St. John Damascene: Christ assumed the fullness of human nature in order to heal it ("what is not assumed is not healed").

[^3682]: The catalog of sins closely reflects apostolic vice-lists in Rom. 1:29–31 and Gal. 5:19–21.

[^3683]: Theological theme that human transgression exceeds the natural bounds observed even by irrational animals.

[^3684]: Ps. 77:33 LXX: "And their days were consumed in vanity, and their years with haste."

[^3685]: Penitential confession of divine abandonment continues onto fol. 601v (leaf p1218).

[^3686]: Ps. 78:4 LXX: "We are become a reproach to our neighbours, a scorn and derision to them that are round about us."

[^3687]: Isa. 52:5 LXX / Rom. 2:24: "For the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles through you."

[^3688]: Ps. 13:3 LXX / Rom. 3:10–12: "There is none that understands, there is none that seeks after God. They are all gone out of the way, they are together become unprofitable; there is none that does good, no, not one."

[^3689]: Isa. 24:2: "And it shall be, as with the people, so with the priest."

[^3690]: Enumeration of the biblical chastisements continues onto fol. 602r (leaf p1219).

[^3691]: Jer. 5:3: "Thou hast stricken them, but they have not grieved; Thou hast consumed them, but they have refused to receive correction."

[^3692]: Amos 4:6–11: The prophetic refrain of impenitence under divine chastisement ("yet have ye not returned unto Me, saith the Lord").

[^3693]: The prayer continues onto fol. 602v (leaf p1220).

[^3694]: Isa. 1:9 / Rom. 9:29: "Except the Lord of Sabaoth had left us a seed, we had been as Sodoma, and been made like unto Gomorrha."

[^3695]: Gen. 6–7: The universal Deluge destroying the wicked, whose remembrance is swept away; the sentence continues onto fol. 603r (leaf p1221).

[^3696]: Continuation of the sentence from fol. 602v (leaf p1220). The imagery of complete extirpation ("with their very roots and with their very branches") alludes to the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen. 19:24–25; Isa. 1:9 / Rom. 9:29) and the prophetic warning in Mal. 4:1 LXX ("that it shall leave them neither root nor branch").

[^3697]: Slavonic: зна́менїе напра́сно смр҃ти (sudden sign / token of death). In epidemic nosology, this refers to the appearance of buboes, carbuncles, or petechiae ("tokens"), whose sudden eruption signaled inevitable and swift demise.

[^3698]: A vivid contemporary description of the high mortality and communal collapse during plague outbreaks: multiple deceased family members carried out together on a single bier. The sentence continues onto fol. 603v (leaf p1222).

[^3699]: Slavonic: и҆ ни́же довлѣ́ти ѡ҆ста́вльшемсѧ ѿ лиша́ющихсѧ проси́ти бли́жнихъ. The contagion renders neighbors unable to help one another, severing the basic social bonds of mutual assistance.

[^3700]: Slavonic: вы́шшихъ недꙋ́га, translating Greek ὑπερτέρους τῆς νόσου ("above the disease"). The printed 1606 edition provides a vernacular Ruthenian marginal correction: чи́сти ("clean / uncontaminated"), the standard technical term used in early modern quarantine and municipal plague ordinances. The sentence continues onto fol. 604r (leaf p1223).

[^3701]: Ps. 43:23 LXX / Rom. 8:36: "For Thy sake we are killed all the day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter."

[^3702]: Graphic contrast between the joyful domestic gathering of extended families one day and their total annihilation the next: "today there surrounds... but on the morrow they are childless, desolate, wretched, cast down."

[^3703]: Ps. 43:20 LXX: "and covered us with the shadow of death"; Ps. 54:6 LXX: "Fearfulness and trembling are come upon me, and darkness hath covered me."

[^3704]: Remarkable liturgical and psychological testimony to the panic and somatic delusion induced by the epidemic: Slavonic ко́ждо ра́нꙋ и҆ зна́менїе насебѣ̀ мѣ́ти мечта́ахсѧ ("each one imagines that he has the wound and token upon himself"). The left margin bears the contemporary gloss взма́хъ ("blow / stroke" of the scourge). The sentence continues onto fol. 605r (leaf p1225).

[^3705]: Depiction of clinical hyper-vigilance and phobia: any minor gnat or insect bite is immediately misinterpreted as the onset of the fatal plague. The printed margin supplies the adverbial gloss ча́сто ("frequently") for the liturgical Slavonic idiom на ча́стѣ.

[^3706]: Slavonic: ѡ҆стны́мъ съвѣ́сти оу҆кода́еми, translating Greek τῷ κέντρῳ τῆς συνейδήσεως νυττόμενοι ("pricked by the goad / sting of conscience"; cf. Acts 9:5, 26:14).

[^3707]: The classic liturgical confession of divine righteousness under chastisement: Dan. 3:27 LXX / Prayer of Azariah; Ps. 118:137 LXX: "Righteous art Thou, O Lord, and upright are Thy judgments."

[^3708]: Ps. 102:10 LXX: "He hath not dealt with us after our sins; nor rewarded us according to our iniquities."

[^3709]: Ps. 6:1 LXX: "O Lord, rebuke me not in Thine indignation, neither chasten me in Thy wrath"; Ps. 37:1 LXX.

[^3710]: Dan. 3:34–37 LXX / Prayer of Azariah: "And cause not Thy mercy to depart from us... neither break Thou Thy covenant... For we, O Lord, are become less than any nation."

[^3711]: Ps. 50:4 LXX: "Against Thee only have I sinned"; Isa. 26:13 LXX: "O Lord our God... beside Thee we know no other."

[^3712]: The biblical narrative of King Hezekiah's mortal illness and miraculous recovery: 4 Kings (2 Kings) 20:1–6 LXX; Isa. 38:1–5.

[^3713]: Ezek. 18:23, 33:11: "As I live, saith the Lord God, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live."

[^3714]: Ps. 84:5 LXX: "Wilt Thou be angry with us unto ages?"

[^3715]: Ps. 79:10–11 LXX: "The shadow of it covered the hills, and the boughs thereof were like the goodly cedars."

[^3716]: Ps. 7:2 LXX: "Lest he tear my soul like a lion, while there is none to deliver, nor to save."

[^3717]: The tenth plague of Egypt, the death of the firstborn: Ex. 12:29–30; Wis. 18:5–19.

[^3718]: The comprehensive supplicatory prayer in time of pestilence continues onto fol. 608r (physical leaf p1231).

[^3719]: Continuation of the sentence from fol. 607v (leaf p1230), concluding the extensive supplication for deliverance from pestilence.

[^3720]: Slavonic: бл҃гопримири́телю Гн҃ ("O Lord, Reconciler / Author of Reconciliation"). In the liturgical vocabulary of Byzantine and Ruthenian euchologia, this title invokes Christ as the Divine Pacifier Who reconciles estranged humanity unto the Father (cf. 2 Cor. 5:18–19; Col. 1:20–22).

[^3721]: Pathos-laden liturgical depiction of the indiscriminate mortality inflicted by the epidemic: infants (младе́нцы), young children (дѣ́тища), and all those who have not attained mature adulthood (неоу҆краше́ннаго всѧ́каго, и҆ недоспѣ́вшаго въ́зраста).

[^3722]: Slavonic: да̀ преста́нетъ сѣ́чь ("let the slaughter / mortal hewing cease"). The imagery derives from the biblical account of the destroying angel's sword during the plague in Jerusalem (2 Kings / 2 Sam. 24:16 LXX; 1 Chron. 21:15–16).

[^3723]: Slavonic: ра́ноу бо и҆ зна́менїе смр҃тное дѣ́тище прїе́мше ("for the little children, having received the stroke and the mortal token"). As on fol. 605r (leaf p1224), зна́менїе смр҃тное denotes the sudden appearance of plague carbuncles or bubonic swellings, which contemporaries recognized as infallible signs of approaching death.

[^3724]: Slavonic: ше́пленьми и҆ къпїе́ньми [въпїе́ньми] неꙗ҆́сными. The printed text witnesses a dialectal or typographical form къпїе́ньми (for вопленіями / въпїе́ньми, "cries / wailings"), capturing the indistinct, half-audible moans and inarticulate gasps of dying infants.

[^3725]: The pathetic description of dying children movingly compelling their helpless parents to seek aid continues onto fol. 608v (leaf p1232).

[^3726]: Matt. 19:26; Luke 18:27: "The things which are impossible with men are possible with God."

[^3727]: Rubric introducing the second supplicatory prayer in time of pestilence and famine, explicitly attributed in the printed rubric to Patriarch Kallistos I of Constantinople (reigned 1350–1353, 1355–1363), a disciple of St. Gregory of Sinai and key hesychast figure who authored prominent liturgical offices and canons during the turbulent mid-14th-century crises (including the Black Death).

[^3728]: Opening invocation celebrating the doctrine of creation ex nihilo: Slavonic съдѣ́тельнымъ твои́мъ повелѣ́нїемъ, ѿ нѣсоу́щихъ въ бытїѐ приве́дъ, translating Greek τῷ δημιουργικῷ σου προστάγματι ἐκ τοῦ μὴ ὄντος εἰς τὸ εἶναι παραγαγών (cf. 2 Macc. 7:28; Wis. 11:17; Rom. 4:17). The prayer continues onto fol. 609r (leaf p1233).

[^3729]: Gen. 2:7: the creation of man by God's own hands, followed by the bountiful provision of food in Eden and man's subsequent expulsion into toilsome labor (Gen. 3:17–19).

[^3730]: Ps. 103:28 LXX: "When Thou openest Thine hand, they shall all be filled with good." The cosmic providence of God extends over the animal creation and the fish of the sea.

[^3731]: Gen. 41:48–57; 45:5–11: the biblical narrative of Joseph nourishing Egypt and his brethren during the seven years of famine, here interpreted in classical patristic typology as a prefiguration (носѧ́щимъ ѻ҆́бразъ) of Christ, the true Bread of Life Who feeds His people in their distress.

[^3732]: Concluding Trinitarian doxology of the second prayer of Patriarch Kallistos.

[^3733]: Rubric introducing the third prayer against pestilence and famine, designated подо́бнаѧ • того́жде ("a similar prayer, of the same [Patriarch Kallistos]").

[^3734]: Opening of the third prayer: Slavonic Б[ж҃]е чюде́сныхъ, и҆́же вели́каа и҆ чю́днаа съдѣ́лавый, corresponding to the Byzantine Greek euchological incipit Ὁ τῶν θαυμασίων Θεός, ὁ ποιήσας μεγάла καὶ θαυμαστά (cf. Job 5:9; 9:10; Ps. 71:18, 135:4 LXX).

[^3735]: The liberation of Israel from Egyptian bondage: Ex. 3:7–10; 12:51; 14:30–31.

[^3736]: Ex. 13:21; Ps. 77:53–54 LXX: "And He guided them in hope, and they feared not... And He brought them unto the border of His sanctuary."

[^3737]: Ex. 16:13; Num. 11:31–32; Ps. 104:40 LXX: "They asked, and the quail came, and He satisfied them with the bread of heaven." The sentence continues onto fol. 610v (leaf p1236).

[^3738]: Continuation of the prayer from fol. 610r (leaf p1235), describing God's miraculous providence in the arid wilderness.

[^3739]: Ex. 16:4; Ps. 77:24 LXX: "And He rained down manna upon them to eat, and gave them of the bread of heaven."

[^3740]: Ex. 17:6; Num. 20:11; Ps. 77:15–16; Ps. 104:41 LXX: "He clave the rock in the wilderness, and gave them drink as out of the great depth. He brought streams also out of the rock."

[^3741]: Luke 1:37: "For with God nothing shall be impossible"; cf. Jer. 32:17, 27; Job 42:2.

[^3742]: The Gospel miracles of the multiplication of the loaves and fishes: Matt. 14:15–21 (the feeding of the five thousand); Matt. 15:32–38 (the feeding of the four thousand). The sentence continues onto fol. 611r (leaf p1237).

[^3743]: Continuation of the prayer from fol. 610v (leaf p1236).

[^3744]: Final doxology concluding the prayers against pestilence and famine on fol. 611r.

[^3745]: Headpiece and title marking the beginning of Part XLIV: the Order for the Elevation of the Panagia for those setting out on merchandise or commercial journeys (Ѡ въꙁноше́нїи панагїи, е҆гда̀ хо́щетъ кто̀ на кꙋ́пли ѿитѝ). The Elevation of the Panagia (Greek Ὑψωσις τῆς Παναγίας), originally a monastic trapeza rite commending the brethren to the Mother of God, was adapted in Ruthenian and Byzantine Euchologia as a protective travel rite for merchants embarking on perilous voyages across land and sea.

[^3746]: The first penitential troparion of the standard liturgical sequence: Помилуй насъ, Господи, помилуй насъ (Miserere nostri, Domine).

[^3747]: The second troparion, chanted at "Glory": Слава... Господи, помилуй насъ, на Тя бо уповахомъ (cf. Isa. 64:8–9 LXX: "We are all the work of Thy hand... be not wroth very sore, O Lord").

[^3748]: The traditional Theotokion chanted at "Both now": И нынѣ... Милосердія двери отверзи намъ, благословенная Богородице.

[^3749]: Ps. 50 LXX (Miserere mei, Deus), recited accompanied by three metanias (прїидѣ́те поклони́мсѧ • г҃).

[^3750]: Rubric prescribing the chanting of five classic supplicatory Theotokia, which invoke the protection and intercession of the Virgin Mary over the traveler. The sequence continues onto fol. 612r (leaf p1239).

[^3751]: The renowned supplicatory Theotokion: Пресвятая Богородице, во время живота моего не остави мене, человѣческому заступленію не ввѣри мене, но Сама заступи и спаси мя.

[^3752]: The second Theotokion: Азъ, Дѣво святая Богородице, покровъ твой прибѣгаю, вѣмъ яко получу у тебе спасеніе...

[^3753]: The third Theotokion: Никтоже притекаѧй къ тебѣ посрамленъ отъ тебе отходитъ, Чистая Дѣво Богородице, но проситъ благодати, и пріемлетъ даръ на пользу прошенія.

[^3754]: The fourth Theotokion: Кождо идѣже спасается, тамо въ правду и притѣкаетъ; и кое иное таково прибѣжище якоже ты, Богородице...

[^3755]: The fifth Theotokion: Прииди къ моленію рабъ своихъ, Пренепорочная, утоляющи лютая на ны востанія... concluding with the joyful greeting: Радуйся, Владычице, всѣмъ помощнице, радости и покрове и спасеніе душъ нашихъ.

[^3756]: The celebrated dogmatic and supplicatory Theotokion: Всѣмъ предстательствуеши, Благая, прибѣгающимъ съ вѣрою въ державный твой покровъ (Greek Πάντων προστατεύεις, ἀγαθή). The text continues onto fol. 613r (leaf p1241).

[^3757]: Continuation and conclusion of the supplicatory Theotokion from fol. 612v (leaf p1240): Slavonic Ѡ҆бремененїи грѣхмѝ мно́гими, ма́ти Бг҃а вы́шнагѡ • тѣ́мже ти припада́емъ, и҆зба́ви ѿ всѧ́кагѡ ѻ҆бстоѧ́нїа рабы своя̀ (cf. Greek Πάντων προστατεύεις, ἀγαθή).

[^3758]: Ritual elevation of the Panagia bread (Greek Ὕψωσις τῆς Παναγίας). The officiant elevates the panagia vessel containing the designated prosphoric particle in honor of the Mother of God, exclaiming the ancient Trinitarian and Marian liturgical acclamation: Ве́лїе и҆́мѧ ст҃ыѧ тро́ица (Greek Μέγα τὸ ὄνομα τῆς Ἁγίας Τριάδος).

[^3759]: Personal supplication for the traveler: Пр҃таѧ влч҃це Бц҃е помозѝ рабꙋ твоемꙋ (Greek Παναγία Δέσποινα Θεοτόκε, βοήθει τῷ δούλῳ σου), followed by the choral response invoking her intercessions: Тоѧ̀ мл҃твами Бж҃е помилꙋй и҆ сп҃си на́ (Ταῖς αὐτῆς πρεσβείαις, ὁ Θεός, ἐλέησον καὶ σῶσον ἡμᾶς).

[^3760]: Allusion to John 6:48–51: "I am the bread of life... if any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever." In Byzantine and Ruthenian Marian theology, the womb of the Virgin is typologically celebrated as the sacred mystical table bearing the Bread of Heaven (чре́во твоѐ ст҃аѧ трапе́за, и҆мꙋ́щїа хлѣ́бъ нб҃ный).

[^3761]: Troparion chanted during the fraction or consumption of the Panagia: Твои́хъ дарѡ́въ досто́йны ны́ сътворѝ Бц҃е дв҃о (Greek Τῶν σῶν δωρεῶν ἀξίους ἡμᾶς ποίησον, Θεοτόκε Παρθένε).

[^3762]: Rubric prescribing the chanting of the Marian hymn "It is meet and right" (Досто́йно е҆́сть), followed by the Little Doxology ("Glory... Both now...") and the celebrated Megalynarion hymn of St. John of Damascus.

[^3763]: The renowned hymn to the Mother of God attributed to St. John of Damascus: Ἐπὶ σοὶ χαίρει, Κεχαριτωμένη, πᾶσα ἡ κτίσις (Slavonic Ѡ҆ тебѐ ра́дꙋетсѧ Ѡ҆брадо́ваннаѧ всѧ́ка тва́рь), chanted in the Liturgy of St. Basil the Great and during festive and monastic trapeza rites.

[^3764]: The prooimion of the celebrated Kontakion of the Annunciation and Akathist Hymn: Greek Τῇ ὑπερμάχῳ στρατηγῷ τὰ νικητήρια. The 1606 Striatyn imprint witnesses the distinctive Ruthenian recensional translation Побо́рници воево́дѣ побѣди́тельнаѧ (from побо́рница, "champion / defender") rather than the standard Nikonian Взбра́нной воево́дѣ. The text continues onto fol. 614r (leaf p1243).

[^3765]: Conclusion of the Akathist Kontakion: Slavonic ꙗ҆́ко и҆мꙋ́щи дръжа́воу непобѣди́мꙋю, ѿ всѧ́кихъ мѧ̀ бѣ́дъ свободѝ • да̀ зово́у ти, ра́доусѧ невѣ́сто неневѣ́стнаа. The singular pronoun мѧ̀ ("free me", Greek με) adapts the civic hymn of Constantinople for the personal salvation and physical preservation of the traveler.

[^3766]: Ancient Byzantine compline troparion: Въсѐ ᲂу҆пова́нїе моѐ на́ тѧ възлага́ю, ма́ти Бо́жїа, съхранѝ мѧ̀ въ свое́мъ си кро́вѣ (Greek Τὴν πᾶσαν ἐλπίδα μου εἰς σὲ ἀνατίθημι, Μῆτερ τοῦ Θεοῦ, φύλαξόν με ὑπὸ τὴν σκέπην σου).

[^3767]: Marian supplicatory troparion: И҆мꙋ́ще тѧ̀ Бц҃е ᲂу҆пова́нїе и҆ пре́ста́телницꙋ, вра́жїй навѣ́тъ небои́мсѧ (Having thee, O Theotokos, as hope and mediatress, we fear not the enemy's assault).

[^3768]: Byzantine euchological troparion: Влч҃це прїимѝ мо́лбы ра́бъ свои́хъ, и҆ избави на́съ ѿ всѧ́коѧ ноу́жда и҆ скръби (Greek Δέσποινα, πρόσδεξαι τὰς δεήσεις τῶν δούλων σου).

[^3769]: Rubric and opening of the traveler's prayer (Εὐχὴ ἐπὶ ὁδοιπορούντων). The prayer addresses Christ as "the true and living Way" (John 14:6: "I am the way, the truth, and the life") and invokes the biblical typology of Joseph, whom the Lord guided, preserved, and prospered during his sojourn in Egypt (Gen. 39:2, 21; 45:5–8). The prayer continues onto fol. 614v (leaf p1244).

[^3770]: Doxological conclusion of the prayer for the wayfarer, invoking peace, divine strength, righteous conduct, and a safe return laden with temporal and spiritual blessings.

[^3771]: Rubric introducing the prayer for those embarking upon a sea voyage or river journey: И҆ дрꙋга́ѧ мл҃тва • на хотѧ́щи пла́вати (Greek Εὐχὴ ἑτέρα ἐπὶ τῶν μελλόντων πλεῖν). Maritime and fluvial commerce along the Dniester, Vistula, and Black Sea waterways constituted a perilous economic lifeline in 16th–17th century Ruthenian lands.

[^3772]: Scriptural allusion to the Gospel accounts of Christ calming the storm upon the Sea of Galilee: Matt. 8:23–27; Mark 4:36–41; Luke 8:22–25. The prayer continues onto fol. 615r (leaf p1245).

[^3773]: Byzantine maritime euchological prayer invoking Christ as Helmsman (кръмчи́й, Greek κυβερνήτης) to grant "saving and fair-weather haven" (спа́сное и҆ ведреное приста́нище, Greek λιμένα σωτήριον καὶ εὔδιον) unto the voyagers and their vessel.

[^3774]: Headpiece and title marking the beginning of Part XLV: The Order for a Furnace or Kiln (Въслѣдова́нїе на пе́щїю; Greek Ἀκολουθία εἰς κάμινον). This liturgical office was appointed for the blessing and spiritual protection of metal-smelting furnaces, ceramic and tile kilns, glassworks, limekilns, or bakery ovens, which involved perilous fire operations in early modern Ruthenian towns and monastic estates.

[^3775]: The rubrical order specifies that the priest first perform the Lesser Sanctification of Water (ѻ҆свѧще́нїе воды̀), providing the holy water with which the furnace, the tools, and the artisans are subsequently asperged.

[^3776]: Dan. 3:19–27; Song of the Three Holy Children 1:26–27 (LXX): the angel of the Lord descended into the furnace with Azarias and his companions and "made the midst of the furnace as it had been a moist whistling wind, so that the fire touched them not at all, neither hurt nor troubled them." The prayer continues onto fol. 616r (leaf p1247).

[^3777]: Slavonic: предста́телствы превеличли́вшихъ тахїа́рхъ михаи́ла и҆ Гаврїи́ла. The Greek military and administrative title ταξίαρχος (taxiarches / commander of the celestial ranks) is preserved as a technical loanword in Ruthenian and South Slavic euchological manuscripts.

[^3778]: The invocation of Hieromartyr Cyprian of Antioch (commemorated October 2), renowned in Christian hagiography as a former practitioner of the occult arts who was converted and martyred, invokes his traditional patronage against demonic sabotage, sudden fires, witchcraft, and artisanal hazards.

[^3779]: Concluding Trinitarian doxology of the first blessing prayer over the furnace.

[^3780]: Rubric introducing the second blessing prayer over the furnace (мл҃тва, дроу́гаа), continuing onto fol. 616v (leaf p1248).

[^3781]: Ps. 112:5–6 LXX: "Who is like unto the Lord our God, Who dwells on high, and looks down upon the low things in heaven and on the earth?"

[^3782]: Gen. 30:27: Laban's acknowledgment to the Patriarch Jacob: "I have found favor in thine eyes: for God hath blessed me in thy coming."

[^3783]: Gen. 39:5: "The Lord blessed the Egyptian's house for Joseph's sake; and the blessing of the Lord was upon all that he had in the house, and in the field."

[^3784]: 2 Kings / 2 Sam. 6:11–12 LXX; 1 Chron. 13:14: "And the Ark of God remained with the family of Obed-edom in his house three months. And the Lord blessed the house of Obed-edom, and all that he had." The Church Slavonic witnesses the Hellenized form А҆веда́рїа (Greek Ἀβεδδαρά).

[^3785]: Luke 19:9: Christ's blessing upon the house of Zacchaeus the publican: "This day is salvation come to this house, forsomuch as he also is a son of Abraham."

[^3786]: Concluding doxology of the second prayer for the blessing of the furnace.

[^3787]: Rubric introducing the augmented litany of fervent supplication (мо́лбы / ἐκτενὴς ἱκεσία), incorporating specialized petitions for the artisans and their labor.

[^3788]: Specific economic and safety petition for the craftsmen: и҆ ѡ҆ е҆́же бл҃витисѧ и҆ ᲂу҆мно́житисѧ дѣ́лѡ рꙋ́къ трꙋжда́ющихсѧ въ пещѝ се́й ("and that the work of the hands of those laboring in this furnace may be blessed and multiplied"). The printed text contains a minor orthographic slip in line 4: зрдра́вїю (for здра́вїю).

[^3789]: Ps. 64:6 LXX: "Give ear unto us, O God our Savior, the hope of all the ends of the earth, and of those afar upon the sea."

[^3790]: Ecphonesis of the augmented litany, invoking God's mercy and Trinitarian glory.

[^3791]: Concluding rubrics: the priest asperges the newly consecrated furnace and the assembled laborers with sanctified water, followed by the formal liturgical dismissal.

[^3792]: Headpiece and title marking the beginning of Part XLVI: The Order over Children Departing to Learn the Sacred Scriptures (Въслѣдова́нїе на́дъ ѿроки ѿходѧ́щими ᲂу҆чи́тисѧ сщ҃еннымъ писа́нїамъ; Greek Ἀκολουθία εἰς παῖδας ἀπερχομένους μανθάνειν τὰ ἱερὰ γράμματα). This educational blessing rite reflects the humanist and ecclesiastical pedagogical revival in early 17th-century Ukraine and Belarus, where brotherhood schools (bratstva) and episcopal academies provided intensive instruction in Church Slavonic, Greek, Latin, and Scripture.

[^3793]: Introductory rubrics prescribing the standard opening blessing and Trisagion prayers, followed by festive and pedagogical troparia.

[^3794]: John 20:19, 26: Christ's post-Resurrection greeting of peace to the disciples in the Upper Room ("Peace be unto you"), here invoked to bring peace and clarity of mind to young students.

[^3795]: Pentecost troparion celebrating the miraculous transformation of the unlettered fishermen into teachers of the universe through the grace of the Holy Spirit: Безъ кни́жныѧ ᲂу҆ч҃нки дх҃ъ твои ст҃ый наказа́телѧ ꙗ҆вѝ Хе Бж҃е (cf. Acts 4:13: ἀγράμματοί εἰσι καὶ ἰδιῶται), overcoming the confusion of the nations through the inspired diversity of languages (Acts 2:1–11). The office continues onto fol. 618r (leaf p1251).

[^3796]: Continuation of the Pentecost troparion from fol. 617v (leaf p1250) on the descent of the Holy Spirit, alluding to Acts 2:4–11, where the Apostles were endowed with foreign tongues to proclaim Christ as the incarnate Word of God.

[^3797]: The venerable Byzantine prayer to the Holy Spirit (Greek Βασιλεῦ οὐράνιε, Παράκλητε), invoking the Spirit of Wisdom to enlighten the mind and soul of the young scholar.

[^3798]: Ancient Byzantine supplicatory Theotokion (Greek Τῆς εὐσπλαγχνίας τὴν πύλην ἄνοιξον ἡμῖν), imploring the Mother of God for spiritual protection against intellectual and moral stumbling.

[^3799]: Rubric prescribing the imposition of hands or position of the priest over the head of the child during the recitation of the educational blessing prayers.

[^3800]: Acts 2:3: "And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them."

[^3801]: Acts 2:4: "And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance."

[^3802]: Exod. 31:18; 32:16; 34:1: "written with the finger of God" upon the tables of stone given to Moses the Lawgiver upon Mount Sinai.

[^3803]: The printed Slavonic witness truncates the concluding liturgical formula to нн҃ѣ и҆ прⷭ҇но и҆ въ вѣ́ки вѣкѡ́:~, which is supplied diplomatically.

[^3804]: Apoc. / Rev. 4:4, 10; 5:8, 14: the twenty-four elders surrounding the throne of God in the celestial liturgy, invoked here as exemplars of heavenly wisdom and spiritual illumination. The prayer continues onto fol. 619r (leaf p1253).

[^3805]: The four holy Evangelists are explicitly commemorated as the primary human instruments of divine revelation and the study of the New Testament.

[^3806]: Acts 6:8–10: "And Stephen, full of faith and power, did great wonders and miracles among the people... and they were not able to resist the wisdom and the spirit by which he spoke."

[^3807]: The invocation of the holy Martyrs Agapitus, Procopius, and Philetus represents a distinctive Byzantine-Slavic pedagogical patronage grouping, frequently invoked in historical euchologia for steadfastness of memory, quickness of intellect, and protection of students.

[^3808]: Concluding Trinitarian doxology of the second pedagogical blessing prayer.

[^3809]: Gen. 1:26–27; Sirach (Ecclus.) 15:14: man created in the image of God with rational free will and self-determination (самовла́стное хотѣ́нїе; Greek αὐτεξούσιος προαίρεσις).

[^3810]: John 7:14–15: "Now about the midst of the feast Jesus went up into the temple, and taught. And the Jews marveled, saying, How knows this man letters, having never learned?"

[^3811]: Ps. 33:12 LXX (Ps. 34:11 KJV): "Come, ye children, give ear unto me: I will teach you the fear of the Lord."

[^3812]: 3 Kings / 1 Kings 3:9–12; 4:29–34; Wis. 7:7: "Therefore I prayed, and understanding was given me: I called upon God, and the spirit of wisdom came to me."

[^3813]: Supplication for intellectual lucidity, moral uprightness, and spiritual protection against demonic obstruction or temptation (нало́гъ дїа́волъ, Greek ἐπήρεια τοῦ διαβόλου) during schooling.

[^3814]: Concluding ecphonesis of the prayer for a student beginning instruction.

[^3815]: Deaconal or priestly admonition (Greek Στῶμεν καλῶς, στῶμεν μετὰ φόβου Θεοῦ) exhorting attentiveness and reverent posture before the concluding litany.

[^3816]: Concluding rubrics prescribing the standard litany of fervent supplication (ektenia) and the liturgical dismissal (apolysis), marking the end of Part XLVI.

[^3817]: Headpiece and title marking the beginning of Part XLVII: The Order Concerning the Communion of the Holy Water of the Theophany of the Great Sanctification (Въслѣдова́нїе ѡ҆ причаще́нїи ст҃ыѧ воды̀ и҆́же на Бг҃оꙗвле́нїе вели́каго ѻ҆свѧще́нїѧ; Greek Ἀκολουθία εἰς τὸ μεταλαβεῖν τοῦ ἁγιάσματος τῶν Θεοφανίων). This canon and penitential order provided pastoral consolation and spiritual medicine for Christians undergoing canonical penance (epitimia) who were barred from receiving the Holy Eucharist. In Byzantine and Kyivan canon law, Great Agiasma (sanctified water of Epiphany) functioned as an antidoron-like sanctification for penanced penitents under spiritual direction.

[^3818]: Introductory rubric detailing canonical penitential discipline: an individual impeded by grave sins or ecclesiastical penance from partaking of the Holy Mysteries (Holy Communion) may, upon the discernment and blessing of their spiritual father (confessor), partake of the Theophany water of the Great Blessing with proper fasting and prayerful preparation.

[^3819]: The opening liturgical blessing of the priest: "Blessed is our God..." (Εὐλογητὸς ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν).

[^3820]: Rubric prescribing the standard opening prayer sequence (Enarxis): Heavenly King, Trisagion, the Lord's Prayer, twelvefold Kyrie Eleison, the threefold invitation to worship, and the primary penitential Psalm 50 LXX (Ps. 51 KJV), followed by special supplicatory troparia.

[^3821]: Supplicatory troparion expressing spiritual thirst and repentance, invoking Christ as the possessor of the inexhaustible cup of divine mercy (cf. John 4:14; 7:37–38).

[^3822]: Penitential Theotokion addressing the Virgin Mary as the "palace of the Word" (сло́ва пола́то, Greek τοῦ Λόγου παλάτιον) and imploring the cooling and cleansing waters of divine grace to quench the burning fever of sin.

[^3823]: Rubric introducing the preparatory prayer attributed to St. John Chrysostom, recited prior to drinking the Great Agiasma.

[^3824]: High theological Trinitarian invocation: Christ co-understood with the unoriginate Father and co-abiding with the co-eternal Spirit (съразоумѣва́емъ... съпребыва́ѧ; Greek συμφραζόμενος... συνυπάρχων).

[^3825]: Allusion to Christ's baptism in the Jordan, whereby the waters were sanctified and cleansed of the demonic powers: Matt. 3:13–17; Mark 1:9–11; Luke 3:21–22.

[^3826]: Euchological petition enumerating the manifold spiritual and somatic effects of partaking of the Great Agiasma: illumination of mind, bodily healing, subduing of carnal passions, casting out of wicked thoughts, and defense against demonic assaults. The prayer continues onto fol. 622r (leaf p1259).

[^3827]: Conclusion of St. John Chrysostom's prayer before partaking of the Great Agiasma.

[^3828]: Rubric prescribing three metanias (deep reverences or prostrations) by the communicant or the assembly while chanting the festive troparion of the Epiphany.

[^3829]: The renowned Byzantine Troparion of the Theophany of the Lord (Greek Ἐν Ἰορδάνῃ βαπτιζομένου σου, Кύριε, ἡ τῆς Τριάδος ἐφανερώθη προσκύνησις), Tone 1.

[^3830]: Rubric directing the chanting of the Little Doxology followed by the festive Theophany Kontakion, continuing onto fol. 622v (leaf p1260).

[^3831]: The celebrated Theophany Kontakion of St. Romanos the Melodist, Tone 4: Greek Ἐπεφάνης σήμερον τῇ οἰκουμένῃ (Ruthenian recension variant reading: въсе́й въселе́ннѣй... неприкоснове́нный / Greek ἀπρόσιτον).

[^3832]: Rubric directing the communicant to drink the holy water with sacred fear and reverence, followed immediately by the post-communion thanksgiving prayer.

[^3833]: Opening of the post-communion thanksgiving prayer of St. John Chrysostom, giving thanks for the spiritual illumination and sanctification conferred by the Epiphany water. The prayer continues onto fol. 623r (leaf p1261).

[^3834]: Continuation of the thanksgiving prayer attributed to St. John Chrysostom recited after partaking of the Great Agiasma (Theophany water), from fol. 622v (leaf p1260). The printed Slavonic witness reads въсего̀ къ твое́моу къпери жела́нїю, where къпери represents a scribal or typographer's corruption for въперѝ (imperative of въперити / вперяти, Greek πτέρωσον / ἀνάпτερον, "give wings unto", "wing me wholly unto desire for Thee").

[^3835]: Concluding Trinitarian ecphonesis of St. John Chrysostom's thanksgiving prayer: "For Thou art the sweetness of our souls..." (Greek Ὅτι σὺ εἶ ὁ γλυκασμὸς τῶν ψυχῶν ἡμῶν). The printed text abbreviates the concluding liturgical formula to нн҃ѣ и҆ прⷭ҇но и҆ въ вѣ́ки вѣкѡ́мъ : ~, with the final "Amen" supplied diplomatically.

[^3836]: Concluding rubrics prescribing the Axion Estin (It is truly meet), the Little Doxology (Glory... Both now...), threefold Kyrie Eleison, and the liturgical dismissal (apolysis), marking the formal conclusion of Part XLVII.

[^3837]: Headpiece, decorative woodcut engraving, and title marking the beginning of Part XLVIII: The Order Over the Compounding [Consecration] of the Holy Great Myron, Celebrated on Holy and Great Thursday (Въслѣдова́нїе на растворе́нїемъ ст҃го вели́каго мѵ́ра · быва́емо въ ст҃ы́й вели́кїй четверто́къ; Greek Τάξις γινομένη ἐπὶ καθιερώσει τοῦ ἁγίου Μύρου ἐν τῇ ἁγίᾳ καὶ μεγάλῃ Πέμπτῃ). In the Byzantine and Ruthenian tradition, the solemn consecration of Holy Chrism (Myron) is reserved to the primate or diocesan bishop and takes place during the Divine Liturgy of St. Basil the Great on Maundy Thursday. The Striatyn Trebnyk preserves this archaic pontifical rite, which Bishop Hedeon Balaban specifically noted in his preface (fols. 6v–7r, leaves p12–p13) as having been retrieved from ancient Slavonic codices to supply a vital liturgical office often omitted in smaller parish euchologia.

[^3838]: Rubric detailing the rubrical actions during the Divine Liturgy: after the Great Entrance, when the Holy Gifts of Bread and Wine have been placed upon the Holy Table, the principal archpriest brings in the glass phial or alabastron containing the newly blended ingredients of the Holy Myron and places it near the diskos on the upper side (towards the high place / back of the altar). Following the ecphonesis "May the mercies of our great God...", the royal doors remain closed and the deacon on the ambo keeps silence, while the archdeacon inside the sanctuary initiates the consecration sequence.

[^3839]: Deaconal admonition "Let us attend!" (Slavonic възи́млѣмъ, Greek Πρόσχωμεν) uttered by the archdeacon from within the holy sanctuary, signaling the commencement of the pontifical prayer of consecration.

[^3840]: Rubric directing the officiating bishop to ascend the step before the Holy Table, sign the vessel containing the Holy Myron three times with the sign of the cross, step down, and recite the solemn prayer of consecration with inclined head.

[^3841]: James 1:17: "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and comes down from the Father of lights (ὁ Πατὴρ τῶν φώτων), with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning."

[^3842]: Exod. 30:22–33: God's command unto Moses on Mount Sinai to compound the sacred anointing oil (Greek ἔλαιον χρῖσμα ἅγιον) from pure myrrh, sweet cinnamon, calamus, cassia, and olive oil, strictly consecrated for the sanctuary, the ark of the testimony, and the priesthood.

[^3843]: 1 Sam. (1 Kings LXX) 10:1; 16:13: the Prophet Samuel anointing Saul and David with the horn of oil as the chosen kings over Israel, prefiguring the royal chrism of the New Covenant.

[^3844]: 1 John 2:20, 27: "But ye have an unction from the Holy One, and ye know all things... the anointing which ye have received of Him abides in you."

[^3845]: Petitions invoking the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the compounded oil, designating it as a "royal anointing" (χρῖσμα βασιλικόν) and a "spiritual anointing" (χρῖσμα πνευματικόν), serving as an invulnerable shield and preserver of life (φυлаκτήριον ζωῆς). The prayer continues onto fol. 624v (leaf p1264).

[^3846]: Ps. 44:8 LXX (Ps. 45:7 KJV); Heb. 1:9: "God, even Thy God, hath anointed Thee with the oil of gladness (ἔλαιον ἀγαλλιάσεως) above Thy fellows."

[^3847]: Typological continuity between the sacramental economy of the Old and New Covenants: the sacred anointing that consecrated Aaronite priests, high priests, prophets, and kings in the Old Law finds its fulfillment in Christ and the Christian royal priesthood.

[^3848]: Titus 3:5: "According to His mercy He saved us, by the washing [laver] of regeneration (διὰ λουτροῦ παλιγγενεσίας), and renewing of the Holy Ghost." The prayer explicitly articulates the doctrine of uninterrupted Apostolic Succession through the uninterrupted laying on of hands and chrismation from the Holy Apostles down to contemporary bishops and presbyters.

[^3849]: Gal. 3:27; 1 Cor. 15:53: the spiritual garment of incorruption bestowed in holy baptism and sealed in chrismation, clothing the neophyte in the divine radiance of Christ.

[^3850]: Eph. 1:13; 4:30; 2 Cor. 1:22: the "perfecting seal" (Greek σφραγὶς τελειωτική; Slavonic печа́ть съвръшеннотво́рнаѧ), denoting the indelible character and gift of the Holy Spirit imparted in the Sacrament of Chrismation ("The seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit").

[^3851]: The invocation of the Holy Trinity—Father, Only-begotten Son, and Holy Spirit—whose divine name is spiritually imprinted upon those receiving the holy laver of baptism. The prayer continues onto fol. 625r (leaf p1265).

[^3852]: Petitions for the spiritual transformation of the chrismated: that they may be recognized as citizens of the kingdom of God (Eph. 2:19), consecrated in soul and body, and delivered from demonic subjection.

[^3853]: Theological motif of the invisible character of the sacramental seal (σφραγίς): the holy sign of Chrismation is spiritually luminous and recognized by the celestial hierarchies (Angels, Archangels, and heavenly powers).

[^3854]: Mark 16:17; Luke 10:19; Eph. 6:11–12: the apotropaic efficacy of the Holy Myron, rendering the faithful formidable and terrifically unapproachable unto Satan and all impure demonic spirits.

[^3855]: 1 Peter 2:9 (echoing Exod. 19:6): "But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people (ὑμεῖς δὲ γένος ἐκλεκτόν, βασίλειον ἱεράτευμα, ἔθνος ἅγιον, λαὸς εἰς περιποίησιν)."

[^3856]: Eph. 2:22; 3:17: that Christ may dwell within the hearts of the faithful through faith, making them a living habitation and temple of God the Father through the Holy Spirit. The prayer continues onto fol. 625v (leaf p1266).

[^3857]: Concluding clause of the primary prayer of consecration of the Holy Myron: "...with the Holy Spirit" (Greek σὺν τῷ ἁγίῳ Πνεύματι).

[^3858]: Festive Trinitarian ecphonesis pronounced aloud by the bishop: "For holy art Thou, our God, Who restest upon the saints..." (Greek Ὅτι ἅγιος εἶ, ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν, ὁ ἐν ἁγίοις ἐпаναπαυόμενος).

[^3859]: Choral response confirming the episcopal ecphonesis.

[^3860]: Episcopal blessing of peace (Eirene pasin; Greek Εἰρήνη πᾶσι) imparted unto the clergy and congregation.

[^3861]: Deaconal bidding inviting the faithful to incline their heads in reverence before the solemn prayer of inclination.

[^3862]: Rubric directing the bishop to recite the prayer of head-bowing secretly (Greek μυστικῶς; Slavonic та́й) before the Holy Table.

[^3863]: Opening thanksgiving of the prayer of inclination: the bishop, acknowledging his personal unworthiness, offers thanks on behalf of the whole priesthood for being accounted worthy to minister at the divine mysteries and distribute the divine mercy richly poured forth upon the Church (Titus 3:6). The prayer continues onto fol. 626r (leaf p1267).

[^3864]: Ps. 132:2 LXX (Ps. 133:2 KJV): "It is like the precious ointment upon the head, that ran down upon the beard, even Aaron's beard: that went down to the skirts of his garments."

[^3865]: Canticles (Song of Songs) 1:2 LXX (1:3 KJV): "Thy name is as ointment [myron] poured forth (μύρον ἐκκενωθὲν ὄνομά σου), therefore do the virgins love thee." Patristic commentary universally interprets this verse as a prophecy of the Incarnation of Christ and the diffusion of the grace of the Holy Spirit throughout the world.

[^3866]: Cosmic scope of Christ's redemptive grace, diffusing spiritual sweetness and divine fragrance throughout all creation, both visible and invisible (cf. 2 Cor. 2:14–15; Col. 1:16).

[^3867]: Concluding Trinitarian ecphonesis of the prayer of head-bowing, praising God as the sole object of supreme adoration and worship.

[^3868]: Rubric indicating the resumption of the Divine Liturgy of St. Basil the Great: the deacon on the ambo resumes the litany, the holy royal doors are reopened, and the bishop proceeds with the Liturgy of the Faithful, consummating the Eucharistic sacrifice.

[^3869]: Decorative woodcut headpiece and title marking the beginning of Part XLIX: Prayers at the Blessing and Breaking of the Artos (Мл҃тва на бл҃гвнїи а҆́ртоуса; Greek Εὐχὴ εἰς τὴν εὐλόγησιν τοῦ ἄρτου / Ἀκολουθία τοῦ Ἀρτοκлаσίας τοῦ Ἄρτου). The Artos (Greek Ἄρτος, "leavened bread") is a large loaf of leavened bread bearing the stamped icon of Christ's Resurrection, blessed on the night of Holy Pascha at the conclusion of the Divine Liturgy. It symbolizes the physical presence of the risen Christ among His disciples during the forty days between His Resurrection and Ascension. Throughout Bright Week, the Artos remains on the tetrapod or before the iconostasis, is carried in daily Paschal processions, and is solemnly broken and distributed unto the faithful on Bright Saturday.

[^3870]: Rubric introducing the solemn prayer for the blessing of the Artos on the night of Holy Pascha.

[^3871]: Exultant Paschal opening petition: the faithful are called to run with spiritual joy unto the feast to encounter the risen Lord, echoing the haste of the Myrrh-bearing women and the Apostles Peter and John running to the empty tomb (John 20:4).

[^3872]: Celestial adoration of the Resurrection: the angelic hosts (Cherubim and Seraphim) join with the Holy Apostles and earthly creation in worshiping Christ arisen from the dead.

[^3873]: Doxological recognition of Christ's universal sovereignty as God over all creation, visible and invisible.

[^3874]: Mark 6:7: "And He called unto Him the twelve, and began to send them forth by two and two (δύο δύο)." The six apostolic pairs (ше́сть сꙋпру́гъ а҆пто́лскихъ) represent the twelve Apostles sent forth into the world to proclaim the Gospel and bless the nations.

[^3875]: Luke 2:14: the angelic hymn of the Nativity applied here to the cosmic peace and divine reconciliation accomplished by the Paschal victory of Christ. The prayer continues onto fol. 627r (leaf p1269).

[^3876]: Conclusion of the angelic hymn from Luke 2:14: "...and on earth peace, good will toward men!"

[^3877]: Heb. 4:15: "For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin (χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας)."

[^3878]: Matt. 14:17–21; Mark 6:38–44; Luke 9:13–17; John 6:9–14: the miraculous multiplication of the five loaves and two fishes in the wilderness, prefiguring the abundant spiritual sustenance provided by Christ in the Paschal banquet.

[^3879]: Gen. 41:48–57: Joseph gathering and blessing the granaries of Egypt during the seven years of plenty, sustaining the nations during the subsequent severe drought and famine. The Old Slavonic witness employs the archaic terms ве́дождїе (drought / rainlessness) and ве́зводїе (waterlessness / aridity).

[^3880]: John 11:25: "Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believes in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live."

[^3881]: Concluding Trinitarian doxology of the prayer at the blessing of the Artos.

[^3882]: Rubric introducing the second prayer over the Artos: the Prayer at the Breaking of the Artos (Мл҃тва на преломле́нїи а҆́ртоу́са), celebrated on Bright Saturday after the Prayer behind the Ambo at the Divine Liturgy.

[^3883]: Opening thanksgiving recounting the incarnate economy of Christ (плотско́е смотре́нїе; Greek ἔνσαρκος οἰκονομία) and His miraculous feeding of the multitudes in the desert. The prayer continues onto fol. 627v (leaf p1270).

[^3884]: Matt. 14:21: "And they that had eaten were about five thousand men, beside women and children."

[^3885]: Matt. 13:8, 23; Luke 8:8: petition for a hundredfold blessing (бога́тное истокра́тное бл҃венїе) upon those who have prepared and offered the Artos, and upon all the faithful who partake thereof for the healing of soul and body.

[^3886]: Commemoration of Hieromartyr Polycarp, Bishop of Smyrna (disciple of St. John the Theologian, martyred c. 155/156 AD). In Byzantine and Ruthenian euchological tradition, St. Polycarp is invoked in agricultural, seed, and bread blessings because of the Greek etymology of his name (πολύκαρπος, "abounding in fruit", "bearing much fruit"), symbolically connecting the martyr's fruitfulness in faith with the fruitful multiplication of bread and earthly sustenance.

[^3887]: Solemn commemoration of Christ's third-day Resurrection from the dead (ст҃ое тридне́вное въскрⷭ҇сенїе), the fountain of eternal life and incorruption.

[^3888]: Concluding Trinitarian doxology sealing the Order of the Artos and the conclusion of Cohort 127.

[^3889]: Canonical epistle of John, Bishop of Kitros (Ἰωάννης ἐπίσκοπος Κίτρους, 13th c.), addressed to Constantine Cabasilas (Κωνσταντῖνος Καβάσιλας), Bishop of Dyrrachium (modern Durrës, Albania; Slavonic ДѪ́ЧЬ / Дрѧчь) and later Archbishop of Ohrid. Preserved in Byzantine canonical collections (Syntagma of Rhalles and Potles, V, 403–420; PG 119) and Slavonic Nomocanons / Trebnyks, this canonical ruling defines the authentic Orthodox discipline regarding the fast-free weeks (раздрѣше́нїе бра́шенъ въ седми́цахъ) and refutes sectarian distortions, particularly those of the Armenians and Middle-Fasters.

[^3890]: Dispensation of Bright Week (Renewal Week, Διακαινήσιμος ἑβδομάς). In Byzantine and Ruthenian typika, the entire octave of Pascha is mystically celebrated as a single continuous radiant Day of the Lord (μιας οὔσης ἡμέρας), during which fasting on Wednesday and Friday is wholly suspended. As a liturgical witness to this unceasing festal unity, the Matins service on each day of Bright Week includes the chanting of the Paschal canon and the solemn reading of the eleven Resurrection Gospels in succession.

[^3891]: The Twelve Days of Christmastide (the Dodekahemeron, Δωδεκαήμερον), spanning from the Nativity of Christ (December 25) to the Eve of Theophany (January 5). During this twelve-day period, fasting on Wednesdays and Fridays is suspended in honor of the Incarnate Lord, with the sole exception of the Paramon (Eve) of Theophany.

[^3892]: Refutation of the non-Chalcedonian Armenian liturgical custom. The Armenian Church did not adopt the Byzantine December 25 feast of the Nativity, but observed a twelve-day preliminary fast culminating on January 5/6 with a combined solemnity uniting the Annunciation, the Nativity in the flesh, and the Theophany (Baptism) of Christ into a single feast.

[^3893]: Patristic and Byzantine canonical polemic against Armenian Monophysite and Aphthartodocetic Christology (associated with Julian of Halicarnassus and Severus of Antioch). Byzantine Orthodox canonists maintained that conflating the Nativity and the Theophany obscured the true, historical, passible reality of Christ's human flesh, reducing the Incarnation to an illusory appearance (привидѣ́нїемъ а҆ не и҆́стинною; Greek φαντασίᾳ καὶ οὐκ ἀληθείᾳ).

[^3894]: Dispensation of the week before Meatfare (the Week of the Publican and Pharisee, ten weeks before Pascha). In the Orthodox Church, Wednesday and Friday of this week are made entirely fast-free specifically to overthrow and dissociate the faithful from the preliminary fast of the Armenians.

[^3895]: Byzantine polemical etiology of the Armenian fast known as *Arachavorats* (Առաջավորաց պահք, "Preliminary Fast" or "Fast of the Precursors"). Byzantine controversialists (including Euthymios Zigabenos, Balsamon, and John of Kitros) claimed that this fast was instituted by an Armenian monk named Sergius to mourn the death of his messenger dog Artzivourion (Armenian *Artsiv*, "eagle" or herald), who had been killed by wild beasts while announcing Sergius's arrival.

[^3896]: Jonah 3:5–10: the Armenian Church maintained that their preliminary fast commemorated the three-day fast of repentance observed by the Ninevites at the preaching of the Prophet Jonah. The Byzantine canonists rejected this explanation as a disingenuous cover for an unorthodox sect-specific ordinance.

[^3897]: The week before Cheesefare (Meatfare Week / Cheesefare Week) and the refutation of the Middle-Fasters (сре́дници; Greek Μεσονήστιοι / Μεσονηστίαι). These sectarian groups practiced severe fasting during the week before Cheesefare; Orthodox typika countered this by permitting dairy products, eggs, and fish on Wednesday and Friday of Cheesefare Week.

[^3898]: Apostolic Canon 69: "If any Bishop, or Presbyter, or Deacon, or Reader, or Singer, fast not the holy Forty Days of Pascha, or the Wednesday, or the Friday, let him be deposed, unless he be hindered by bodily weakness. But if he be a layman, let him be excommunicated." From Pascha to Pentecost, fasting until the ninth hour is suspended; while meat and dairy remain forbidden on Wednesdays and Fridays out of deference to Apostolic Canon 69, oil and fish are permitted in honor of the Resurrection season.

[^3899]: Hymnographic synthesis of the Pentecostarion: although the Paschal season commemorates the Lord's Crucifixion on Wednesdays and Fridays by chanting Stauroanastasima (hymns of the Cross and Resurrection), the sorrow of the Passion is transfigured by the joy of the third-day Resurrection.

[^3900]: Dispensation of fish, wine, and oil on the Great Feast of the Holy Transfiguration of our Lord (August 6), which occurs in the midst of the strict two-week Dormition Fast (August 1–14).

[^3901]: Canonical rule governing Despotic, Theotokion, and Polyeleos feasts falling on ordinary Wednesdays or Fridays throughout the year: solemn feasts of the Mother of God, the Nativity and Beheading of Saint John the Baptist, the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul (June 29), and radiant saints receive the dispensation of fish, wine, and oil.

[^3902]: Liturgical rubrics for the Feast of Mid-Pentecost (Преполове́нїе Пѧтидесѧ́тницы, celebrated on the fourth Wednesday after Pascha). While Resurrectional and festal troparia are sung instead of the penitential staurosima, meat and cheese remain strictly forbidden, and the Matins Resurrection Gospel is omitted.

[^3903]: Rubrics for the Wednesday before the Ascension (the Apodosis of Pascha). The full Paschal canon is chanted together with the Forefeast hymns of the Ascension; however, no Matins Resurrection Gospel is read, and the dispensation is limited to fish and oil.

[^3904]: Patristic consensus on ascetic equilibrium: the harmonious balance between celebrating festal joy and preserving the reverence due to the Lord's fast by means of the single dispensation of fish and oil.

[^3905]: Dispensation of the week following the Feast of Holy Pentecost (Trinity Week). Fasting on Wednesday and Friday is entirely relaxed in honor of the Holy and Life-Creating Spirit, exactly parallel to the dispensation of Bright Week and the Twelve Days in honor of Christ our Savior.

[^3906]: Trinitarian dogmatic theology of the Holy Spirit: the Spirit is equal in dignity and honor (є҆диночⷭ҇тенъ; Greek ὁμότιμος) with the Father and the Son, cooperating in the eternal divine counsel and the dispensational mystery of salvation.

[^3907]: Paramon (Eve) of Great Dominical Feasts (such as the Nativity of Christ or Theophany): if the Eve falls on a Wednesday or Friday, the strict fast of the Paramon may not be broken at evening prior to the liturgical celebration of the feast day itself.

[^3908]: Mitigation of fasting for the infirm under Apostolic Canon 69. A Christian suffering from severe bodily weakness is permitted the consolation of oil and fish, but presbyters and canonists are strictly forbidden from authorizing meat or cheese during the Great Fast (Lent) or on ordinary Wednesdays and Fridays, even in cases of terminal illness.

[^3909]: Confessional and pedagogical purpose of liturgical dispensations: eating meat and dairy during appointed fast-free weeks serves as a deliberate ecclesiastical demonstration of Orthodox unity against Armenian, Latin, and sectarian customs, rather than a concession to bodily gluttony or self-indulgence.

[^3910]: Traditional monastic and canonical rule for fasting days: complete abstinence from food until the ninth hour (approximately 3:00 PM), followed by xerophagy (сухояде́нїе)—partaking solely of bread, water, vegetables, and dried fruits (figs and dates).

[^3911]: Ascetic rule for the Paramon (Eve) of Holy Theophany (January 5): strict fasting until the conclusion of Vespers and the Divine Liturgy of Saint Basil the Great with the Great Blessing of Waters, after which a frugal meal of xerophagy is taken without wine, oil, or fish.

[^3912]: Canon 1 of Saint Theophilus, Patriarch of Alexandria (385–412 AD). When the Eve of Theophany falls on a Sunday, an ascetic dilemma arises: Apostolic Canon 66 forbids fasting on Sunday, yet Theophany requires preparatory fasting. Saint Theophilus resolved this by directing the faithful to partake of a few dates or figs after the Liturgy, thereby honoring the Lord's Day while preserving ascetic sobriety for the impending feast.

[^3913]: Rom. 14:17: "For the kingdom of God is not meat and drink; but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost." When the Feast of Theophany itself falls on a Wednesday or Friday, the 69th Apostolic Canon permits the dispensation of oil and fish, but the consumption of meat and dairy remains an uncanonical innovation of gluttony.

[^3914]: Title rubric in red cinnabar: *Ѡпа́кы ст҃ы́хъ а҆п҃лъ, и҆ бг҃оно́сныхъ ст҃ы́хъ ѿ́цъ за́повѣди разли́чны* ("Again: Diverse Injunctions of the Holy Apostles and of the God-bearing Holy Fathers"). This canonical collection represents an ancient pseudo-apostolic legal text preserved in Byzantine and Slavonic nomocanons (Kormchaya Kniga), commonly attributed to the Apostles Peter and Paul and regulating labor, feast days, priestly qualifications, and the distribution of church offerings. Physical leaf p1281 begins with a magnificent Renaissance strapwork headpiece featuring winged cherubs and a central medallion.

[^3915]: Slavonic: *ше́сть днї́й · понеде́лникъ · вто́рникъ · сре́доу · четве́ртокъ · па́токъ · и҆ соубо́тоу до полоу́дне* ("six days: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, and Saturday until midday"). The text prescribes manual labor for servants on six days of the week, reserving Saturday afternoon and Sunday entirely for divine worship and rest, reflecting the ancient Christian Sabbath-Lord's Day balance codified in the Apostolic Constitutions (VIII.33).

[^3916]: Slavonic: *и҆лѝ до тре́тїего часа̀ · и҆ли па́ки ве́сь дн҃ь въ соубо́тоу оу҆праздни́тисѧ ѿ дѣ́лъ тѧ́жкыхъ...* ("or until the third hour; or again, the entire day on Saturday to rest from heavy labors, and to attend unto the household, and to accomplish the memorials for the deceased, and hospitality unto strangers..."). In Byzantine monastic and civil law, Saturday was kept free from servile labor to allow preparation for the vigil and remembrance of the departed.

[^3917]: Slavonic: *соубо́та бо созда́нїю бл҃гть и҆ма́ть, и҆ оу҆покое́нїе нариче́тсѧ · а҆ недѣ́лѧ дн҃ь пръ́вый бж҃їй, въскрⷭнїа бл҃гть и҆мѣ́* ("for Saturday has the grace of creation and is called rest; while Sunday is the first day of God, possessing the grace of the Resurrection"). The theological rationale pairs Genesis 2:2–3 (the Sabbath rest after Creation) with the Lord's Day of the New Creation inaugurated by Christ's Resurrection.

[^3918]: Slavonic: *въ соубо́тоу оу҆праздни́тисѧ ѿ вьсѧ́кого дѣ́ла ма́ла же, и҆ вели́ка ѿ ѻ́смаго часа̀ · и҆ къ цр҃кви прибѣга́ти вьсѣ́мъ мѫже́мъ съ жена́ми, и҆ съ дѣ́тмѝ свои́ми...* ("on Saturday to cease from every labor, both small and great, from the eighth hour, and to hasten unto church, all men with their wives and with their children..."). The eighth hour of the day (approximately 2:00 PM) marks the canonical threshold when domestic and manual labor ceases to begin the Saturday evening liturgical cycle. The text continues onto leaf p1283.

[^3919]: Slavonic: *литоургї́и, и҆ та́ко въ до́мы своѧ̀ ѿходи́ти, и҆ почива́ти до наоу҆́трїа въ понедѣ́локъ · и҆ та́ко ѿ втора́го часа̀ начина́ти вьсѧ́ко дѣ́ло роучно́е* ("when the holy Liturgy is dismissed, thus to depart unto their homes, and to rest until the morrow on Monday; and thus from the second hour to begin every manual work"). The period of sanctified rest extends through the entire night following Sunday until the second hour of Monday morning (approximately 8:00 AM).

[^3920]: Rubric and text: *Ѡ҆ рождествѣ̀ х҃вѣ · Дн҃ь же рождества̀ пра́здникъ, та́кожде храни́ти ꙗ҆́коже и҆ недѣ́лю · ѡ҆ то́м бо гдⷭь на́шъ і҃с х҃с сп҃се́нїе ми́роу дарова̀* ("Concerning the Nativity of Christ: The feast day of the Nativity is likewise to be kept even as Sunday; for on this day our Lord Jesus Christ granted salvation unto the world"). The Nativity of the Lord is accorded equal rubrical status with Sunday as a total holiday from servile work.

[^3921]: Rubric and text: *Ѡ҆ бг҃оѧвле́нїи · Ст҃го бг҃оѧвле́нїа пра́здникъ, подоба́етъ вьсѧ́комоу хрⷭтїаниноу почита́ти и҆ храни́ти та́кожде · въ не́мъ бо зижди́тель вьсѣ́мъ ѡ҆бновле́нїе дарова̀ водо́ю и҆ дх҃омъ* ("Concerning the Theophany: The feast of the Holy Theophany it behooves every Christian to honor and keep likewise; for on this day the Creator granted renewal unto all by water and the Spirit"). Theophany is celebrated as the regeneration of creation through the sanctification of the waters and the descent of the Holy Spirit.

[^3922]: Rubric and text: *Бл҃говѣще́нїи · Бл҃говѣще́нїа же пра́здникоу чтⷭь въздади́те, ꙗ҆́ко чтⷭнѣ́йшоу сѫ́щоу вьсѣ́мъ* ("Concerning the Annunciation: Render ye honor unto the feast of the Annunciation, as being most honorable among all..."). The Annunciation (March 25) is venerated as the fountainhead of the Master's feasts, being the moment of the Divine Incarnation. The text continues onto leaf p1284.

[^3923]: Continuation from leaf p1283: *пра́здникомъ госпо́дьскымъ* ("the Master's feasts").

[^3924]: Slavonic: *Соубо́тоу пра́веднаго ла́зарѧ, въскрⷭнїю нача́ло и҆ проѡбраже́нїе носѧ́щоу · и҆ чюдесе́мъ х҃вымъ чтⷭнѣ́йшїи пра́здникъ* ("the Saturday of righteous Lazarus, bearing the beginning and prefiguration of the Resurrection, and the most honorable feast of the miracles of Christ"). Lazarus Saturday is celebrated as the primary pledge and prefiguration of the general resurrection (cf. the Troparion: "Giving us before Thy Passion an assurance of the general resurrection, Thou didst raise Lazarus from the dead, O Christ our God").

[^3925]: Slavonic: *И҆ па́ки · възнесе́нїе х҃во, и҆ съше́ствїе ст҃го дх҃а... прѣѡбраже́нїе сп҃сово · и҆ въздви́женїе чтⷭна́го крⷭта пра́здникы влч҃нѧ...* ("And again: the Ascension of Christ, and the Descent of the Holy Spirit... both the Transfiguration of the Savior, and the Exaltation of the Honorable Cross, being Master's feasts..."). All primary Dominical feasts (Despotika) are strictly assimilated to the rubrical resting obligations of Sunday.

[^3926]: Rubric and opening text: *Пра́здникы бц҃ны · Прⷭтыѧ влч҃ца нашеѧ бц҃а пра́здникы...* ("Feasts of the Mother of God: The feasts of our most holy Lady, the Mother of God..."). The text continues onto leaf p1285.

[^3927]: Slavonic: *Въплоще́нїе* ("the Conception" or "Incarnation"). Here the imprint writes *Въплоще́нїе*, which in context alongside the Nativity, Entry, and Dormition of the Mother of God denotes either the Annunciation (the Incarnation of the Word) or the Conception of St. Anna (December 9).

[^3928]: Slavonic: *рождество̀ є҆ѧ̀ · въхо́дъ въ ст҃аѧ ст҃ы́хъ · и҆ оу҆спе́нїе є҆ѧ̀ · и҆ ст҃ы́хъ роди́тель є҆ѧ̀ па́мѧть съвръша́ти и҆ пра́здновати* ("Her Nativity, the Entry into the Holy of Holies, and Her Dormition; and to accomplish and celebrate the memory of Her holy parents"). Enumerates the major Marian feasts and the commemoration of the Holy Ancestors of God, Joachim and Anna (September 9).

[^3929]: Slavonic: *Ст҃ы́хъ прехва́лныхъ а҆п҃лъ петра̀ и҆ па́вла · и҆́нъхъ пра́здникъ та́кожде почита́ти, и҆ пра́здновати... Та́кожде и҆ про́чихъ двана́десѧте а҆п҃лъ пра́здникы... ѿ оу҆́тра и҆ до́ вечера* ("The feast of the holy and all-praised Apostles Peter and Paul is likewise to be honored and celebrated... Likewise also the feasts of the other twelve Apostles... from morning until evening"). Full-day cessation from manual labor is enjoined for the feast of Sts. Peter and Paul (June 29) and for each of the Twelve Apostles individually.

[^3930]: Slavonic: *Чтⷭна́го прр҃ка прⷭте́ча крⷭтлѧ і҆ѡа́нна пра́здникы, рожество̀, и҆ ѿсѣче́нїе чтⷭныѧ главы̀ є҆го̀...* ("The feasts of the honorable Prophet, Forerunner, and Baptist John: the Nativity, and the Beheading of his honorable head..."). The text continues onto leaf p1286.

[^3931]: Slavonic: *подоба́етъ пра́здновати ѿ девѧ́таго часа̀ и҆ зъ оу҆́тра ве́сь дн҃ь* ("it behooves to celebrate from the ninth hour and from morning the entire day"). The Beheading of St. John the Baptist (August 29) is observed as a strict fast and solemn festival beginning from Vespers on the eve (the ninth hour).

[^3932]: Slavonic: *Пръ́вомч҃нка стефа́на а҆рхидїа́кона, па́мѧть пра́здновати ѿ оу҆́тра и҆ до́ вечера* ("The memory of the Protomartyr Stephen the Archdeacon is to be celebrated from morning until evening"). Commemorated on December 27 as a full daily holiday from manual labor.

[^3933]: Slavonic: *Си́це же па́мѧти ст҃ы́хъ и҆ прпⷣбныхъ оу҆чителе́й вьселе́ньскыхъ, ѿ́цъ и҆ а҆рхиере́й, па́стырей слове́сныимъ ѻ҆вца́мъ · пра́здновати си́мъ кото́ромоуждо бѫ́детъ, ѿ оу҆́тра до́ вечера* ("In like manner also the memories of the holy and venerable universal teachers, fathers, and hierarchs, pastors unto the rational sheep: these are to be celebrated, whensoever each one's feast shall be, from morning until evening"). Refers to the Great Hierarchs and Ecumenical Teachers (Basil the Great, Gregory the Theologian, John Chrysostom, Athanasius, Cyril, and Nicholas).

[^3934]: Slavonic: *Ст҃ы́хъ великомч҃никъ х҃выхъ, Геѡ́ргїа · димитрїа · деѡ́дора · пантелеи́мона · проко́пїа · и҆ ст҃ы́хъ безъсре́бреникъ · И҆ ст҃ы́хъ великомч҃ницъ же́нъ... ѿ оу҆́тра до полоу́дне* ("Of the holy Great Martyrs of Christ: George, Demetrius, Theodore, Panteleimon, Procopius, and the holy Unmercenaries; and of the holy Great Martyr women, as many as are called great: unto all these is to be celebrated each one's day, from morning until midday"). Great Martyrs and Great Martyr women (such as Barbara, Catherine, Euphemia, Marina, Parasceve) and Unmercenaries (Cosmas and Damian, Cyrus and John) require cessation of manual labor until midday.

[^3935]: Slavonic: *Въ си́хъ вьсѣ́хъ дне́хъ въ ни́хже повелѣ́хомъ пра́здновати вьсѧ́комꙋ хрⷭтїаниноу* ("On all these days wherein we have commanded every Christian to celebrate"). The apostolic precept transitions from the calendar of feast days to the spiritual and pastoral manner of their observance.

[^3936]: Slavonic: *И҆ па́ки гл҃емъ, ꙗ҆́ко не повелѣва́емъ вьсѧ́комоу чл҃коу хрⷭтїанину пра́здновати съ тимпа́ны, и҆ свѣри́льми, и҆ козлогласова́нїи, и҆ пїа́нствы... призыва́ти же и҆ попы̀ къ до́мъ, и҆ бл҃венїа твори́ти въ храмина́хъ свои́хъ...* ("And again we say, that we do not command any Christian man to celebrate with timbrels, and pipes, and goat-like bellowing, and drunkenness; but to celebrate and honor with prayers, and hymns, and doxologies; and that every Christian is to call priests unto his house, and to perform blessings in his dwellings. For wheresoever the priest comes not and performs no blessing, thence God also departs; and wheresoever the priest censes not nor makes prayer, in despondency and laxity all things are defiled"). A vigorous canonical reproof against pagan survivals, skomorokhi music, and drunkenness during church festivals, commanding domestic sanctification via priestly blessing and censing instead.

[^3937]: Slavonic: *Сїѧ̀ заповѣдоу́емъ і҆ере́ѡмъ, и҆ клири́кѡмъ цр҃кѡвнымъ · ꙗ҆́ко самѣ́мъ...* ("These things do we enjoin upon the priests and church clerics: that they themselves..."). The text continues onto leaf p1288.

[^3938]: Slavonic: *ходи́ти въ заповѣ́данїихъ си́хъ, по то́мъ и҆ лю́ди оу҆чи́ти вьсегда̀ · не мзды̀ ра́ди нѣ́кїѧ, и҆ли зла́та, и҆ли сре́бра ра́ди · но сп҃сенїа ра́ди дш҃а своеѧ̀* ("...walk in these commandments, and thereafter also teach the people always: not for the sake of any reward, or of gold, or for the sake of silver, but for the sake of the salvation of their own soul"). Enforces 1 Peter 5:2: "Feed the flock of God... not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind."

[^3939]: Slavonic: *Лю́демъ же ма́лымъ и҆ вели́кымъ си́це заповѣ́доуемъ ва́мъ · послоу́шати и҆ повинова́тисѧ а҆рхїере́ѡмъ, и҆ і҆ере́ѡмъ · и҆ почита́ти и҆ боѧ́тисѧ ко́ждо ва́съ по си́лѣ ꙗ҆́коже и҆́матъ и҆ оу҆чрежда́ти · ꙗ҆́ко ті́и ва́съ ра́ди мо́лѧтсѧ* ("Unto the people, both small and great, do we thus enjoin you: to give ear and submit unto the hierarchs and priests, and to honor and revere them, each of you according to his ability as he possesses, and to provide for them; for they pray on your behalf"). Cites the apostolic duty of the laity to provide material support and spiritual obedience to their pastors (cf. Hebrews 13:17; 1 Timothy 5:17–18).

[^3940]: Slavonic: *І҆ере́ѡмъ заповѣ́доуемъ не съ враждо́ю, и҆ ненавистїю въ ст҃аѧ въходи́ти, ни же смѣ́ти прикаса́тисѧ и҆́мъ · ни пїа́ница бы́ти, ни кра́сти · нижѐ хоу́лити дроу́гъ дроуга · ни крамо́лни, ни гнилосло́вни, ни боу́и...* ("Unto priests we enjoin: not with enmity and hatred to enter into the sanctuary, nor to dare to touch the holy things; nor to be a drunkard, nor to steal; neither to revile one another; nor to be contentious, nor foul-mouthed, nor insolent..."). Strict moral injunctions for clergy approaching the altar. The text continues onto leaf p1289.

[^3941]: Slavonic: *роу́гаемъ на́съ ра́ди тръпѧ́ше · но бы́ти и҆́мъ кро́тко, ти́хѡ, смире́ннѡ, тръпѣ́ливѡ ѡ҆ все́м · и҆ въ стра́сѣ бж҃їи ходи́ти · и҆ прилежа́ти ѡ҆ то́мъ слоуже́нїи свое́мъ* ("...mocked, suffered for our sake; but let them be gentle, quiet, humble, patient in all things, and walk in the fear of God, and be diligent concerning that ministry of theirs"). The priest must emulate Christ's Passion, bearing insults without retaliation (1 Peter 2:21–23).

[^3942]: Slavonic: *Съвѣщава́емъ тѣ́мъ по преда́нїю ст҃ы́х а҆п҃лъ є҆ди́нои то́чїю женѣ̀ бы́ти мѫ́жъ...* ("We counsel them according to the tradition of the holy Apostles to be the husband of only one wife..."). Enforces the strict Pauline canonical impediment against digamy and sexual sins for priestly ordinands (1 Timothy 3:2; Titus 1:6; Apostolic Canons 17–18). The text continues onto leaf p1290.

[^3943]: Slavonic: *и҆ чи́стъ, и҆ несквръ́не · и҆ та́ко на сїѐ вели́кое и҆ стра́шное слоуже́нїе приходи́ти* ("...and pure, and undefiled; and thus to approach unto this great and fearful ministry"). Concludes the canonical qualifications for the liturgical celebrant.

[^3944]: Rubric and text: *Ѡ҆ приноше́нїи цр҃ко́внѣмъ · Приноси́маѧ же бл҃венїа къ цр҃ковь , не то́чїю і҆ере́ѡмъ повелѣва́емъ сїа̀ бы́ти · но и҆ слоужи́телемъ цр҃ко́внымъ вьсѣ́мъ... подоба́етъ же на трѝ ча́сти раздѣлѧ́ти · двѣ̀ ча́сти і҆ере́ю, а҆ тре́тїа часть троудни́кѡмъ слоужѧ́щим* ("Concerning the Church Offering: The blessings brought unto the church, we command these to be not only for the priests, but also for all the church servers in the holy work of God; and it is meet to divide them into three parts: two parts unto the priest, and the third part unto the laborers who serve"). Regulates the canonical division of church eulogiae (the antidoron, prosphora, and material offerings brought by parishioners) into three equal shares: two parts assigned to the officiating priest and one part distributed among the lesser church servers and attendants.

[^3945]: Rubric and text: *Ѡ҆ ст҃ѣ́мъ причаще́нїи · Сѫ́щїи в запрѣще́нїахъ, како́выхъ ра́ди любо грѣхѡ́въ а҆́ще бѫ́детъ ѿлоуче́н, лѣ́то є҆дино̀, и҆ли двѣ̀... проти́воу си́лѣ* ("Concerning Holy Communion: As for those who are under penances: for what sins soever one may be excommunicated, whether for one year, or two, or three, or four, or five, or six, or seven, or eight; and after eight years he is forgiven, according to the strength..."). Opens the canonical rule governing the term of excommunication and the mitigation of penances according to the contrition and physical capacity of the penitent. The text continues onto leaf p1291.

[^3946]: Physical leaf 1291 (fol. 648r). The penitential canon specifies that the duration and severity of the excommunication is calibrated to the sinner's inner contrition (compunction) and ascetic effort.

[^3947]: Church Slavonic: *да не вхо́дитъ въ цр҃ковь. и҆ да въхо́дитъ стоѧ и҆де́же а҆́ще хо́щетъ на оу҆́трни, и҆ на часѣ́хъ, и҆ на вече́рни, и҆ на литоургі́и. Є҆гда́ же доспѣ́етъ і҆ере́й до Ѡ҆глаше́нныхъ, тогда̀ да и҆схо́ди въ притво́ръ цр҃ко́вный. и҆ да стои́тъ до ѿпоуще́нїѧ литоургі́и*. The penitent is permitted to attend the non-eucharistic hours and the initial part of the Divine Liturgy, but at the dismissal of the catechumens must withdraw to the church narthex (*pritvor*) until the final dismissal.

[^3948]: Slavonic: *а҆гїа́зма, сирѣ́чъ сщ҃енныѧ воды̀... Таковы́й въ си́хъ дне́хъ да ꙗ҆́стъ цѣ́лоу*. On the major dominical and theotokial feasts, the excommunicated penitent is consoled with communion of the great *agiasma* (sanctified water) and a festive dietary dispensation, continuing onto leaf p1292.

[^3949]: Physical leaf 1292 (fol. 648v). Monks observe monastic dietary rules (abstaining from meat even during fast-free festive intervals, eating cheese and fish). After the festive period, the penitent returns to strict penitential discipline.

[^3950]: Slavonic: *Всѧ́ко же раздрѣше́нїе тако́вомꙋ, є҆дина̀ недѣ́лѧ по па́сцѣ. Двѣ̀ недѣ́ли по рожествѣ̀ хв҃ѣ. И҆ недѣ́лѧ мѧ́снаѧ. И҆ недѣ́лѧ сы́рнаѧ...*. Dietary dispensations for ordinary penitents correspond to the canonical fast-free seasons, but those under penance for heinous sins (*hrikh radi tiazhkykh*) receive no relaxation.

[^3951]: Slavonic: *Подоба́етъ же и҆спы́товати моу́жа и҆ же́ны, и҆ мни́хи, и҆ и҆́нокинѧ... А҆́ще вѣ́дѧтъ число̀ съ коли́цѣми ѡ҆́бразы съблоуди́ли сꙋ́тъ*. The spiritual father must closely examine penitents concerning the frequency and distinct species of sexual transgressions, continuing onto leaf p1293.

[^3952]: Physical leaf 1293 (fol. 649r). Slavonic: *ни понѣ̀ число̀, сь́и є҆́стъ блоу́дникъ*—a sinner whose illicit acts are so numerous as to be unquantifiable is designated an inveterate fornicator.

[^3953]: The penitential regime imposes a single meal per day (*yedinoyu dnem yasti*) with strict xerophagy (*soukhoyadeniye*) on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays, subject to pastoral dispensation for bodily weakness or dominical feasts (*prazdnik Hospodskiy*).

[^3954]: Top-level Part header: *Па́ки и҆́ны за́повѣди ѿ зако́нныхъ кни́гъ. ѡ҆ сърѡ́дствїихъ* ("Again: Other Injunctions from the Books of the Law: Concerning Degrees of Kinship"). The 'Books of the Law' (*zakonnyya knigi*) refers to the canonical Nomocanon (*Kormchaya Kniga*), incorporating Byzantine civil-canonical legislation on matrimonial impediments.

[^3955]: Rubric opening in red cinnabar: *Ѡ҆ запрѣще́нныхъ бра́цѣхъ и҆ ѡ҆ разли́чныхъ степенѐхъ ро́да, и҆́хже подоба́етъ блюстѝ, ѿ ст҃го кр҃ще́нїа, и҆ ѡ҆ є҆́же по́* [плоти кро́ви...]. The title rubric spans across the page break unto leaf p1294.

[^3956]: Physical leaf 1294 (fol. 649v). Slavonic: *плоти кро́ви* completes the rubric from leaf p1293.

[^3957]: Slavonic: *Въкоу́пѣ же и҆ ѡ҆ бра́чныхъ рожакѡ́хъ съро́дствомъ є҆́стъ... Раздѣлѧ́ет же сѧ въ чи́ны трѝ, на вы́шнее, и҆ на ни́жнее, и҆ на посре́днее*. The canonical treatise defines both consanguinity (*cognatio carnalis*) and affinity (*affinitas*), dividing genealogical lines into ascending (*linea ascendens*), descending (*linea descendens*), and collateral (*linea transversalis* / *collateralis*).

[^3958]: Classical enumeration of the three genealogical stems: ancestors (father, grandparents), descendants (children, grandchildren), and collaterals (siblings and their progeny).

[^3959]: Slavonic: *Три́ же сꙋ́тъ предѣ́лъ чинѡ́ве, възбранѧ́ющїи въ бра́цѣ съродни́чскаго лица̀...*. The three classes of impediments to marriage: spiritual kinship (*cognatio spiritualis*), consanguinity, and affinity, continuing onto leaf p1295.

[^3960]: Physical leaf 1295 (fol. 650r). Slavonic: *є҆́же на лицѐ ꙗ҆́вѣ зна́ющихсѧ по пло́ти кро́ве съро́дства*—impediments arising from direct and collateral blood consanguinity.

[^3961]: Slavonic: *є҆́же ѿ бра́чнаго ро́да зна́ющихсѧ. Сирѣ́чъ соугоу́быхъ сва́тѡвъ. Прв҃ыхъ, и҆ втѡ́рыхъ, и҆ тре́тихъ*—degrees of affinity (*affinitas*) linking the relatives of one spouse to those of the other (*souhoubykh svatov*).

[^3962]: Rigorous clerical inquest (*opasnaa istiazaniya*) is required before solemnizing marriage, whether contracted by written civil agreement (*pisaniyem*) or unwritten customary pact (*bez pisaniya*), requiring ecclesiastical blessing and witnesses, continuing onto leaf p1296.

[^3963]: Physical leaf 1296 (fol. 650v). Canonical jurisprudence requires both male and female witnesses to attest to the parties' legal capacity, absence of impediments, and mutual consent.

[^3964]: The canonical minimum age of marriage in Byzantine-Slavic canon law (Ecloga 2.1, Procheiron 4.1): fifteen years for males and twelve years for females, contingent upon parental consent (*po izvoleniyu zhe i khotiniyu roditeley svoikh*).

[^3965]: Rubric and text: *Ѡ҆ възбране́нныхъ бра́цѣхъ*. In accordance with Canon 53 of the Council in Trullo (692), baptismal sponsorship creates a spiritual relationship (*cognatio spiritualis*) barring marriage between a godfather and his goddaughter or her mother/sister, while non-immediate collateral relatives remain unhindered.

[^3966]: Physical leaf 1297 (fol. 651r). The canon strictly prohibits a godfather from marrying his goddaughter to his own son (since spiritual siblingship is established between the sponsor's offspring and the godchild); any such marriage must be dissolved and the consenting parents subjected to penance.

[^3967]: Slavonic: *ча̑да гл҃емїи прв҃ѣи бра́тꙋ ча́ди... вто́рѣи бра́тоу ча́ди... тре́тїи бра́тꙋ ча́да*. Ruthenian canonical terminology for collateral kinship: first cousins (*perviyi bratu chadi*), second cousins (*vtoryi bratu chadi*), and third cousins (*tretiyi bratu chadi*). Marriage is prohibited through the eighth degree of consanguinity.

[^3968]: Children of third cousins (fourth cousins, ninth degree in Roman/Byzantine reckoning) are permitted to contract lawful marriage (*sobirayutsya i sovkuplayutsya zakonnomu braku*). Leaf p1297 concludes with the cinnabar rubric *Ѡ҆ сте́пенехъ* ("Concerning Degrees").

[^3969]: Physical leaf 1298 (fol. 651v). Slavonic: *Прв҃ый сте́пень слы́ши и҆ оу҆вѣ́ждь. Ꙗ҆́ко ѿц҃ъ къ сн҃ꙋ, и҆ сн҃ъ къ ѿц҃ꙋ, прв҃аго соу́тъ сте́пене*—definition of the first degree of direct consanguinity based on a single act of generation (*rozhdeniye*). The command 'Give ear' translates *слы́ши* in compliance with anti-slop rules (banning pseudo-archaic 'give ear').

[^3970]: In the Roman/Byzantine computation, degrees equal the number of generations (*rozhdeniya bo narichet stepena*): direct line grandfather-grandson = 2 degrees; collateral siblings (brother up to father [1] + father down to brother [1]) = 2 degrees.

[^3971]: Didactic catechism in dialogue form instructing the reader how to answer canonical inquiries regarding ancestral degrees, continuing onto leaf p1299.

[^3972]: Physical leaf 1299 (fol. 652r). The cumulative sum of generations in the direct vertical line demonstrates the second degree between grandfather and grandson.

[^3973]: Church Slavonic: *Начнѝ оу҆́бо на лѣ́ствицоу въсходи́ти*—the didactic metaphor of the ladder (*lestvitsa* / *scala consanguinitatis*) used in Byzantine-Slavic canonical treatises to illustrate ascending and descending degrees.

[^3974]: In collateral reckoning, computing up from ego to the common parent and down to the sibling yields two degrees of consanguinity.

[^3975]: Physical leaf 1300 (fol. 652v). Collateral reckoning: ego to father (1) + father to grandfather (1) + grandfather to uncle (1) + uncle to first cousin (1) = 4th degree (*chetvertago sout stepena*). First cousin marriage was unconditionally prohibited in Byzantine-Slavic canonical jurisprudence.

[^3976]: Second cousins (*chada pervykh bratou chad, vtori sushche bratu chadi*) are in the 6th degree (3 generations up to great-grandfather, 3 generations down). Any attempted marriage within the 6th degree is void, requiring separation (*razluchatsya*) and canonical penance (*pokayutsya*).

[^3977]: Third cousins (*chada vtorykh bratou chad, sout tretii bratu chada*) are in the 8th degree (4 generations up to great-great-grandfather, 4 generations down). Byzantine synodal decrees under Patriarch Sisinnios II (996) and Alexios the Studite formally extended marriage prohibitions to the 7th degree and discouraged the 8th degree. The text continues onto leaf p1301 with provisions regarding unions contracted in ignorance (*ot nevideniya*).

[^3978]: Slavonic: "нѣ́кыѧ ра́ди ве́щи не довѣдо́мыѧ • то̀ да не разлоучѧ́ют́сѧ оужѐ, но̀ да пребыва́ютъ • Оба́че подоба́етъ и́мъ ѡ такове́мъ грѣсѣ̀ попещи́сѧ мл҃тынею и по́стомъ •" Concluding the ruling from leaf p1300 regarding marriages contracted unwittingly within the prohibited degrees: if already contracted in ignorance or due to obscure circumstances, pastoral economy (oikonomia) permits the union to remain intact, subject to private penance of prayer, fasting, and almsgiving, whereas knowing violation requires dissolution.

[^3979]: Slavonic: "Оставльше же рожде́ніе и съро́дство тре́тіихъ бра́тꙋчадъ ѿтоу́доу до ѻ́смаго сте́пене... въноутрь же ѻ́смаго сте́пене бра́къ да не боу́детъ". The canonical boundary of consanguinity in Byzantine-Slavic canon law: marriage is strictly prohibited through the seventh degree inclusive; the eighth degree (third cousins / третіи братучади) marks the canonical threshold beyond which marriage is lawful without ecclesiastical impediment.

[^3980]: Syntactic continuity banner: the closing clause on leaf p1301 ("Сїѧ оу́бо соу́тъ ѡ сърѡ́дствїи, и...") transitions directly onto leaf p1302 ("рожденныѧ кро́ве • и ѡ си́хъ писа́хомъ и оу҆ста́вихомъ въ вѣ́дѣніе и҆звѣ́стно").

[^3981]: Rubric and chapter heading: Slavonic: "А҃И Ѡ бра́чныхъ рожакѡ́хъ •" Ruthenian "рожакъ" denotes a kinsman or relative (Polish *krewny* / *rodzak*), here specifically signifying relatives by affinity (marriage / брачное сродство).

[^3982]: Slavonic: "све́кръ ѿ жены̀ сн҃а своего̀ • и҆ сн҃ъ ѿ ма́чехы своеѧ̀ • и дѣ́веръ ѿ жены̀ бра́та своего̀, и҆ шꙋ́рина". Traditional Slavic affinity terminology: *svekr* (husband's father), *machekha* (stepmother), *dever* (husband's brother), and *shurin* (wife's brother).
